records.article:
# Does the Cypherpunk Manifesto read as an LP2 running key?

**This specific running-key test did not produce a convincing whole-page reading.** We tried every contiguous offset of a pinned copy of Eric Hughes’s *A Cypherpunk’s Manifesto* against [LP2-00](#/reader/lp2-00), [LP2-31](#/reader/lp2-31) and [LP2-54](#/reader/lp2-54). Under both declared ways of turning its letters into key values, each page’s best score was matched or beaten by several fully searched shuffled keys. The same search ranked a planted known reading first under **both** mappings.

![Whole-page scores for two manifesto key mappings on three LP2 pages against fully searched shuffled-key controls](experiments/records/cypherpunk-manifesto-running-key/whole-page-scores.svg)

## What was tested

The [source page](https://activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html) is attributed to Eric Hughes and dated 9 March 1993. We preserved the HTML bytes retrieved on 23 October 2026 and used only its essay body, from the first “Privacy is necessary” through “Onward.” The title, signature, address and date were excluded. Uppercasing and retaining A–Z leaves **4,072 letters**. The source URL, raw and normalized hashes, and exact extraction rule are in the [plan](experiments/records/cypherpunk-manifesto-running-key/plan.json).

We tested two **different alphabet assumptions**, named in the figure:

- **A–Z shifts:** A=0 through Z=25, one letter per key step. This matches the convention in the [Emerson running-key test](#/experiments/emerson-running-key); it is not itself a GP transcription.
- **GP rune key:** Parse the letters greedily as canonical Gematria Primus Latin labels, including TH, NG and other two-letter labels, with V/K/Z/Q mapped to U/C/S/C. This produces **3,893 key units**. Erasing the source’s spaces permits a two-letter label to cross a former word boundary; another boundary policy is outside this test.

For each mapping and each of the three pages, we tried **every zero-based offset** leaving enough key units to cover the **entire page**. At each rune position we calculated `plaintext = ciphertext − key (mod 29)`, joined the resulting GP Latin labels, and used the pinned English quadgram score. The three page lengths are 262, 269 and 232 runes. The source and the sixteen shuffled copies were searched with exactly the same offsets and score. The shuffles preserve each mapping’s key-value counts; they do not model alternative meaningful books.

## Result and limit

For A–Z shifts, **13, 16 and 13** of the sixteen shuffled-key searches equalled or beat the manifesto’s best whole-page score on LP2-00, 31 and 54. For the GP rune key the counts were **11, 14 and 9**. Those are comparisons of *maxima from complete offset searches*, so a lucky offset is compared with other equally searched opportunities. The figure shows the score and full shuffle range for each case; the [result file](experiments/records/cypherpunk-manifesto-running-key/results.json) retains all top-five offsets and decoded strings.

Before examining LP2, we encoded the full 264-rune known reading on LP1-04 using each mapping at offset 3301. In both cases, the identical exhaustive search selected that offset first and recovered the planted reading exactly. This checks the decoder and scorer on a known plaintext. It cannot establish that either mapping is the one used by LP2.

Sixteen shuffled searches give a coarse reference, not a calibrated tail probability. The English scorer can also miss meaningful non-English or unusually rendered plaintext. The result is confined to this archived edition, these two mappings, subtraction direction, page-start clock, three target pages and whole-page English scoring. It does **not** rule out the manifesto under a different rule or running keys in general.

## Reproduce

Download this record’s files and run `python experiments/records/cypherpunk-manifesto-running-key/run.py --check` from the repository root. The independent `check.py` parses the source with a separate HTML parser and recomputes every original and shuffled offset maximum. `plot.py --check` verifies the figure. All three scripts use Python’s standard library and the pinned files; they do not fetch the source again.
records.reader_finding: The manifesto did not stand out from shuffled keys on the three tested pages. Every best-score result was matched or beaten by several shuffled-key searches.

# A column solver with a short-key limit

**Result.** The source's column-frequency solver produced 165 complete-page readings using fixed key lengths 2, 3 and 5. None reached the predeclared English score line. The solver recovered **one planted readable passage in 107 of those 165 page-and-key-length settings**; it did not recover the passage in the other 58. Among all LP2 outputs, the highest score was −6.78 on LP2-55 at key length 5, but that setting did not recover the plant. The highest-scoring LP2 output in a setting that recovered the plant was LP2-49 at key length 3 (−6.95). A full-search shuffle comparison found 107 of 199 trials with a maximum at least as high as the overall LP2 best.

![Of 165 page-and-key-length outputs, 107 recovered a planted reading, and none of those passed the English score line.](experiments/records/d4v1-column-unigram-key-recovery/summary.svg)

The [pinned C++ solver](https://github.com/d4v1-sudo/my_cicada_tools_cpp/blob/6bba820aed72184837611a82c79c4587157080aa/src/utils.cpp) asks for a page and a key length. It removes the source's listed possible interrupter positions, divides the remaining runes into repeating-key columns, and chooses the shift in each column that best matches a frequency table from solved pages. Its first preview applies the inferred key to the **original, unfiltered** page. We reproduced that direct numeric preview for fixed lengths 2, 3 and 5 on LP2-00–55, omitting the number-only LP2-50. This is **one source method with three bounds**, not three different cipher ideas.

| Check | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Nine archived readings encrypted with fixed repeating keys | Exact key recovered on 9/9 at length 2, 9/9 at length 3, and 8/9 at length 5 |
| The same readable passage fitted to each target page's length, with its exact source interrupter positions | 107/165 key recoveries; every planted passage also clears the English score line |
| LP2 complete-page outputs | 0/165 clear the −5.5 English score line, including 0/107 in settings that recovered the plant |
| 199 shuffled-page trials, each rerunning all pages and all three lengths | 107 global maxima equal or exceed the strongest actual output; plus-one tail 108/200 |

This check used **one constructed passage**, adjusted to each target page's length. Recovering it shows that a setting can work on that passage; failing to recover it leaves that setting without this positive check. It is not a statistical power estimate or a guarantee for other English text. The source removes listed rune positions **before finding the key**, which can change column phase, but decrypts the unfiltered page afterward. On the 23 pages where listed positions fall inside the page, many plants fail for that reason. A different key schedule or an implementation that preserves phase after removals is outside this replay. The source's automatic key-length setting also chose a longer period rather than the planted length 3 for all nine complete known-reading controls, so this record makes no negative claim about automatic mode.

The English quadgram score and its −5.5 line are **our added screen**, calibrated against the nine complete readings and 199 complete-search shuffle controls. The original program derives its unigram target from known solved readings; checks on those readings are in-sample for that key-inference target, not an independent language-generalization test. Its unigram fitness alone does not certify English. We did not count its alternate rune, Latin or patched-key transforms as tested here. The [source-order correction note](experiments/records/d4v1-column-unigram-key-recovery/execution-note.json) documents a discarded exploratory implementation whose floating-point summation could change a tied shift. The final key inference agrees with compiled original C++ on nine fixed page-and-length cases, and an independent checker reconstructs every target row, plant and shuffle.

## Reproduce

The [frozen plan](experiments/records/d4v1-column-unigram-key-recovery/plan.json), [complete results](experiments/records/d4v1-column-unigram-key-recovery/results.json), [source interrupter map](experiments/records/d4v1-column-unigram-key-recovery/interrupt-map.json) and [source target frequencies](experiments/records/d4v1-column-unigram-key-recovery/source-target.json) are supplied with the experiment. From the repository root run `python experiments/records/d4v1-column-unigram-key-recovery/run.py --check`, followed by `check.py` and `plot.py --check`. The checks require Python with NumPy and Numba, but no network fetch or upstream source checkout. The unlicensed source program is linked and pinned by revision rather than copied into the archive.
records.reader_finding: This short-key solver produced no English-like LP2 output. It recovered the planted passage in 107 of 165 page-and-key-length settings; the other 58 did not recover it. Shuffled searches often scored higher than the best manuscript result.
records.reader_limit: The test uses key lengths 2, 3 and 5, one planted passage, and the source’s exact rule for removing possible interrupters. It does not rule out repeating-key ciphers or longer keys.

records.summary: A source program launches two numeric keys and route searches after three consecutive missing-prime word sums. Its unigram score passes every one of 199 shuffled controls for both keys on a known reading, and route order cannot change that score.

record_type.label: Control
record_type.description: Checks a search, decoder or scorer using synthetic inputs or reference text; it does not identify the cipher of an unsolved page.

scope.representation: Pinned source secrets.cpp 256-pair stream and 180 missing primes; one 157-rune known direct reading from source Page 5. Synthetic three-word anchor and 199 shuffled conditional score controls; no unsolved LP2 target search.
scope.procedure: Verify source constants and five grid case differences; test three-word trigger, invert two key streams and six source route positions on a known reading; scan all 29 source Atbash shifts on 199 seeded shuffles for each key and use unigram invariance for routes.

Yet all 199 shuffled controls for each key exceeded the source score bar after trying 29 Atbash shifts; all 199 route shuffles also passed, and any route permutation leaves this unigram score unchanged. No unsolved-page anchor counts or decodes were run.

The original score bars are weak on this fixture, but the key and route hypotheses are not excluded. records.article:
# Missing-prime keys and routes: checking the score

**Result.** A pinned C++ search looks for three consecutive words whose rune-prime sums point to the 2013 missing-prime list. Only then does it try two repeating keys and several routes. Its final screen asks whether a candidate has rune frequencies like solved pages. On one known 157-rune reading, **all 199 shuffled controls passed that screen for each key** after the source's 29 Atbash shifts. Reordering runes cannot change this frequency score at all. These controls do not support treating a score above the source's threshold as a recovered reading.

![Both source keys pass all 199 shuffled controls; changing a route cannot change the unigram score.](experiments/records/d4v1-missing-prime-anchor-gate/control-screen.svg)

| What we checked | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| Three consecutive synthetic words with prime sums 73, 79 and 83 | The source trigger fired once. Inserting one nonmatching word stopped it. |
| The 256-pair key and the 180 missing-prime key | Both recovered a deliberately encrypted known reading. After shuffling the ciphertext, **199/199** controls for each key still exceeded the source's strict 0.91 score threshold at some Atbash shift. |
| Column, diagonal and inward-spiral routes at widths 3 and 7 | All six inverse-constructed examples recovered the reading. Every route preserves the same rune counts, so its score is unchanged for a fixed shift. All **199/199** shuffled route controls exceeded the source's strict 0.90 threshold. |

The test uses **one known reading that contributed to the source's solved-page frequency target**. These plants check the operator and the trigger; they do not estimate performance on other English passages. The shuffled texts are controls, not alternative proposed decipherments. We did **not** count anchor sequences on unsolved pages or run a manuscript decryption here. A later test needs a fixed reading-sensitive score and a full-search control before it can say whether these keys or routes help.

## Source and transcription

The [pinned program](https://github.com/d4v1-sudo/my_cicada_tools_cpp/blob/6bba820aed72184837611a82c79c4587157080aa/src/utils.cpp) uses the 180 primes from 73 through 1223. Those match the archived **2013 telnet-command gap**, which is distinct from CicadaOS `prime_echo`. Its 256-pair source key is spelled exactly like the current LP2-49–51 transcription. The same program's `pages.h` differs from its `secrets.cpp` at five letter-case cells. Those five disagreements and the still-uncertain glyphs are documented in [the grid transcription comparison](#/experiments/grid-radix-reconciliation) and [stem review](#/experiments/grid-stem-uncertainty). This check preserves the source's `secrets.cpp` key without silently correcting it.

The source and current site agree on the rune order of all 56 mapped LP2 pages. Punctuation changes word boundaries on LP2-04, LP2-21 and LP2-41, so any future count of three-word anchors must name which transcription it uses. The exact-source version uses the pinned `pages.h` text. No target-page result is reported here.

## Reproduce

The [frozen pretarget plan](experiments/records/d4v1-missing-prime-anchor-gate/plan-frozen.json), [control-calibration amendment](experiments/records/d4v1-missing-prime-anchor-gate/calibration-amendment.json), [source-derived fixture](experiments/records/d4v1-missing-prime-anchor-gate/fixture.json) and [all 199 control maxima](experiments/records/d4v1-missing-prime-anchor-gate/results.json) are included. Run `python experiments/records/d4v1-missing-prime-anchor-gate/run.py --check`, then `check.py` and `plot.py --check`. The independent checker recomputes both full shift searches and verifies six route plants. The optional [C++ fixture](experiments/records/d4v1-missing-prime-anchor-gate/source-controls.cpp) can be compiled against the pinned upstream source to confirm its tokenizer, trigger and key transforms; upstream code is linked by revision and hash rather than bundled.
records.reader_finding: The source’s score accepted all 199 shuffled controls for each key. Rearranging the runes cannot change this score, so it cannot select a route. A high score here does not establish a readable message.
records.reader_limit: This checks the scoring rule on one known passage. It does not test the keys on unsolved pages or rule out the proposed keys and routes.

records.title: Positional totient shifts on complete LP2 pages
records.question: Do any of the source-defined 100 positional totient shifts yield English-like complete LP2 pages?
records.summary: A pinned public C++ proposal subtracts φ(position+offset) modulo 29. We screened offsets 0–99 on all 55 rune-bearing unsolved pages with a controlled English whole-page scorer.

record_type.label: Bounded solving test
record_type.description: Applies a fixed decoding, extraction or payload-retrieval rule to declared unsolved material, or excludes a specific direct-generation rule. Its result covers only those bounds.

scope.representation: Archived GP29 rune order including headings, page-local rune clock; LP2-50 excluded because pinned transcription has no runes.
scope.procedure: Apply P_i=(C_i−φ(i+offset)) mod29 for offsets 0–99 to each full page, score canonical GP Latin output with a pinned English quadgram model, calibrate with nine readings and offset-17 planted encryptions, and compare the global best with 199 full-search pagewise shuffles.
scope.parameters: 100 offsets × 55 pages = 5,500 outputs; −5.5 English line; nine solved readings; 199 full-search shuffled trials.
scope.exclusions: No current-word prime-sum totient branch, offsets outside 0–99, other signs or resets, other languages, key layers or general totient mechanism.

records.finding: Nine known-reading plants recovered at rank one. None of 5,500 LP2 outputs reached the predeclared English score line. The best was −6.603 on LP2-55, and 87 of 199 full-search shuffles did at least as well. The separate original-source positional hit gate recovered only seven of nine planted readings, so its zero target hits cannot exclude the method.
records.limitations: Only the source positional branch, offsets 0–99, page-reset rune clock, one transcription and English GP Latin quadgram score were tested. The source current-word prime-sum totient branch is unresolved. Post-target source-gate audit is not a preregistered English test.
records.article:
# Positional totient shifts on complete LP2 pages

**Result.** None of the 5,500 complete-page outputs from the 100 fixed positional totient offsets reached the predeclared English score line. The best was LP2-55 at offset 64 (−6.60); 87 of 199 full-search shuffled controls did at least as well. Nine known readings passed the English scorer; all nine deliberately encrypted controls were decoded exactly and ranked their true offset first, so this is a useful bounded screen of this particular rule. It does **not** identify or exclude a general totient cipher.

![The best LP2 output sits below the known readings and among full-search shuffled controls.](experiments/records/d4v1-positional-totient-streams/summary.svg)

The tested rule is simple: number the runes from zero at the start of each page, compute Euler's totient of the position plus an offset, and subtract that number modulo 29. For example, offset 17 starts with shifts φ(17), φ(18), φ(19), and so on. The [pinned source code](https://github.com/d4v1-sudo/my_cicada_tools_cpp/blob/6bba820aed72184837611a82c79c4587157080aa/src/utils.cpp) tries offsets 0–99. Our new screen retained that operator and range, then used an independently pinned English quadgram score and a complete-search shuffle comparison. It is **not** a claim that the author ran this English scoring test.

| What was checked | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| LP2-00–55, excluding the number-only LP2-50 | 55 rune-bearing pages × 100 offsets = 5,500 outputs |
| Fixed English line | Zero outputs reached −5.5; best −6.60 |
| Nine archived complete readings | All nine reached the line and beat all 199 own shuffles |
| Nine known readings encrypted with offset 17 | All nine recovered exactly and ranked offset 17 first |
| 199 pagewise shuffle trials, each searching every offset and page | 87 trials equaled or exceeded the actual global best; plus-one tail 88/200 |

The [original source's positional hit rule](experiments/records/d4v1-positional-totient-streams/source-positional.json) differs from this English test: it requires both a within-page offset z-score above 3.5 **and** a solved-rune unigram fitness above 0.90. A post-target audit found no source-rule LP2 hit, but its plant gate triggered for only seven of nine known readings; 41 of 199 complete-search shuffles produced at least one hit. The source unigram target was built from known solutions, so this plant check is in-sample. Therefore the source rule's zero is not a powered exclusion. The 0.85 threshold in that source belongs to a separate current-word branch, not this positional branch. The [dated correction](experiments/records/d4v1-positional-totient-streams/plan-amendment.json) preserves the original frozen plan and states this source-rule distinction; the 0.85 diagnostic is limited to 1,000 random strings of one length.

The source's other option-29 rule derives a shift from the GP-prime sum of the **current ciphertext word**. That input-dependent word rule did not pass a complete-reading plant check and remains unresolved; it is not included in the 5,500 outputs. An exploratory known-warning preimage check found words for which the proposed plaintext has no ciphertext preimage under the simple same-word interpretation, and the source handles some separators differently when advancing its word clock. A faithful replay needs to preserve that clock and establish a working positive control first.

This screen uses the archived GP29 rune streams, including headings, and scores the canonical GP Latin rendering as English. The source page numbers 17–72 align with LP2-00–55 after normalizing the J-rune glyph spelling; LP2-50 has no runes in the pinned transcription. Other offsets, signs, separator rules, languages, key layers and different totient constructions remain untested here.

## Reproduce

Download the experiment files and run `python experiments/records/d4v1-positional-totient-streams/run.py --check`, then `check.py`, `source_gate.py`, `source_positional.py`, and `plot.py --check` from the repository root. The [frozen plan](experiments/records/d4v1-positional-totient-streams/plan.json) pins all page, reading and scorer inputs; the [complete result](experiments/records/d4v1-positional-totient-streams/results.json) includes per-page winners and all 199 null maxima. `check.py` independently reconstructs the 5,500 outputs and all shuffled searches. Python with NumPy and Numba is required; no upstream source code or network fetch is needed for these checks.
records.reader_finding: None of the 100 position-based totient shifts produced English-like text on any of the 55 tested pages. The strongest result was no better than many shuffled searches. All nine deliberately encrypted controls were decoded correctly.
records.reader_limit: This checks one positional rule and offsets 0–99, using an English scorer. It does not rule out other totient rules or the separate word-sum proposal.

records.article: ## The comparison The pale tree on [LP2-55](#/reader/lp2-55) resembles the photograph [DeadTree.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DeadTree.jpg), credited to R. Neil Marshman / Brookie. This test asks a narrower, checkable question: when the source photograph is scaled and translated over the manuscript tree, does a horizontal reflection fit better than its original orientation? It does **not** seek a decryption rule or recover the original image-editing steps. The published [Commons original](exports/sources/commons/DeadTree.jpg) is 1,894 × 2,606 pixels. Its local SHA-256 is `608288991f92b8ab901a9fbb39937f93ebdfeb5fd84edeecfa637d5262ff7b29`; its SHA-1 matches the checksum on the [Commons file record](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DeadTree.jpg). The LP2-55 JPEG is the archived 2,400 × 3,600-pixel page. The script rejects either image if its bytes change. ![Mirrored source, pale manuscript tree and their half-opacity overlay](exports/figures/dead-tree-alignment.png) The figure shows the selected mirrored fit at left, the LP2-55 tree region in the middle and a 50% overlay at right. Both source and manuscript are converted to grayscale response maps, enlarged for inspection; this is **not** an unmodified image or a reconstruction of the author’s layer. The source is R. Neil Marshman / Brookie, [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/), horizontally reflected, cropped, resized, threshold-mapped and blurred here. [Open the original photograph](exports/sources/commons/DeadTree.jpg) · [Open the unmodified manuscript page](images/lp2-55.jpg). ## Frozen comparison rule The source crop is `[100, 500, 1750, 1950]`; the LP2-55 crop is `[550, 1300, 1850, 2550]`, with right and bottom edges excluded. In each grayscale crop, values darker than the chosen brightness level become a stronger tree response. The source uses `clip((170−L)/130,0,1)` and the manuscript `clip((250−L)/45,0,1)`. Gaussian blur with sigma 7 tolerates differences in stroke width and some missing twigs. Those values were chosen after inspecting the images, so the following scores are descriptive rather than a blind significance test. For each orientation, the script checks 23 scales from 0.370 through 0.700 in increments of 0.015, plus every integer translation that keeps the whole template inside the manuscript crop. The fit score is normalized cross-correlation. In a second run, only the upper 60% of the source template chooses the transform; the lower 40% is scored at that fixed transform. This lower-region check tests whether the upper-branch fit extends further down the same image. It is not a wholly independent holdout because the photograph, crops and processing were selected after viewing both images. | Orientation | Best whole-crop correlation | Upper 60% fit | Lower 40% at that fit | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Original | 0.377 | 0.564 | −0.095 | | Horizontal reflection | **0.623** | **0.813** | **0.456** | The reflected upper fit uses scale 0.550 and translation `(230,94)` relative to the LP2-55 crop. Its major forks, central branch structure and rightward lower limb overlap in the visualization. The unreflected comparison does not carry its upper fit into the lower region. [Download every scale, coordinate and score](exports/dead-tree-alignment.json). ## What this establishes and what remains open The two declared alignments favor a horizontally reflected source photograph, including the lower region that did not choose the fit. This supports a specific image-source relationship more strongly than a general resemblance between bare trees. The test does not calculate a chance probability against a collection of other tree photographs. It does not establish the exact crop, layer opacity, drawing/filter steps or software used to make LP2-55. Fine branches and the lower trunk differ visibly in the overlay. The [branches guide](#/wiki/branches?section=shared-tree) compares the related treatments on LP2-32 and in the 2016 message. Those carriers are **not** fit by this script. A related experiment now gives each its own crop, response rule and orientation control. Nothing in this image alignment implies a rune operation. ## Reproduce Download the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/dead-tree-alignment.zip) and extract it preserving folders. It contains the [Commons original](exports/sources/commons/DeadTree.jpg). Download the [LP2-55 original](images/lp2-55.jpg) separately or extract the original-images ZIP into the same folder. Install Python 3, NumPy and OpenCV (`opencv-python`); the recorded run used OpenCV 5.0.0. Verify the files using the bundled `START-HERE` instructions, then run: ```text python experiments/records/dead-tree-alignment/run.py --check ``` To regenerate a report and figure under other settings, edit a **copy** of the script and save separate outputs. Report altered crops, thresholds, blur, scale range and orientation choices. The exact source file, [plan](experiments/records/dead-tree-alignment/plan.txt), [script](experiments/records/dead-tree-alignment/run.py), [results](exports/dead-tree-alignment.json) and [visualization](exports/figures/dead-tree-alignment.png) are linked here for inspection.

records.article:
## One source family, two different treatments

The [LP2-55 source comparison](#/experiments/dead-tree-alignment) favored a horizontally reflected version of R. Neil Marshman’s [DeadTree.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DeadTree.jpg). Two related images remain: a broad, soft tree on [LP2-32](#/reader/lp2-32), and a faint tree behind text in the [2016 message](images/message-2016.jpg). This record measures them separately. The first comparison uses LP2-55 as the reference image; the second returns to the Commons photograph. It does not assume identical blur, brightness or scale across carriers.

The result supports the shared tree artwork under the declared comparisons. It does not recover how the author processed any image, prove a decryption step or assign a probability of chance resemblance across other photographs.

## LP2-55 → LP2-32: same orientation

The script compares the tree region of two original 2,400 × 3,600 JPEGs. It maps their differently rendered dark and pale shapes to grayscale responses, blurs with sigma 15 and searches scales 0.650–1.225 in 0.025 steps. It searches every integer translation keeping the source crop fully inside the LP2-32 crop. Both the original LP2-55 orientation and its horizontal reflection are scored.

![LP2-55 tree aligned to LP2-32, with target and overlay](exports/figures/dead-tree-manuscript.png)

The displayed panels are contrast-mapped and blurred for this comparison; open the [unmodified LP2-55](images/lp2-55.jpg) and [LP2-32](images/lp2-32.jpg) images to inspect the real artwork. The unchanged orientation aligns the broad top forks and carries more of that alignment into the lower trunk. The figure shows its upper-region fit and a half-opacity overlay, not an original image layer.

| LP2-55 orientation | Whole-region best | Upper 60% fit | Lower 40% at upper fit |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Same | **0.623** | **0.704** | **0.600** |
| Horizontally reflected | 0.483 | 0.514 | 0.353 |

The same-orientation upper fit uses scale 0.900 and translation `(123,186)` inside the LP2-32 crop. This says that the two *manuscript treatments* preserve orientation relative to each other. It does not contradict the preceding experiment, where both were compared with an originally unreflected photograph.

## Commons photograph → 2016: reflected orientation

The 2016 JPEG is only 563 × 569 pixels and puts pale message text over a very dark tree. The script crops the central tree, maps pixel brightness above the black background to a response, and masks pixels brighter than 100 to reduce the white lettering. It uses Gaussian sigma 1.5 and searches 26 scales from 0.065 to 0.140. The source photograph’s original and horizontally reflected orientations are both compared.

![Mirrored Commons tree aligned to the faint 2016 background tree, with target and overlay](exports/figures/dead-tree-message.png)

This figure increases contrast and removes much of the bright text **for inspection only**; it is not the original message. The source photograph is R. Neil Marshman / Brookie, [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/), cropped, mirrored, resized and contrast-mapped here. [Original Commons JPEG](exports/sources/commons/DeadTree.jpg) · [original 2016 message](images/message-2016.jpg).

| Original | 0.566 | 0.644 | 0.442 |
| Horizontal reflection | **0.854** | **0.826** | **0.858** |

The reflected upper fit uses scale 0.089 and translation `(69,29)` within the message crop. The lower region matches at that fixed transform despite not setting the transform in the declared search. The photograph, crop, text mask and response were still chosen after seeing the images, so these correlations are descriptive, **not** a calibrated chance probability.

## Bounds, files and next checks

The [complete result JSON](exports/dead-tree-cross-carrier.json) records both orientations, 24 and 26 scale values, crops, settings, coordinates and scores. This is one family of related source-image comparisons, not a blanket assertion that every tree image was made with the same filter. Fine branches and the amount of visible trunk vary. No source was inferred from manuscript text or rune values.

The lower 40% check is useful but not fully independent: all preprocessing choices and the two target images were selected during exploration. A stronger source-identification test would score a preregistered set of unrelated tree photographs under the same search budget and report the winner and gap. An exact production reconstruction would need to explain the tonal treatment and branch omissions as well as geometry. Those questions remain open.

Download the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/dead-tree-cross-carrier.zip); it contains the Commons photograph, plan, script, report and figures. Place the original LP2-55, LP2-32 and 2016 JPEGs in its `images/` directory, or extract the site’s original-images ZIP there. Install Python 3, NumPy and OpenCV (the recorded run used OpenCV 5.0.0), verify the bundled files and image hashes using the `START-HERE` instructions, then run:

```text
python experiments/records/dead-tree-cross-carrier/run.py --check
```

The [plan](experiments/records/dead-tree-cross-carrier/plan.txt) lists every input and preprocessing choice. Edit a copy and save separate results for any changed crop, mask, threshold, scale range or image set. The [script](experiments/records/dead-tree-cross-carrier/run.py) does not access a network or AI service.

records.article:
# Five-digit chain-addition keys

Could a five-digit decimal primer generate the shifts for the beginning of an unsolved page?

## Finding

**None of the 100,000 primers recovered a fixed known opening.** We tested both addition and subtraction against the first 12 runes of all 55 rune-bearing unsolved pages. That is **99 million exact comparisons** with nine preselected known readings, with zero 12-rune matches. The longest shared prefix was **five runes**. Four page/reading/sign combinations admit a primer for those first five runes, but the sixth rune breaks each one. Five chosen digits can fit five chosen shift values; those short fits do not support a decryption.

![A five-digit decimal primer generates later key digits by adjacent-pair addition modulo ten.](experiments/records/decimal-chain-opening-cribs/primer-clock.svg)

The example starts with `31415`. Its sixth digit is `(3 + 1) mod 10 = 4`; its seventh is `(1 + 4) mod 10 = 5`. The same rule continues. The [American Cryptogram Association's GROMARK sheet](https://www.cryptogram.org/downloads/aca.info/ciphers/Gromark.pdf) specifies a five-digit primer and this chain addition, but the complete cipher also uses a mixed alphabet. **This experiment isolates the digit stream** and uses its digits as direct GP29 shifts. It is a newly constructed LP2 baseline, not a replay of a documented historical attempt or a test of full GROMARK.

## What was checked

Every decimal primer from `00000` through `99999`, including leading zeroes, produced 12 key digits. For each page, we reset the stream at the first visible rune, kept the header, and ignored non-rune marks. We computed `plaintext = ciphertext ± digit (mod 29)` and compared with the same nine 12-rune openings used in earlier bounded tests. The [result file](experiments/records/decimal-chain-opening-cribs/results.json) gives the complete prefix-length histogram for both signs. A synthetic known reading encrypted with primer `31415` is recovered under each sign.

The [plan](experiments/records/decimal-chain-opening-cribs/plan.json) fixes the primer range, recurrence and criterion. Run `python experiments/records/decimal-chain-opening-cribs/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/decimal-chain-opening-cribs/check.py` from the repository root. The checker independently reads page JSON and counts matching prefixes by enumerating all 100,000 streams. Other page positions, unknown openings, nondecimal primers, alternate GP alphabets, interruptions and full GROMARK are outside this result.

records.title: Can a correct key fail under the wrong alignment rule?
records.question: How do rigid and skip-aware decoders recover known rune sequences under four declared encoder mechanisms?
records.summary: Planted controls separate exact rune recovery, permitted alignments, beam pruning and English score acceptance across 216 plants and 2160 decoder results.

record_type.label: Control
record_type.description: Checks a search, decoder or scorer using synthetic inputs or reference text; it does not identify the cipher of an unsolved page.

family.title: Decoder alignment controls
family.question: Can declared decoders recover planted plaintext under matching and mismatched alignment rules?

variant.label: Four encoders with fixed rigid and beam decoders

scope.representation: First min(240, available) output rune indices from all nine known-reading traces; canonical GP labels only for scoring.
scope.procedure: Plant ordinary addition, probabilistic collision skipping, value rewriting and one unrelated advance plus skipping; decode with correct/wrong deterministic key fixtures using rigid subtraction and four bounded beams.
scope.parameters: Nine traces, three seeds, key-value repetitions 1 and 4, 10000 slots; beam widths 16/64 crossed with skip limits 1/3; cumulative quadgram selection, normalized acceptance -5.5; 216 plants and 2160 decoder results.
scope.exclusions: No manuscript cipher identification, general recovery guarantee, language identification, uniform-pad assumption, key search or calibrated false-positive probability.

records.finding: Correct-key ordinary addition recovers exactly throughout. Skip limits exclude some true alignments; a wider beam cannot repair them. Rewriting often passes the language threshold without exact rune recovery. All wrong-key controls fail exact recovery and the threshold.
records.limitations: Artificial encoders and dependent known-text controls, not a fitted manuscript model. Exact alignment and exact plaintext are distinct. Cumulative and normalized scores have different objectives. Human review pending.
records.article:
## Can a correct key still fail?

Yes, under a mismatched decoding rule. This experiment starts with known rune sequences, encrypts them using four precisely specified mechanisms, and asks what rigid subtraction and a skip-aware beam decoder recover. Knowing the answer lets us measure exact recovery rather than judging whether a candidate merely sounds plausible.

All ordinary-addition controls recover exactly with the correct key. With key skipping and single-value keys, the beam allowing three skips recovers 26 of 27 plants exactly, while rigid subtraction recovers one. Repeating each key value four times changes that result: the same beam recovers eight of 27, with the true recorded alignment outside its transition rules in the other 19. Increasing beam width from 16 to 64 does not repair that structural limit.

These findings concern the declared artificial encoders. They do not show that the unsolved manuscript uses key skipping, rewriting, or any particular key generator.

## Four ways to consume the same key

Every operation uses rune indices modulo 29. Ordinary addition emits `c = p + k`; subtraction recovers `p = c − k`. A key slot is a position in the generated sequence, not its numerical value. Several slots can hold the same value.

| Encoder | What happens when the proposed ciphertext repeats the previous rune? | Key alignment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ordinary addition | Emit it unchanged. | One slot per plaintext rune. |
| Key skipping | With probability 83/100, reject that key slot and retry the same plaintext rune. | Rejections consume additional slots. |
| Value rewriting | With probability 83/100, add one to the proposed ciphertext value modulo 29. | Still one slot per plaintext rune. |
| Unrelated advance plus skipping | Apply the skip rule, but also consume one extra slot halfway through the plaintext, regardless of repetition. | Contains an advance that the collision-only model may not permit. |

The first emitted rune has no predecessor. The rejection draw occurs only on a collision. Each plant resets its state, and every draw, rejected slot, accepted slot and rewrite is preserved in the report. Exhausting the key is an error; no zero padding is allowed.

The key fixture hashes a fixed seed label and counter with SHA-256, then reduces each byte modulo 29. This reduction is biased because 256 is not divisible by 29. It is a reproducible test input, not a claim of uniform randomness or a one-time pad. The second fixture repeats each value across four successive slots. Neither fixture was adjusted to match manuscript statistics.

For an introductory numerical diagram, see [key alignment, skip limits and beam search](#/wiki/key-alignment).

## What the beam can represent

The rigid decoder consumes one slot at every step. The beam keeps several candidate prefixes. At each step it considers accepting the next key slot, or skipping up to its declared limit. A skipped slot is permitted only when it would have generated a repeat of the preceding ciphertext rune under that candidate plaintext.

Beam width controls how many prefixes survive scoring. The skip limit controls which paths can exist at all. These are different bounds: retaining more paths does not introduce a transition that the model forbids.

We test widths 16 and 64, each with skip limits one and three. Candidates are ordered by cumulative English quadgram score, then lexicographic key-slot path and rune sequence. The final normalized score is reported separately. Because some rune labels contain multiple letters, maximizing cumulative score is not the same as maximizing normalized score. The experiment preserves this declared selection rule rather than changing it after seeing results.

## The complete control grid

The nine known-reading traces supply their first 240 rune indices, or their full length if shorter. Three seed IDs, two key fixtures and four encoders produce 216 plants. Every plant is decoded with the correct and wrong key using all five decoder configurations: 2,160 results. These reuse source texts and are not independent trials from a population.

The figures show every correct-key configuration. The complete summary CSV also includes every wrong-key configuration, all of which produced zero exact recoveries and zero accepted scores. That finite result is not a general false-positive rate and does not calibrate a large key search.

Selected counts below explain the figures; the CSV retains all 80 grouped cells and the JSON retains every individual result. Each cell has 27 plants. “Accepted” means normalized score at least −5.5, not a correct answer.

| Encoder and key fixture | Decoder | Exact | Accepted |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Ordinary addition, either fixture | Every tested decoder | 27/27 | 27/27 |
| Skipping, single values | Rigid | 1/27 | 2/27 |
| Skipping, single values | Beam 64 / 3 | 26/27 | 27/27 |
| Skipping, four-slot runs | Beam 64 / 1 | 0/27 | 0/27 |
| Skipping, four-slot runs | Beam 64 / 3 | 8/27 | 18/27 |
| Rewriting, single values | Every tested decoder | 1/27 | 27/27 |
| Rewriting, four-slot runs | Every tested decoder | 0/27 | 27/27 |
| Unrelated advance, single values | Beam 64 / 3 | 2/27 | 22/27 |
| Unrelated advance, four-slot runs | Beam 64 / 3 | 0/27 | 15/27 |

## Why a passing score is insufficient

Rewriting leaves much of the original text intact. The score therefore accepts many candidates even though some rune indices are wrong. This is an especially clear example of why “looks like language” and “reproduces the full plaintext” must be recorded separately. The [scorer-language controls](#/experiments/english-scorer-controls) examine another failure mode: meaningful text in some languages can receive a poor English score.

An admissible true path also need not finish first. In the single-value skip condition with a three-skip beam, every true path is permitted and none is pruned, yet one plant's winning candidate is not exact. A competing retained path scores higher under the declared ordering. The report distinguishes this from structural failure and records the first pruning step if one occurs; no true-prefix pruning was observed in this grid.

An unrelated advance does not always force failure. If its skipped value happens to satisfy the collision rule, the model can represent it. This explains why some plants in that condition still recover. Conversely, a structurally invalid *recorded alignment* is not a proof that no alternative alignment could spell the same plaintext. Exact candidate recovery is measured independently of the encoder's slot path.

## Even the correct key can be ambiguous

A tiny example makes the issue visible without a language model. Work modulo three with key slots `[0, 0, 1]` and always reject collisions. Plaintext `[0, 1]` emits ciphertext `[0, 1]` using slots zero and one. Plaintext `[0, 0]` emits the same ciphertext by rejecting slot one and accepting slot two. The key and ciphertext alone do not distinguish these two plaintexts under this mechanism.

The stored encoder trace resolves that ambiguity for verification because it contains the answer's alignment. A solver does not receive that trace. The trace-assisted inversion check is an oracle control, not an available decryption attack.

## Reproduce and inspect

Download this experiment's ZIP and preserve the directory structure. Python 3 standard-library modules are sufficient; no network access, API, external model download or third-party package is required.

```text
python experiments/records/decoder-skip-controls/run.py --check
python scripts/check_decoder_skip_controls.py experiments/records/decoder-skip-controls/results.json --receipt my-decoder-audit.json
python experiments/records/decoder-skip-controls/plot.py
```

The producer checks every frozen input hash. The independent checker imports no producer functions: it reconstructs source prefixes, generated keys and encoder decisions, replays beam selection, and checks every returned rune sequence and diagnostic. It also recomputes full-text scores using a separate calculation. All 216 plants and 2,160 decoder results passed. Ten small-control tests include exhaustive transition comparisons, long rejection runs, rewrite wraparound, exhaustion, ambiguity, and beam output checked against complete path enumeration. Human review remains pending.

## Scope and next steps

This is a fresh control inspired by [Dukotah's benchmark work](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/benchmark/README.md), not a replication of that repository's reported percentages. Known readings, including any non-prose material within their selected prefixes, are retained without editing. We do not infer manuscript language, identify its cipher, prove a pad construction, or claim that all skip-aware algorithms share these failures.

A later experiment can change the encoder or alignment rule, but must record those changes and test recovery again. Searching many wrong keys also needs a separate control of the *best score from each entire search*, not just a collection of individual wrong-key scores. See [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) for why the size and selection rule belong in the claim.

records.article:
# Direct Hill keys at LP2 page starts

**Question.** Can a single invertible linear block key over the 29-rune alphabet turn the first twelve runes of an unsolved LP2 page into a fixed known-reading opening?

**Result.** No such key fits any of the **495 page-and-opening pairs** for two-rune blocks or the **495 pairs** for three-rune blocks. This is a complete key-feasibility check for the stated block rule: it does not sample a few matrices or assume a convenient key.

![One matrix must preserve the relationships among every block.](experiments/records/direct-hill-key-feasibility/block-rule.svg)

## What the test means

Each rune has its usual Gematria Primus index from 0 to 28. We divide the first twelve runes into consecutive blocks of two or three, starting at the first rune of each page. For one proposed opening, the same unknown matrix **D** must satisfy **P = D·C (mod 29)** for *every* corresponding ciphertext and plaintext block. A later block cannot be handled with a different key. The nine target openings were fixed in the earlier known-readings test.

We do not need to try the enormous set of possible keys. First choose independent ciphertext blocks. Their proposed plaintext blocks determine what D must do on that span. Every other ciphertext block is a combination of those basis blocks, so its target must obey the same combination. Finally the target basis must remain independent; otherwise D cannot be invertible. If the ciphertext span is incomplete, the check counts every possible invertible extension instead of falsely rejecting it. For rank *r* in dimension *n*, that count is the product of **29ⁿ − 29ʲ** for **j = r, …, n−1**.

Here all 55 tested page starts have full ciphertext rank in both dimensions. Their first independent blocks therefore determine a unique possible matrix. In every one of the 990 comparisons, a remaining block disagrees with that matrix. None of the nine opening readings is obtained under this exact direct rule.

## Limits and reproduction

The test covers **LP2-00–55 except runeless LP2-50**, page-local origin zero, the first twelve runes including headings, dimensions two and three, and nine fixed 12-rune openings. It does not test other plaintexts, later positions, block offsets or directions, an affine constant, padding, transposition, or a key that changes between blocks. It does not test the LP2 number square as a key schedule.

Download the experiment files and run `python experiments/records/direct-hill-key-feasibility/run.py --check` followed by `python experiments/records/direct-hill-key-feasibility/check.py` from the repository root. The second program reads the independent page JSON, uses a separate stacked-rank criterion for all 990 cases, and checks small-field predictions against **all** invertible 2×2 and 3×3 matrices over F₂ and F₃. Those controls include full-rank, rank-deficient, zero-input, and inconsistent cases. The per-case result file records the page, opening, rank, and number of compatible keys.
records.reader_finding: No key works for any of the 55 tested page starts and nine known twelve-rune openings, using blocks of two or three runes. The check covers every invertible key under that fixed rule.
records.reader_limit: Blocks start at the first rune and use the usual 29-rune indices. Other openings, starting positions, added offsets and keys that change between blocks remain untested.

records.summary: All 880 page/representation/degree checks have difference gcd 1, excluding this direct-output model for every modulus greater than one. Polynomial keys mixed with plaintext are not tested.

scope.procedure: Compute forward differences of orders 2–9 and their integer gcd for each nonempty page and representation; independently verify using binomial sums from page JSON.

records.article:
# Can a low-degree polynomial directly generate an LP2 page?

**No, under the exact model tested here.** Every nonempty rune page in archived LP2-00–55 fails a necessary condition for direct polynomial generation of degree at most eight, in both rune-index and prime-value coordinates. The obstruction applies to every integer modulus greater than one, not just a searched list of moduli.

This says nothing about a polynomial **key** added to unknown plaintext. In that model the polynomial generates only the key, while this test compares its output directly with the manuscript symbols.

## The proposed construction

Number the retained runes on one page i = 0, 1, 2, … . The tested rule is:

```text
c[i] ≡ P(N + s*i) (mod m)
```

Here P has integer coefficients and degree at most eight; N is any integer starting position; s is any fixed integer stride, including negative or zero; and m is any fixed integer greater than one. Coefficients, origin, stride and modulus may differ between pages. The output c[i] is either the rune's zero-based index or its literal Gematria Primus prime value. There is no additional alphabet mapping.

## Why differences can rule out infinitely many parameters

A forward difference subtracts each value from the next. For the squares 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, the first differences are 1, 3, 5, 7, the second differences are 2, 2, 2, and the third differences are 0, 0. Each difference lowers polynomial degree by at least one. A polynomial of degree at most d therefore has zero differences at order d+1.

Reducing a sequence modulo m may change those differences from zero into multiples of m. It cannot change the requirement that **m divides every difference at that order**. Consequently, m must divide their greatest common divisor (gcd). If that gcd is 1, no modulus m > 1 can work.

Substituting N+s*i into a polynomial does not increase its degree in i. This is why arbitrary origins and fixed strides are covered without enumerating them. The proof uses the algebraic form of the rule; it does not estimate a probability.

## A small example you can check by hand

| Sequence | Values | First differences | Second differences | Third differences |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Squares | 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 | 1, 3, 5, 7 | 2, 2, 2 | 0, 0 |
| Change only the last value | 0, 1, 4, 9, 17 | 1, 3, 5, 8 | 2, 2, 3 | 0, 1 |

The modified example has gcd(0, 1) = 1 at order three. It cannot be a quadratic polynomial stream modulo any m > 1 under the stated rule. A gcd other than 1 would merely leave possible divisors to investigate; it would not establish that a polynomial exists.

## Manuscript result and coverage

The retest uses the repository's archived rune text, retains headings, removes nonalphabet characters, and starts a separate stream for each page. Decimal labels, separators and line breaks do not advance the position. It tests degrees 1–8 separately; constant polynomials are included within every degree bound.

| Coverage | Count |
| --- | ---: |
| Page files LP2-00–55 | 56 |
| Nonempty rune streams | 55 |
| Representations per stream | 2 |
| Degree bounds per representation | 8 |
| Checks with gcd 1 | 880 of 880 |

LP2-50 contains no alphabet runes in this transcription and is explicitly skipped. Its alphanumeric grid is not converted into a rune stream. LP2-56 and LP2-57 are outside the scope.

For a concrete witness, LP2-00's zero-based rune indices have ninth differences beginning **−1078, 1882, −2478, 1805**. Their successive gcds are 1078, 2, 2, 1. Those four values alone exclude every modulus greater than one for degree at most eight. The downloadable ledger contains all differences and a short gcd-one prefix for each of the 880 checks.

## What would reopen the question?

A polynomial key mixed with plaintext, a higher-degree polynomial, irregularly skipped positions, internal resets, a different rune selection, or an additional output mapping changes the model. Those require their own tests. The result does not eliminate arithmetic ciphers, running keys, recurrences or periodic ciphers as general classes.

The result is tied to the supplied transcription, not to a new visual audit of every rune. If the transcription changes, rerun the calculation. Agreement between the text and page-JSON versions checks computation and packaging; those versions share their archival source.

## Reproduce and independently check

Extract the experiment ZIP with folders intact, or use the repository. Python 3's standard library is sufficient. No network requests, AI calls or additional packages are needed.

```text
python experiments/records/direct-polynomial-streams/run.py --check
python experiments/records/direct-polynomial-streams/check.py
```

The first command takes successive neighboring differences. The second reads page JSON and computes each difference directly with the binomial-coefficient formula, without importing the first implementation. It also checks 128 synthetic polynomial streams across degrees, moduli, origins and strides, plus the modified-square example above. Both commands must pass.

## Relationship to the earlier archive

This is a fresh reproduction of the supplied closure register's direct-polynomial claim (C10/C22), using the current published corpus. It is not an original discovery. The earlier archive describes formal Lean checks; this package supplies an elementary proof and independently checked integer calculations, and does not claim to rerun that Lean development. Other entries in the register are not certified by this experiment.
records.reader_finding: No polynomial with integer coefficients and degree at most eight can directly generate any of the 55 tested pages under the fixed-step rule, even allowing any fixed integer modulus greater than one. Both rune indices and GP prime values fail the required check.
records.reader_limit: This tests the polynomial as the entire output, not as a key mixed with plaintext. Higher degrees, skipped positions, resets and extra symbol mappings remain untested.

records.article:
# The same six runes on LP2-27 and LP2-55

**`ᛞᛄᚢ-ᛒᛖᛁ` appears once on each of these two pages.** The six runes are conventionally transliterated `DJU-BEI`; the hyphen is a visible separator and does not count as a rune. In the archived text they begin at rune offset **28 on LP2-27** and **70 on LP2-55**, counting from zero at the start of each page.

![The same six-rune DJU-BEI sequence appears at zero-based offsets 28 and 70 on LP2-27 and LP2-55.](experiments/records/dju-bei-cross-page/offsets.svg)

| Page | Where to look | Zero-based rune offset | One-based rune position | Exact source slice |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| [LP2-27](#/reader/lp2-27) | line 2, columns 11–17 | 28 | 29 | `ᛞᛄᚢ-ᛒᛖᛁ` |
| [LP2-55](#/reader/lp2-55) | line 4, columns 4–10 | 70 | 71 | `ᛞᛄᚢ-ᛒᛖᛁ` |

The offset counts only the 29 Gematria Primus runes. Spaces, hyphens, punctuation and row ends are skipped, but the page's rune order is preserved. The count resets at each page. Thus this verifies the two locations reported in the supplied discussion without relying on an ambiguous character count that includes separators.

The recurrence is a **source observation**, not a decryption. It does not show that the phrase is plaintext, that one page supplies a key to the other, or that it explains suppressed doublets. The match was already known before this audit, so we do not attach a chance probability to it. This record checks these two stored transcriptions only; it does not claim a manuscript-wide search or fresh adjudication against the page images.

To reproduce, run `python experiments/records/dju-bei-cross-page/run.py --check` from the repository or extracted experiment bundle. The [script](experiments/records/dju-bei-cross-page/run.py) reads the archived [LP2-27](data/pages/lp2-27.json) and [LP2-55](data/pages/lp2-55.json) page records, checks their rune counts, and verifies the stored [coordinate report](experiments/records/dju-bei-cross-page/results.json). Compare the [original LP2-27 image](images/lp2-27.jpg) and [LP2-55 image](images/lp2-55.jpg) if a proposed interpretation depends on the exact visual form or adjacent marks.

records.article:
# Where the 86 doublets cross a separator

The standard LP2-00–55 count removes non-runes within each page. That makes some equal runes neighbors in the filtered stream even when a hyphen or row break separates them in the archived text. This audit locates those pairs and tests the site's seven stored LP2 reviewed-text edits.

**Sixty of the 86 pairs are directly adjacent rune characters.** Three have only a row-wrap marker between them, 22 cross a hyphen, and one crosses other punctuation. No doublet crosses an apostrophe alone or with a soft row wrap. These categories are exclusive: a hyphen plus row wrap counts in the hyphen row.

![A bar and legend split the 86 equal-rune pairs by intervening marks: 60 contiguous, 3 row-wrap only, 22 hyphen and 1 other punctuation.](experiments/records/doublet-boundaries/boundaries.svg)

| Intervening marks | Equal pairs | All rune pairs in that class | Rate |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| None: rune characters touch | 60 | 9,637 | 0.623% |
| Row wrap only (`/`, CR/LF) | 3 | 388 | 0.773% |
| Apostrophe, perhaps with wrap | 0 | 3 | 0% |
| Hyphen, perhaps with wrap | 22 | 2,721 | 0.809% |
| Other separator | 1 | 152 | 0.658% |
| **All within-page filtered pairs** | **86** | **12,901** | **0.667%** |

The first three rows follow the site's published rune-token convention: slash row markers and physical line breaks are removed, and an internal apostrophe is allowed. Under that convention, **63 of 10,028 within-token pairs** match (0.628%). This is a transcription-based token definition, not an image-verified judgment that every such pair lies within a manuscript word. Conversely, the 22 hyphen-crossing doublets would disappear from a strictly word-internal doublet count. Rates across these groups are descriptive; the small row-wrap and apostrophe groups do not justify a mechanism claim.

## What the stored corrections change

The current archive has separate LP2 reviewed-text layers for pages 05, 07, 11, 15, 35, 37 and 38. They alter notation marks but preserve the ordered rune stream. Applying all seven leaves the **86 pair identities and all five doublet category counts unchanged**. None of the stored punctuation changes falls between a doublet in a way that moves it to another class.

This answers a deliberately limited question. The other LP2 pages have no separate reviewed layer here. The seven layers are not a second complete independent transcription, and this experiment does not recheck 86 pairs against the original 2400×3600 scans. A new rune correction could change both pair identities and counts; a new separator correction could change the word-internal classification without changing 86.

The [full doublet guide](#/wiki/doublets) explains the 86-event count and provides source coordinates. The [transcription guide](#/wiki/transcription-checking?section=coverage) lists which pages have reviewed layers. The [short-lag profile](#/experiments/doublet-lag-profile) keeps the filtered within-page rule and compares equality at rune distances one through five. These analyses answer different questions.

The [EA frequency control](#/experiments/ea-frequency-control) asks a separate question: whether the 86 observed repeat positions are numerically plausible as plaintext EA under one exact running-sum equation. It uses decoded GP indices from solved pages rather than assigning English digraphs by eye.

The [placement audit](#/experiments/doublet-placement) asks whether the event positions cluster by page or sit unusually close together after preserving the number of available within-page edges.

## Reproduce and inspect

Extract the experiment ZIP without flattening folders. Python 3.12 and its standard library suffice:

```text
python experiments/records/doublet-boundaries/run.py --check
python experiments/records/doublet-boundaries/check.py
```

The producer records SHA-256 hashes for the alphabet, all 56 archived page texts, and the seven page records with reviewed layers. `results.json` lists every doublet by page, zero-based rune index, source character offsets, intervening marks and reviewed-layer classification. Run `--write` to regenerate the report and SVG. The independent checker extracts runes with a separate regular-expression path, recounts separator classes, and checks all 86 offsets against the existing source-location ledger. That verifies the archived data handling; it does not authenticate the photographed glyphs.

records.article:
# Removing or splitting adjacent repeats

**Result.** Three fixed edits all suppress adjacent repeats when applied as a final operation to the archived LP2-00–55 rune stream. They do **not** reveal which edit, if any, was used to make that stream. Both insertion rules can also give the same output from different inputs, even if the decoder knows the input length. A reverse-edit step therefore needs extra information that the proposal did not supply.

![The original stream has 86 adjacent repeats. Deleting the later rune leaves none; inserting fixed F leaves eight; inserting a different rune leaves none.](experiments/records/doublet-collision-edits/collision-edits.svg)

The supplied list proposed deleting one copy of a repeat (`ABBC → ABC`) or splitting it with a filler (`ABBC → ABDBC`). We pinned one complete pass for each, plus a deliberately stronger insertion control. They are three **variants of one collision-edit idea**, not three independent LP2 decryptions.

| Forward edit on LP2-00–55 | Runes afterward | Adjacent repeats afterward |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Original archive | 12,956 | 86 |
| Collapse each run to its first rune | 12,870 | 0 |
| Put `F` between each original repeat | 13,042 | 8 |
| Put the next GP rune between each original repeat | 13,042 | 0 |

The eight repeats left by fixed `F` insertion occur where the original repeated rune is itself `F`; an `F` inserted between two `F`s does not separate them. Choosing a filler guaranteed to differ from the repeated rune removes that edge case, but this adaptive choice was **our control rule**, not a specified historical key. These are forward edits to an already sparse ciphertext. Reaching zero doublets by editing it says little about how its original 86 arose.

## Why undoing an edit is harder

The deletion rule loses positions. For instance, the three four-rune strings `FFFTH`, `FFTH TH` and `FTH TH TH` (spaces here only separate GP rune labels) all collapse to `FTH`. Knowing there were four runes does not choose among them.

Insertion can also be ambiguous, even with a declared filler. Under the fixed-`F` rule, `TH F TH TH` and `TH TH F TH` both become `TH F TH F TH`. Exhaustive enumeration over the small alphabet `{F, U, TH}`, holding original length fixed, first finds **two** ambiguous outputs among length-four originals for each insertion rule. That toy result proves these fixed transforms are not generally one-to-one; it does not estimate how many LP2 readings they permit. The [complete preimage counts](experiments/records/doublet-collision-edits/results.json) cover original lengths one through five.

The source example also mentions moving a repeated rune (`ABBC → ABCB`), but it does not say how to handle the end of a stream, runs longer than two, or new collisions. We have not turned that open rule into an invented test. Likewise, the filler glyph, the stage at which editing happens, and a decoder's removal clock were not fixed in the source.

## Exact scope and next test

We filtered the [archived LP2 page texts](#/reader/lp2-00) to GP runes and edited each of the 56 pages separately. Page breaks never become adjacent pairs. The [plan](experiments/records/doublet-collision-edits/plan.json) states the pass order and run handling; [results](experiments/records/doublet-collision-edits/results.json) give the before/after count on every page. The original supplied discussion is identified by its attachment SHA-256 in the plan.

A proposed LP2 decryption using one of these edits would need a frozen preceding cipher, filler or deletion-position rule, and a way to recover a planted known reading before scoring unsolved text. The [decoder controls](#/experiments/decoder-skip-controls) show why a plausible-looking output is not enough to establish exact recovery.

Run from the repository root or the experiment ZIP with Python 3.12 or later:

```text
python experiments/records/doublet-collision-edits/run.py --check
python experiments/records/doublet-collision-edits/check.py
python experiments/records/doublet-collision-edits/plot.py --check
```

The independent checker reconstructs edits by maximal equal-rune runs instead of the producer's adjacent-pair loop. It checks all page totals, input hashes, and toy preimage counts. Neither program treats a reduced doublet count as a plaintext reading.

records.article:
# What surrounds the 86 ciphertext doublets?

The [doublet guide](#/wiki/doublets?section=ea-constraint) describes one proposed equation in which a repeated ciphertext rune would mark a plaintext EA. That statement is easy to overread. It fixes the **plaintext symbol at a transition** under the equation; it does not say that the repeated *ciphertext* rune is the EA rune, or that the neighboring ciphertext runes should spell an English word. This experiment records those local ciphertext values and asks whether they have extra ordering structure under a declared conditional control.

![Counts of all 29 ciphertext symbols at the 86 doublet positions, compared with means from fixed-mask within-page permutations.](experiments/records/doublet-context/context.svg)

## What the equation predicts

For `Cᵢ = Cᵢ₋₁ + Kᵢ(Pᵢ − 28) mod 29` with nonzero `Kᵢ`, `Cᵢ = Cᵢ₋₁` if and only if `Pᵢ = 28` (EA). The doublet's visible rune is `Cᵢ`, the **current ciphertext state**. It can be any of the 29 runes. A doublet on AE does not make AE the proposed plaintext; a doublet on EA does not offer special confirmation.

If the *following* plaintext rune is not EA and its key is independently uniform on 1–28, its difference `Cᵢ₊₁ − Cᵢ` is uniform on those 28 nonzero residues. The next ciphertext rune is then uniform over the 28 symbols **other than** `Cᵢ`. It is not independent of `Cᵢ` in absolute symbol terms, because equality is forbidden. If the following plaintext is EA, the next difference is zero and a triple results. The observed doublet mask has no consecutive zeros, so this record cannot use a fixed-mask control to judge how surprising that absence is.

## The actual local inventory

From the archived LP2-00–55 text, filter to the 29 GP runes, keep headings, and compare neighbors only within pages. This gives **86 zero differences in 12,901 transitions**. Each event is recorded by page and zero-based rune index in the [result ledger](experiments/records/doublet-context/results.json). One event has no preceding within-page difference; one has no following one. None has a zero difference immediately beside it. The remaining 85 preceding and 85 following differences are tabulated separately in all 28 nonzero residues.

The event-symbol counts range from **0 to 7**, rather than 3 to 7. GP index 17 (B) has no event; index 25 (AE) has seven; index 28 (EA) has three. The latter labels are ciphertext symbols, not decoded plaintext. Across all 29 bins there are **123 pairs of events sharing the same ciphertext symbol**. The local before-versus-after residue imbalance, defined in the [plan](experiments/records/doublet-context/plan.txt), is **27.786**. Both summaries were selected before this control was run, but the underlying doublet observation had already been seen.

## A control that holds the known anomalies fixed

For each page, retain its first ciphertext rune, the positions of all zero differences and the multiset of all nonzero differences. Shuffle only the nonzero difference order within that page, then cumulatively add the differences modulo 29 to rebuild a synthetic ciphertext page. This preserves the **86-event mask exactly** and also preserves each page's difference histogram. It asks whether *placement relative to those zeros* adds anything beyond those known properties. It does not simulate English, a key generator, or the chance of obtaining 86 zeros in the first place.

| Diagnostic | Observed | Central 95% of 5,000 conditional permutations | Trials at least observed |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Same-symbol pairs among doublet events | 123 | 108–150 | 2,950 / 5,000 |
| Before/after difference imbalance | 27.786 | 12.745–34.259 | 854 / 5,000 |

Both observed values sit inside these conditional ranges. In the figure, blue bars are the complete observed 29-symbol inventory and red ticks are the average count for each bin across the permutations. The ticks are not 29 separate significance cutoffs. The report also includes all 28 before and after residue bins, every event location, the seed (`330122`), and both inclusive rank directions.

This is **not independent corroboration** of the earlier [nonzero-difference histogram](#/experiments/ea-difference-independence). The same source differences are reused, and the new control deliberately fixes their pagewise histograms. The broad question “are these 86 positions really plaintext EA?” remains unanswered. A proposed key schedule would have to predict something further that can be checked without freely choosing plaintext neighbors after seeing the ciphertext.

## Do hyphen-crossing doublets have different neighbors?

The [boundary ledger](#/experiments/doublet-boundaries) classifies **22** doublets as crossing a hyphen, **63** as within a rune token under the site's rule, and **one** as crossing other punctuation. The last event is kept in the [complete companion ledger](experiments/records/doublet-context/boundary-context.json) but excluded from this two-group comparison. Calling all 64 non-hyphen events “within-word” would misclassify that one event; even the 63-token group is a transcription convention, not a fresh image review.

For a repeated ciphertext rune at position `i`, the immediately preceding rune is at `i−2` and the following rune at `i+1`, if those positions exist within the same page. The table counts **ciphertext** GP labels. Circular distance means the smaller of the two distances between their indices around the 29-symbol alphabet; it does not measure English-letter similarity.

| Doublet group | Events | Before available / distinct labels | Mean before distance | After available / distinct labels | Mean after distance |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Hyphen-crossing | 22 | 22 / 16 | 5.95 | 22 / 17 | 8.23 |
| Within-token | 63 | 62 / 25 | 8.06 | 62 / 25 | 7.87 |
| Other separator, excluded from comparison | 1 | 1 / 1 | 2.00 | 1 / 1 | 5.00 |

There is a visible difference in the *mean preceding circular distance*, but that summary was inspected after this question arose. For a broader comparison fixed in the [companion plan](experiments/records/doublet-context/boundary-context-plan.json), we sum the two-group Pearson association scores over all 29 before-rune labels and all 29 after-rune labels, retaining a separate category for a missing page-edge neighbor. The observed score is **51.321**. We then keep every observed before/after context vector intact and permute which 22 of the 85 eligible events carry the hyphen label. In **6,495 of 10,000** global shuffles the score is at least this large; the central 95% of shuffled scores is **39.592–71.390**. A second control preserves each page's hyphen count and yields **8,626 of 10,000** at least as large, with a central range of **46.195–75.474**. Only **13 pages and 40 events** have labels that can move in that stricter control.

These are exploratory conditional ranks, not prospective p-values or a test that the 22 marks were placed randomly. The 22-event group is small, many labels are sparse, and page layout can affect both boundary status and ciphertext context. The whole-label statistic does not stand out under either stated comparison; it does not rule out a particular word-boundary cipher rule. In the proposed EA-stalling equation, the runes around a doublet remain ciphertext states. They cannot be compared directly with English words containing EA without a separately fixed key and boundary clock.

## Reproduce and limits

Extract the experiment ZIP without flattening it, then run:

```text
python experiments/records/doublet-context/run.py --check
python experiments/records/doublet-context/check.py
python experiments/records/doublet-context/boundary_context.py --check
```

The producer reruns all 5,000 seeded conditional permutations and checks the saved JSON and SVG byte for byte. The separate checker re-extracts the Runic Unicode block, recomputes all 86 event locations and both diagnostics, and verifies each source hash. The companion script hashes both source ledgers, joins all 86 events by page and rune position, verifies neighboring runes against the archived page text, and reruns both 10,000-draw boundary-label controls. This checks the archived text, not a fresh image transcription. Neither control nor the exact algebra identifies the cipher, and these exploratory ranks are not adjusted for the wider history of questions asked of the same 86 events. See the [boundary audit](#/experiments/doublet-boundaries) and [placement audit](#/experiments/doublet-placement) for other, non-interchangeable scopes.
