records.article:
# Are the nonzero differences independent under the EA-stalling model?

The [EA-frequency control](#/experiments/ea-frequency-control) compared the 86 LP2 doublets with decoded GP EA on solved pages and examined the index of coincidence (IoC) of successive ciphertext differences. This companion check asks what the **specific independent-nonzero-key version** of that equation predicts beyond the zero count. It keeps the observed zero positions and page boundaries fixed; it does not search for plaintext or keys.

Under `Cᵢ = Cᵢ₋₁ + Kᵢ(Pᵢ − 28) mod 29`, with each key independently uniform on 1–28 and independent of a fixed plaintext, every plaintext EA gives difference zero. For any other plaintext rune, multiplication by its nonzero offset permutes 1–28. Therefore, **conditional on the zero mask**, the other differences must be independent uniform draws from those 28 residues. This is a prediction of the declared key model, not of every running-sum cipher. A periodic, deterministic or nonuniform key need not have it.

![Counts of the 28 nonzero difference residues on LP2-00–55, with their equal-count reference marked in red.](experiments/records/ea-difference-independence/differences.svg)

## Input and two diagnostics

Read archived LP2-00–55, including headings. Retain the 29 GP runes, discard other characters, and subtract each previous rune index from the next **within the same page** modulo 29. There are 12,901 differences: **86 zero** and **12,815 nonzero**. No pair is formed across a page boundary. The zero mask remains at its observed positions in all simulations.

The first diagnostic is the Pearson chi-square of the 28 nonzero residue counts against an equal-count reference. The expected count per residue is **12,815 / 28 ≈ 457.68**. The second counts equal neighboring nonzero differences. Both difference positions must be consecutive within one page; a zero between them breaks the comparison. That leaves **12,676 eligible pairs**, with **452.71** expected equalities if the nonzero draws are independent uniform residues.

| Diagnostic | Observed | Central 95% of 2,000 conditional draws | Draws at least observed |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 28-bin Pearson chi-square | 42.056 | 14.403–43.092 | 69 / 2,000 |
| Equal neighboring nonzero differences | 432 / 12,676 | 412–492 | 1,685 / 2,000 |

The histogram statistic is near the high end of this seeded conditional reference. The order-sensitive count sits within it. The simulation uses seed `33012026`; every trial fills only nonzero-mask slots with independent draws from 1–28. In a positive control, those synthetic differences were accumulated into ciphertext and differenced again, recovering the simulated values exactly. The complete result stores all 28 observed bins, both tails of each simulated rank, source hashes and the plan.

## The histogram is not independent evidence from the previous IoC

Let `m = 12,815` and let `c₁ … c₂₈` be the nonzero difference counts. The chi-square is `28 Σ cᵣ² / m − m`. With the **86 zero differences fixed**, the full difference IoC has numerator `86 × 85 + Σ cᵣ(cᵣ − 1) = 86 × 85 + Σ cᵣ² − m` and a fixed denominator `12,901 × 12,900`. Both statistics are increasing functions of the same `Σ cᵣ²`. They rank every conditional simulated histogram in exactly the same order. The histogram makes the individual residues inspectable; its 69/2,000 upper rank is **not a second independent hint** alongside the earlier IoC result.

Neighboring equality instead uses the **order** of nonzero differences. A page can keep every residue count—and thus the chi-square and IoC—while a rearrangement changes this adjacent-pair statistic. Here 432 equalities are below the 452.71 uniform expectation but inside the simulated central range. It would be a mistake to infer a periodic key, or its absence, from this one lag-one check.

## What the result leaves open

The model and diagnostics were selected after the low doublet count and difference IoC were already known. These inclusive Monte Carlo ranks are descriptive and unadjusted for that selection or for examining two related summaries. They do not provide a prospective probability that the manuscript uses this cipher. A near-uniform residual distribution is compatible with many mechanisms; a small departure would challenge only the independently uniform nonzero-key version under these boundaries and transcription choices.

No plaintext EA positions have been verified, no key has been recovered, and no unknown page has been read. A deterministic key schedule, a clock that pauses on EA, word or page resets, changed rune mapping, and alternate transcription layers require separately declared tests. See the [doublet guide](#/wiki/doublets?section=ea-constraint) for the algebra and the [placement audit](#/experiments/doublet-placement) for the spatial distribution of the 86 zeros.

## Reproduce

Extract this experiment's ZIP without flattening folders. Python 3.12 and its standard library suffice:

```text
python experiments/records/ea-difference-independence/run.py --check
python experiments/records/ea-difference-independence/check.py
```

The producer reruns the 2,000 conditional draws and checks the saved JSON and SVG byte for byte. The independent checker extracts the Runic Unicode block with a different parser, verifies every source hash, recomputes the 28 bins and adjacent statistic, and calculates chi-square from an exact rational formula. Both use archived text, not a fresh manual rereading of the JPEGs. The [test plan](experiments/records/ea-difference-independence/plan.txt), [result data](experiments/records/ea-difference-independence/results.json) and [figure](experiments/records/ea-difference-independence/differences.svg) are available separately.

records.article:
# Does EA occur often enough in solved text?

A proposed running-sum explanation for the rare repeated runes makes a testable prediction: wherever its rule applies, two equal neighboring ciphertext runes would mark an EA rune in the hidden plaintext. This record asks whether EA occurs about as often in known readings as those repeats occur in unsolved LP2. Matching rates would satisfy one necessary condition; it would not recover plaintext or establish the cipher.

The proposed equation is `Cᵢ = Cᵢ₋₁ + Kᵢ(Pᵢ − 28) mod 29`. Here `C` is the ciphertext rune index, `P` the plaintext index, EA has index 28, and each key value `Kᵢ` must be nonzero. Under those conditions, a ciphertext doublet is equivalent to plaintext EA at that transition. This is an **exact property of the proposed equation**, not evidence that Liber Primus uses it.

The site's solved LP1 controls contain **20 EA runes in 2,782 within-page transition positions** (0.719%). Unsolved LP2-00–55 has **86 doublets in 12,901 within-page positions** (0.667%). If the solved LP1 rate were simply carried over, it would correspond to about **92.7 EA positions** at the unsolved length. That is close to 86, but many different ciphers or text-generation rules can produce the same marginal rate.

![Observed EA and doublet rates with illustrative Wilson ranges; the solved LP1 sample has a wider range.](experiments/records/ea-frequency-control/comparison.svg)

| Source and measurement | Events | Positions | Rate |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Solved LP1-01, 03–16: decoded GP EA | 20 | 2,782 | 0.719% |
| Solved LP2-56–57: decoded GP EA | 0 | 178 | 0% |
| Unsolved LP2-00–55: equal neighboring ciphertext runes | 86 | 12,901 | 0.667% |

As a scale for sampling variation, a 95% **Wilson score interval** for 20/2,782 is **0.466–1.108%** if those positions were independent draws with one fixed EA probability. The observed unsolved rate, 0.667%, lies inside that interval. The same calculation for 86/12,901 gives **0.540–0.822%**. These intervals overlap, but do not establish equal rates or a cipher: adjacent rune positions in prose are dependent, and the LP1 and LP2 sources are not random samples from one common process.

To reproduce the endpoints for either count, set `p = events / positions`, `n = positions`, and `z = 1.9599639845`. The endpoints are `[p + z²/(2n) ± z√(p(1−p)/n + z²/(4n²))] / [1 + z²/n]`. The page-resampling range below addresses a different source of variation. It also remains descriptive, not a probability distribution for unknown plaintext.

The two solved LP2 pages are short; their zero EA count is not a robust estimate for the much longer unsolved portion. The LP1 pages also differ in section and method from that portion. Resampling the 15 solved LP1 pages 10,000 times gives a descriptive range of roughly **54–132 EA positions** when each draw's rate is scaled to 12,901 positions. This shows how the small control set changes with page mix. It is **not** a predictive interval for unknown LP2 plaintext: the pages are section fragments, not independent random samples from a known common language process.

## Why the spelling conversion matters

The known-reading source preserves actual decoded **GP rune indices** alongside their literal Latin labels. In all 17 solved control pages, removing row wraps and greedily taking the longest GP labels **within each printed token** reconstructs the stored index sequence exactly. That is a check on this literal source layer, not a license to parse normalized English the same way.

If all token boundaries are erased first, greedy parsing finds **31 EA labels** across the solved LP1 pages instead of the actual **20 EA runes**. The eleven extras are cross-word `E|A` joins such as `ONE | ALONG` and `STRUGGLE | AND`. The downloaded report lists all eleven. Even inside one ordinary English word, the letters `EA` do not prove the manuscript used the single EA rune: `REACT` could be segmented `R·EA·C·T` or `R·E·A·C·T`. In Gematria Primus, EA has prime value 109, while E plus A totals 67 + 97 = 164. Preserve original rune boundaries when testing a frequency or prime sum.

## What about the difference IoC?

Subtract each within-page ciphertext rune from the next modulo 29. This gives 12,901 differences, including 86 zeros. Their observed index of coincidence is **0.035325**. Under an additional idealized assumption—condition on exactly 86 zero differences, then draw all 12,815 nonzero values independently and uniformly from residues 1–28—the expected IoC is **0.035284**. In 2,000 seeded simulations, the central 95% interval was **0.035249–0.035326**; 54 trials reached or exceeded the observed value.

So 0.0353 is near the upper edge of this **conditional nonzero-uniform** reference: 54 of 2,000 draws were at least as high (2.7%). The observed value is still inside the central 95% simulation range. This is a mild tension with that one extra uniform-key assumption, not a test of the running-sum equation as a whole and not standalone confirmation. The reference was chosen after the zero deficit and IoC were known, and other features and baselines have also been examined. Shuffling the ciphertext runes within pages would change the zero count and ask a different question. Uniform nonzero differences are what independently uniform nonzero keys would imply at non-EA positions for this particular equation; other key schedules can behave differently.

The key layer explains the limitation. Write the observed difference as `Dᵢ = Cᵢ − Cᵢ₋₁`. For each **nonzero** Dᵢ and every one of the **28 non-EA plaintext symbols** Pᵢ, there is exactly one allowed nonzero key, `Kᵢ = Dᵢ(Pᵢ − 28)⁻¹ mod 29`. Thus an unconstrained key per position can fit *any* proposed non-EA plaintext at those positions. Conversely, an independently uniform nonzero key makes Dᵢ uniform on 1–28 regardless of how uneven the non-EA plaintext letter frequencies are. The conditional IoC can challenge that extra independent-uniform-key assumption; it cannot identify plaintext, establish EA at the 86 positions, or test an unspecified deterministic key schedule. **No fixed key schedule has been applied to unsolved LP2 in this record.** Doing so would be a different, stronger experiment with a declared generator and fixed parameters. Simply deleting the 86 zero differences leaves the same 12,815 nonzero values whose histogram is tested in the [companion record](#/experiments/ea-difference-independence). Deleting ciphertext runes instead creates new adjacencies and is a different operation.

Under the archived boundary rule, **22 of the 86 doublets cross a hyphen**. They are legitimate consecutive runes in the filtered stream but are not within-token repeats. If the proposed recurrence resets at word boundaries, those 22 edges no longer fall under its doublet⇔EA identity. If the key continues over boundaries, the identity still applies to the second rune of each edge, with the hyphen ignored by the cipher clock. The [separator audit](#/experiments/doublet-boundaries) lists every such position; the current count cannot decide which clock Cicada used.

All of these comparisons were designed after the low doublet count was known. A confirmatory version would need a key schedule, starting state, boundary/reset rule, rune mapping and success criterion fixed from evidence independent of the test output, then a prediction of untouched ciphertext or a verified plaintext passage. Merely changing an interval method or reserving positions after inspecting this corpus cannot turn the existing rate match into a prospective test.

The [doublet placement audit](#/experiments/doublet-placement) tests a different implication: whether the 86 candidate EA positions have unusual page counts or short gaps under explicit event-placement controls. Those controls also cannot establish a plaintext reading.

The [nonzero-difference companion](#/experiments/ea-difference-independence) keeps the observed zero positions fixed and checks residue balance and adjacent differences. Its 28-bin chi-square is algebraically the same information as the difference IoC reported above, so the two histogram summaries must not be counted as independent evidence.

## Reproduce and limits

Extract the experiment ZIP without flattening it. Python 3.12 and its standard library suffice:

```text
python experiments/records/ea-frequency-control/run.py --check
python experiments/records/ea-frequency-control/check.py
```

The producer hashes the known-reading extract, alphabet and all 56 unsolved text files. The independent checker recounts decoded EA indices, reconstructs literal labels, verifies the cross-word joins, and recalculates the exact difference IoC. The source extract uses established decoded readings and a documented LP1-10 correction; this experiment is not a fresh image audit. It cannot tell whether the 86 doublets are plaintext EA, nor recover the nonzero key sequence. See [the doublet guide](#/wiki/doublets?section=ea-constraint) for the equation and its assumptions, and the [boundary audit](#/experiments/doublet-boundaries) for where the 86 pairs sit relative to stored separators.

# Historical Emerson book-cipher control

## Purpose and what this does not test

A book cipher needs a source edition and counting conventions, not just a book title. This record reproduces the documented 2014 opening-image coordinates against the frozen Emerson Self-Reliance PDF derivative. It gives newcomers a working control and a trace they can inspect before proposing new book-cipher experiments.

**The answer was known before this rerun.** This is a historical replication, not blind discovery, an independent confirmation of source selection, or a decipherment of an unsolved manuscript page. No hidden-service address was visited.

## Frozen plan and prior reconstruction history

The rerun plan and wrapper were committed as `1f67f70` before this execution. Source files, the existing lookup script and the known result were hashed in the plan. An earlier reconstruction had corrected the treatment of embedded verse after inspecting mismatches: the verse remains inside prose paragraph 36 rather than creating extra paragraphs. That earlier adjustment is disclosed in the existing evidence manifest and is not presented here as a rule discovered independently.

The PDF is the contemporary snapshot linked in the historical walkthrough. Its hash is fixed, but the original creator's exact edition is not authenticated by this reproduction.

## Counting conventions

Re-extract the pinned PDF with pypdf 6.19.0 in layout mode. Begin at the first prose paragraph, exclude numeric page footers, and use four-space prose indentation to begin paragraphs. Seven-space verse remains in its surrounding paragraph. Apply Unicode NFKC normalization and join wrapped lines according to the stored extraction rule. All 50 extracted paragraphs must match the frozen derivative.

Coordinates are one-based paragraph:sentence:word:letter positions. Sentences split at `.`, `!` and `?`; words split on whitespace with edge punctuation removed; only ASCII letters count inside the selected word. Single-character entries are copied literally. These are the documented reconstruction conventions, not a universal natural-language sentence parser.

## Result

The complete trace matches the archived control. Fifteen coordinate lookups and seven literal characters reconstruct:

```
auqgnxjtvdbll3pv.onion
```

This is a historical output string. Reproducing it says nothing about any current service at that name. The supported claim is only that these exact inputs and rules reproduce the recorded trace.

## Complete coordinate trace

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1:2:3:1 | 1 | always | a |
| 3:3:13:5 | 2 | genius | u |

| 4:3:3:1 | 2 | being | b |

| 3 | Literal | Copied directly | 3 |
| 13:2:5:4 | 6 | corpse | p |

| o | Literal | Copied directly | o |
| n | Literal | Copied directly | n |

The first coordinate, 1:2:3:1, selects the third word of the second sentence in paragraph 1: `always`. Its first letter is `a`. The JSON output includes each full selected sentence, so a reader can check the counting rather than trusting the final string alone.

## Reproduce from files

Use Python 3.12.10 and pypdf 6.19.0. Install the exact dependency in your preferred environment:

```
python -m pip install pypdf==6.19.0
python experiments/records/emerson-book-cipher-control/run.py --check
```

Dependency installation needs package access; the actual experiment makes no network request. The wrapper checks every frozen input hash, invokes the existing reproduction script with `--check-pdf`, compares all 50 paragraphs, and checks the complete output trace. It then compares the new report with the saved one. Missing dependencies or changed inputs fail visibly.

To save a separate report:

```
python experiments/records/emerson-book-cipher-control/run.py --output my-emerson-control.json
```

Existing output files are never overwritten. [Download the complete trace](experiments/records/emerson-book-cipher-control/results.json). [Download the pinned PDF](exports/sources/emerson-self-reliance.pdf) and [paragraph derivative](exports/sources/emerson-paragraphs.json). The [coordinate payload](exports/steganography/opening-2014.body.txt) is the extracted message body; extraction and signature verification are separate steps described in the opening-image guide.

For a standard-library-only replay of the frozen paragraphs, run `python scripts/reproduce_emerson.py` without `--check-pdf`. That shorter check does not re-extract the PDF and must not be reported as having done so.

## Retest and review

Codex ran the PDF reconstruction and lookup twice on 20 October 2026. Both produced the same 50 paragraphs and identical complete trace. No counting rule or source changed during this rerun. The diagram was generated afterward from the saved first lookup. Human review remains pending, and the lookup implementation is the existing historical reproduction code rather than a newly independent decoder.

## Family and future variants

A different edition, paragraph convention or source text needs a separate variant with the exact change recorded. An attempt to apply a book cipher to an unsolved LP2 page also needs an independently defined source of coordinates and a success criterion. This historical control is useful for checking an implementation; it does not establish that such a transfer has already been tested.

See [book-cipher conventions](#/wiki/book-ciphers), [Emerson and the historical source](#/wiki/emerson-self-reliance), and [the opening image](#/wiki/opening-2014).

# Does the preserved Emerson text work as an LP2 running key?

Under **one fully specified additive rule**, the tested LP2 pages do not show a convincing Emerson-key opening or continuation. We searched every **43,325 contiguous offsets** of the archived *Self-Reliance* extract for each of LP2-00, LP2-31 and LP2-54. The best 96-rune openings score near maxima from eight complete searches using shuffled versions of the same source letters. Their next 96 runes remain far below a planted known-reading control. This does not exclude other running-key rules, source editions, alphabets or page positions.

![Opening and held-out continuation scores for Emerson and shuffled-source searches](experiments/records/emerson-running-key/search-scores.svg)

## Why this source and what rule was frozen

Emerson's *Self-Reliance* is a documented source for a **2014 book-coordinate cipher**, reproduced separately in the [historical control](#/experiments/emerson-book-cipher-control). That history makes it a concrete candidate to test; a coordinate cipher does not establish a running key for LP2. We used the site's preserved **50-paragraph PDF derivative**, not an authenticated creator edition. Its original file, extraction convention and SHA-256 are described in the [Emerson source guide](#/wiki/emerson-self-reliance).

Join the 50 stored paragraphs with spaces, uppercase, and retain ASCII A–Z. The result has **43,516 letters**. Map A to 0 through Z to 25. For each LP2 page, take its first 192 archived alphabet runes in order, including headings. At each offset, subtract successive source-letter values from rune indices modulo 29; the source does not wrap, and punctuation advances neither stream. This is deliberately a Latin-letter-to-rune numeric key, not a claim that Emerson's prose was written in Gematria Primus.

Score the first **96 decoded runes** after concatenating their canonical Latin labels. The score is the mean base-10 log probability of overlapping four-letter groups under the pinned [English quadgram model](#/experiments/english-scorer-controls); unseen groups receive count 0.01. Select the highest first-window score, breaking ties toward the lowest source offset. Only then score the **next 96 runes** at that same offset. Search eight deterministic full-stream letter shuffles with exactly the same offset budget and selection rule. Those controls preserve the source's letter counts while breaking its order. The [plan](experiments/records/emerson-running-key/plan.json) fixes these choices and hashes every input.

## Complete search maxima

Higher scores are more English-like under this exact scorer. The shuffle ranges below contain the **best selected candidate from each complete shuffled-source search**, not scores of arbitrary unselected offsets.

| Target | Best Emerson offset | First 96 | Eight shuffle maxima | Next 96 at chosen offset | Shuffle continuations |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| LP2-00 | 19,692 | −6.364 | −6.372 to −6.143 | −7.575 | −7.807 to −7.054 |
| LP2-31 | 1,162 | −6.353 | −6.444 to −6.218 | −7.368 | −7.875 to −7.306 |
| LP2-54 | 21,646 | −6.462 | −6.536 to −6.255 | −6.817 | −7.754 to −6.997 |

The LP2-54 continuation scores higher than all eight shuffled-source continuations. That observation is retained, not dismissed: there are only eight controls, its first window was not stronger than their maxima, and its continuation score is still far below the known-reading plant. These values are **descriptive**, not a calibrated p-value or an English-language decision threshold. The [full result](experiments/records/emerson-running-key/results.json) preserves the top five offsets and both decoded windows for every search, so a reader can inspect the candidate text rather than rely on one number.

## Did the search have a fair chance to find a real key?

As a positive control, take the first 192 **decoded** rune indices of LP1-06, add the same Emerson key beginning at zero-based offset **3,301**, and search the resulting synthetic ciphertext without telling the search its offset. The complete 43,325-offset search ranks **3,301 first**, recovers the known indices exactly there, and scores **−4.096** on the first 96 and **−3.883** on the next 96. This proves the pipeline can recover a planted instance of the specified rule at this length. It does not establish its power for every possible plaintext or source text.

The scorer itself has documented language limits: it can reject meaningful Welsh, for example, while accepting some non-English text. Canonical rune labels also differ from ordinary English spelling. A low score therefore cannot exclude a non-English plaintext or every English representation. The result only weakens this **single Emerson / A–Z shifts / subtractive modulo-29 / page-opening** variant. A proposal with a different source conversion, offset reset, interrupted clock, or selected passage is a different search and must count those choices.

## Reproduce

With Python 3 standard library, from the repository root or extracted [experiment ZIP](downloads/experiments/emerson-running-key.zip):

```text
python experiments/records/emerson-running-key/run.py --check
python experiments/records/emerson-running-key/check.py
python experiments/records/emerson-running-key/plot.py --check
```

The producer checks all source hashes and replays every complete offset search. The independent checker reconstructs the source, shuffles, rune streams and planted ciphertext; it scores by counted quadgrams rather than the producer's sliding sum, and verifies every maximum, top-five list and holdout. The plotter checks the published figure. No API, model download or network call is needed.
records.reader_finding: No convincing Emerson-key reading emerged. LP2-54’s continuation beat the eight shuffled controls, but the selected openings did not stand out and the continuations scored far below the planted reading.
records.reader_limit: Only the first 192 runes of LP2-00, 31 and 54 were tested, across 43,325 offsets in one extract. The rule uses A–Z values, uninterrupted subtraction and English scoring.

## Would our scorer recognize a real answer?

A search can recover meaningful text and still discard it if its scoring rule expects the wrong language. This experiment isolates that last step: give a fixed English four-letter scoring model known text in eight languages, then shuffle the same letters as a control. No cipher or decoder is involved.

The model accepts all English and French samples in this run, some German, Italian, Portuguese and Spanish samples, and none of the Finnish or Welsh samples. It accepts none of the 7,680 shuffled controls. That is useful separation from these shuffles, but **acceptance is neither English identification nor proof of a decryption**. Rejection also cannot rule out meaningful plaintext in another language.

## Source and scope

The idea follows the scorer-language investigation in [Dukotah's repository](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/PAPER.md). We pin that revision and reuse its English quadgram count file and −5.5 threshold. We run a new, narrower control on our existing aligned FLORES translations; we do not reproduce the repository's full decoder benchmark or import its conclusions about the unsolved cipher.

The [language comparison experiments](#/experiments/parallel-languages) ask which reference profiles resemble manuscript statistics. This experiment instead asks what a candidate-selection tool accepts when the input is already known text. There are no unsolved-page inputs here.

## Fixed procedure

Divide each of the eight 1,012-sentence translations into the same eight consecutive sentence blocks: four of 127 sentences and four of 126. Join sentences with spaces. Apply each of two rules: uppercase and retain A–Z only; or uppercase, canonically decompose Unicode, remove combining marks, and then retain A–Z. The second rule folds many accented letters but is not a general transliteration system. Uppercasing can expand characters, such as ß to SS. The report records retained lengths and discarded alphabetic characters for each block.

Take the first 120, 240 and 400 retained letters from every block. These are nested samples, not three independent passages. Aligned sentence blocks preserve source content boundaries, but equal character prefixes do not necessarily end at the same translated idea. Generate 20 deterministic shuffles of each excerpt, preserving its exact letter counts. Keep all 384 original cells and all 7,680 controls; there is no selection by score.

For each overlapping group of four letters, use log₁₀(count / total model count). An unseen group receives log₁₀(0.01 / total). Average over the length minus three groups. Accept a sample when this average is at least −5.5. This threshold belongs to this model and preprocessing; it is not portable to an arbitrary language scorer.

## All conditions

Each cell below is accepted originals out of eight blocks. Every condition also has 160 shuffles per language; all have zero accepted shuffles. The figure shows individual original scores and the full observed shuffled range, not a confidence interval.

| Language | A–Z 120 | A–Z 240 | A–Z 400 | Folded 120 | Folded 240 | Folded 400 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| English | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 |
| Finnish | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 |
| French | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 |
| German | 6/8 | 6/8 | 6/8 | 6/8 | 6/8 | 8/8 |
| Italian | 7/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 7/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 |
| Portuguese | 5/8 | 7/8 | 7/8 | 6/8 | 7/8 | 7/8 |
| Spanish | 6/8 | 7/8 | 7/8 | 8/8 | 7/8 | 7/8 |
| Welsh | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 |

## What this does and does not establish

This scorer can reject intact language while accepting a different non-English language. A successful candidate therefore needs more than crossing a threshold: a reproducible decoding rule, declared choices, coherent extended output and checks against controls appropriate to the whole search.

The shuffles preserve single-letter frequencies but destroy order. They are not wrong-key outputs from a specified cipher. Zero acceptances in this finite collection does not imply zero false positives, especially after searching millions of candidates and keeping the maximum. The overlapping sample lengths, reused translations and shared model also prevent treating these cells as independent trials or a general accuracy estimate. Model-training overlap with the benchmark has not been independently excluded.

This is not decoder recovery power: it bypasses decoding entirely. The completed [planted decoder controls](#/experiments/decoder-skip-controls) separately measure exact recovery and score acceptance under fixed encoder, key and skip rules. The [bounded search-maximum controls](#/experiments/search-maximum-controls) retain the maximum from each complete null search rather than treating individual null strings as equivalent to selected winners. These are separate experiments; neither retroactively turns this scorer-only test into a manuscript decryption test. The [newcomer control walkthrough](#/wiki/first-experiment?section=search-controls) explains how to read them together.

## Reproduce and inspect

Download the experiment bundle and extract it with its directory structure. No network access, API key or third-party Python package is required.

```text
python experiments/records/english-scorer-controls/run.py --check
python scripts/check_english_scorer_controls.py experiments/records/english-scorer-controls/results.json --receipt my-scorer-audit.json
python experiments/records/english-scorer-controls/plot.py
```

The producer checks every pinned input hash. The independent checker reconstructs the source excerpts and shuffles, calculates scores by counting four-letter groups rather than importing the producer, and checks every decision within an absolute numerical tolerance of 10⁻¹². Both computations passed; human review remains pending. The saved JSON includes excerpts, hashes, seeds, individual scores and normalization diagnostics, so every plotted mark can be traced back to its input.

scope.representation: 55 rune-bearing LP2 pages as concatenated canonical GP Latin labels; headings included, punctuation omitted, key clock per Latin character, reset each page.
scope.procedure: Independently reproduce both source + operators. Exhaustively enumerate the F-preserving operator image at each of 11 key slots and test complete page outputs for forbidden letters. Invert only the ordinary operator and score complete outputs against known readings and 199 whole-selection page shuffles.
scope.parameters: Fixed AIRAUMFERAE key, phase zero; 55 pages × two source branches; 11×26 image enumeration; nine solved-reading controls; 199 whole-selection shuffles for the ordinary branch.
scope.exclusions: No inverse is asserted for F-preserving; no other phase, key, word reset, 29-rune operation, language, dynamic Playfair or hidden layer.

records.finding: The F-preserving operator is noninvertible and has one forbidden output at each nonzero key slot. Fifty-three of 55 pages violate that exact rule; LP2-03 and LP2-55 pass only this necessary test. The ordinary fixed-key inverse peaks at English score −7.894, below the −5.5 control threshold; 152 of 199 complete-search page shuffles scored at least as high. Nine known-reading and nine planted ordinary-key controls passed.
records.limitations: The source code takes uppercase A–Z input and did not specify an LP2 transcription or publish a manuscript sweep. The result assumes canonical GP Latin labels joined per page, phase zero, and a key clock per Latin character. Image membership is only necessary; it does not decrypt the two compatible pages. Other phases, alphabets, resets, languages and related keys remain untested.
records.article:
# Fixed-key Vigenère with a preserved F

**Result.** Under a page-local, 26-letter GP transliteration, the source's F-preserving encoder cannot produce **53 of 55** rune-bearing LP2 pages: each contains at least one letter that this operator can never output at its key position. LP2-03 and LP2-55 pass this necessary condition; that alone supplies no reading. The ordinary, invertible Vigenère branch produced **no English-like whole-page output** with the source's fixed key.

![At one key position F and X both become F, while N cannot appear; 53 of 55 pages violate the resulting output rule.](experiments/records/eternalth-f-preserving-vigenere/summary.svg)

The pinned [C++ draft](https://github.com/Eternalth/Liber-Primus/blob/a662136a916435767a74e6198f0549d5878b1d0a/VigenereFenglish.cpp) prints two versions with the eleven-letter key `AIRAUMFERAE`: ordinary A–Z Vigenère addition, and the same addition while leaving input `F` unchanged. Its key counter advances on every character, including `F`. We compiled the original and checked both outputs against an independent formula on [three synthetic inputs](experiments/records/eternalth-f-preserving-vigenere/source-parity.json). The source does not include a manuscript input or a recorded search result; the LP2 application here is a new bounded test.

## Why the F branch can be checked exactly

At the second key position the key letter is `I`, an offset of 8. The source maps input `F` to `F` because it preserves it. It also maps input `X` to `F` by addition. **No input maps to `N`** at that position: ordinary addition would require `F`, which the special rule does not shift. This makes the operator noninvertible. We enumerated all 26 inputs at every key position and checked that the same single forbidden output exists wherever the key offset is nonzero.

For the complete LP2 pages, concatenate the canonical Latin labels of the runes, including headings. Punctuation and spaces do not advance the key. Start the key at its first letter on each page. The resulting strings contain **291 forbidden-position letters** across 53 pages; LP2-00, for example, first violates the rule at zero-based Latin character 12. LP2-03 and LP2-55 contain none. A different transliteration, key phase, reset rule, or rune-level version is outside this result.

## Ordinary branch

The ordinary branch has a unique inverse: subtract the fixed key from the page's Latin letters. The best complete-page English quadgram score was **−7.894** on LP2-34, below the predeclared **−5.5** control threshold. None of the 55 pages crossed it. When the same complete-page search was repeated on 199 seeded pagewise rune shuffles, **152** shuffled searches scored at least as high as the actual best page. The shuffle comparison is a selection control, not a model of the cipher.

Nine archived 66-rune readings passed the English-score gate, and nine ordinary-key plants decoded exactly. Source-generated F-branch outputs passed the exhaustive forbidden-letter check; deliberately inserting a forbidden letter failed. The F branch has no general inverse, so we did not present subtraction with a preserved F as a source decryption algorithm.

The [plan](experiments/records/eternalth-f-preserving-vigenere/plan.json) fixes the page list, representation, key, controls and shuffle rules. [Results](experiments/records/eternalth-f-preserving-vigenere/results.json) give each page's forbidden-letter count and complete ordinary output. Run `python experiments/records/eternalth-f-preserving-vigenere/run.py --check`, then `python experiments/records/eternalth-f-preserving-vigenere/check.py` for an independent enumeration and full null check. The source repository has no license file, so its C++ file is linked and pinned rather than bundled.
records.reader_finding: This exact F-preserving rule cannot produce 53 of the 55 tested page strings. The two compatible pages remain undecoded. With the same key, no ordinary Vigenère output passed the English-score check.
records.reader_limit: This assumes the stated Latin conversion and a key restarted from its first letter on each page. Other key phases and rules were not tested.

records.title: Delete F runes, then test lag-13 repeats
records.question: Does deleting every F reveal excess exact two-rune repetition at lag 13?
records.summary: After deleting all F runes, 18 exact lag-13 two-rune repeats occur; 104 of 499 page-preserving shuffles have at least 18.

record_type.label: Manuscript measurement
record_type.description: Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule.

scope.representation: Archived LP2-00–55 rune-only page streams; 29 GP indices, F=0.
scope.procedure: Remove every F separately on each page; count exact two-rune matches at lag 13 and scan lags 2–28. Compare both with 499 matched within-page shuffles.
scope.parameters: 458 F runes deleted; 12,498 retained; 499 shuffles, seed 13003301; lags 2–28.
scope.exclusions: Alternative F behavior, selective F skips, key consumption, doublet collision rules, I/M resets and actual plaintext decoding.

records.finding: After deleting every F, the lag-13 exact two-rune count is 18 over 11,728 opportunities; 104/499 shuffles match or exceed it. The best of 27 lags is lag 5 and 109/499 shuffled searches match or exceed that best ratio.
records.limitations: The source did not prescribe complete F deletion or an exact two-rune motif. This is one new bounded interpretation, not a replay of the reported cipher attempt. Page shuffles are not a cipher model.
records.article:
## Finding

Deleting every F rune does **not** reveal an unusual lag-13 two-rune repeat under this fixed test. The archived LP2-00–55 stream has **17** exact matching two-rune blocks at lag 13. After deleting all **458 F runes** within their pages and joining the retained neighbors, the count is **18**. In **499** page-preserving shuffle trials, the middle 95% of counts is **8–22**, and **104** trials reach at least 18.

![Lag-13 exact two-rune matches before and after removing F, with the shuffled reference.](experiments/records/f-delete-lag13/comparison.svg)

The displayed counts have different numbers of opportunities: **12,186** before F deletion and **11,728** afterward. The fixed lag-13 result is therefore best read beside its own shuffled reference, not as a one-count improvement by itself.

## Full lag search

The program also repeats the same exact-block test at every lag from **2 through 28**. It divides each observed count by that lag's mean under shuffled pages, then compares the largest ratio with the largest ratio from every shuffled trial. The observed best is **lag 5**, with a ratio of **1.707**; **109 of 499** shuffled searches do at least as well. Lag 13 was proposed in the discussion, but the broader scan guards against quietly choosing another attractive lag afterward.

## Rule and limit

This test interprets an “F skip” as deleting **every** F (GP index 0) from the rune-only stream, independently on each page. It does not say that the source participant used this deletion rule. Their account did not specify whether F is copied, removed, or consumes a key slot. Nor does this test model collision-driven skips, I/M resynchronization or a key stream. It tests only whether this one removal operation exposes exact two-rune repeats at the proposed lag.

Run `python experiments/records/f-delete-lag13/run.py --check` from the repository root. The [saved report](experiments/records/f-delete-lag13/results.json) retains per-lag counts, reference means, input hashes and the seed so the comparison can be reproduced.
records.reader_limit: Tests one F-deletion interpretation and one exact motif; it does not test the complete proposed stream cipher.

records.title: Direct GP readings of gaps between F runes
records.question: Can every consecutive F gap on LP2-00–55 map literally to one GP index or prime value without reduction or omissions?
records.summary: Pins all 458 F positions and tests four literal gap-to-GP interpretations under both joined-page and within-page boundaries.

record_type.label: Bounded solving test
record_type.description: Applies a fixed decoding, extraction or payload-retrieval rule to declared unsolved material, or excludes a specific direct-generation rule. Its result covers only those bounds.

scope.representation: The 29-GP-rune transcription of LP2-00–55, with all F positions stored as page-local and concatenated rune ordinals; non-rune separators omitted, headings retained.
scope.procedure: Take each consecutive F pair globally or within a page, compute position distance or intervening-rune count, and map the literal integer to a zero-based GP rune index or exact GP prime; preserve each unmapped value at its original position.
scope.parameters: 458 F runes; 457 joined-page gaps or 403 within-page gaps; two distance conventions × two literal value maps × two boundary policies = eight cases. A complete reading requires all gaps to map.
scope.exclusions: No modulo 29, skipping, subset selection, F presence bits, absolute-position encoding, variable-length packing, post-hoc fragment selection, keys or plaintext scoring.

records.finding: None of eight boundary/reading cases produces a complete direct symbol stream. Among 403 within-page gaps, 273 and 281 map to GP indices under distance and intervening-count rules; 157 and 140 map to exact GP prime values. All unmapped gaps and their source F positions are retained, and synthetic known-gap controls pass.
records.limitations: This is a new, narrow operationalization of a broad F-location idea, not a replay of a historical decoding claim. It excludes absolute positions, binary presence, modulo reduction, chosen subsequences, variable-length numbers and keys. Incomplete literal mappings do not rule out every F-location channel.
records.article:
# Can the gaps between F runes be read directly?

The suggestion that F/Fehu *locations* carry a separate message has several possible meanings. This test fixes one narrow one: **take every gap between consecutive F runes and read its number directly as a Gematria Primus rune index or prime value.** It does not skip awkward gaps or reduce them modulo 29.

**None of the four literal readings produces a complete symbol stream.** LP2-00–55 has **458 F runes**, making **457** consecutive gaps when pages are joined or **403** when each page starts afresh. Every direct mapping leaves values outside its 29-symbol alphabet.

![Four natural direct readings of the 403 within-page F gaps each leave unmapped values; an additional encoding rule would be needed.](experiments/records/f-interrupter-gap-direct-read/gaps.svg)

| Gap number and symbol map | Within-page gaps mapped | Joined-page gaps mapped |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Position distance → zero-based index 0–28 | 273 / 403 | 287 / 457 |
| Position distance → exact GP prime | 157 / 403 | 172 / 457 |
| Runes *between* Fs → zero-based index 0–28 | 281 / 403 | 296 / 457 |
| Runes *between* Fs → exact GP prime | 140 / 403 | 150 / 457 |

“Position distance” subtracts the two F rune positions. “Runes between” is that distance minus one. For example, the second and third Fs in the joined stream are **41** positions apart. That cannot be a zero-based GP index, which must be 0–28. The largest observed position distance is **218**. All gaps, including cross-page gaps in the joined version, remain in the [full result](experiments/records/f-interrupter-gap-direct-read/results.json) with both source F ordinals and page labels. Unmapped values remain explicit `null` entries in the ordered symbol vectors; no attractive fragment is selected from the mapped subset.

This result says that those **four direct conventions** need an extra coding rule to make a complete reading. It does not reject an F-location message in general. Positions rather than gaps, F/non-F bits, variable-length numbers, deliberate nulls or a key could encode something else. The [59-Fehu coordinate replay](#/experiments/fehu-coordinate-triad) tests a different rule that deliberately reduces selected offsets modulo 29; its result cannot be counted as a direct-gap reading. The [F-deletion lag test](#/experiments/f-delete-lag13) asks about rune repeats after deletion, also a different question.

## How the count was made

The test keeps exactly the 29 GP runes from each LP2-00–55 transcription, including headings, and drops punctuation and spaces. It stores the page-local and joined-stream position of every F. A joined stream includes 54 gaps crossing page boundaries; the within-page version omits those gaps. A number maps only when it literally equals a zero-based index from 0 to 28 or one of the 29 GP prime values. No modulo, wrap, skipped value or chosen page subset is used.

Two synthetic streams place Fs at known positions so their distances map to the first GP prime symbols and to known GP index symbols. An out-of-range control stays unmapped. The independent checker rebuilds all 458 positions from per-page JSON text, compares its rune streams with the archived text files, and verifies every gap and mapped/unmapped position.

From the repository root:

```text
python experiments/records/f-interrupter-gap-direct-read/run.py --check
python experiments/records/f-interrupter-gap-direct-read/check.py
```

The [plan](experiments/records/f-interrupter-gap-direct-read/plan.json), [results](experiments/records/f-interrupter-gap-direct-read/results.json) and [checker](experiments/records/f-interrupter-gap-direct-read/check.py) pin the exact scope. This is a newly defined bounded reading of a broad idea, not a replay of a historical decoding attempt.

records.title: Feedback ciphers with fixed starting values
records.question: Do scalar-primed feedback rules recover a known 12-rune opening at an unsolved LP2 page start?
records.summary: Neither feedback rule recovers a known opening across 1,856 fixed configurations on 55 pages. Different openings and other starting sequences remain untested.

record_type.label: Bounded solving test
record_type.description: Applies a fixed decoding, extraction or payload-retrieval rule to declared unsolved material, or excludes a specific direct-generation rule. Its result covers only those bounds.

scope.representation: Canonical GP indices from 12,956 runes on the 55 nonempty pages of LP2-00–55. Hyphen/period delimit words; slash/newline do not.
scope.procedure: Subtract feedback modulo 29; before the chosen lag use a repeated scalar primer, then an earlier ciphertext or plaintext value. Test continuous-page and per-word initialization. Compare each output's first twelve runes with nine fixed known-reading openings.
scope.parameters: 2 feedback sources × 16 lags × 29 scalar primers × 2 boundary rules = 1,856 configurations; 55 pages and nine opening cribs = 918,720 exact comparisons.
scope.exclusions: Unknown openings, later crib positions, arbitrary primer vectors, added key layers, symbol skipping, other arithmetic signs and other alphabets.

records.finding: No tested configuration recovers any of the nine exact 12-rune openings. The longest matching prefix is three runes. All 1,856 synthetic recovery controls and the independent full-census checker pass.
records.limitations: This is an exact-crib census rather than a language or cipher-identification test. A correct plaintext with another opening would fail this acceptance rule. The proposed feedback rules are solver hypotheses, not established instructions from the manuscript.
records.article:
# Feedback ciphers with fixed starting values

**None of these rules recovered any of nine known 12-rune openings at the beginning of an unsolved LP2 page.** We checked 1,856 configurations, each applied to 55 pages, for 918,720 exact comparisons. These are variations of two feedback rules, not 1,856 separate historical proposals.

The question is narrow: could these feedback rules reproduce an opening already seen in a documented reading? A different plaintext opening could still be correct. A failed crib match therefore closes this particular comparison, not the feedback-cipher family.

## The rules

Each decoded rune is its ciphertext index minus a feedback value, modulo 29. Before enough runes have been read, that value is the selected scalar primer. After the chosen lag, the feedback value comes from either an earlier ciphertext rune or an earlier decoded rune.

| Choice | Tested values |
| --- | --- |
| Feedback source | Earlier ciphertext or earlier plaintext |
| Lag | 1 through 16 runes |
| Primer | Each index 0 through 28, repeated during initialization |
| Word boundaries | Continue through the page, or restart after every hyphen and period |
| Target | Each nonempty page on LP2-00–55, starting fresh at every page |
| Acceptance | Exact equality with one of nine fixed 12-rune known-reading openings |

Slashes and line breaks are layout marks in this parser. All 12,956 archived runes are retained; number-only LP2-50 supplies no rune stream. The nine openings are pinned to their original reproduction CSVs in the [manifest](experiments/suites/feedback-opening-census/manifest.json).

The longest matching prefix is **three runes**, attained by four configurations. No English-language score or statistical significance is assigned to those fragments. The [complete result file](experiments/suites/feedback-opening-census/cases.json) lists every tested rule and a digest of its full decoded output.

## How the batch is checked

The producer encrypts a synthetic plaintext and recovers it under every configuration. A separate checker reads the structured page records, implements the recurrence independently and recomputes all case digests, opening comparisons and prefix ties. It also compares the relevant one-step results with the earlier [LP2-54 header experiment](#/experiments/lp2-54-header-feedback).

This batch does not test arbitrary primer vectors, another alphabet, adding rather than subtracting feedback, skipped symbols, unknown plaintext openings, a key layer, or cribs at later positions. Those choices belong in another explicit manifest or engine version.

## Reproduce

```text
python experiments/records/feedback-opening-census/run.py --check
python experiments/suites/feedback-opening-census/check.py
```

The scripts use Python's standard library and run without a network connection. The declared rules and pinned input files are included in the experiment ZIP.
records.reader_limit: Unknown openings, arbitrary primer vectors, another alphabet, extra key layers and matches later in a page are outside this batch.

records.title: LP2: replaying the 59-Fehu coordinate triad
records.question: Does the reported LP2-only Fehu-coordinate construction reproduce its three numerical targets, and is its ordered match unique among starts under that fixed rule?
records.summary: The three reported coordinate streams and GP sums reproduce exactly at F182. It is the only exact ordered match among 350 eligible starts under the frozen rule; selection-aware significance and decryption remain untested.

record_type.label: Method replay
record_type.description: Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading.

scope.representation: Concatenated LP2-only runes in page order, punctuation excluded; numbered F positions and zero-based rune offsets; GP alphabet indices and prime values from the archived index.
scope.procedure: Reconstruct the three overlapping 59-Fehu windows at 29-Fehu start increments, apply the source's X/Y coordinate and origin choices, compare full coordinate streams and prime sums, and enumerate all eligible starts.
scope.parameters: Grid width 29; windows 59 Fehus; X, Y, X axis order; origins first, first, third window; targets 3001, 2819, 2579; exact ordered equality; 350 starts.
scope.exclusions: LP1, alternate windows or axes, target permutations, message-segment adjustments, other origins, near misses, chance probability across the exploratory search, and a cipher key or plaintext.

records.finding: The exact reported construction is verified: 13,136 LP2 runes contain 466 F runes; F182 begins at zero-based rune index 4,949; sums are 3001, 2819 and 2579; F182 is the only exact ordered hit among 350 eligible fixed-rule starts. No decryption follows.
records.limitations: The discussion selected or refined the window length, grid, axes, origins and adjusted message targets while exploring. The 1-of-350 conditional match is not an unconditional p-value; the full search history and private source attachments are unavailable for audit. Human review pending.
records.article:
# A 59-Fehu coordinate triad in LP2

**Finding.** A reported construction is arithmetically reproducible on Liber Primus part two (LP2). Of 350 eligible starting Fehu runes, one start—**F182**—produces the ordered sums **3001, 2819, 2579** under the source's fixed three-window rule. All 177 coordinate labels in the three supplied streams also agree with the archived rune data. This is a numerical match, not a decryption or a probability that Cicada intended the construction.

The proposal treats every F/Fehu rune as a position marker. First concatenate LP2-00 through LP2-57 in page order, keeping the 29 manuscript runes and dropping punctuation. Number the resulting Fehus F1, F2, and so on. This produces 13,136 runes and 466 Fehus. The count is **LP2-only**: adding LP1 changes every later Fehu number. F182 occurs at zero-based rune index 4,949 in this stream.

For each chosen Fehu, subtract an origin Fehu's rune index. Put that distance on a grid 29 columns wide: its remainder after division by 29 is X, and the quotient modulo 29 is Y. Read X or Y as a zero-based Gematria Primus rune index and add the corresponding prime values. For example, F182 has offset zero from itself, so its X value is 0, the F rune worth 2. F183 is 60 runes later: `60 mod 29 = 2`, the TH rune worth 5. The source writes V for the rune indexed 1; this archive labels it U. The indices and prime values are the same.

| Window | Coordinate and origin | Recomputed GP sum | Reported target |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| F182–F240 | X, origin F182 | 3001 | 3001 |
| F211–F269 | Y, origin F182 | 2819 | 2819 |
| F240–F298 | X, origin F240 | 2579 | 2579 |

The starts are 29 Fehus apart. The middle window crosses the shared F240 seam; the last window resets its origin there. These details matter. Using F240 as the middle origin or keeping F182 as the last origin asks a different question. The archived [plan](experiments/records/fehu-coordinate-triad/plan.json) fixes all three choices before the replay. The [results](experiments/records/fehu-coordinate-triad/results.json) retain the three sums at every eligible start, not just the match.

![Three stacked line plots show the coordinate-prime sums across all 350 eligible starts. Dashed horizontal lines mark the three reported targets and a vertical line marks F182.](experiments/records/fehu-coordinate-triad/coordinate-scan.svg)

Only F182 yields all three exact targets in order among the 350 complete start positions **under this one rule**. That does not make the chance of the reported finding 1 in 350. The source describes an exploratory sequence: a 59-Fehu window, a 29-column grid, X and Y choices, target message segments with F included or removed, and an origin reset were selected or refined while looking at the data. The number of tried alternatives is unknown. Many such choices can create a unique exact hit, especially when large prime sums are used as targets. We have not run a selection-aware maximum over that wider search family or checked a predicted key or plaintext on untouched LP2 material.

The three target numbers are presented in the supplied discussion as adjusted sums from a 2016 message. This record reproduces the **LP2-side coordinate arithmetic** and checks the source's supplied coordinate streams; it does not independently establish that those message adjustments were specified in advance. The reported 2017 value 2131 has no placement in this triad. Nor does a match explain how coordinate values would decode neighboring runes.

## Reproduce the bounded check

Python 3.12 and its standard library suffice, offline:

```text
python experiments/records/fehu-coordinate-triad/run.py --check
python experiments/records/fehu-coordinate-triad/check.py
python experiments/records/fehu-coordinate-triad/plot.py --check
```

The producer verifies the three full label streams from the supplied discussion and enumerates all 350 starts. The separate checker recounts Fehus from each stored page line, recalculates every start with a different loop, and checks the one exact ordered match. The plan and report identify the local source extract by SHA-256; the private discussion transcript is not a retrievable public citation. See the [F-interrupter guide](#/wiki/interruptions), [prime-sum guide](#/wiki/prime-sums), and [search-space guide](#/wiki/search-space) before treating a numerically precise fit as a cipher rule.

records.title: Reading every nth rune
records.question: Does any fixed step from 2 to 29, with any starting phase and either page-local or joined position counting, produce English-like LP2 text?
records.summary: A complete 868-setting fixed-step search found no output that stood out against matched full searches on shuffled pages.

record_type.label: Bounded solving test
record_type.description: Applies a fixed decoding, extraction or payload-retrieval rule to declared unsolved material, or excludes a specific direct-generation rule. Its result covers only those bounds.

scope.representation: All 12,956 canonical GP runes from the 55 rune-bearing LP2-00–55 pages; punctuation and artwork excluded.
scope.procedure: For p=2..29 and every residue phase, select forward rune positions under page-reset or joined-book clocks. Pool within-page quadgram sums for reset cases, score joined cases as one stream. Compare the largest of 868 English scores to 256 maxima from shared within-page-shuffle full-grid searches. Plant the known GP readings into each selected stream as a sensitivity control.
scope.parameters: 868 settings (2 clocks × sum of p for p=2..29); all have ≥360 Latin quadgrams against a frozen 100-quad eligibility gate. Shared null seeds 33017121–33017376. Source-backed bound p≤29 uses GP alphabet size, without treating it as a detected period.
scope.exclusions: Periods greater than 29, backward selection, adjustable page order, inferred or interrupted clocks, number-derived keys, further cipher layers, non-English texts and claims that this grid represents every historical attempt.

records.finding: The best setting was step 24, zero-based phase 2 with page resets: score −7.151 over 563 selected runes. In 182 of 256 shared page-shuffle full searches, the best setting scored at least as high (global add-one 183/257≈0.712).
records.limitations: Only forward steps 2–29, both stated page clocks and direct English scoring are covered. A cipher layer, other language, reversed order, alternate period range or rule chosen from page artwork remains untested. The catalog is an idea list, not evidence of a particular historical search.
records.article:
# Reading every nth rune

**Question.** Does taking every *n*th rune, at some starting phase, reveal English when the counter restarts on each page or runs across the book?

**Result.** No tested setting stands out. The best score came from **step 24, phase 2, restarting on each page**: take zero-based positions 2, 26, 50 and so on, which are the third, twenty-seventh and fifty-first runes. Its 563 selected runes scored **−7.151** under the fixed English model. In **182 of 256** shuffled-page controls, the *best* of the same 868-setting search scored at least as well (global add-one estimate **183/257 ≈ 0.712**). The output is not a reading; it begins `EBNGHITHJTHLDU|MBHEASSTHGEAAX|UPNEOINWAEN…`, where bars mark page boundaries.

![The best observed every-n score sits within the range of complete shuffled searches and below their median.](experiments/records/fixed-step-position-extraction/full-search-scores.svg)

## What was searched

We used the **12,956** archived GP runes on LP2-00–55, excluding the empty LP2-50. For each step **2 through 29**, we tested every phase from **0 through step − 1**. Twenty-nine is a declared upper bound from the size of the GP alphabet, not evidence of a cipher period. Each phase was tried with two clocks: reset to position zero at every page, or continue through all pages joined in numerical order. That makes **868 settings** of one method family. Punctuation and layout never advance the counter.

We converted each selected rune to its canonical GP Latin label and scored English four-letter groups. With the page-reset clock, each page's selected text was scored separately and those score sums pooled; no four-letter group crossed a page boundary. All **868** settings supplied at least **360** within-segment four-letter groups and cleared the preregistered 100-group minimum. A valid reading in another language or under a second cipher layer would not necessarily score well here.

To judge a whole phase search fairly, each control trial shuffled the rune order **within every complete page once** and reused those same 55 shuffled pages for all 868 settings. This preserves each page's rune frequencies while disrupting position-specific text. The comparison is between the **best observed setting** and the **best setting in each trial**, not between an attractive observed phase and an average random phase. The median control maximum was **−7.122**, slightly above the observed −7.151. As a sensitivity check, all **868** synthetic controls with known GP reading indices planted at the selected positions recovered those indices exactly and cleared the frozen English-recognition threshold; their lowest score was **−4.509**.

The test covers forward fixed steps 2–29 with these two page clocks and direct English scoring. It does not test periods beyond 29, reversed streams, transposition after selection, number-derived keys, other languages, or arbitrary rules chosen after viewing the output. The source idea list suggested every-*n* extraction but did not specify a historical search to replay.

## Inspect and reproduce

[`streams.tsv`](experiments/records/fixed-step-position-extraction/streams.tsv) contains **all 868 exact extracted streams** as runes and Latin labels, with `|` showing page boundaries. [`results.json`](experiments/records/fixed-step-position-extraction/results.json) contains every observed score and all 256 complete-control maxima. From the repository root, run `python experiments/records/fixed-step-position-extraction/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/fixed-step-position-extraction/check.py`; both require NumPy and Numba. The second script independently reads the page JSON, rebuilds every stream, and recomputes all observed scores and 256 full searches with a different quadgram implementation.

records.title: Four alternating rune streams: concentration check
records.question: Do the four position-modulo-four streams in the unsolved LP2 rune sequence retain unusually high rune concentration?
records.summary: Each of the four manuscript phases has an ordinary collision rate under page-preserving shuffles. A planted four-stream substitution example is clearly detected.

record_type.label: Manuscript measurement
record_type.description: Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule.

family.title: Alternating-stream checks
family.question: Does splitting positions into fixed alternating streams expose a specified signal?

variant.label: Four global phases; monogram collision concentration

scope.representation: The 29 GP runes on LP2-00–55 except the number-only LP2-50, concatenated in image-page order. Four phases use global position modulo four, with no reset at a page break.
scope.procedure: Measure the mean and maximum of the four phase IoCs. Shuffle rune order independently within each page 1999 times, rerunning the split and both measures. Plant a four-stream shifted-copy control from the solved LP1 warning page.
scope.parameters: 55 rune-bearing pages; 12956 runes; random.Random(330122), 1999 page-shuffle trials; upper plus-one tails; Bonferroni for two measures.
scope.exclusions: The source's full 185-operation decoder sweep, other phase assignments, feedback ciphers, separate polyalphabetic keys and plaintext recovery.

records.finding: The observed phase-mean IoC is 0.034511, exceeded by 361 of 1999 page-shuffled controls (upper-tail p=0.181). The largest phase IoC is 0.034564, exceeded by 945 controls (p=0.473). The two-measure-adjusted minimum is 0.362. A planted four-stream control has mean IoC 0.064029, reached by none of 1999 whole-stream shuffles.
records.limitations: This is a narrow new test, not an independent replay of the source's 185 variants. IoC only tests phase-wise symbol concentration. The original source's rune-bearing segment numbering omits number-only LP2-50, so its phrase pages 0–54 corresponds to actual pages 0–55 except 50. Its public model-building dependencies are incomplete.
records.article:
## Finding

**Splitting the unsolved rune stream into four alternating streams does not expose the concentration expected from four simple substitution alphabets.** The four measured collision rates lie within the middle 95% of page-preserving shuffled comparisons. A planted four-stream example is detected by the same measure. This says nothing decisive about four separate running keys, feedback ciphers or a different way to assign runes to streams.

![Successive rune positions assigned to four phases, followed by each phase's observed collision rate and the shuffled reference interval.](experiments/records/four-phase-ioc/phase-comparison.svg)

Take every fourth rune, starting with positions zero, one, two and three. For each resulting stream, the index of coincidence (IoC) is the chance that two different positions contain the same rune. A fixed substitution or a fixed additive shift changes rune labels but preserves that concentration. An independent keyed stream that continually changes its substitution need not preserve it. [How IoC works](#/wiki/index-of-coincidence).

| Check | Manuscript | Page-shuffle comparison |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Mean IoC across four phases | 0.034511 | 0.034416–0.034551 middle 95%; 361 of 1,999 shuffles at least as high |
| Highest phase IoC | 0.034564 | 0.034460–0.034697 middle 95%; 945 of 1,999 shuffles at least as high |

The two upper-tail estimates are **0.181** and **0.473**. Neither is unusual; correcting for checking both measures gives a smallest adjusted estimate of **0.362**. Each comparison shuffles rune order *within each page*, keeping its length and rune counts. It then repeats the four-way split from the start of the concatenated book. Thus the test asks whether the original order adds a four-phase concentration signal beyond the fixed page histograms.

## What was actually tested

The source is the [published “literal imperatives” sweep](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round22/C-literal-imperatives/RESULTS.md), which includes decimation and four-way interleaving among 185 operations. **This is an independent, narrower test, not a replay of its decoder verdict.** Its public checkout omits the generated nine-register language model and at least one corpus needed to rebuild it, so a fresh clone cannot currently rerun that entire scorer. The present record uses only the archived runes and a fully specified statistical comparison.

The source's phrase “LP2 pages 0–54” hides a numbering detail. Its loader drops an all-number page before numbering rune-bearing segments. Its 12,956-rune stream matches the actual images **LP2-00 through LP2-55, excluding number-only LP2-50**. We use those actual page labels: 55 rune-bearing pages, with the phase count continuing across page breaks. [Manuscript reader](#/reader).

As a power check, we Atbash-decoded the 184-rune [LP1 warning page](#/reader/lp1-01), made four copies shifted by 0, 3, 7 and 11 rune places, and interleaved them. Their mean phase IoC was **0.0640**. None of 1,999 whole-stream shuffles reached it. This confirms that the measure can see a strong four-stream substitution signal; it is not a control for every plausible cipher.

## Repeat the check

Download [this experiment](downloads/experiments/four-phase-ioc.zip) for the script, fixed plan, input text, results and figure. From the repository root run:

```text
python experiments/records/four-phase-ioc/run.py --check
python experiments/records/four-phase-ioc/check.py
```

The [plan](experiments/records/four-phase-ioc/plan.json) fixes the page mapping, two measures, shuffling rule and 1,999 trials. The [results](experiments/records/four-phase-ioc/results.json) retain the observed scores and tail counts. An [independent arithmetic check](experiments/records/four-phase-ioc/check.json) repeats the mean-IoC comparison with another random seed. The result is conditional on this particular four-phase concentration model; it does not close the broader hint or the source's other operations.
records.reader_limit: A fixed positional split and a monogram statistic are narrower than the cited 185-operation sweep.

records.title: GP prime values as a plaintext autokey
records.question: Do page-local plaintext-rune GP prime values, used one step back or as a running sum, yield unusually English-like complete LP2 pages?
records.summary: Neither of two fixed plaintext-prime feedback rules stood out in a whole-page LP2 search: 144 of 199 matched shuffled searches scored at least as high as the best observed candidate.

record_type.label: Bounded solving test
record_type.description: Applies a fixed decoding, extraction or payload-retrieval rule to declared unsolved material, or excludes a specific direct-generation rule. Its result covers only those bounds.

scope.representation: 12,956 GP29 rune indices across the 55 nonempty LP2-00–55 pages, ignoring punctuation and artwork; prime values from the canonical 29-rune alphabet.
scope.procedure: Decode every whole page by either previous-plaintext-prime feedback or cumulative plaintext-prime-sum feedback; rank complete GP-to-Latin outputs under the pinned English quadgram model. Repeat the entire selection on 199 independently seeded within-page-shuffled corpora.
scope.parameters: 2 equations × 29 scalar seeds × 2 arithmetic signs × 55 pages = 6,380 observed candidates; 199 complete-grid shuffles, seeds 33017200–33017398. Page-local starts, one key advance per rune.
scope.exclusions: Previous ciphertext-prime feedback (separate source W5), word-level prime sums, skips, word or line resets, cross-page state, additional key layers, other alphabets/languages, parable-specific reductions beyond the exhaustive seed residues and any unspecified iterative 'shedding' operation.

records.finding: Across 6,380 complete-page candidates, the best score was −6.835 on LP2-32. In 144 of 199 page-shuffled full-grid controls, at least one candidate scored as high. All 116 arithmetic inversions and 12 full-length model-selection plants passed.
records.limitations: These two equations were defined for this bounded test, not supplied by the original proposal. The test does not define or test 'shedding,' word resets, skipped runes, across-page state, other languages or arbitrary gematria recurrences. A shuffled corpus is a conditional control, not a cipher model.
records.article:
## Finding

We tested two precise ways for a newly recovered rune's [Gematria Primus prime value](#/alphabet) to set the next key. Neither stood out in a complete-page search. The best of **6,380** LP2 candidates was on LP2-32, but **144 of 199** matched shuffled-page searches found an English score at least as high. The leading output begins `NGDIAIATTHEWABAETEEAHT...`; this isolated fragment is not a reading.

![Two prime-valued feedback rules and their full-search comparison.](experiments/records/gp-prime-plaintext-feedback/feedback-overview.svg)

The same search recovered all **12 planted full-length messages** made from the archived Warning reading. An independent checker reproduced all 6,380 decoded outputs and scores, checked every shuffled input, and reran three complete null grids. These controls show the bounded test works; they do not prove that every possible autokey would be found.

## The two rules

Let `C[i]` be a ciphertext rune index, `P[i]` its decoded index, and `g(x)` the GP prime value at index `x`, reduced modulo 29. We tried every initial value `s = 0…28` and both signs `e = −1,+1`:

| Rule | Decoding |
| --- | --- |
| Previous plaintext rune | `P[0] = C[0] − e·s`; then `P[i] = C[i] − e·g(P[i−1])` |
| Running plaintext prime sum | Start `S[0] = s`; then `P[i] = C[i] − e·S[i]` and `S[i+1] = S[i] + g(P[i])` |

All arithmetic is modulo 29. Each complete LP2 page starts afresh. Punctuation does not advance the key. We did not delete text, skip runes, reset at words, carry state across pages, or iterate whole-text passes. Those would be different rules; the proposal's imagery of “shedding” does not define one of them.

We defined these two rules to explore numerical autokey. The original proposal did not specify either equation. Each parable number has the same effect as one of the 29 starting values already tested; this test gives none of them a special role. Other records cover [index-valued feedback](#/experiments/feedback-opening-census), [known readings used as a fixed key](#/experiments/solved-reading-running-key), and [partial feedback-table fits](#/experiments/crib-inferred-feedback-table). The [word-boundary replay](#/experiments/dukotah-word-boundary-key-clocks) tests previous-ciphertext prime values and word-level sums. Those are different update rules.

## What the comparison means

We scored the full decoded page for four-letter English patterns, after writing each rune in its standard Latin form. The exact score is average quadgram log likelihood. Each of 199 controls shuffles rune order independently within every page, then repeats **the whole search** over both rules, signs, seeds and pages. This is a conditional check of whether the selected best score is unusual given page lengths and rune counts; a shuffle is not a cipher model. The observed best score was **−6.835**; the shuffled-search median was **−6.760** (larger scores are better). Results and every candidate are available in [results.json](experiments/records/gp-prime-plaintext-feedback/results.json) and [cases.csv](experiments/records/gp-prime-plaintext-feedback/cases.csv).

The test uses the site's 55 nonempty LP2-00–55 transcriptions and one pinned English score model. Another alphabet mapping, language, primer construction, key layer, or stopping rule remains outside this record. No candidate here establishes an LP2 reading or an encryption mechanism.

## Reproduce

The [frozen plan](experiments/records/gp-prime-plaintext-feedback/plan.json) records the equations, inputs, seed range, score and shuffled-control schedule. From the repository root, run `python experiments/records/gp-prime-plaintext-feedback/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/gp-prime-plaintext-feedback/check.py`. The first uses NumPy and Numba; the independent checker uses only the Python standard library. The saved outputs are also in the experiment ZIP.
