The 29-offset comparison was motivated by the observed source result. The source scales the target chi-square for display in a way that does not preserve its null reference.
records.article:
# Can a simple cipher imitate LP2's rare repeated runes?

A [published comparison](https://github.com/Leo-Y-Zhang/LiberPrimusAnalysis/blob/a32bdc0e06ea58532fbaf4329acae4a0b1020513/fingerprint.py) encrypts the same 2,979 runes of known Liber Primus text in 23 specified ways, then compares each output with the still-unread LP2 text. The measurements are repeated adjacent runes, overall rune balance, and matches two positions apart. We reproduced **all 23 rows** of its archived table from pinned inputs.

## Finding

![LP2's adjacent-repeat rate is 0.664%; the source's chain simulation is 0.672%. The match comes from the frequency of one plaintext rune.](experiments/records/leo-cipher-model-fingerprints/repeat-rate.svg)

LP2 has **86 identical adjacent pairs in 12,955 opportunities** (0.664%). One source simulation, `cipher = previous cipher + plaintext + 1` modulo 29, has **20 in 2,978** (0.672%). Its overall rune balance is also near uniform. These are real matches to the selected summaries, but they **do not identify LP2's encryption**.

The repeat-rate match has a simple explanation. Under that chain rule, a new cipher rune equals the previous one exactly when the plaintext rune is **EA**, index 28. EA occurs **20 times** after the first position in the chosen known reading. We verified that identity both algebraically and by generating and reversing the stream. The observation is therefore determined by this plaintext sample's rune frequency; the chain has not predicted a readable LP2 passage.

As an explicitly **post-observation** check, we held the same chain rule and plaintext fixed while trying all 29 additive constants. The source's `+1` is the closest of the 29 to LP2's observed repeat rate. That rank describes this particular chosen sample and one statistic; it is not a probability that the source cipher is correct. The [complete model and offset table](experiments/records/leo-cipher-model-fingerprints/results.json) preserves every value.

## What the comparison covers

The 23 rows include fixed-period keys, prime and Fibonacci streams, plaintext and ciphertext feedback, two running-key examples, affine substitution, random output, and several F-pass-through variants. The source generated **one** instance of each random-key model on the same 2,979-rune known reading. It compared those with 12,956 unread runes. This is a useful fingerprint demonstration, not a search over every key, every plaintext or every boundary rule.

One displayed source number needs care: it multiplies LP2's uniformity χ² by `2,979 / 12,956`, turning the actual **26.36** into **6.06** for its table. A chi-square statistic does not retain its original reference distribution after that scaling. We reproduce the printed value to audit the source, but do not use it to rank cipher models. The source's final “running key English with F-interrupts” row passes F unchanged while continuing to index the key by absolute position; it does not pause the key clock.

## Reproduce

Use [Leo's pinned source](https://github.com/Leo-Y-Zhang/LiberPrimusAnalysis/tree/a32bdc0e06ea58532fbaf4329acae4a0b1020513) with its separately pinned [relikd input](https://github.com/relikd/LiberPrayground/tree/719380ebee0523ad7f2fbf389c6f960d51bea5a4) installed as that source expects. The scripts check the source, dataset, archived receipt and baseline file hashes. From the Liberpedia repository root, substitute the Leo checkout path for `LEO`:

```text
python experiments/records/leo-cipher-model-fingerprints/run.py --source-root LEO --check
python experiments/records/leo-cipher-model-fingerprints/check.py --source-root LEO
python experiments/records/leo-cipher-model-fingerprints/plot.py --check
```

The runner reconstructs the 23 outputs independently of the source implementation and compares all displayed rows with the saved receipt. The checker freshly runs the source script, compares its 23 rows again, tests the chain inverse, and independently verifies all 29 repeat-count identities. This record does not copy the source code or its third-party input texts.

records.title: Do LP2 sections share a running key?
records.question: Does the source difference-IoC cross-section scan reveal an alignment that survives a complete-search control?
records.summary: A planted shared key is detectable, but the strongest distinct LP2 section alignment is near the shuffled-search median. The saved source score disagrees with the pinned current formula at a tested alignment.

record_type.label: Manuscript measurement
record_type.description: Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule.

scope.representation: Nine pinned relikd LP2 unsolved section rune streams; 12,956 runes total.
scope.procedure: Replay the source synthetic shared-key power example; scan all 45 unordered section pairs over shifts with at least 300 rune overlap, then 99 seeded full-search section-order shuffles. A clearly post-observation follow-up restricts to 36 distinct-section pairs and 99 separate full-search controls.
scope.parameters: GP29, 1,200-rune synthetic overlap, 300 source-style null draws, 99 all-pair shuffles and 99 distinct-pair follow-up shuffles.
scope.exclusions: Other transcriptions, key models, alternate boundaries or shifts, reverse transforms and full decryption.

records.finding: The top distinct-section score is 6.0117 (pages 3–7 versus 33–39, shift 25, overlap 1120); 53 of 99 shuffled whole searches match or exceed it. The all-pair maximum 11.319 is a self-pair at lag one, not cross-section evidence. The source printout gives z=3.3 for another tested alignment, while pinned current code gives z=5.68; an older SD approximation is numerically consistent with 3.3, but the historical formula used is unverified.

records.article:
# Do LP2 sections share a running key?

If two rune streams use the **same additive key at the same position**, subtracting their ciphertexts cancels that key. A [published source test](https://github.com/Leo-Y-Zhang/LiberPrimusAnalysis/blob/a32bdc0e06ea58532fbaf4329acae4a0b1020513/tests5.py) measured whether the resulting differences look more structured than chance across nine LP2 sections and many relative shifts. This record replays that calculation and checks its strongest alignments.

## Finding

![A cross-section peak of 6.01 sits almost on the shuffled-search median of 6.03; 53 of 99 shuffled complete searches reach at least the observed score.](experiments/records/leo-shared-key-differences/cross-section-control.svg)

The strongest alignment **between different sections** is pages 3–7 against pages 33–39, shifted by 25 runes with 1,120 runes overlapping. Its normalized difference score is **6.01**. After seeing that result, we ran a separate whole-search control: shuffle rune order within each of the nine sections, then search all 36 distinct section pairs and every eligible shift again. **53 of 99** shuffled searches reached at least 6.01; their median maximum was **6.03**. This is an exploratory, post-observation comparison, not a discovery probability fixed in advance. The observed cross-section peak does not stand out under this control.

The source also included each section paired with itself. Under the pinned current code, the largest all-pair score is **11.32**, from adjacent runes within pages 40–53. It is a local difference-pattern measurement, not evidence that two sections share a key. None of 99 whole-section-shuffle searches reached this self-pair score, which confirms the local ordering signal but does not identify its cause. The manuscript's uneven difference distribution and word structure are plausible contributors; this test does not separate them.

## Why the archived numbers differ

The source's saved [result printout](https://github.com/Leo-Y-Zhang/LiberPrimusAnalysis/blob/a32bdc0e06ea58532fbaf4329acae4a0b1020513/results/tests5.txt) lists pages 15–22 against pages 33–39 as its top pair at shift 1,598, overlap 305, score **3.3**. That *same* alignment has score **5.68** under the standard-deviation formula in the pinned `lp.py`. Applying an approximation of `0.75 / √n` to its unchanged difference count gives **3.25**, which rounds to the archived 3.3. This shows a numerical inconsistency between the saved printout and the pinned current formula. The approximation is one possible explanation; we have not established which code version or formula produced the printout.

The source's synthetic example is a useful positive control. Two known rune texts encrypted with one shared key have difference IoC **1.047**; 300 source-style unaligned comparisons average **1.000**. Kappa also rises from a null mean of **0.0367** to **0.0592**. The statistic can detect this planted relationship at that length. It does not imply the LP2 sections have it.

## Method and limits

The [frozen plan](experiments/records/leo-shared-key-differences/plan.json) names the nine exact section files, the 1,200-rune synthetic example, all 45 unordered pair scans (including nine self-pairs), every shift with at least 300 runes overlapping, and 99 full-search shuffles. The [post-observation plan](experiments/records/leo-shared-key-differences/followup-plan.json) explicitly filters to 36 different-section pairs. Results and every selected alignment are [saved](experiments/records/leo-shared-key-differences/results.json); the [follow-up results](experiments/records/leo-shared-key-differences/followup-results.json) preserve all 99 control maxima. An [independent check](experiments/records/leo-shared-key-differences/check.py) recomputes each reported winning window directly and verifies both source receipts.

Shuffling entire sections breaks real short-range rune structure, so the control answers a conditional question about this scoring/search procedure. It does not test every possible key reset, transposition, cipher layer or alignment. A high difference score alone is not a decryption.

## Reproduce

The source text is a separately pinned [relikd transcription](https://github.com/relikd/LiberPrayground/tree/719380ebee0523ad7f2fbf389c6f960d51bea5a4); the scripts verify every input SHA-256. With that checkout at `REL` and the pinned Leo source checkout at `LEO`, run from the repository root:

```text
python experiments/records/leo-shared-key-differences/run.py --source-root REL --check
python experiments/records/leo-shared-key-differences/followup.py --source-root REL --check
python experiments/records/leo-shared-key-differences/check.py --source-root REL --source-test-root LEO
python experiments/records/leo-shared-key-differences/plot.py --check
```

The full search uses NumPy and Numba; the independent window checker uses Python's standard library. The source license allows reading and checking, but this record does not copy its implementation.

# Does a periodic signal survive transformations of LP2?

**Finding.** A previously reported peak reproduces: in the pinned LP2 pages 27–32 transcription, taking each rune minus the rune two places earlier gives a normalized coincidence score of **1.412** at period **238**. That is the highest score in this source profile. It is an observation about this transform and transcription, not a recovered key.

![The source peak, shuffle controls and planted positive control](periodic-profile.svg)

The harder question is whether the scoring rule reliably points to a periodic source. We scanned the source's five representations—original runes, neighboring differences, neighboring sums, two-step differences and nonzero neighboring ratios—over every eligible period through 300. In 499 shuffles of the same page group's runes, one shuffle reached or exceeded the real-data peak when we took the best result across all five representations and periods. The resulting **conditional** tail fraction is 2/500. Allowing for selection among the nine page groups gives a simple bound of 18/500. Neither calculation covers the separate concatenated-page scan, other statistics or earlier choices that led to this analysis.

Our frozen positive control makes the practical limit clear. We planted a strong 13-rune cycle, replacing 10% of its symbols at random. Its ordinary coincidence score at period 13 was **23.464**. The source's within-profile ranking selected period **143 = 11 × 13**, so the literal planned criterion of finding 13 or a multiple **passed**. Yet its maximum standardized score fell below **452 of the 499** shuffle maxima. This score alone would not distinguish that known periodic source from its shuffle controls. The real period-238 peak should not be treated as evidence that the manuscript has a 238-rune encryption cycle.

## What was measured

We used the nine unsolved text sections and alphabet from the pinned [relikd transcription](https://github.com/relikd/LiberPrayground/tree/719380ebee0523ad7f2fbf389c6f960d51bea5a4). The operator and unweighted average over residue-column coincidence scores follow [Leo's test](https://github.com/Leo-Y-Zhang/LiberPrimusAnalysis/blob/a32bdc0e06ea58532fbaf4329acae4a0b1020513/tests3.py). The complete profile also records repeated four-rune spacing, visible word-edge counts and a separate all-section concatenation. Those additional scans are descriptive; the shuffle fraction above is conditional on the pages 27–32 scan only.

At period 238, a 1,431-symbol two-step-difference stream leaves only six or seven symbols per residue column. That makes an unusually high average sensitive to small-column coincidences. The source reports this peak as about 1.412 and z 6.0; the independent replay gives 1.412285 and z 5.950736 before rounding.

## Reproduce

Obtain the pinned relikd checkout. From the repository root, substitute its path for `PATH`:

```text
python experiments/records/leo-transform-periodic-profile/run.py --source-root PATH --check
python experiments/records/leo-transform-periodic-profile/check.py --source-root PATH
```

The first command recomputes the nine section profiles and all 499 shuffles from the source bytes. The second independently checks the source hashes, the full pages 27–32 period profile, visible word edges and control arithmetic without importing the producer. Exact source text is linked rather than redistributed here. Neither command tests a decryption or rules out periodic ciphers.

# Do short LP2 words resemble shifted dictionary words?

## Finding

The [published word-pattern test](https://github.com/Leo-Y-Zhang/LiberPrimusAnalysis/blob/a32bdc0e06ea58532fbaf4329acae4a0b1020513/tests2.py) reproduces from its pinned inputs. A Caesar-shifted dictionary word has the same sequence of differences between neighboring runes. Among LP2 words of four through eight runes, Caesar-pattern matches are **165/511, 12/317, 0/256, 0/216 and 0/156**. The 2,000 random rune words sampled at each length yield **627, 45, 4, 0 and 0** matches. Longer LP2 words give no Caesar-pattern hits in this dictionary; short words alone are weak evidence because the dictionary covers many possible patterns.

Allowing any invertible affine multiplier raises the LP2 matches to **511, 166, 13, 1 and 0**. The matched random-word rates are very similar, especially for lengths four through six. The solved-page plaintext check has Caesar matches in **322 of 325** words at these lengths, confirming that the dictionary can recognize most known reading words under the same segmentation. These observations do not identify a cipher or rule out other vocabularies and word-boundary choices.

![Affine dictionary-pattern match rates for LP2 words and uniform-random rune words, grouped by word length. They are similar at each length.](experiments/records/leo-word-pattern-dictionary/word-patterns.svg)

## What was compared

We used the nine unsolved-section rune transcriptions and `dictionary_all-rune.txt` from [relikd/LiberPrayground at commit `719380e`](https://github.com/relikd/LiberPrayground/tree/719380ebee0523ad7f2fbf389c6f960d51bea5a4). Word separators follow that source; line wraps are ignored. The [plan](experiments/records/leo-word-pattern-dictionary/plan.json) pins SHA-256 hashes for all 18 section files and the 10.3 MB dictionary. The script checks those hashes before counting. It also repeats the original test's single seeded stream of 2,000 independent uniform-random words per length.

The source calls one column “reversed.” Its code reverses the **difference tuple**. Literal reversal of a word also changes the sign of each difference: `Δ(reverse(word)) = −reverse(Δ(word)) (mod 29)`. We retain the source's values for an exact replay and report literal reversed-word values separately in [results.json](experiments/records/leo-word-pattern-dictionary/results.json). This correction affects that column's interpretation, not the Caesar or affine findings.

## Reproduce

Fetch the pinned relikd revision above, then run `python experiments/records/leo-word-pattern-dictionary/run.py --source-root PATH --check` and `python experiments/records/leo-word-pattern-dictionary/check.py --source-root PATH`. `PATH` is its checkout directory, containing `pages/` and `data/dictionary_all-rune.txt`. The input files are linked and hash-checked but not redistributed here. The separate checker rebuilds the complete LP2 Caesar and affine counts using first-rune anchored offsets, checks source fingerprints and verifies the reversal identity. The seeded random and solved-text controls are recomputed by `run.py`; the checker compares their published counts. `plot.py` regenerates the figure from `results.json`.

records.question: Do fixed rune positions or line boundaries reveal deliberate ciphertext forcing beyond the effects of physical line layout?
records.summary: One of 21 position and boundary checks flags line initials against a flat shuffle. Reflowing shuffled text by fitted glyph widths makes that apparent anomaly ordinary; six bounded English reading families and the other checks find no supported message.

scope.procedure: Replay source C-02 Arm A (10 positional histograms), Arm B (six English-scored keyless reading families with within-family best-of-search nulls), Arm C (five position-conditioned repeat/difference checks), the post-hoc width-fit/reflow confound and planted forcing power curve. Independently parse physical lines, verify position and doublet tables, fit widths and reflow with a separate seeded simulation.

records.finding: Independent parsing confirms 12,956 runes on 594 physical lines. The line-initial chi-square is 78.656 against a flat-null mean near 27, but a layout-aware reflow gives p=0.177 in the pinned source and p=0.195 in an independently seeded replay. The other nine position tests and five rejection tests do not clear their gate. Six English-reading families remain below their own best-of-family null maxima; planted controls are recovered. The six message families score English under a bounded keyless transform set. Boundary-rejection tests have little power with only four line-crossing doublets. Source message-family nulls were repeated with independent per-family seed states, so sampled extrema differ from the archived serial receipt.
records.article:
## Finding

**One of 21 pre-registered checks flagged the first rune on each physical line. The apparent signal disappears when line wrapping is included in the comparison.** The other nine position checks, six keyless reading families, and five rejection-pattern checks did not meet their declared gates in the pinned source run. Our replay independently reconstructed the 55-page input and all observed position counts, and reran the source's position, rejection, layout, and planted-message controls. The source's six-family message replay is included as a separate result file.

The conspicuous line-start result is real: its rune-frequency statistic is **78.66**, above every one of 200,000 draws from *fixed positions* in the manuscript. But line starts are not random positions. Wide rune glyphs are more likely to be pushed over a line's right margin. When shuffled text is broken into new lines using fitted glyph widths, the mean statistic rises from about **27 to 66**. The observed 78.66 falls within that distribution: **p = 0.177** in the source's 5,000 reflows, and **p = 0.195** in our separately seeded 2,000 reflows. This shows that the frequency excess alone does not establish a deliberate first-rune signal; the reflow model is an approximation, so it does not prove how the original pages were typeset.

![A flat comparison makes line initials look extraordinary; reflowing the shuffled text places the observed value near the ordinary range.](experiments/records/line-initial-layout-control/layout-control.svg)

## What the source tested

The pinned transcription contains **12,956 runes** on **594 physical lines** across **55 nonempty LP2 pages**. We recovered those counts, plus **2,928 hyphen-delimited words**, **219 sentence units**, **86 adjacent identical-rune pairs**, and **four pairs crossing a line**. The source's original plan had two preliminary split-count errors; the published runner corrected them before testing, without changing its gate. Each of its 21 pre-registered checks used a threshold of **0.001 ÷ 21**.

| Check | What it asks | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Ten positions | Are the first, last, second, or penultimate runes of lines, and the edges of words, pages, and sentence units, unusually distributed? | Only **line initials** clear the fixed-position gate. All other nine are negative. |
| Six reading families | Do line initials, per-page acrostics, diagonals, every-Nth-line initials, page edges, or word edges form an English-like message after a bounded set of rune transformations? | All six are negative against a separate *best-of-family* null. Short per-page readings look tempting by raw score but fare worse than the same search on random draws. |
| Five rejection checks | Does the low adjacent-repeat rate change at line or word positions, or does the nonzero difference channel carry a boundary signal? | None clears the gate. The line-boundary test has only **four repeats among 539 transitions**, so its negative result has little power against subtle suppression. |

The reading families enumerate **56,376 candidate transformations** in total. That is a count of variants within six tests, not 56,376 independent ideas. Each family compares its best score with the best score obtained by running the *same search* on size-matched random manuscript draws. The source's two planted English line-initial messages, plain and Caesar-shifted, were both recovered. This checks that its English scorer can recognize a sufficiently strong message in the tested format. It does not test other languages or more complex decoding rules.

For throughput, some message-family nulls were rerun separately from a fresh seed state. Their observed searches are identical to the pinned receipt; their sampled null extrema are independent repeats, not byte-for-byte copies of the source's serial RNG stream. The result file records the actual number of null replicates for each family.

## Why the line-start check changed

The source fitted relative widths for 29 runes and two separators from **539 nonfinal lines**, then used those widths to greedily reflow shuffled rune streams. Our independent fit also produces shorter variation in estimated line widths than treating every rune as equal width (**0.0828 vs 0.1063** coefficient of variation). A width-weighted expectation reduces the observed line-start departure from **78.66 to 38.73**. The source reflow and our independently seeded reflow give compatible results.

One archived precision claim needs correction: the source calls **53.5%** an “exact line-length” fit. Its code counts an existing line if its tokens fit the width budget, without checking whether the following token would also fit. A stricter resynchronised comparison matches **42.9%** of line lengths exactly; **82.5%** are within one token. That is adequate to demonstrate the flat-null confound, but it is not a reconstruction of the original typesetter. The source reports a **0.879** correlation with a BabelStone rune font; that external font file was absent from the pinned checkout and is **not independently verified here**.

## What a negative can and cannot rule out

The source planted a fixed English phrase into synthetic, layout-aware streams in two ways: always write the chosen rune, or let an anti-repeat rule override a collision. With 200 trials per setting, the corrected line-start statistic detected **all** trials when at least **60%** of line initials were forced under either mechanism. At 40%, it detected **59.5%** and **46.0%**, respectively; at 20%, neither setting registered. At zero forcing, the flat statistic falsely fired in **49%** of trials, while the layout-corrected statistic fired in **0 of 200**. These are conditional powers for these two synthetic mechanisms and this phrase, not a bound on every possible hidden message.

![The corrected detector sees both planted mechanisms consistently once sixty percent of line initials are forced, but has little sensitivity below forty percent.](experiments/records/line-initial-layout-control/power-curve.svg)

The tested rejection signature is especially weak at line breaks. A scheme that *prevents* additional boundary doublets can remain invisible with only four observed boundary events. The six reading searches are English-quadgram checks over identity or Atbash, 29 shifts, forward or reversed order, and keeping or dropping the F interrupter. They leave column readings, ornament-defined sets, different languages, and other transformations open.

## Reproduce and inspect

From the repository root, run the independent measurement and checker with Python 3 and NumPy:

```text
python experiments/records/line-initial-layout-control/run.py
python experiments/records/line-initial-layout-control/check.py
python experiments/records/line-initial-layout-control/plot.py
```

The bundled [results](experiments/records/line-initial-layout-control/results.json) give our line-start, line-final, width-fit, planted-control, and reflow measurements. The `replay-armA.json`, `replay-armB.json`, `replay-armC.json`, `replay-layout.json`, and `replay-power.json` files retain each full source-arm replay; the corresponding original scripts, pre-registration, and pinned result receipts are in `source/`. The independent checker builds the ten position sets from a second parser and verifies the observed counts and rejection tables before comparing source receipts. To rerun all 21 source checks, use the commands in the bundled `source/RESULTS.md` at the pinned revision. Its message-family nulls are computationally expensive; inspect the included results and replicate counts first.

records.article:
## Finding

Three similar-looking feedback rules make different predictions. For **additive** feedback, `c[i] = p[i] + c[i−1]`, a ciphertext doublet requires `p[i] = 0`. For **Beaufort-style** feedback, `c[i] = c[i−1] − p[i]`, the same is true. Their literal inverse outputs are negatives of each other modulo 29, so they identify **exactly the same 86 zero positions** in LP2-00–55. Doublet placement alone cannot distinguish these two rules.

For the **subtractive** variant, `c[i] = p[i] − c[i−1]`, the inverse is `p[i] = c[i] + c[i−1]`. Its zero condition is a pair summing to zero, not a repeated pair. The archived stream yields **437 zero outputs** under that literal inverse, rather than 86.

![Zero-output counts for additive, Beaufort and subtractive feedback.](experiments/records/linear-ciphertext-feedback/zero-outputs.svg)

These are structural statements about precisely written recurrences. Neither 86 nor 437 tells us that the corresponding inverse is readable plaintext. A key term, symbol remapping, zero skip, or interrupted clock would change the model. The [literal multiplication check](#/experiments/multiplicative-ciphertext-autokey) addresses another feedback rule with a stronger, absorbing-zero contradiction.

## Reproduce

Python 3.12 standard library, from the repository root:

```text
python experiments/records/linear-ciphertext-feedback/run.py --check
python experiments/records/linear-ciphertext-feedback/check.py
```

The first command rebuilds the [29-bin output frequencies](experiments/records/linear-ciphertext-feedback/results.json), page-by-page zero counts and figure. The second independently recounts the three zero conditions from each transcription and checks the modular identity.

records.article:
## What was tested

Can one fixed rule `(a × p + b) mod m` rearrange all 29 Gematria Primus prime values into a different ordering of the same values? Here p is the literal prime, not a rune index. Every output must belong to the same prime alphabet, and distinct inputs must give distinct outputs.

For **every integer modulus m greater than 109**, the only resulting permutation is the identity: each prime stays itself. This is a fresh reconstruction of the supplied research archive’s C07 claim, not a new discovery or a rerun of its original certificate. No manuscript page or proposed plaintext is used.

## Results

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Distinct images of inputs 2 and 3 | 29 × 28 = 812 choices |
| Exact integer permutations without modular wrapping | One: a=1, b=0 |
| Remaining anchor choices | 811 |
| Candidate maps requiring modular checks | 13,212 |
| Nonidentity full-alphabet permutations | None |

This does not exclude shifts modulo 29 on **rune indices**, prime-derived running keys, or position-dependent transformations. It is specifically about a single affine map of the full literal-prime alphabet.

## Why the infinite range is finite to check

Let u be the output of 2 and v the output of 3. Subtract their congruences:

```text
2a + b ≡ u (mod m)
3a + b ≡ v (mod m)
a ≡ v − u (mod m)
b ≡ 3u − 2v (mod m)
```

No modular division is needed. Composite moduli and coefficients that are not invertible modulo m are included. For each u,v define the unreduced integer expression `L(p)=u+(p−2)(v−u)`.

If L sends every prime into the palette as ordinary integers, its nonzero slope makes it injective. Exhaustive anchor checking finds only L(p)=p in this branch. Otherwise choose a palette input p whose integer image L(p) is outside the palette. To obtain an allowed modular output y, **m must divide the nonzero integer L(p)−y**. Enumerating those divisors for all 29 possible targets gives every candidate modulus for that anchor pair.

The identity works for every m>109 because all primes are canonical residues. Every other branch has a nonzero divisibility witness, so it is finite. There is no unsearched large-modulus tail. The report lists every anchor, witness and candidate modulus.

## A worked branch

Suppose 2 maps to 3 and 3 maps to 5. Then L(p)=2p−1, so L(5)=9 is outside the palette. For any allowed output y from 2 through 109, the nonzero difference 9−y has absolute value at most 100. No modulus above 109 can divide it. This anchor pair therefore has no candidates.

Other pairs have larger differences and require checks. The program applies the reduction to every pair; this example alone is not the proof of the complete result.

## Where the conclusion stops

| Relaxed assumption | Counterexample | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drop injectivity | a=0, b=2, m=110 maps every prime to 2 | Output membership alone does not force identity |
| Use a partial palette | a=109, b=5, m=110 swaps 2 and 3 | The subset {2,3} has a nonidentity permutation |

The subset example is not a result about any actual manuscript page. A page using fewer than all 29 symbols requires its own support-specific test. Neither counterexample recovers plaintext.

## Reproduce

Extract the experiment bundle with its folders intact:

```text
python experiments/records/literal-prime-affine/run.py --check
python experiments/records/literal-prime-affine/check.py
```

Both commands use Python’s standard library and make no network or AI requests. The first reconstructs the full report. The second does not import the producer: it checks candidate completeness by scanning each witness’s bounded modulus range directly, then enumerates all coefficient pairs for moduli 110 through 125. Those sixteen controls check the implementation; coverage above them comes from the divisibility argument, not extrapolation. The checker also verifies the two counterexamples.

Both checks passed on 20 October 2026. The question, planned procedure and controls are in `plan.txt`. No search bounds, scoring rules or exceptions were changed after seeing the result. Source alphabet, scripts and output hashes are included in the record. Computational review is complete within this scope; human review is pending. No Lean or other proof-assistant build is claimed.

See [rune indices and prime values](#/wiki/rune-values), [prime indices](#/wiki/prime-indices), [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants), and [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) before applying this result to another proposal.

The [completed page-support variant](#/experiments/literal-prime-affine-pages) checks the actual archived LP2 supports. It retains two additional LP2-55 maps, illustrating this distinction with manuscript data.

records.article:
## What changes from the baseline?

The [baseline](#/experiments/literal-prime-affine) requires one affine map to permute the entire 29-prime alphabet. This variant uses the prime values actually present on each archived LP2-00–55 page. Outputs may be any of the 29 allowed primes, but distinct observed inputs must still have distinct outputs. A page may use its own fixed coefficients and modulus.

The modulus range remains **every integer m greater than 109**. We do not score English or select a proposed reading. The supplied archive’s C08 claim predicted two LP2-55 exceptions; the fresh calculation retained all survivors rather than filtering for that prediction.

## Results

| Archived page support | Pages | Candidate maps checked per distinct support | Nonidentity maps |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| All 29 prime values | 53 pages | 13,212 | None |
| 28 values, missing 7 | LP2-49 | 14,901 | None |
| 25 values, missing 7, 29, 59, 103 | LP2-55 | 14,901 | Two |
| No rune values | LP2-50 | Not tested | No conclusion |

Thus **54 of the 55 nonempty rune pages allow only identity** under this exact model. LP2-55 has two additional maps. LP2-50 contains the alphanumeric panel rather than a rune stream; this procedure does not interpret its characters as GP runes.

The counts refer to distinct input supports, not a separate rerun for each of the 53 identical full-support cases. There are 43,014 candidate-map checks across the three supports. The all-modulus identity branch is handled separately.

## The two LP2-55 exceptions

| Coefficients (a, b, m) | Image of prime 2 | Images of observed odd primes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (58, 57, 114) | 59: rune label T | Unchanged |
| (102, 101, 202) | 103: rune label Y | Unchanged |

Both have the form `a=m/2+1`, `b=m/2`. For an odd prime p,

```text
ap+b = p + (m/2)(p+1) ≡ p (mod m)
```

because p+1 is even. At p=2, the result is `2+m/2`: 59 for m=114 and 103 for m=202. Each map therefore changes only F to T or Y on this page. It does not decode the remaining runes or recover word boundaries.

Neither 59 nor 103 occurs in LP2-55’s observed input support. Sending 2 to either value therefore does not collide with another observed input. On the full alphabet, the odd input 59 or 103 is fixed too, so two inputs would have the same output. That is why these exceptions do not contradict the baseline.

The coefficients 58 and 102 are not units modulo 114 and 202 respectively: each gcd is 2. Requiring the affine map to be invertible on the entire residue ring would discard them. Our stated model requires injectivity only on the observed prime support, so they must be retained.

## Complete enumeration without a modulus cutoff

Every nonempty page support contains primes 2 and 3. Assign distinct allowed images u and v to them, giving 812 anchor choices per support. These determine `a=v−u` and `b=3u−2v` modulo m.

For each pair, examine the unreduced expression `L(p)=u+(p−2)(v−u)` on the page’s support. If every integer output is already allowed, record that branch separately. In this dataset the only such branch is identity. Otherwise choose the first supported prime whose L(p) is outside the full palette. Every valid modulus must divide one of the nonzero differences `L(p)−y`, where y is an allowed target prime.

The script tests every resulting divisor above 109, requiring both allowed outputs and no collisions on the observed support. The complete report retains each anchor’s witness and candidate list, the two surviving maps and their full outputs, and every page’s source hash. There is no arbitrary upper modulus bound.

## Reproduce

Extract this variant’s bundle with its folders intact:

```text
python experiments/records/literal-prime-affine-pages/run.py --check
python experiments/records/literal-prime-affine-pages/check.py
```

Python’s standard library is sufficient. The bundle includes the baseline’s divisor helper and all 56 archived page texts. No network or AI requests are made.

The independent checker does not import the producer or divisor helper. It reconstructs page support by counting each alphabet symbol, verifies page hashes, enumerates the possible moduli directly within each witness’s mathematical bound, and checks every survivor. It also verifies that both LP2-55 exceptions fix all its odd input primes and move 2 to a previously absent value.

Both commands passed on 20 October 2026. The method and controls were recorded in `plan.txt`; no input boundaries, candidate criteria or modulus bounds were changed after inspecting the result. Human review is pending. This is an elementary calculation with a checked certificate, not a proof-assistant build or a new decipherment.

## Limits

The result concerns the archived rune transcription and one fixed literal-prime affine map per page. It does not cover corrected symbol streams that change a page’s support, position-dependent transformations, noninjective maps, nonlinear rules, rune indices modulo 29, or prime-derived keystreams. A change in any of those assumptions requires a separate variant.

See [rune values](#/wiki/rune-values), [the full-alphabet baseline](#/experiments/literal-prime-affine), and [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) for the distinction between checking a model completely and claiming a general decryption.

records.article:
## What was tested

Suppose a rune is replaced by its Gematria Primus prime value: F becomes 2, U becomes 3, and so on through the 29-value alphabet ending at 109. Could one fixed quadratic formula rearrange that entire alphabet without producing any values outside it?

We tested `f(x) = ax² + bx + c (mod m)` for **every integer modulus m greater than 109**. A modulus sets the wraparound size: values that differ by a multiple of m count as the same output. We required the formula to send all 29 primes to **29 distinct primes from that same alphabet**. The result is identity only: under these assumptions, each prime must map back to itself.

This is a replication of the quadratic claim in the supplied research archive. The earlier scripts and reported result were inspected before the plan was written. It is not a new discovery or a blind test. A fresh enumerator and a separately implemented checker agree; human review remains pending.

This extends the [full-alphabet affine experiment](#/experiments/literal-prime-affine) by allowing an x² term. It does not rule out every arithmetic cipher. A changing key, a formula applied only to a page's observed runes, or an operation on rune **indices** rather than prime values asks a different question.

## Why an infinite range can be checked

Trying moduli up to a convenient maximum would leave every larger modulus unresolved. Instead, three chosen inputs restrict which moduli can work.

Call the prime alphabet S. The images of 2, 3 and 5 must be three different members of S; write them as u, v and w. There are `29 × 28 × 27 = 21,924` ordered choices. These three images determine the following integer expression:

```text
Q(x) = 2u(x−3)(x−5) − 3v(x−2)(x−5) + w(x−2)(x−3)
```

For any polynomial fitting those three images, `6f(x) ≡ Q(x) (mod m)`. The factor 6 matters: it cannot simply be cancelled when the modulus is divisible by 2 or 3.

For each choice of u, v and w, find the first alphabet value x for which Q(x) is not six times an alphabet value. If the final output is some y in S, then m must divide the **nonzero integer** `Q(x) − 6y`. A nonzero integer has only finitely many positive divisors. Taking the divisors for all 29 possible y therefore gives a complete finite list for this branch, including moduli larger than a guessed search cutoff.

The downloaded certificate records each branch's three images, the chosen witness x, its Q(x), and every candidate modulus. For each candidate the scripts recover all possible coefficients and check the entire output alphabet directly.

## The branch without a finite witness

Exactly one choice escapes that divisor reduction: `(u,v,w) = (2,3,5)`. In this branch Q(x) is exactly 6x as an integer, so a different argument is needed. All its possible maps have the form

```text
f(x) = x + a(x−2)(x−3) (mod m), with 6a ≡ 0 (mod m).
```

For every integer x, `(x−2)(x−3)` is either 0 or 2 modulo 6. The only possible changes from identity are therefore a shift by 2a; the input 7 already tests that shift. If it is nonzero, its circular distance from zero is m/3. But two members of this alphabet differ by at most `109−2 = 107`. A valid nonidentity map in this branch would consequently need `m ≤ 321`.

The checker directly scans the coefficient residues for all moduli 110 through 321. None gives a nonidentity permutation of the alphabet. The argument above handles every larger modulus; those larger moduli are not silently dropped.

## Results

| Finite branches | Candidate-modulus checks | Coefficient checks | Surviving maps |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Modulus coprime to 6 | 261,346 | 261,346 | 0 |
| Modulus divisible by 2 or 3 | 2,420,451 | 7,993,284 | 0 |

These counts are branch checks: a modulus can occur under several different choices of anchor images. They are not counts of distinct modulus values across the whole experiment.

The separate identity-anchor branch contains 318 coefficient expressions representing identity within the checked interval. **Different coefficients need not mean a different function.** For example, modulo 110,

```text
55x² + 56x = x + 55x(x+1) ≡ x.
```

The product x(x+1) is always even, so the extra term is divisible by 110. Reporting that quadratic coefficient as a nonidentity solution would be a mistake.

## Where the conclusion stops

The requirement to preserve the **whole** alphabet is essential. On only the three inputs `{2,3,5}`, the quadratic `22x² + 16x + 10 (mod 127)` swaps 2 and 3 and fixes 5. However, it sends 7 to 57, outside the prime alphabet. A smaller observed alphabet can therefore permit maps excluded by the full-alphabet test. See the [affine page-support variant](#/experiments/literal-prime-affine-pages) for a separate example of why page-level scope matters.

Injectivity is essential too: the constant function f(x)=2 always stays inside S, but destroys the distinctions between runes. Working with rune indices instead of their literal primes changes the domain. Higher-degree formulas, word-dependent operations, varying coefficients, and polynomial key sequences combined with unknown plaintext are also outside this experiment.

No candidate plaintext was scored. There was no selection of words that happened to look meaningful, and no claim about the language of the unsolved pages follows from this result.

## How to reproduce it

Use Python 3 with its standard library. No network service or model is needed. From the repository root, choose output filenames that do not already exist:

```sh
python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_quadratic_palette.py
python scripts/run_quadratic_palette.py --output quadratic-certificate.json
python scripts/check_quadratic_palette.py quadratic-certificate.json --receipt quadratic-audit.json
```

The first command compares both coefficient solvers against every coefficient triple for moduli 2 through 18, including cases where division by 6 is invalid. It also checks divisor generation and the scope counterexamples above.

The producer scans divisor pairs up to the square root and solves congruences using modular inverses after accounting for the greatest common divisor. The checker imports none of that code: it reconstructs divisors by prime factorization and obtains coefficient solutions by lifting a congruence to integer equations. It then checks every finite branch and the bounded identity branch against the saved certificate. The receipt identifies the certificate and checker by SHA-256.

Agreement between these implementations supports the computation. The all-modulus conclusion additionally depends on the reduction explained above. It has not been presented as a proof-assistant result or as completed human review.

records.article:
# What remains when the four LP1 message borders are removed?

The four signed messages hidden in **LP1-10–13** display the same seven-row ASCII number diagram with a changing outer digit. In page order, the border digits are **3, 3, 0, 1**. Remove the top and bottom rows and the first and last character from each remaining row: the interior is byte-identical in all four messages, without rotation or reflection.

![Four ASCII diagrams with their changing perimeter marked in orange and common interior in blue](experiments/records/lp1-payload-outer-ring/four-borders-one-interior.svg)

This checks a reported observation connected to the solved text's phrase about *shedding the circumference*. The source note says removing the outer number of each repeated square leaves an identical number grid. It does **not** supply an LP2 decryption rule or an output. The match is a property of the four embedded messages, not evidence that stripping a perimeter solves an unsolved manuscript page.

## The four source objects

Each page image has an extracted OutGuess payload containing a PGP-signed instruction. The repository retains the exact body text and page metadata recording successful signature verification. This audit rechecks the body hashes and that recorded verification status; it does not independently re-run GPG. The bodies instruct the reader to create a Tor hidden service and submit three magic squares. Their diagrams have the same spacing and numeric interior. LP1-10 and LP1-11's whole body files are byte-identical; LP1-12 and LP1-13 change the diagram's border digit.

| Embedded body | Border digit | Retained numeric rows |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| LP1-10 | 3 | `10 12 10` / `12 14 12` / `10 12 10` |
| LP1-11 | 3 | Same |
| LP1-12 | 0 | Same |
| LP1-13 | 1 | Same |

The [fixed plan](experiments/records/lp1-payload-outer-ring/plan.json) defines the operation before comparison. It requires exactly one diagram bounded by two 16-character rows of equal digits; removes only that one-character perimeter; retains spacing in the five interior rows; and parses the three numbered rows. The [complete result](experiments/records/lp1-payload-outer-ring/results.json) preserves every original and retained line, the source hashes, and the derived matrix.

The common matrix is:

```text
10  12  10
12  14  12
10  12  10
```

Its row sums are **32, 38, 32**. It is therefore not a magic square under the ordinary equal-row-sum definition. The border sequence happens to read `3301` in page order; the audit does not infer a further instruction from that fact.

## A distinct reading that fails

There are also two *visible* five-by-five LP1 squares: the mixed number-and-rune square on LP1-05, which needs Gematria Primus conversion, and the decimal square on LP1-16. If “remove the outer ring” is instead applied to those, their central three-by-three grids differ:

```text
LP1-05 converted       LP1-16 printed
199 130 320            812 934 280
245  91 245            620 809 620
320 130 199            280 934 812
```

None of the five-by-five core values occurs in the other core. Rotation or reflection cannot make them identical. These are not the repeated signed-message diagrams described in the source discussion. Keeping the objects separate matters: the same verbal instruction cannot be reported as verified on a different pair of squares.

## Reproduce the comparison

From the repository root, with Python 3 and no added packages:

```text
python experiments/records/lp1-payload-outer-ring/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp1-payload-outer-ring/check.py
python experiments/records/lp1-payload-outer-ring/plot.py --check
```

The run script extracts the diagrams from four hashed message bodies and converts the separate LP1-05 and LP1-16 page transcriptions for the exclusion check. The independent checker parses the ASCII blocks with a different pattern and compares all four exact lines and all nine core values against an explicit oracle. The result is an input and source-identity audit. It does not test whether a perimeter-removal operation helps decrypt LP2.

# Does preserving each section change the column-balance result?

The fixed 464-word arrangement remains unusually flat under a null that shuffles word lengths only within their original four sections. All original section slots and the continuous sixteen-column layout are preserved. This is a sensitivity variant of `lp1-word-length-balance`, not an independent discovery.

| Quantity | Unrestricted baseline | Within-section variant |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Observed integer score | 128256 | 128256 |
| Observed column-mean variance | 501/13456 | 501/13456 |
| Observed variance / model expectation | 0.25150357 | 0.25209625 |
| Null trials | 49,999 | 49,999 |
| Trials at or below observed, including ties | 54 | 88 |
| Plus-one lower-tail estimate | 0.0011 | 0.00178 |

The constrained expectation is calculated separately. Its exact expected integer score is `612019253902976/1202967183`, and expected column-mean variance is `4781400421117/32374252828896`. The unchanged observed variance divided by that expectation is `1205373117366/4781400421117`.

The four sections contain 45, 124, 208 and 87 words. Their boundaries do not reset the column position. The report preserves every section's slot counts in all sixteen columns, exact expected column sums and variances, and all 49,999 null scores. A singleton-section boundary and unequal section sizes are covered by small exhaustive controls.

## What changes between the two models?

The baseline permits any word length to move to any of the 464 slots. This variant permits a word length to move only to a slot in its original section. The lengths themselves, section order and observed arrangement remain unchanged. A section may occupy different numbers of slots in different columns, so keeping its slots matters as well as keeping its histogram.

The slot diagram shows those fixed memberships. Colors identify the four sections, not high or low word lengths. The same word may have several interchangeable positions within its color. A single section boundary can cut across a row; the next section continues at the next column.

The two histogram panels use identical integer-score bins, displayed on a common column-mean variance scale. The dashed line is the unchanged observed variance. Lower variance means more similar column means. Every one of the 49,999 null scores per model contributes to its panel; the complete bin counts are downloadable as CSV. The shared seed number does not pair individual trials because the procedures consume random choices differently.

## Why the expectation changes

Under unrestricted shuffling, every slot samples the same pool of lengths. Under within-section shuffling, each slot samples only its section's pool. The four pools have different means and variances. Columns also contain different section slot counts. Consequently, their expected sums need not be identical, even though every column still contains 29 words.

For section size N, population variance v and c slots in one column, its sum contributes variance `c*(N-c)*v/(N-1)`. Contributions from independently shuffled sections add. The expected squared distance from the fixed overall mean also includes the difference between each column's expected sum and the overall mean. The script uses exact fractions; the checker obtains the same expectation through pairwise position moments. The ratio in the table therefore uses each model's own expectation.

## Reproduce

Extract the experiment ZIP with folders intact, or use the repository. Python 3 standard library is sufficient. Run `python experiments/records/lp1-section-balance/run.py --check` to reproduce all constrained scores, run the independent checker and verify the figures. Use `--output section-replay` to retain new files in a new directory.

The individual stages can also be run from the root with new output paths:

```sh
python scripts/test_lp1_section_balance.py
python scripts/lp1_section_balance.py --output section-results.json
python scripts/check_lp1_section_balance.py section-results.json --receipt section-audit.json
```

The [protocol](experiments/plans/lp1-section-balance.md) was committed before constrained shuffles were generated. The producer uses the hashed word ledger and source dependencies. The checker independently scans the original archived text, verifies all 464 words, reconstructs every permutation with explicit index swaps, and calculates the expectation through position-pair second moments. It imports no producer code. Both implementations share Python's pseudorandom primitive.

## Interpretation and publication status

Both estimates are below the predeclared 0.05 threshold. Preserving section-level length distributions does not remove the low-variance result in this fixed test. The two tests share the same selected arrangement; their p-values must not be combined as independent evidence. The original exploration is not included in either null. Neither model preserves sentence syntax, and neither tests a grille, carrier text, authorial intent or a decryption.

Human review remains pending. Saved results and the independent receipt are preserved here without overwriting the original baseline. The figures and histogram CSV are generated from those saved reports; the baseline distribution is reused from its published record, not simulated as part of this variant.

## Related explanations

See [the unrestricted baseline](#/experiments/lp1-word-length-balance), [word-length conventions](#/wiki/word-lengths), and [null models and selection](#/wiki/null-models). The [section-order variant](#/experiments/lp1-section-order) now searches all 24 orders with matching selection in every control. Preserving sentences remains a separate, untested constraint.

# LP1 column balance after searching section orders

This variant belongs to the LP1 word-length and column-balance family. Human review remains pending.

## What was tested

The original 464-word sequence fills a table of 29 rows and 16 columns. Its column totals are unusually similar under the previously declared shuffle controls. This variant asks whether that comparison changes when a solver may rearrange the four intact sections and keep whichever arrangement has the most similar column totals.

The sections are Warning (45 words), Welcome (124), first koan (208), and second koan (87). Word order within each observed section remains unchanged. Every arrangement fills the table continuously, without resetting at section boundaries. The score is `Q = sum((16 * column_total - 1796)^2)`; lower scores mean more balanced columns.

The [protocol](experiments/plans/lp1-section-order.md) was committed before calculating the order search. It disclosed the already-known fixed-order results. Each of 49,999 controls shuffles lengths within the original sections, searches the same 24 orders, and retains its minimum. It would be unfair to search the observed data but compare that selected result with controls given only one arrangement.

## Results

No alternative order improves the original score, **128256**. Four orders tie for that minimum because they are cyclic rotations of the original arrangement.

| Representative order | Score Q |
| --- | ---: |
| Warning → Welcome → first koan → second koan | 128256 |
| Warning → Welcome → second koan → first koan | 295680 |
| Warning → first koan → Welcome → second koan | 257280 |
| Warning → first koan → second koan → Welcome | 407296 |
| Warning → second koan → Welcome → first koan | 215808 |
| Warning → second koan → first koan → Welcome | 337664 |

Each row represents four cyclic rotations with exactly the same score. Rotating the 464-word sequence shifts its sixteen column totals without changing their balance, since 464 is divisible by 16. Thus the 24 arrangements form six classes; this does **not** make the six scores independent.

**440 of 49,999 controls** have a selected minimum no greater than the observed minimum, ties included. The plus-one estimate is `(440 + 1) / 50000 = 0.00882`. The fixed-order within-section comparison was `0.00178`. The larger estimate reflects the extra opportunities given to every control, even though the observed minimum did not improve.

The result remains below the protocol's 0.05 threshold. It describes this precise word sequence, table width, score, shuffle model and section-order search. It does not estimate the probability of intentional design, provide a decryption, or correct for the wider exploration that originally selected the 464-word object and sixteen-column layout. The two estimates use the same shuffled sections and are not independent evidence.

## Verification and reproduction

The independent checker reconstructs the source tokens, generates permutations through explicit index swaps, and computes all 24 scores in every control using section-column accumulation. It does not import the producer. It checks **1,199,976 null order scores**, all observed orders, every minimum and tie list, and the full tail count. Every baseline-order control score also matches the earlier section-preserving report. Both implementations share Python's pseudorandom primitive.

The toy tests exhaust small section permutations with unequal section sizes and repeated values. A non-divisible example demonstrates why the cyclic reduction requires complete rows.

From the repository root, choose new output paths:

```sh
python scripts/test_lp1_section_order.py
python scripts/lp1_section_order.py --output order-replay.json
python scripts/check_lp1_section_order.py order-replay.json --receipt order-replay-audit.json
```

The producer checks the frozen input hashes. Compare the replay report's SHA-256 with `report_sha256` in the independent audit receipt. The downloadable result retains the full order mapping, observed scores, all six class scores for every trial, and all minimizing orders; none of the searched arrangements is omitted from that representation.

## Read the figures

The order diagram lists all 24 arrangements in six groups. Every arrangement in one group has the same Q; the bar represents that shared score. Letters label sections, not rune values. The histogram shows the minimum score retained from every complete 24-order search. Its vertical scale counts trials, and its dashed line is the observed minimum. All 49,999 trials are included; the bin counts are downloadable as CSV.

## Run the complete reproduction

Extract the experiment ZIP with folders intact. Run `python experiments/records/lp1-section-order/run.py --check` from its root. Python 3 standard library is sufficient; the run is offline. Use `--output order-replay` to retain results in a new directory. The wrapper repeats the simulation, independently checks every order score, and reproduces the figures and histogram.

See the [fixed-order section-preserving comparison](#/experiments/lp1-section-balance), [original baseline](#/experiments/lp1-word-length-balance), and [search-space explanation](#/wiki/search-space).

# LP1 seven-word GP-825 match

One proposed LP2 reading was compared with a seven-word stretch of the solved LP1 warning. This test checks the **LP1 side of that comparison**: how many seven-word stretches have exactly 21 runes and a Gematria Primus sum of 825?

## Result

Among **652** seven-word windows kept within their solved LP1 sections, **one** meets both conditions. It starts at zero-based word 9 of the warning: `YOU CNOW TO BE TRUE TEST THE`. The decoded-rune trace gives it 21 runes, GP sum 825 and zero-based rune-index sum 232. The source discussion reported 716 windows; that denominator does not reproduce with these seven sections and word boundaries. Even joining all 694 words across section breaks gives only 688 possible starts.

![One qualifying LP1 window among 652 section-internal windows](experiments/records/lp1-seven-word-825-census/windows.svg)

The result confirms an exact match in LP1 under the declared trace. It does **not** establish that the proposed LP2 phrase has the stated rune spelling or sum, that the two passages are linked, or that a decryption rule follows. The phrase and numeric criteria were selected during exploration, so `1/652` is a census of these LP1 windows, not a chance probability for the full search.

## Reproduce

Run `python experiments/records/lp1-seven-word-825-census/run.py --check` from the repository root. The [saved census](research/source-intake/lp1-seven-word-825-audit.json) includes all seven section counts and input hashes. Word separators come from the archived runes; decoded symbols come from the published reading traces. The [source note](research/source-intake/lp1-seven-word-825-audit.md) explains the one documented LP1-10 rune swap and the Latin-label spelling difference.

records.article:
## Does searching other widths change the balance result?

The original comparison arranged 464 word lengths in sixteen columns. This variant asks a different question: if we may choose among six widths, how unusual is the smallest normalized column imbalance we can obtain? Every shuffled control receives exactly the same choice.

The fixed rule selects **width 2**, with normalized imbalance R about **0.01694**. Of 49,999 shuffled controls, 6,035 obtain a minimum no greater. The plus-one lower-tail estimate is **0.12072**, above the declared 0.05 threshold. This test does not support an unusually small minimum-R under its unrestricted-shuffle model.

That conclusion needs a precise qualification: **this is not an adjustment of the smallest fixed-width p-value**. Width 32 has the smallest unadjusted tail in the table below; width 2 has the smallest R. Choosing between those criteria after seeing the results would change the experiment.

## What is fixed, and what changes?

Use the same Warning, Welcome, first koan and second koan as the [464-word baseline](#/experiments/lp1-word-length-balance). Keep their order, headings, interruption runes, word boundaries and internal apostrophes. Count native runes per word. The source population contains 464 words and 1,796 runes.

Try only widths **2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64**. Word i, counted from zero, goes in column i modulo the width. Do not rotate the start, reorder sections or pad the final row. Widths 32 and 64 leave unequal column sizes, so the statistic explicitly weights by the number of words in each column.

The width set follows the earlier power-of-two discussion, including 64. The original width-16 result and qualitative observations about other widths were known before this protocol. The protocol was committed before these new measurements; that does not erase the earlier exploration.

## Why divide by an expectation?

Let n be the number of words, T their total length, n_j the size of column j and S_j its length sum. Define weighted imbalance as Q = sum(S_j² / n_j) − T² / n. Lower Q means more similar column means. Let D = sum(x_i²) − T² / n, where x_i is each word length.

Under an unrestricted permutation of those fixed lengths, the expected Q for k columns is (k−1)D/(n−1). We use **R = Q / expected Q**. At width 16, this equals the baseline's normalized variance of column means. The derivation and exact arithmetic are preserved in the research README.

Dividing by the expectation makes the mean equal to one under each width's null distribution. It does **not** make those distributions have the same shape. An R of 0.02 at one width can be less unusual than an R of 0.3 at another. The declared selection rule nevertheless chooses the minimum R, and its control distribution must repeat precisely that rule.

## Every tested width

The fixed-width tails below include ties and use the plus-one correction. They are diagnostic, unadjusted comparisons—not independent evidence or six corrected tests.

| Width | Words per column | Observed R | Fixed-width tail / 49,999 | Unadjusted estimate |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2 | 232 | 0.01694 | 6,006 | 0.12014 |
| 4 | 116 | 0.14684 | 3,429 | 0.06860 |
| 8 | 58 | 0.34531 | 3,317 | 0.06636 |
| 16 | 29 | 0.25150 | 54 | 0.00110 |
| 32 | 14 or 15 | 0.31188 | 5 | 0.00012 |
| 64 | 7 or 8 | 0.73060 | 2,044 | 0.04090 |

The width-16 exact R and 54-control tail reproduce the original baseline. The same random seed and fresh-copy shuffle sequence are used, so this agreement is a reproduction check, not an independent replication.

## Matching the selection in every control

Generate 49,999 unrestricted permutations using Python's Random with seed 330146. For each one, calculate all six R values and retain the minimum, including every tying width. Compare those minima with the observed minimum using exact rational arithmetic. The result is (6,035 + 1)/(49,999 + 1) = **0.12072**.

The null figure includes all controls. Its bins are for display only; the tail count uses the exact values, not histogram bins. The saved report retains all 299,994 null width scores, their minima and ties.

This does not account for every width, every possible grouping of text, the original selection of the 464-word object, or choosing the statistic itself. It also does not preserve coherent sentences or each section's length distribution in the controls. The [within-section variant](#/experiments/lp1-section-balance) and [section-order variant](#/experiments/lp1-section-order) address different choices. No result here identifies a grille or the unsolved cipher.

## Reproduce and inspect

Download this experiment's ZIP and extract its folders. Python 3's standard library is sufficient; the bundle includes the source transcriptions and baseline dependencies. No network access, API or model is used.

```text
python experiments/records/lp1-width-selection/run.py --check
```

To retain a fresh replay instead of using a temporary directory:

```text
python experiments/records/lp1-width-selection/run.py --output my-width-replay
```

The producer reconstructs the baseline words and scores nested power-of-two columns with exact integer ratios. The independent checker imports neither the producer nor its word tokenizer: it scans the source characters, explicitly replays Fisher–Yates and calculates each Q from direct column slices with rational arithmetic. It checks all observed scores, all 299,994 null scores, minima, ties and tail counts. Both computations agree; human review remains pending.

records.article:
## Question

Do the original-order rune-word lengths from the Warning, Welcome, first koan and second koan give unusually similar means in sixteen columns, compared with unrestricted permutations of those same lengths?

This record reproduces a supplied numerical observation. The arrangement and approximate result were already known. It tests one stated comparison, not whether the authors intentionally designed the text this way.

## Reconstruct the object before testing it

Use the archived ciphertext, in manuscript order. Count runes, not Latin letters: a rune labeled TH still has length one. Include headings and the interrupting F runes. Remove slash and newline wrapping, concatenate successive pages within each section, and retain other word boundaries. An internal apostrophe belongs to the same word and contributes no rune.

| Section | Pages | Words | Runes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Warning | LP1-01 | 45 | 184 |
| Welcome | LP1-03–04 | 124 | 515 |
| First koan | LP1-06–09 | 208 | 778 |
| Second koan | LP1-14–15 | 87 | 319 |
| Total | Nine pages | 464 | 1796 |

All 464 reconstructed lengths match the supplied vector exactly. Treating the apostrophe in DON'T as a word separator instead produces 465 tokens: two pieces of lengths three and one replace one four-rune word. That would shift all later column assignments.

The table is filled across each row from left to right, sixteen words at a time. There are 29 rows. Word 1 goes in row 1, column 1; word 16 in row 1, column 16; word 17 in row 2, column 1. Section boundaries do not reset the column counter.

The full [29-by-16 length table](experiments/records/lp1-word-length-balance/length-table.csv) is downloadable. The [word ledger](experiments/records/lp1-word-length-balance/words.json) gives each word's original ciphertext, rune length, section, contributing pages, row and column. A word crossing a page boundary records both pages. Neither file silently substitutes contextual English.

## Statistic and exact expectation

Let N = 464, k = 16 columns and m = 29 words per column. For column j, let S_j be its total rune count and M_j = S_j / m its mean word length. Let M be the overall mean word length, 1796/464.

Use the population variance across the sixteen column means:

```
V = sum((M_j - M)^2) / k
R = V / E[V under the declared shuffle model]
```

Each shuffle uniformly permutes the same list of 464 lengths. It keeps the overall distribution and total rune count but destroys word order, sentence structure and section membership. Duplicate lengths remain duplicate observations; there is no sampling of newly invented words.

For population variance sigma² of the fixed 464 lengths, the finite-population expectation is:

```
E[V] = sigma² × (k - 1) / (N - 1)
```

Why? Each column is a sample of m positions without replacement. Its mean has variance sigma² × (N-m)/(m(N-1)). The grand mean is fixed, so averaging the squared deviations of the column means has this same expectation; N = km gives the expression above. Independence between columns is not assumed.

The script uses exact rational arithmetic for this expectation and the observed ratio. For shuffle comparisons it uses an integer multiple of V, avoiding floating-point decisions at the tail boundary.

## Findings

The sixteen column totals are:

```
113, 105, 119, 111, 112, 118, 110, 111,
112, 112, 109, 101, 109, 126, 111, 117
```

Each total is divided by 29 to get its mean. Their deviations from the mean column total, 112.25, have squared sum 501.

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Observed variance of column means | 501/13456 |
| Exact shuffle expectation | 922305/6230128 |
| R | 77321/307435 = 0.25150356986029565 |
| Shuffles | 49,999 |
| Seed | 330146 |
| Shuffles with variance no greater than observed | 54 |
| Corrected lower-tail Monte Carlo estimate | (54 + 1)/(49,999 + 1) = 0.0011 |

The observed variance is about 25.15% of this model's expectation. It falls in the lower tail of the specified comparison, below the predeclared 0.05 threshold. The ratio and expectation are exact; the tail probability is estimated by simulation. Its Monte Carlo standard error is roughly 0.00015, not zero.

The [results file](experiments/records/lp1-word-length-balance/results.json) includes every simulated integer score, not only the tail count. The chart shows the observed column means. It does not plot the null distribution.

## What this does and does not establish

The counts, ordering and stated ratio reproduce from the archived runes. Under unrestricted permutations of this fixed multiset, arrangements at least this flat were uncommon in our run.

This is not a test against ordinary English. Unrestricted shuffling discards linguistic and section structure; an unusual result under that model need not be unusual among coherent texts. It is also not the probability that the observation is a coincidence, that the text was deliberately constructed, or that this arrangement is useful for decryption.

The original observation resulted from exploration. We knew the selected four sections, width and approximate ratio before this run. The plan was committed before this simulation, but that does not make the original discovery prospective. The reported tail estimate does not account for all earlier choices of populations, widths, orders and statistics.

The supplied Alice, Gateless Gate and other-LP window counts have not been reproduced here. Exact corpora and conversion rules would be needed. Overlapping windows are dependent, so a fraction of matching windows is not automatically an independent-trial significance calculation.

Keeping punctuation and word boundaries fixed while applying one-output-rune-per-input-rune substitutions preserves these lengths. Decoding does not provide independent confirmation of the same length pattern. Read [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants) and [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) before extending the claim.

## Reproduce and inspect

Extract this experiment's ZIP with its directory structure intact. Python 3 is sufficient; there are no third-party dependencies or network calls.

```
python experiments/records/lp1-word-length-balance/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp1-word-length-balance/check.py
```

The first command repeats all 49,999 shuffles and compares the complete results and word ledger. The independent checker uses a character scanner rather than the runner's regular expression, compares every token and length, calculates the observed variance directly from rational column means, and validates the null expectation by exhaustively enumerating two four-element teaching populations. It also independently calculates the first 32 null scores and audits the full saved tail count. A full rerun agreed.

To regenerate the CSV and chart from the saved outputs:

```
python experiments/records/lp1-word-length-balance/plot.py
```

Computational review is complete; human review is pending. The scripts and fixed input hashes define this result. The supplied vector is included only as a comparison target, not used to generate the measured lengths.

## Related questions remain separate

A within-section shuffle is a natural sensitivity test: preserve each section's length distribution while changing its internal order. Other variants can compare section orders, widths or removal rules, with a declared selection procedure.

Section-contribution ledgers, sentence-removal scans, unchanged-rune grilles and the proposed 928-word carrier answer different questions. They are not findings of this record. In particular, 464 is a word count and 1,796 is a rune count; subtracting a count of unchanged runes from 464 would mix units.

## Sources and selection history

Inputs are the nine archived LP1 transcription files, with SHA-256 hashes in the plan and record. The complete supplied numerical vector is preserved in submitted-lengths.json. No missing screenshots, spreadsheets or named attachments were treated as available data. The initial count and exact-R reconstruction preceded the frozen simulation plan; that exploratory step is disclosed rather than described as a blind test.

records.article:
## Finding

**The lag-35 peak is real in the transcription, but it is not unusual once the search over 242 lags is counted.** On LP2-00–02, 42 of 694 rune pairs separated by 35 positions are equal, a standardized score of **3.759** against a uniform 29-rune reference. It is the largest score among lags 1–242. Yet **82 of 999** step-shuffled controls have a peak at least this large after undergoing the *same* 242-lag search (one-sided plus-one proportion **83/1,000**).

![The lag-35 score is in the upper, but ordinary, part of the best-of-242 control distribution.](experiments/records/lp2-00-02-lag35-selection/selection.svg)

## Why the search matters

[A public analysis](https://github.com/Leo-Y-Zhang/LiberPrimusAnalysis/blob/a32bdc0e06ea58532fbaf4329acae4a0b1020513/lag_and_parity_tests.py) reported lag 35 as the highest coincidence score in the 729-rune opening section and observed no repeated peaks at 70, 105 or 140. That arithmetic reproduces here. If **35 had been specified before looking**, none of our 999 controls would reach its score at that fixed lag. But 35 was selected as the strongest among 242 candidates; the comparison must select the strongest lag in every control as well.

| Lag | Equal pairs | Standardized score |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 35 | 42 / 694 | 3.759 |
| 70 | 22 / 659 | −0.155 |
| 105 | 26 / 624 | 0.983 |
| 140 | 22 / 589 | 0.382 |

The controls keep the exact inventory of all **728 modular differences between adjacent runes**—including four zero steps, the section's adjacent doublets. Each trial shuffles those differences, reconstructs a 729-rune stream from the original first rune, scans lags 1–242, and retains its largest score. The strongest control scores range from **2.007 to 5.318**; their median is **2.950**. This is a conditional reference for the observed step composition, not a simulation of the manuscript's encryption. The [results](experiments/records/lp2-00-02-lag35-selection/results.json) include all 242 observed lag counts and all 999 maxima.

## What the test can say

There is no convincing **period-35 recurrence by this coincidence statistic**. A genuine repeating key could leave a peak at 35 or a harmonic, but a weak or interrupted one might not. The absence of harmonics here is descriptive; it does not rule out every interrupted, changing or compound key. The control scan only corrects for choosing among these 242 lags in this section. It does not adjust for choosing the section itself, alternative transcriptions, scoring rules, or many other ideas tried elsewhere.

As a basic power check, the script plants a 35-periodic 29-symbol sequence with 55% of positions independently replaced. Its strongest scanned lag is 35, with z **29.139**. This is deliberately easy to detect; it verifies the code can recognize a substantial planted recurrence and does not establish power for subtle ones.

Reproduce offline with `python experiments/records/lp2-00-02-lag35-selection/run.py --check`, then run `python experiments/records/lp2-00-02-lag35-selection/check.py`. The independent checker recounts the manuscript peak and rebuilds the first ten controls through a separate pair-count calculation. Both scripts use Python's standard library and the archived transcription.
