records.article:
# Möbius values of the LP2-15 number panel

A [reported suggestion](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=lp2-15-mobius-square-transform) applies the arithmetic Möbius function to the numbers at the top of [LP2-15](#/reader/lp2-15). This is a small but exact question: what comes out when we transform **all sixteen printed entries in place**? The source transcript refers to an output image that is not retained in the supplied text, so this is a reconstruction of the stated operation, **not an exact comparison with that historical image**.

The numbers in the upper part of each cell below are printed on the page; the `μ` values beneath them are calculated. The red `3299` stays in its original row and column. Neither a Fibonacci spiral nor subtraction from 3301 is applied here.

![Four-by-four LP2-15 panel showing each printed decimal number above its calculated arithmetic Möbius value. Only the second row is nonzero.](experiments/records/lp2-15-mobius-panel/panel.svg)

[Open the diagram](experiments/records/lp2-15-mobius-panel/panel.svg) · [View the original page](images/lp2-15.jpg)

The output matrix, in printed row order, is:

| Row | Column 1 | Column 2 | Column 3 | Column 4 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | −1 | −1 | −1 | +1 |
| 3 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 4 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

For a positive integer `n`, the arithmetic Möbius function is **zero if a prime square divides `n`**. Otherwise it is `−1` for an odd number of distinct prime factors and `+1` for an even number. That rule accounts for each cell; no visual judgement is required to obtain this matrix.

| Printed cell | Factorization | μ |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| r1c1 · 3258 | 2 × 3² × 181 | 0 |
| r1c2 · 3222 | 2 × 3² × 179 | 0 |
| r1c3 · 3152 | 2⁴ × 197 | 0 |
| r1c4 · 3038 | 2 × 7² × 31 | 0 |
| r2c1 · 3278 | 2 × 11 × 149 | −1 |
| r2c2 · **3299, printed red** | 3299 (prime) | −1 |
| r2c3 · 3298 | 2 × 17 × 97 | −1 |
| r2c4 · 2838 | 2 × 3 × 11 × 43 | +1 |
| r3c1 · 3288 | 2³ × 3 × 137 | 0 |
| r3c2 · 3294 | 2 × 3³ × 61 | 0 |
| r3c3 · 3296 | 2⁵ × 103 | 0 |
| r3c4 · 2472 | 2³ × 3 × 103 | 0 |
| r4c1 · 4516 | 2² × 1129 | 0 |
| r4c2 · 1206 | 2 × 3² × 67 | 0 |
| r4c3 · 708 | 2² × 3 × 59 | 0 |
| r4c4 · 1820 | 2² × 5 × 7 × 13 | 0 |

Twelve entries vanish; the only nonzero row is `−1, −1, −1, +1`. All but the red entry are even, but **evenness alone does not imply μ = 0**: the three other numbers in row 2 are squarefree. The table shows which prime square makes every zero. The row alignment is an observation of this fixed transform, not a decryption or a significance estimate after possible functions and arrangements have been considered.

## Reproduce it

From a checkout or the experiment download, run:

```text
python experiments/records/lp2-15-mobius-panel/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp2-15-mobius-panel/check.py
python experiments/records/lp2-15-mobius-panel/plot.py --check
```

The [plan](experiments/records/lp2-15-mobius-panel/plan.json) fixes the source page hash and all sixteen inputs. The producer uses integer factorization; the separate checker searches independently for prime-square divisors and counts distinct prime factors. The [results](experiments/records/lp2-15-mobius-panel/results.json) preserve every coordinate, number, factorization, calculated μ value and the matrix. The diagram is generated from that ledger. The source transcript is identified by hash in the [reported-attempt register](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=lp2-15-mobius-square-transform), rather than reproduced without its missing image.

**What this establishes:** the stated arithmetic operation is reproducible on the complete printed panel. It does not show that this was exactly the unseen image in the discussion, that a particular row or spiral is a key, or how a `−1/0/+1` stream would act on the runes. A solving test would first have to fix that operation, its order, boundaries and acceptance criterion, then compare continuous output with controls.

# Does the LP2-15 prime-gap tail repeat?

A supplied proposal finds **8, 20, 10, 6** at the end of the LP2-15 spiral prime gaps after reduction modulo 28. The numbers are correct. The pattern appears **once** in the fifteen shown gaps. Extending the same [Fibonacci-indexed prime construction](#/wiki/lp2-15-panel?section=construction) gives **4**, not the predicted **8**, for the next gap.

![The shown tail, its period-four prediction, and the different next four residues.](experiments/records/lp2-15-prime-gap-cycle/gap-cycle.svg)

The source's 4×4 array is a **derived prime array**, not the decimal values printed on LP2-15. Following its spiral gives `2, 3, 5, 7, 13, 23, 43, 79, 149, 263, 463, 829, 1481, 2593, 4507, 7817`. All fifteen reported consecutive differences and modulo-28 residues check out. The last four residues occupy gap positions **12–15** and occur nowhere else as an exact consecutive four-number run in the shown data.

Before extending the sequence, we fixed the proposal's most direct cycle reading: repeat the final four residues for the **next eight** gaps, without rotating or searching phases. The next Fibonacci prime index after 987 is 1597; its prime is 13477. Thus the first new gap is `13477 − 7817 = 5660`, and **5660 mod 28 = 4**.

| Continuation | Next eight residues mod 28 |
| --- | --- |
| If the four-number tail repeats | 8, 20, 10, 6, 8, 20, 10, 6 |
| Same Fibonacci prime-index generator | **4, 2, 20, 2, 24, 26, 26, 26** |

None of the eight positions matches the fixed cycle. This is a check of **one arithmetic recurrence claim**, not a test of rune decryption or an exclusion of other panel paths. The proposal does not explain why to use modulus **28**; the Gematria Primus alphabet has **29** runes. Changing modulus or mapping residues to runes would require a separately stated rule. For a declared comparison, these eight gaps modulo 29 are `5, 4, 7, 12, 25, 10, 22, 22`; no plaintext is inferred from them.

## Reproduce

From the checkout or [experiment ZIP](downloads/experiments/lp2-15-prime-gap-cycle.zip), run from the root of the extracted bundle:

```text
python experiments/records/lp2-15-prime-gap-cycle/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp2-15-prime-gap-cycle/check.py
python experiments/records/lp2-15-prime-gap-cycle/plot.py --check
```

The [frozen plan](experiments/records/lp2-15-prime-gap-cycle/plan.json) fixes the tail, eight-step continuation and no-phase-search criterion. The [source-number transcription](experiments/records/lp2-15-prime-gap-cycle/source.json) preserves the full array, gaps and residues with the three supplied screenshots identified by SHA-256; the screenshots themselves are not republished. The [results](experiments/records/lp2-15-prime-gap-cycle/results.json) retain all 24 primes and 23 gaps. The producer checks the source array against the archived [LP2-15 construction ledger](exports/fibonacci-prime-panel.json); the independent checker rebuilds the primes with a sieve.

records.article:
# A totient variant of the LP2-15 number panel

The printed [LP2-15](#/page/lp2-15) panel has sixteen integers. One is prime: the red **3299**. A supplied January 2026 discussion proposes taking Euler’s totient of the prime entries, subtracting the results from 3301, and reading Fibonacci gaps in the resulting prime positions. Its three 4×4 arrays make most of that proposal checkable. They do **not** specify a rule for turning the numbers into plaintext.

This audit keeps the reported arrays intact. The exact posted gap at row 4, column 1 is **317**, and the row 2, column 2 gap is marked uncertain; neither is silently corrected. The [source intake entry](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=lp2-15-totient-before-prime-gap) identifies the supplied transcript and its SHA-256 hash.

![Every printed panel cell beside the source's prime candidate, ordinal and proposed Fibonacci gap](experiments/records/lp2-15-totient-gap-audit/panel-audit.svg)

## What the arithmetic actually does

Euler’s totient φ(n) counts positive integers at most n that are coprime to n. For a prime p, φ(p) = p − 1. Only **3299** is prime among the sixteen printed cells, so this first step changes only that cell, to **3298**. The source’s post-totient array matches the computed array in all 16 positions. It now has two adjacent 3298s.

For each post-totient value x, we calculated **both** 3301 − x and 3301 + x. The source’s second array matches one of these two values at every cell, and all sixteen selected values are prime. Fourteen selected values use subtraction; the entries **4516** and **1206** in the bottom row use addition, producing **7817** and **4507**. Thus the posted label “3301 − X” does not describe the whole array. A single literal subtraction rule would miss those two cells.

Primality alone leaves a further choice at both 3298 cells: **3** and **6599** are prime. Their zero-based prime ordinals are **1** and **852** respectively. Requiring a *Fibonacci-valued ordinal* selects 3, since 1 is a Fibonacci value and 852 is not. This filter leaves one sign per cell, but the source does not state it as a forward sign-selection rule. The two 3298 cells both become prime **3**, so ordinal **1** is duplicated and ordinal **0** (prime 2) is absent.

| Stage | Match with posted array | Qualification |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Prime-only totient of printed panel | 16/16 | Changes only red 3299. |
| Candidate from 3301 ± transformed cell | 16/16 | Two cells require `+`; primality alone leaves two cells with either sign. |
| Selected candidate has Fibonacci zero-based prime index | 16/16 | This condition resolves the sign ambiguity after the candidate set is inspected. |
| Posted Fibonacci predecessor gap | 14/15 specified | Row 4, column 1 reports 317, while index 987 follows 610 and gives 377; one other cell is marked `?`. |

The gap calculation is easiest to see in the first row. Prime **43** has zero-based ordinal **13**; the preceding distinct Fibonacci value is **8**, so its gap is **5**. Prime **79** has ordinal **21**, following 13, so its gap is **8**. At bottom left, prime **7817** has ordinal **987**, following **610**, so the corresponding gap is **377**, not the posted 317. The source’s comment `0 /* ? */` leaves the other exceptional cell unresolved. Because the canonical Fibonacci sequence starts **0, 1, 1**, the predecessor of an occurrence of ordinal 1 also depends on which repeated 1 that occurrence is assigned to. The post does not give that assignment.

## What this settles—and what it does not

The arithmetic reproduces a coherent **derived pattern** from the printed square if the two plus signs and Fibonacci-index sign filter are allowed. It does not construct the original square from independent inputs: it begins with the printed numbers, changes the red one, and then selects signs that produce the reported primes. The established [Fibonacci-indexed prime construction](#/wiki/lp2-15-panel) starts independently with a declared index list, uses absolute distance from 3301, and matches all sixteen printed cells. These are different claims.

No rule is supplied for which of the source’s arrays should become a cipher key, how it advances through runes, what to do with the duplicate 3 or uncertain gap, or how to score a result. The discussion itself suggests only that a related manipulation *might* apply to the text. This record therefore audits the numbers; it is **inconclusive as a decoding method**.

## Reproduce the audit

From the repository root or this experiment’s extracted ZIP, use Python 3 with no external packages:

```text
python experiments/records/lp2-15-totient-gap-audit/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp2-15-totient-gap-audit/check.py
python experiments/records/lp2-15-totient-gap-audit/plot.py --check
```

The [plan](experiments/records/lp2-15-totient-gap-audit/plan.json) fixes the source’s three arrays and source hash. The [results](experiments/records/lp2-15-totient-gap-audit/results.json) retain both signs, primality and prime ordinal for every cell. The independent checker uses a sieve and a coprimality count rather than the producer’s factoring and totient implementation. Neither script chooses a plaintext interpretation.

The stored second rune is `A`, worth 97. Substituting `F`, worth 2, would lower 786 to 691 exactly. That is a **sensitivity check, not a correction**: no source supplied here justifies changing that rune. An image-level disagreement or a different claimed span would need its own evidence.

records.article:
# LP2-31: periodic IoC for periods 2–20

**Computationally checked; human review pending.** Codex reran the script and reviewed the separate position-pair oracle on 20 October 2026. This is a bounded statistical result, not a decipherment or a human-reviewed conclusion.

Put every 13th rune of LP2-31 in the same column and ask whether equal runes meet within those columns more often than they would after shuffling the page. Period 13 gives the largest score among the tested periods 2–20, but **213 of 999 shuffled pages reached at least that high a best-period score**. The experiment does not support singling out period 13 at its declared 0.05 threshold. The question, counting rule and other limits follow below.

## Question

Does LP2-31 have an unusually large within-column coincidence score at any period from 2 through 20, relative to random reorderings of the same rune multiset?

This is a test of one ordering statistic. It does not attempt decryption or determine whether the page uses Vigenère.

## Scope fixed before the first run

The plan is in `plan.json`, committed as `e515465` before computing the first result. It selects LP2-31, periods 2–20 inclusive, offset zero, 999 shuffles, seed 330131 and a 0.05 threshold. These are declared choices for this run, not a claim that the question or page was selected independently of all prior research.

The input is the complete archived rune stream, including headings. Remove every character outside the 29-rune alphabet before assigning positions. No corrections, decryption, region selection or cross-page concatenation are applied. The resulting length is 269 runes. Input paths and SHA-256 hashes are in `record.json` and `results.json`.

## Method

For period k, put positions with the same remainder modulo k in the same column. Count matching ordered pairs in each column and add them. Divide by the total number of ordered pairs available within all columns:

```
pooled IoC(k) = sum over columns and symbols of n(c,s)*(n(c,s)-1)
                / sum over columns of N(c)*(N(c)-1)
```

This weights columns by their number of pairs; it is not the unweighted mean of column IoCs. No pairs between different columns count.

Take the maximum over all 19 periods. Shuffle the original rune list afresh for each trial, preserving its exact symbol counts. Repeat the entire 19-period scan on every shuffled version and retain that trial's maximum. Compare maxima to maxima, rather than comparing the selected observed peak with an unselected single-period null distribution.

The random generator is Python's `random.Random(330131)`, using `shuffle`. Exact rational comparisons include ties. The Monte Carlo value is:

```
(1 + number of shuffled maxima >= observed maximum) / (999 + 1)
```

All observed period scores are retained. Each shuffled trial stores all 19 numerators, aligned with the observed periods. Their denominators do not depend on rune order and are stored once in the observed rows. The trial maximum is also stored as an exact fraction.

## Reproduce

From the repository root, using Python 3.12.10 and its standard library:

```
python experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/check.py
python experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/run.py --check
```

The independent check enumerates pairs of positions directly, instead of counting frequencies in columns. It checks a constant string, an alternating string, and every tested period of the actual page. The alternating control has pooled IoC 1 at period 2.

The full rerun compares every stored field, including all shuffle scores and input hashes. It should report exact reproduction and:

```
n: 269
best_periods: [13]
exceedances: 213
monte_carlo_p: 0.214
below_threshold: false
```

To save a separate report:

```
python experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/run.py --output my-periodic-ioc.json
```

An existing output file is never overwritten. No network service, model, API key or third-party package is used. A changed input hash or random-generator behavior can prevent byte-for-byte reproduction; investigate rather than replacing the expected output automatically.

## Results

![Observed pooled IoC by period. The highest bar is period 13; the maximum-adjusted shuffle comparison is p = 0.214.](experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/period-scan.svg)


Period 13 has the unique largest observed score: 216 / 5300 = 0.04075471698. Its columns contain 20 or 21 runes.

Of 999 random reorderings, 213 have a maximum at least this large somewhere in the same period range. The corrected Monte Carlo value is 214 / 1000 = 0.214. It is not below the declared 0.05 threshold.

For scale, the approximate Monte Carlo standard error of the estimated tail frequency is 0.013, using sqrt(q*(1-q)/999) with q = 213/999. This describes simulation uncertainty, not uncertainty about a cipher or plaintext. The reported Monte Carlo value has increments of 0.001.

## Interpretation and limitations

This run does not provide evidence, at the declared threshold, for singling out period 13 from this scan. It does not establish that LP2-31 lacks periodic structure. A cipher may produce structure that this statistic, input convention or period range does not detect.

The null model treats rune order as exchangeable conditional on its counts. It does not preserve word lengths, punctuation positions, local repeated patterns or possible region boundaries. Rejecting it would not prove any particular encryption method. Failing to reject it does not prove randomness.

The maximum comparison accounts for selecting among periods 2–20 in this run. It does not correct for choosing LP2-31, trying different text regions or previous unrelated tests. Periods outside the range, other pages, corrected streams, alternative statistics and actual key searches remain untested here.

No shift or Vigenère key is inferred. The period-13 peak is retained as a descriptive result, not promoted to a solution.

## Sources and related work

- [LP2-31 record and original-source links](https://jelliottdev.github.io/#/page/lp2-31)
- [IoC definition, baseline and invariants](https://jelliottdev.github.io/#/wiki/index-of-coincidence)
- [Reproducibility requirements](https://jelliottdev.github.io/#/wiki/reproducibility)

The whole-page baseline does not test ordering: shuffling preserves global IoC. This experiment adds an order-sensitive column statistic and a declared shuffle comparison. No earlier experiment is imported as a completed run.

## Retest and changes after inspection

On 20 October 2026, the independent position-pair check passed, and all observed and simulated numerical fields reproduced exactly. The only difference from the first saved output was the SHA-256 of `data/index.json`, whose page metadata had since changed. The plan and rune input hashes were unchanged. No period range, threshold, seed, sample count, or scoring rule was changed.

The original report is preserved as [original output](experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/results-original.json). The [current report](experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/results.json) records the current input hash. The checked script reproduces the current report exactly, including all 999 trials. The [chart script](experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/plot.py) reads that report without running another experiment.

This record is the baseline for the periodic-IoC shuffle family. Future variants must identify each changed scope field and give their own plan, output and interpretation. A [within-row shuffle variant](#/experiments/lp2-31-row-shuffle-ioc) now preserves each archived row’s length and rune counts while leaving the observed statistic unchanged. Human review is still pending; the computational review was performed by Codex, not by an independent human researcher.

# LP2-31 periodic IoC: preserving row composition

## Why change the null model?

The baseline shuffles all 269 runes together. That preserves the page's total counts but can move any rune to any row. If rows differ in composition, that comparison removes those differences as well as the ordering under investigation.

This variant instead preserves each archived row's length and exact rune counts, shuffling only within that row. It asks a conditional question about order after holding row composition fixed. This is not automatically a better model; it makes a different assumption visible.

LP2-31 has twelve ordinary text rows and no separately identified heading. No row was removed or renamed as a heading for this test. Archived transcription lines provide the boundaries.

## Plan and relation to the baseline

The plan and runner were committed as `8dfc7c0` before executing the variant. The variant was motivated after the whole-page result was known; it is not independent confirmation and does not account for selecting among null models.

Only the shuffle procedure changes. The input remains the same 269 runes, periods remain 2–20 inclusive, the statistic remains pooled within-column matching pairs, and each trial's maximum is compared with the observed maximum. There are still 999 trials, seed 330131, greater-than-or-equal ties, plus-one Monte Carlo correction, and a 0.05 threshold.

The twelve row lengths are:

```
23, 22, 24, 24, 22, 22, 21, 22, 21, 24, 22, 22
```

Remove non-alphabet characters inside each row, shuffle that row's runes, then concatenate rows in their original order. Column positions run across the concatenated page; they do not restart at row boundaries. The same seed does not make the two models' individual shuffled pages equivalent or create a paired statistical test.

## Results

| Quantity | Whole-page baseline | Within-row variant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input runes | 269 | 269 |
| Observed peak period | 13 | 13 |
| Observed peak fraction | 216/5300 | 216/5300 |
| Null maxima at least observed | 213/999 | 245/999 |
| Plus-one Monte Carlo p | 0.214 | 0.246 |
| Below declared 0.05 threshold | No | No |

The observed scores agree exactly for every period, as they should: the observed input and scoring procedure did not change. The within-row comparison is 246/1000 = 0.246. Its approximate Monte Carlo standard error is 0.014, using sqrt(q*(1-q)/999) with q=245/999. This describes simulation uncertainty, not confidence in a cipher.

The two runs give the same threshold decision under their different assumptions. The difference between 0.214 and 0.246 is not evaluated as a separate statistical effect, and neither p-value is the probability that period 13 is the true key length.

## Reproduce

From a repository checkout with Python 3.12.10:

```
python experiments/records/lp2-31-row-shuffle-ioc/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp2-31-row-shuffle-ioc/check.py
```

The runner compares every observed field and all 999 stored trial records. The separate checker verifies the twelve row lengths, exact agreement with the baseline's observed scores, and a position-pair oracle for all observed periods and the first three seeded null trials. That oracle directly enumerates position pairs rather than using column-frequency counts. The runner also asserts preservation of each row's multiset in every trial.

[Download the complete variant output](experiments/records/lp2-31-row-shuffle-ioc/results.json). All 19 period numerators are stored for every shuffle; the denominators are in the observed rows. The comparison diagram is generated from the two saved reports. Neither the checker nor the plot interprets candidate plaintext or calls an AI service.

## Retest and changes after inspection

Codex reran the complete variant and performed the separate checks on 20 October 2026. Every stored field reproduced. No null rule, period range, input boundary, seed, threshold or statistic changed after the variant's first result. The checker and comparison graphic were added afterward for verification and presentation. Human review remains pending.

## Interpretation and remaining limits

This row-conditioned null preserves more local composition than the whole-page null, but still discards within-row word boundaries and local patterns. It treats all rune permutations within a row as exchangeable. Neither model is a full model of a particular cipher or language.

This variant does not show that the page is random, that period 13 is impossible, or that Vigenère is absent. It also does not test different pages, period ranges, row selections, alternative statistics or key searches. Those changes must be documented separately rather than silently folded into this result.

# LP2-32 grid sums and the 2016 message

This recount reproduces three numerical equalities: **563, 569 and 1136**. They are the first-row sum, first-column sum and central 5×5 perimeter sum of a specified arrangement of LP2-32. The preserved 2016 image measures 563×569 pixels, and its extracted payload contains 1,136 bytes.

“Supported” refers to these exact calculations. It does not establish that the correspondence was intended, statistically unusual or useful for decryption.

## Construct the grid

Use the archived LP2-32 text. Keep all 121 alphabet runes, remove separators, and place the stream left-to-right into eleven rows of eleven. Do not reverse, rotate, pad or omit runes. Replace each rune with its stored Gematria Primus prime value.

This is an analytical rearrangement. It is not a claim that the original manuscript has eleven printed lines. The JSON records every grid cell, its original rune ordinal and its source-text character offset so the rearrangement can be followed back to the page.

## Exactly which cells are summed?

The first row is grid row 1, columns 1–11. The first column is column 1, rows 1–11. They share the top-left cell, so these measurements are not disjoint.

The central 5×5 block occupies rows 4–8 and columns 4–8, using one-based coordinates. Sum its outer border, counting each corner once. That is 16 cells: five across the top, five across the bottom, and three additional cells down each side. Do not include the central nine cells or count corners twice.

In the enlarged figure, the top border sums to 275 and the bottom border to 373. The three remaining left-edge cells sum to 231; the three remaining right-edge cells sum to 257. Thus `275 + 373 + 231 + 257 = 1136`. This decomposition counts each corner exactly once.

| Quantity | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Rune count | 121 |
| Sum of all 121 prime values | 6045 |
| First row | 563 |
| First column | 569 |
| Central 5×5 perimeter | 1136 |
| Original 2016 JPEG width × height | 563 × 569 |
| Preserved OutGuess payload bytes | 1136 |

The output also lists all eleven row sums, all eleven column sums and all 49 placements of a contiguous 5×5 block within this grid. Only the central block has perimeter sum 1136 under these rules. That statement concerns those 49 placements; it is not a chance probability over other layouts, page choices or target numbers.

## What was compared with the grid?

The image measurement comes from the original JPEG frame header, not a displayed preview. Payload length means raw bytes in the preserved extracted signed message, including its armor and formatting. It does not mean visible characters, plaintext letters, pixels or the JPEG file size.

The [later-message guide](#/wiki/later-messages) separately documents an exact OutGuess extraction and signature verification. This recount uses those preserved bytes and hashes them; it does not need to run OutGuess again. The [Wing and Tree guide](#/wiki/wing-and-tree) locates the manuscript drawing. A numerical match does not prove that the two tree images have the same source.

## Reproduce

Extract this experiment’s ZIP with its directory structure intact. It includes the payload, scripts and text inputs. Download the [original 2016 JPEG](images/message-2016.jpg) separately and save it as `images/message-2016.jpg` inside the extracted folder. The ZIP’s image-input manifest gives its checksum. Python’s standard library is sufficient.

```text
python experiments/records/lp2-32-message-grid/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp2-32-message-grid/check.py
```

The producer reads the rune text and parses JPEG segment headers. The checker reads the separate archived page record, uses flat-index cell sets to recount the perimeters, and checks the image’s baseline frame header independently. Both use the same stored alphabet, so their agreement does not independently resolve transcription ambiguities.

## Limits and follow-up

The original lead selected this page, arrangement and central border for inspection. No null model or accounting for other explored arrangements is supplied here. A follow-up can test a stated family of layouts or a fixed shuffle model, but should not describe this one successful comparison as an exhaustive search. See [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) and [null models](#/wiki/null-models).

## Recreate the diagram

The SVG is included in the experiment ZIP. The drawing reads the stored cell ledger directly; its numbers are not manually retyped. Install Matplotlib if you want to recreate it, then choose a new output filename:

```text
python experiments/records/lp2-32-message-grid/plot.py --output my-grid.svg
```

The drawing script refuses to overwrite an existing file. Plotting is optional; the producer and independent checker still use only Python’s standard library.

records.article:
## What was tested?

The lower text block on [LP2-39](#/page/lp2-39) starts with three red runes, followed by punctuation. The first rune is enlarged across several rows. Read in manuscript order, the archived prefix is IA + C + S, with zero-based indices 27, 5 and 15. The Latin labels describe the ciphertext symbols; they are not an English reading.

A **crib** is a proposed plaintext fragment. This experiment takes twenty suggested words and asks whether any single affine substitution maps the word to those three runes. It checks the entire declared key space, rather than adjusting a separate shift for each position.

The candidate list is fixed in plan.json. It is a selected list, not a dictionary or an unbiased sample of possible headings. WHY was already in the list before this calculation; no new words were added after inspecting the result.

## Representation comes before the key search

Words are uppercased and split in every possible way using the 29 Latin labels stored in the [GP alphabet and rune values](#/wiki/rune-values). There are no pronunciation rules or spelling substitutions. TH may be one label or T + H; NG may be one label or N + G.

BEING does **not** have a three-rune representation under these rules. Its two segmentations are B + E + I + NG (four) and B + E + I + N + G (five). The suggested B + EI + NG would need an EI label that is absent from this alphabet. A proposed alias can be tested separately, but it must be declared rather than silently substituted.

THUS has three runes as TH + U + S, or four as T + H + U + S. Their prime sums are 61 and 138 respectively. These sums are recorded for transparency; primality is not used to select a candidate or key. See [word lengths](#/wiki/word-lengths) and [spelling and prime sums](#/wiki/prime-sums).

## Search bounds and complete result

The encryption rule is C = (aP + b) mod 29, using rune indices rather than prime values. Test every a from 1 through 28 and every b from 0 through 28: **812 keys**. Multiplication by any allowed a is invertible modulo 29. This space includes ordinary shifts and shifted alphabet reversals.

The twenty words give 22 segmentations. Seventeen have the required three runes, so the complete search contains **17 × 812 = 13,804 candidate/key trials**. Wrong-length candidates are retained below instead of disappearing from the report.

| Candidate | Rune lengths | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AND | 3 | No affine fit |
| BUT | 3 | No affine fit |
| WHY | 3 | a = 7, b = 7 |
| HOW | 3 | No affine fit |
| WHO | 3 | No affine fit |
| YOU | 3 | No affine fit |
| HER | 3 | No affine fit |
| HIM | 3 | No affine fit |
| HIS | 3 | No affine fit |
| ONE | 3 | No affine fit |
| TWO | 3 | No affine fit |
| WAY | 3 | No affine fit |
| MAP | 3 | No affine fit |
| LAW | 3 | No affine fit |
| GOD | 3 | No affine fit |
| BEING | 5, 4 | Wrong length |
| OLD | 3 | No affine fit |
| THUS | 3, 4 | No affine fit |
| FOLLY | 5 | Wrong length |
| WISDOM | 6 | Wrong length |

Only WHY matches. Its rune indices are W = 7, H = 8 and Y = 26. The single key a = 7, b = 7 produces:

| Position | Proposed index P | 7P + 7 | Reduced modulo 29 | Cipher label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 7 | 56 | 27 | IA |
| 2 | 8 | 63 | 5 | C |
| 3 | 26 | 189 | 15 | S |

## Why this is not a solution

Three symbols provide very little independent constraint. Because the first two proposed indices differ, they determine an affine key; the third position tests that key. Here the check was repeated across seventeen eligible candidates. Finding one fit does not establish that the authors intended WHY, or that this key applies to the following text.

For this three-symbol ciphertext, the 812 invertible affine keys produce 812 distinct three-symbol candidate plaintexts. A short word among those outputs needs further evidence. This is a search-space count, not a probability estimate for English words or for the authors' choices.

This experiment does not score the remaining text, use a language model, or select a key by how promising the continuation sounds. The recorded outcome is **inconclusive** about the reading. The exact header fit is reproducible; a decipherment is not established.

A follow-up should freeze the surviving key and test text outside the three-rune crib against an explicit criterion. If it fails, inventing fresh per-position shifts would define a different method, not rescue this affine result. Keep such changes in separate variants within this family. See [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) and [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants).

## Reproduce and inspect

Download this experiment's ZIP and extract it with its folders intact. Both commands use Python's standard library and run offline:

records.article:
# The red passage on LP2-53

**Question.** Does the long red passage have the equality pattern expected of an ordinary solved-text passage after a simple rune substitution, and does it differ from the black text on the same page?

**Result.** Its 51 runes have an index of coincidence (IoC) of **0.0298** and **26 distinct runes**. None of **2,492** same-length windows from eight archived decoded GP passages is that flat: their lowest IoC is **0.0400** and they use at most 23 distinct runes. But the red result lies *inside* the **0.0259–0.0408** IoC range of 78 black-text windows on LP2-53. Color distinguishes the passage visually; these measurements do not establish a separate cipher.

![The red span compared with matched solved and same-page black windows.](experiments/records/lp2-53-red-equality-invariants/equality-profile.svg)

## The exact span

The original [LP2-53 image](images/lp2-53.jpg) shows a red **ᛏ** as the final rune of text line 6, then three complete red lines. In the archived transcription these are page rune ordinals **128–178**, inclusive: **1 + 24 + 22 + 4 = 51** runes. Punctuation, line slashes, the final dotted mark and artwork do not enter the count. This span is shared with the separately documented LP2-53 key tests; this record asks a different, key-free question.

## Why equality is useful here

A one-to-one substitution can rename runes, but it cannot change which positions are equal. Thus IoC, number of distinct runes and adjacent-equal pairs are **invariants** of every bijective monoalphabetic substitution. We used the `output_index` traces from eight known GP readings, excluding LP2-56’s hash-target passage, and slid a 51-rune window within each reading. These windows overlap; the counts describe the archived corpus and are not independent samples or a probability that the manuscript was produced by a cipher.

The red span has **zero adjacent equal pairs**. That alone is not surprising: every black-window control on the same page also has zero, and **2,155 of 10,000** shuffles of the red runes (21.55%) likewise have none. Shuffling keeps the red symbol counts and IoC unchanged while testing whether their observed order has an unusual immediate-repeat count.

The red span’s much lower IoC than the decoded passages makes a direct one-to-one renaming of those *particular* known-reading-style windows a poor account of its equality structure. It does **not** eliminate simple substitution of another plaintext with different statistics, nor more complex ciphers or section-specific treatment. The same-page black comparison is the clearest limit on calling the red color a separate encryption layer.

Run `python experiments/records/lp2-53-red-equality-invariants/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/lp2-53-red-equality-invariants/check.py` from the repository root. The independent checker reads the page text rather than the page JSON, rebuilds all reading windows, verifies the image hash and 51-rune span, tests substitution invariance with a planted rune permutation, and repeats all 10,000 conditional shuffles. Exact inputs and results are retained with the record.

## Result

**Neither of the two documented LP1 Vigenère keys made LP2-53’s red passage read like the archived English examples.** The best of 42 key/phase/sign settings scored **−6.69**, below the fixed **−5.5** English threshold. Its score was ordinary among matched controls: **460 of 999** shuffled red passages had an equal or higher *best-of-42* score. This is a bounded test of two keys on this passage, not a finding about every possible key or plaintext language.

![The best red-passage score is near the center of shuffled-control maxima and below the scores of nine known readings.](experiments/records/lp2-53-red-known-keys/scores.svg)

## What was tested

The original page changes from black to red at the **last rune of line 6**. That rune and all runes on lines 7–9 make **51 red runes**, page rune positions **128–178** when counting from zero. The archived transcription has 179 runes in total. Hyphens separate words and slashes mark line layout; the red word lengths are **5, 4, 4, 11, 2, 3, 2, 6, 5, 5, 2, 2**. In particular, the leading hyphen on the last line separates its first two runes from the preceding word.

The two keys are the rune-index sequences documented for the **Welcome** and **second koan** readings. For each key we tried every starting phase and both arithmetic directions, calculating `Pᵢ = Cᵢ ± Kᵢ (mod 29)`. Only runes advance the key; punctuation and line breaks do not. Because every phase is included, resetting the key at the red start adds no new candidate. There is no internal full stop in the red span, so a full-stop pause also adds no new candidate. This leaves **42 distinct named settings**.

We scored each result with the site's pinned English quadgram model, applying it to canonical GP transliteration. Higher values look more like that model's English training text. The controls were run before scoring the manuscript: all **nine** archived solved-reading excerpts of the same 51-rune length passed the −5.5 threshold and beat all **200** of their own seeded rune shuffles. When those nine excerpts were enciphered with one of the two keys, their true plaintext ranked first in the same 42-setting search **nine times out of nine**. These controls show that this narrow test can recognize similar plaintext if either declared key is correct; they do not prove that every valid LP2 reading must score as English.

For a family-wise comparison, we shuffled the red rune order 999 times, preserving its rune counts. Each shuffle went through the **whole 42-setting search**, and we compared its best score with the manuscript's best. This controls for choosing the nicest-looking key after seeing all 42 outputs under that shuffle model. It is not a model of the unknown encryption process.

## Reproduce and limits

The [plan](experiments/records/lp2-53-red-known-keys/plan.json) pins the page image, transcription, alphabet, two-key source and scorer. Run `python experiments/records/lp2-53-red-known-keys/controls.py` to verify the quality gate, `python experiments/records/lp2-53-red-known-keys/run.py --check` to recompute all candidates and shuffles, and `python experiments/records/lp2-53-red-known-keys/check.py` for an independent reconstruction. [All 42 outputs and 999 control maxima](experiments/records/lp2-53-red-known-keys/results.json) are saved.

Other keys, position-dependent schedules, interrupts, transpositions, alternate rune mappings and non-English or nonstandard plaintext remain open. The visible red passage could also have a role other than a separately encrypted English sentence.

records.article:
## What is being tested?

A reported periodic-IoC peak on LP2-54–55 motivates this test. The index of coincidence (IoC) measures how often symbols match within groups of positions. We ask whether a specified ciphertext-feedback rule, with some F runes treated as interruptions, makes that score unusually high after searching every permitted interruption pattern and period.

The answer under the declared comparison is **no**: 543 of 999 shuffled inputs produced a maximum at least as high as the manuscript's. This is a new bounded implementation. The source discussion names scripts and plots, but their complete files were not supplied, so we cannot claim to reproduce their exact processing or graphs.

## Ciphertext feedback, step by step

Represent each rune by its zero-based index in the 29-rune alphabet. F has index zero. Keep a state containing the preceding ciphertext value, initially zero. For an ordinary rune:

```
output = (current ciphertext - previous ciphertext state) mod 29
previous ciphertext state = current ciphertext
```

That is ciphertext feedback: the state receives the input rune, not the decoded output. Plaintext autokey is a different recurrence.

For a selected F interruption, emit F unchanged, set the previous ciphertext state to zero, and exclude that emitted F from the scored stream. Unselected F runes follow the ordinary rule. After removing selected Fs, number the remaining output consecutively from zero for the periodic calculation.

The sibling [skip variant](#/experiments/lp2-54-55-autokey-skip) changes only how the state behaves at a selected interruption. A useful distinction: in reset mode, ordinary adjacent ciphertext differencing already uses F=0 as the next state. Selecting an F therefore removes its own scored output without otherwise changing the following arithmetic. Skip mode instead changes the next non-interruption output by retaining the earlier ciphertext value.

## A small control before the manuscript

In a teaching alphabet modulo ten, encrypt plaintext 1,2,0,3,4 with initial state zero and the third position selected as an interruption:

| Rule | Ciphertext |
| --- | --- |
| Reset state at the selected zero | 1,3,0,3,7 |
| Retain state across the selected zero | 1,3,0,6,0 |

The skip result is 13060, not 13064. Once the next ordinary symbol is processed, the state must update again; carrying an extra lag forward changes the cipher. The checker verifies encryption and decryption in both directions, including leading, adjacent and trailing interruptions.

## Inputs and search bounds

Concatenate archived LP2-54 and LP2-55, including the heading and removing punctuation. There are 232 + 76 = 308 runes. The state does not reset at the page break.

The six F positions in this combined stream are 41, 65, 195, 247, 257 and 273, counted from zero. A mask is a compact way to specify a subset: bit zero selects the first F, bit one the second, and so on. Mask 0 selects none; mask 63 selects all six. Every one of the 64 masks is tested.

For each output, test all periods 2 through 30 inclusive. Period k groups output positions by their remainder modulo k. Pool ordered equal-symbol pairs across those columns, then divide by all ordered within-column pairs:

```
pooled IoC = sum over columns and runes of count * (count - 1)
             / sum over columns of length * (length - 1)
```

This weights columns by their available pairs. It is not an unweighted average of column IoCs. The search has 64 × 29 = 1,856 parameter configurations; that count does not claim independent evidence from every configuration. See [index of coincidence](#/wiki/index-of-coincidence) and [search bounds](#/wiki/search-space).

## Comparison model

Each of 999 trials retains all six F positions and shuffles the other 302 ciphertext values. It preserves the complete rune counts and length but discards the order of non-F symbols. Each trial starts from a fresh copy; the random seed is 330154.

Repeat the entire 64-mask, 29-period search on every shuffled input and retain its maximum. Comparing the observed maximum with these maxima accounts for mask and period selection inside this declared search. It does not account for the earlier exploration that suggested the pages, cipher model or broader analysis choices.

The two modes use the same shuffled inputs. Their results are related comparisons, not independent replications. We report individual upper-tail estimates and Bonferroni-adjusted estimates for the two planned modes. This adjustment does not turn the original discovery into a prospective test.

## Result

| Quantity | Measured result |
| --- | --- |
| Unique winning mask | 0: no selected interruptions |
| Winning period | 13 |
| Largest pooled IoC | 332/6992 = 83/1748, approximately 0.04748284 |
| Null maxima at least as large | 543 of 999 |
| Corrected Monte Carlo estimate | (543 + 1)/1000 = 0.544 |
| Adjusted for the two planned modes | 1.0 |

Neither the individual estimate nor its two-mode adjustment is below the declared 0.05 threshold. A period-13 peak exists descriptively in this processing, but the test finds no evidence that the selected maximum exceeds this conditional shuffle reference. This is not a decryption and does not rule out period 13, ciphertext autokey or different interruption rules generally.

The [period profile CSV](experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset/period-profile.csv) records the best mask at each period alongside the no-interruption score. Its chart joins those observed scores for readability; the upper line may switch masks between points. The [complete results](experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset/results.json) retain all 1,856 observed ratios, every null maximum and its winning configurations, plus a source-position trace for each observed winning mask.

## Reproduce and audit

Extract this record's ZIP with its directories intact. The skip variant includes shared code under the reset record's directory; do not flatten the folders. No third-party packages, network calls or AI service are required.

```
python experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset/check.py
```

The full rerun reproduces the observed scores, winning traces and all 999 null maxima. The independent checker uses direct ciphertext indexing instead of mutable feedback state, enumerates same-column pairs to audit every observed score, reconstructs the first two complete null searches with frequency counts, verifies winning traces by re-encryption, and audits the saved tail count. Both checks passed; human review remains pending.

To rebuild the chart and CSV:

```
python experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset/plot.py experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset
```

## Remaining questions

This model conditions on the observed F locations. It does not measure whether those locations themselves are unusual. It also says nothing about a prose-generating model, different interruption symbols, primers, heading omissions, page-local resets, other period ranges or language-scored candidates. Each changed question needs explicit scope and fresh controls. A high score from any such later search must be compared with a reference that repeats that search.

To rebuild the chart and CSV:

```
python experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset/plot.py experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-skip
```

## Remaining questions

This model conditions on the observed F locations. It does not measure whether those locations themselves are unusual. It also says nothing about a prose-generating model, different interruption symbols, primers, heading omissions, page-local resets, other period ranges or language-scored candidates. Each changed question needs explicit scope and fresh controls. A high score from any such later search must be compared with a reference that repeats that search.

# Can the last two pages form an 8×8 word grid?

**Yes, under the proposed heading exclusion.** The archived text has **66 words** beginning on LP2-54–55. The red opening is a one-rune word followed by an eight-rune word. Removing those two leaves **64 words**: 48 begin on LP2-54 and 16 on LP2-55. In manuscript order, they fill exactly six rows and two rows of an 8×8 grid.

![Eight-by-eight grid of word positions: six rows start on LP2-54 and two on LP2-55.](experiments/records/lp2-54-55-word-square/word-square.svg)

This is a clean **arrangement**, not a reading. One of the 64 words crosses the page boundary; the grid keeps it whole and assigns it to the page where it starts. An independent check reconstructs all 66 words directly from the two page transcriptions and agrees with the archived word-token export.

The proposed “labyrinth” continuation does not give a start corner or turning direction. Even the simplest inward orthogonal spiral has **eight** different corner/direction variants on this grid. All visit every cell once, and each begins with a different sequence. The [saved result](experiments/records/lp2-54-55-word-square/results.json) lists all eight routes; it does not select the one whose output looks best. A decipherment test still needs a fixed route, a rule for turning words into cipher material, and an output criterion set before reading it.

# LP2-54: do the simple header autokeys make an eight-rune word?

The red opening of [LP2-54](#/reader/lp2-54) has a single rune followed by eight: `ᚪ-ᛗᛝᛞᛡᚦᛉᛁᛗ`. A reported attempt proposed **A**, **I** or **O** for the first plaintext rune and considered autokey feedback for the next word. The [earlier fixed-rule record](#/experiments/lp2-54-header-feedback) calculates all nine output runes for both simple feedback rules. Here the narrower question is whether **any of those six eight-rune outputs is an English word in a fixed corpus**.

![The six fixed outputs, all without a corpus match.](experiments/records/lp2-54-header-dictionary/header-cribs.svg)

**Result: zero of six match.** The pinned corpus has **19,715 distinct eight-rune spellings** among 138,466 entries. The same six calculations on **all 13** visible one-rune/eight-rune word pairs across LP2-00–55 also produce no corpus matches. Both planted `A MOUNTAIN` controls decode correctly, one for each feedback rule. The all-page comparison is context, **not a p-value**: those 13 pairs were not random draws from English.

The rules are exact. Convert the nine cipher runes to zero-based Gematria Primus indices modulo 29. Choose A, I or O at position zero, which fixes the primer. With ciphertext feedback, each later plaintext index is the current cipher index minus the *previous cipher* index. With plaintext feedback, subtract the *previous plaintext* index instead. Keep the printed one-plus-eight break. We looked up only the resulting eight-rune sequence, after mapping the corpus's alternate J rune to the manuscript's J rune. No word was selected to influence a key or an alignment.

| First rune | Feedback | Eight-rune output, by GP label | Corpus match |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Ciphertext | A TH TH R R EO AE N | No |
| A | Plaintext | A Y Y U U P Y OE | No |
| I | Ciphertext | A TH TH R R EO AE N | No |
| I | Plaintext | N EO J T S EA J H | No |
| O | Ciphertext | A TH TH R R EO AE N | No |
| O | Plaintext | T C/K E N OE NG E U | No |

The repeated ciphertext-feedback row is expected: after the first position, that rule depends only on adjacent ciphertext, so changing the first-rune crib cannot change the second word. The pinned corpus is a finite vocabulary, not every possible English spelling or phonetic rune transliteration. A word miss therefore excludes **these two literal one-step rules with these first-rune choices and this corpus**. It does not test the source discussion's unspecified C/K/D functions, extra cipher layers, changed word boundaries, interruption positions, or a complete LP2 reading. A more flexible search must state its transforms and total candidate count before judging a hit.

## Reproduce

Use the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/lp2-54-header-dictionary.zip) or a checkout, then run:

```text
python experiments/records/lp2-54-header-dictionary/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp2-54-header-dictionary/check.py
python experiments/records/lp2-54-header-dictionary/plot.py --check
```

The [plan](experiments/records/lp2-54-header-dictionary/plan.json) specifies the rules and exclusions. The [full result](experiments/records/lp2-54-header-dictionary/results.json) lists every eligible page pair and all 78 outputs. The preserved word list is separately attributed to [Liber Primus Crib Assist at revision `9c10caf`](https://github.com/mortlach/Liber-Primus-Crib-Assist/tree/9c10cafce02e512840cc9e173127930594a56281/data/1_grams-full); it is not claimed to be the exact dictionary used by the original reporter.

# LP2-54: what do simple autokey rules make of the red header?

The [reported header-crib proposal](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=lp2-54-header-autokey-crib) singles out the nine red runes on [LP2-54](#/reader/lp2-54): one rune, then eight. It suggests a first word such as **A**, **I** or **O**, followed by an eight-rune word. The discussion also corrects a consequential distinction: ciphertext feedback uses the previous **ciphertext** rune, while plaintext feedback uses the previous **plaintext** rune. Those are different recurrences even when both are called “autokey.”

This record tests just those two one-step recurrences, without changing the alphabet or selecting words after seeing output. It is a bounded baseline for the larger proposal, not a replay of the proposed search over hundreds of words and unspecified functions.

The clue-to-rule chain has an important break: the **red one-plus-eight layout is visible on the page**, while A/I/O and either feedback recurrence are solver hypotheses. The manuscript does not explicitly assign those letters or tell us to use autokey. That distinction matters when deciding whether a short output would count as evidence.

## Inputs and fixed choices

The archived red prefix is `ᚪ-ᛗᛝᛞᛡᚦᛉᛁᛗ.`. The hyphen separates the first rune from the following eight, and the period ends the header. In the canonical zero-based Gematria Primus order the nine cipher indices are **24, 19, 21, 23, 27, 2, 14, 10, 19**. The index labels A, I and O are **24, 10 and 3**. A single primer `k` ranges over all 29 indices; each first-rune crib picks one primer, so the six displayed rows are not an open-ended key search.

For ciphertext feedback, `P[0] = C[0] − k` and `P[i] = C[i] − C[i−1]`. For plaintext feedback, `P[0] = C[0] − k` and `P[i] = C[i] − P[i−1]`. All subtraction is modulo 29. Neither rule resets at the word separator, line break or page edge. The complete run processes **all 232 runes on LP2-54**, not just the header. Punctuation is retained in the source but has no arithmetic slot.

The [frozen plan](experiments/records/lp2-54-header-feedback/plan.json) names the source-discussion hash, transcription hash, alphabet and exact bounds. The [full result](experiments/records/lp2-54-header-feedback/results.json) contains all **58** mode-and-primer combinations, including each full 232-rune output. The producer checks that re-encryption returns every original rune; an independent checker verifies the equations at every position.

## Header outputs

![The nine source positions above six fixed-rule outputs, with the separator after the first rune.](experiments/records/lp2-54-header-feedback/header-feedback.svg)

[Open the comparison at full size](experiments/records/lp2-54-header-feedback/header-feedback.svg).

| Feedback | First-rune crib | Primer | Nine output labels, separated after rune one |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| Ciphertext | A | 0 | A · A TH TH R R EO AE N |
| Ciphertext | I | 14 | I · A TH TH R R EO AE N |
| Ciphertext | O | 21 | O · A TH TH R R EO AE N |
| Plaintext | A | 0 | A · A Y Y U U P Y OE |
| Plaintext | I | 14 | I · N EO J T S EA J H |
| Plaintext | O | 21 | O · T C/K E N OE NG E U |

The ciphertext-feedback second word is the **same for all 29 primers**, because every position after the first subtracts two known cipher runes. Choosing A, I or O therefore changes only the first rune in that model. Plaintext feedback propagates the primer choice through later positions. This is why confusing the two clocks can produce a different purported header reading.

These rune-label strings are transparent outputs, not established English or a scored decryption. Even an apparent word from a larger search would require the complete search budget, a fixed word list and transliteration, a known-reading control, and an untouched continuation. An extra encryption layer, alphabet permutation, different lag, interruption rule or manually chosen function could change every output. None is tested here.

## Reproduce

From a checkout or the [downloadable bundle](downloads/experiments/lp2-54-header-feedback.zip):

```text
python experiments/records/lp2-54-header-feedback/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp2-54-header-feedback/check.py
python experiments/records/lp2-54-header-feedback/plot.py --check
```

No external service or Python package is needed. The run was not altered after inspecting output. This census **does not support a header reading by these six simple fixed-rule candidates**, but it does not rule out the broad autokey family or the original proposal’s other, unspecified C/K/D functions. The related [LP2-54–55 interruption tests](#/experiments/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset) ask a separate periodicity question and should not be counted as independent confirmation of this header test.

## Finding

**No tested digest equals a complete aligned block of the 256-byte grid payload from LP2-49–51.** We reused the exact artifact corpus fixed for the [LP2-56 printed-hash check](#/experiments/lp2-56-internal-artifact-hashes): 412 named variants representing **324 distinct byte strings**. Seven hash algorithms produced **16,848 exact block comparisons** and zero matches. This tests one possible structure for the grid bytes; it does not identify what they mean.

![The 256-byte payload divided into 16-, 32- and 64-byte blocks, with seven digest algorithms and no exact matches.](experiments/records/lp2-56-aligned-digest-blocks/blocks.svg)

The question is whether the grid might contain whole hashes of already preserved puzzle material. A hash has a fixed byte length, so we cut the payload from **byte zero** into non-overlapping blocks of that length and compared complete digest bytes. The test used neither a sliding window nor the hexadecimal *text* of a digest.

| Block size | Complete blocks | Hashes checked | Comparisons |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: |
| 16 bytes | 16 | MD5 | 5,184 |
| 32 bytes | 8 | SHA-256, SHA3-256, BLAKE2s-256 | 7,776 |
| 64 bytes | 4 | SHA-512, SHA3-512, BLAKE2b-512 | 3,888 |

The inputs were the **75 original page JPEGs**, four exact newline forms of each of the **75 stored raw page strings**, four forms of each of **nine stored literal sections**, and the resolved payload itself. Duplicate byte strings were hashed once. The [candidate map](experiments/records/lp2-56-aligned-digest-blocks/candidate-map.json) retains all 412 names and their byte hashes; the [input plan](experiments/records/lp2-56-aligned-digest-blocks/plan.json) pins the earlier corpus and payload by SHA-256. The payload comes from the [LP2-49–51 grid extraction](#/experiments/rsa-window-54-source-replay), not from the printed 512-bit value on LP2-56.

## Why the zero is bounded

For each of the seven algorithms, a synthetic 256-byte container held a known candidate digest in its **first and last aligned blocks**. The same scanner found both positions and did not mistake reversed digest bytes for a match. Standard `abc` digest vectors also passed. These controls check the scanner's boundaries, byte order, and hash API; they do not show that a real grid block should be a hash.

Other origins, overlapping or bit-shifted windows, changed input bytes, padding, hash truncation, and different algorithms were outside this test. The result rejects only the precise claim that **one of these 324 candidate byte strings hashes to one of these complete aligned blocks under these seven algorithms**. It cannot rule out a digest embedded elsewhere in the grid or a different interpretation of the payload.

## Reproduce

From the repository root, run:

```text
python experiments/records/lp2-56-aligned-digest-blocks/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp2-56-aligned-digest-blocks/check.py
```

The runner computes each candidate digest once per algorithm and fans it out to the matching block size. The independent checker rebuilds the input bytes and searches in the opposite direction: it indexes candidate digests, then asks which payload blocks appear in that index. Both verify the pinned source files. The [result summary](experiments/records/lp2-56-aligned-digest-blocks/results.json) includes the block counts, comparisons, matches and all seven planted-control outcomes.

# Could the LP2-56 number be four MD5 hashes?

The ending of [LP2-56](#/reader/lp2-56) prints 128 hexadecimal characters: **64 bytes**. One bounded way to read them is as four consecutive 16-byte values, the length of an MD5 digest. We compared each complete block with MD5 of the exact bytes in the preserved Liberpedia artifact corpus.

**Result: none of the four blocks matched.** The corpus contains 412 named variants representing 324 distinct byte strings. We computed MD5 once per distinct input and made **1,296 exact block comparisons**. Each block had zero hits.

![Four consecutive 16-byte blocks of the LP2-56 printed value, each with zero exact MD5 matches in the fixed candidate corpus.](experiments/records/lp2-56-four-md5-target-blocks/blocks.svg)

This closes only the stated construction for these inputs. It does **not** show that LP2-56 is not a sequence of MD5 values: the intended input could be a web page or other bytes absent from the corpus. Nor does it test modified encodings, another reading of the printed value, truncated digests, a different offset, or a different algorithm. If all four blocks had candidate matches, a proposed four-part explanation would still need to justify the input selection and printed order; no such ambiguity arose here.

## Exact input and comparison rule

The target is the five hexadecimal runs between separators in the archived LP2-56 reading, with the terminal slash marks removed. Decoding those 128 characters gives 64 bytes. Blocks start at byte **0, 16, 32, and 48**; each occupies exactly 16 bytes. The comparison uses binary digest bytes, not their printed hexadecimal characters.

The [frozen artifact corpus](#/experiments/lp2-56-internal-artifact-hashes) consists of original page JPEGs, four precise text-encoding variants of stored page raw text and section readings, plus one resolved 256-byte grid payload. Their paths and SHA-256 hashes are pinned in its [source plan](experiments/records/lp2-56-internal-artifact-hashes/plan.json). That earlier experiment tested three 64-byte digest algorithms against the **whole** printed LP2-56 target. This record asks the distinct four-block MD5 question. The [aligned grid-payload test](#/experiments/lp2-56-aligned-digest-blocks) instead compares artifact hashes with blocks of a different, **256-byte grid payload**.

The runner verifies the printed target against the archived page text and all candidate source-file hashes. It checks MD5 of `abc` against its standard test value, then plants known MD5 digests at the first and last blocks of a synthetic 64-byte container. The independent checker rebuilds the candidate bytes, hashes them and checks all four block positions and the controls. The controls pass, including rejection of byte-reversed digest matches.

Run from the repository root:

```text
python experiments/records/lp2-56-four-md5-target-blocks/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp2-56-four-md5-target-blocks/check.py
```

The [plan](experiments/records/lp2-56-four-md5-target-blocks/plan.json), [results](experiments/records/lp2-56-four-md5-target-blocks/results.json) and [checker](experiments/records/lp2-56-four-md5-target-blocks/check.py) pin the bytes, bounds and outputs. This is a new test of a specific construction, **not** a replay of a claimed historical attempt.

## Result

**None of the 1,236 declared hash comparisons equals the 512-bit value printed on LP2-56.** This covers 412 byte candidates and three algorithms. Some text variants produce identical bytes, so there are **324 distinct input byte strings**. The result is a narrow check of these preserved files, not a test of every possible message, encoding or file associated with Cicada 3301.

![Four input families compared under three 512-bit hashes; no exact matches.](experiments/records/lp2-56-internal-artifact-hashes/coverage.svg)

The printed target occupies **five rows totaling 128 hexadecimal characters**, or 64 bytes. It is a plausible digest length but the page does not identify a hash function or an input. Testing a digest requires both. A suggested input chosen after looking at the target creates an unbounded search, so this record fixed a finite set before computing matches.

## What went into the check

| Input | Byte rule | Candidates |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Original manuscript images | Exact bytes of all 75 archived JPEGs | 75 |
| Rune transcriptions | Each of the 75 stored `raw` strings encoded as UTF-8 | 300 variants |
| Stored literal sections | Nine sections made by joining their stored `reading.literal` strings in page order | 36 variants |
| Resolved grid payload | Exact 256-byte payload already extracted in the LP2-54 source replay | 1 |

The nine literal sections include **LP2-56's printed hash text itself**; that entry is an inventory check, not a decoded passage. The other eight are readings. The text counts include four stated byte forms per string: exact UTF-8; LF changed to CRLF; one final LF removed if present; and exactly one final LF ensured. The two cover-page rune strings are empty; they remain in the audit so the inventory is complete. No text was translated, respelled, uppercased, padded or reinterpreted as hexadecimal. Each candidate was hashed with **SHA-512, SHA3-512 and BLAKE2b-512** and compared byte for byte with the printed target.

This revisits a public proposal to hash the page JPEGs under SHA-512 and BLAKE2b. Its saved source table reports 75 values for each algorithm, but did not preserve the source JPEG bytes. This check uses Liberpedia's preserved originals, whose exact SHA-256 values are pinned in the [input plan](experiments/records/lp2-56-internal-artifact-hashes/plan.json). It adds the other declared local artifacts; it does not equate two image sets whose byte identity was not established.

**Whirlpool and Streebog were not run.** No trusted implementation with a verified control vector was available in this environment. A failure to find a match among the three run algorithms says nothing about either excluded algorithm, a different file, a URL response, or an undisclosed byte transformation.

## Reproduce

From the repository root, run `python experiments/records/lp2-56-internal-artifact-hashes/run.py` to recreate the [1,236-row digest table](experiments/records/lp2-56-internal-artifact-hashes/cases.jsonl) and [summary](experiments/records/lp2-56-internal-artifact-hashes/results.json). Then run `python experiments/records/lp2-56-internal-artifact-hashes/check.py`. The checker independently reconstructs every input byte string and digest, verifies source-file hashes and standard `abc` algorithm vectors, and checks the 64-byte target extraction. Both use Python's standard library.

records.article:
## Result

**Neither Whirlpool nor Streebog-512 matches the complete 512-bit value printed on LP2-56** for any of the 412 previously frozen artifact-byte variants. The 412 variants contain **324 distinct byte strings**. We hashed each distinct string once with each algorithm—648 digest operations—then reported every named input comparison. Whirlpool has one digest display; Streebog was compared in both ordinary byte order and the byte-reversed display used in [RFC 6986](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6986.html). That yields **1,236 full-value comparisons, zero matches**. Reversing its display is a notation check, not a third algorithm.

![Whirlpool and Streebog-512 were applied to the frozen artifact bytes; all full-value comparisons missed the LP2-56 target.](experiments/records/lp2-56-whirlpool-stribog/coverage.svg)

This extends the [earlier exact-byte matrix](#/experiments/lp2-56-internal-artifact-hashes) without changing its inputs. It uses all 75 preserved manuscript JPEGs, 75 stored raw rune texts under four declared newline forms, nine stored literal sections under the same forms, and one exact 256-byte grid payload. One literal section is the printed LP2-56 hash itself, not a decoded passage. The [source plan](experiments/records/lp2-56-internal-artifact-hashes/plan.json) pins the files and byte rules; the [extension plan](experiments/records/lp2-56-whirlpool-stribog/plan.json) pins the added algorithms, controls and display rule.

## Algorithm checks

The installed **libgcrypt 1.12.2** provides both 64-byte digests. Before touching manuscript inputs, its Whirlpool output for `abc` matched the [Whirlpool reference vector reproduced in the Linux cryptographic test suite](https://android.googlesource.com/kernel/msm/+/2d94dfc8c38edf63e91e48fd55c3a8822b6a9ced/crypto/tcrypt.h). Its Streebog-512 output matched **both 512-bit examples** in [RFC 6986](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6986.html#section-10). The RFC writes the message and digest as most-significant-byte-first bitstrings; their displayed bytes must be reversed to check a normal byte-oriented library call. The record pins the exact test messages and expected outputs.

The search compared the whole 64-byte digest with the whole printed value. It did not look for partial matches or adjust input bytes to make one appear. The result covers these two installed algorithm implementations and these preserved artifact bytes. It does not rule out a different source file, a keyed or salted construction, another input normalization, or older Whirlpool-0/Whirlpool-T variants.

## Reproduce

On a machine with libgcrypt, run `python experiments/records/lp2-56-whirlpool-stribog/run.py`, then `python experiments/records/lp2-56-whirlpool-stribog/check.py`. Both accept `--libgcrypt PATH` for another installation; the pinned Windows DLL is used by default when present. The runner uses the library's one-shot hash API; the checker independently reconstructs the candidate bytes and uses its streaming API. Both require all three published control vectors to pass. The [result table](experiments/records/lp2-56-whirlpool-stribog/cases.jsonl) and [summary](experiments/records/lp2-56-whirlpool-stribog/results.json) record every full comparison.

records.article:
# Fixed alphabet transformations and the warning opening

## Why test this?

A newcomer can reasonably try reusing the warning's Atbash method, shifting the rune alphabet, or reversing the text. These are small, finite searches. The difficult part is deciding what counts as success without picking an attractive fragment after looking at the output.

This test uses one deliberately narrow criterion: the first 12 decoded rune indices must equal the first 12 decoded runes of LP1-01's warning. The criterion is motivated by an existing reading, but there is no evidence that an unsolved page must repeat that opening. This is not an English detector.

## Plan and scope

The plan and runner were committed as `faab48f` before the first execution. All 56 archived pages LP2-00–55 are included, corresponding to their unsolved status in the source snapshot. This is not a claim about their present-day solving status.

For every page, keep all recognized runes, including headings, and remove other characters. Use indices 0–28. Try both original and whole-stream reversed order. For each order, evaluate both multipliers a = 1 and a = -1 with every additive offset b = 0–28, using `(a * index + b) % 29`.

The positive multiplier covers all constant shifts. The negative multiplier covers alphabet reversal with every shift; ordinary Atbash is a = -1, b = 28. The identity is included. Reversing a complete stream is not the same as reversing individual rows or words.

| Transformation class | Orders | Offsets | Pages | Cases | Exact matches |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Constant shift | 2 | 29 | 56 | 3248 | 0 |
| Reversed alphabet plus offset | 2 | 29 | 56 | 3248 | 0 |
| Total |  |  |  | 6496 | 0 |

These are parameter cases, not a promise that every resulting string is distinct.

## Result and interpretation

All 6496 cases completed. No output began with the specified 12-rune warning prefix. Every full candidate sequence is retained in the JSON output, not only its prefix or an attractive excerpt. Each case records the page, order, multiplier, offset, output indices, and exact-match flag.

This finding is negative only for the declared opening at position zero. It does not rule out meaningful text beginning differently, a heading that needs separate treatment, another region, or an arbitrary substitution. There is no significance estimate because this is an exhaustive exact-match query, not a statistical test of whether the text is English.

## Reproduce and inspect

Use Python 3.12.10 and the repository checkout:

```
python experiments/records/lp2-alphabet-warning-prefix/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp2-alphabet-warning-prefix/check.py
```

The first command regenerates and compares every candidate, input hash, and match flag. The second uses a separately constructed alphabet-walk lookup to verify all output indices and confirms that every parameter tuple is unique. It also checks the known warning's opening A,W,A against indices 24,7,24. Neither command uses a network service.

[Download all candidate outputs](experiments/records/lp2-alphabet-warning-prefix/results.json). To save a fresh report, run the runner with `--output my-prefix-scan.json`; it refuses to overwrite an existing file. Read `alphabet` to map output indices back to runes. Latin transliteration involves additional conventions and is not applied here.

## Retest and changes after inspection

Codex reran the complete scan and the separate oracle on 20 October 2026. All 6496 candidates reproduced exactly. No input-selection rule, prefix length, transformation, or stopping rule changed after the first result. The independent oracle was added after the first run as a verification step, not used to select results. Human review remains pending.

## Next variants

A different known opening, prefix position, heading convention, or transformation range must be declared as a new variant with the changes visible. Do not append extra guesses to this baseline and report only the final combined search. An exact match in any later variant would still require checking the rest of the page.
