# Original JPEGs: guarded OutGuess build comparison

## What this test asks

The original default-key sweep had 41 abnormal exits. Those failures leave an important question: did the retrieval reach an identifiable error condition, and would a more explicit check change the extracted bytes?

This variant uses a clean build with three diagnostic guards. A guard checks a condition before an operation that would otherwise be invalid and stops with an explanatory message. Here the checks concern the retrieval bit position, iterator capacity, and a zero iterator value used by a remainder operation. They are diagnostic changes, not a new decryption method.

The [original baseline](#/experiments/outguess-default-key) remains available with its unchanged results. Both records belong to the same experiment family.

## What stayed fixed

The inputs are all 75 manuscript JPEGs plus the 2014 opening image and compasses cover, in their original bytes. Image hashes, the literal key `Default key`, and the 20-second timeout match the baseline. No image was recompressed or edited. The ten known payload controls run first; a control failure would stop the sweep.

The scope and runner were committed as `40890c5` before execution. The earlier 13-case pilot helped establish the build procedure; those cases are included here and are not presented as unseen validation. This is one complete 77-image comparison, not a search over keys or build settings.

## What changed

The recorded executable was compiled afresh from upstream commit `24810e14327c2bbeedeaadd3e24491f2a4425c02`, with the documented Windows portability changes and explicit guard patches. All 54 C files were compiled; object files from the original build were not reused. The build specification records compiler identity, source hashes and commands.

The clean guarded Windows executable has SHA-256 `bdc1810e59cb1152e7c3da88b38eaedfe49eba1656b4a4ab6f8c2b3f40126273`.

The clean executable differs in hash from the archived pilot executable, although it reproduced all 13 pilot results exactly. The full comparison below uses the clean executable. This does not establish bit-for-bit reproducible compilation across toolchains.

## Results

| Baseline outcome | Guarded outcome | Images |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Successful exit | Same successful exit, diagnostic and bytes | 31 |
| Existing rejection | Same rejection, diagnostic and bytes | 5 |
| Abnormal exit | Explicit zero-iterator guard; unchanged empty output | 41 |

All ten positive controls match. The 31 successful exits consist of those ten controls and 21 unverified outputs. Every one of the 77 payload byte streams matches the baseline exactly; no new candidate output appeared.

All 41 changed cases report `Guard: iterator skipmod zero`, with their individual bit counts and offsets retained in the saved report. For example, LP1-14 reports `Guard: iterator skipmod zero at off=645437 bits=645682`. The guarded build checks this zero value before the iterator's remainder operation.

The [comparison graphic](experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/results/comparison.svg) summarizes the counts. The [per-image comparison](experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/results/comparison.json) and [complete diagnostics](experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/results/report.json) retain the underlying evidence.

## What the result means

The new build gives a specific diagnostic for all 41 previously abnormal cases. This is useful for investigating the implementation and for preventing those failures from being mistaken for clean negative results.

It does not authenticate the 21 candidate outputs. It does not prove any image lacks hidden data. Both executables share the same upstream source and Windows port, so this is not validation by an independent implementation or another platform. The guarded run is also not a captured stack trace from the original executable.

## Reproduce the saved comparison

Download this experiment's bundle and the original-images archive, then extract both into the same folder, preserving their paths. Follow the bundle's START-HERE file to verify the archive and required image hashes. From that folder run:

```text
python experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/compare.py --check
```

This needs Python and the supplied data, but does not execute OutGuess. It verifies the plan dependencies and image hashes, checks both sets of saved outputs, and compares bytes and diagnostics directly. It recomputes the saved comparison instead of trusting its reported equality flags.

To regenerate the chart after that audit:

```text
python experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/figure.py
```

## Repeat retrieval from a source build

Supply a clean checkout of the pinned upstream source and a compatible MinGW-W64 GCC toolchain. The included build script does not fetch or install these dependencies. Choose an output directory that does not yet exist:

```text
python experiments/records/outguess-guard-pilot/build.py --source /path/to/outguess-source --output /path/to/new-build
python experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/run.py --outguess /path/to/new-build/outguess.exe --output /path/to/new-results
```

The runner requires the recorded executable hash. If compilation produces a different hash, preserve its build report and define a separate comparison; do not overwrite the expected hash to make the check pass. The new-results directory must not already exist. The saved-evidence audit above checks the committed results, not this new directory. To rerun retrieval and compare directly with the committed results, use `run.py --outguess /path/to/new-build/outguess.exe --check`.

## Remaining work

Human review is pending. An independently documented platform or implementation would address a different uncertainty from the guard comparison. Candidate-payload analysis should be a separate bounded experiment, retaining all outputs and avoiding the assumption that process success implies a message.

# Six keyed OutGuess probes on LP2

## Result

Six fixed passphrases were tried against each of the 58 original LP2 JPEGs. OutGuess returned nonempty bytes in **232 of 348** runs. None of those byte streams passed the basic checks for a readable message or a common file header. The result is **inconclusive** about hidden data: a successful OutGuess exit does not authenticate its output.

![Count of nonempty retrievals for each of six keys. Bars count outputs, not messages.](experiments/records/outguess-keyed-lp2/figure.svg)

| Literal key | Nonempty outputs | Bytes per nonempty output |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `3301` | 24 / 58 | 54,051 |
| `LIBER PRIMUS` | 57 / 58 | 29,932 |
| `GEMATRIA PRIMUS` | 47 / 58 | 47,513 |
| `CIRCUMFERENCE` | 58 / 58 | 19,957 |
| `DIVINITY` | 34 / 58 | 51,011 |
| `SELF-RELIANCE` | 12 / 58 | 61,831 |

Each key produced exactly one nonempty output length across the pages, though the output hashes differ. Printable ASCII accounts for only 37.5–39.2% of those bytes. No output begins with a PGP, ZIP, PDF, PNG, GIF or JPEG header. These are descriptive checks, not a complete file-format classifier or a proof that no payload exists.

## What was tested

The six literal, case-sensitive phrases above were fixed before the 348-case run. They are a small manuscript-derived probe, not an exhaustive dictionary. The archive's historical keyed attempts were reviewed *after* this list had been frozen and did not change it. Original image bytes and the guarded OutGuess executable are fixed by SHA-256 in the [plan](experiments/records/outguess-keyed-lp2/plan.json).

The control first embeds a known 43-byte text into a separate synthetic JPEG under each key. Its six retained carriers recover that exact text only with their matching key: all **36 correct-key and cross-key checks** passed. Initial synthetic covers exposed a guarded retrieval-bound failure under one of the correct keys. The final 800×800 cover and six working carrier bytes were pinned before the LP2 grid; the exception and replacement are recorded in the plan. This control verifies that this build can recover a message when one is embedded under these keys. It does not validate the unsolved-page outputs.

This is a keyed extension of the [default-key OutGuess baseline](#/experiments/outguess-default-key). It checks this build, these six passphrases and these original JPEGs. Other passwords, transformed images, other steganography tools, and a modified OutGuess implementation remain outside its scope.

## Inspect or repeat

Download the experiment bundle and original JPEG archive, preserving their paths. [The saved receipt](experiments/records/outguess-keyed-lp2/results.json) lists every exit status, diagnostic, output size and SHA-256. [The output archive](experiments/records/outguess-keyed-lp2/outputs.zip) contains the exact 348 retrieved byte files, including empty ones, for independent inspection. A large binary output is not itself evidence of a message.

The bundle includes the [exact guarded Windows executable](experiments/records/outguess-keyed-lp2/tool/outguess-guarded-win64.exe) used for this run (SHA-256 `bdc1810e59cb1152e7c3da88b38eaedfe49eba1656b4a4ab6f8c2b3f40126273`) and its [copyright and license notices](experiments/records/outguess-keyed-lp2/tool/NOTICES.txt). This product includes software developed by Niels Provos. This software is based in part on the work of the Independent JPEG Group. Extract `outputs.zip` into a folder and, on Windows, run:

```text
python experiments/records/outguess-keyed-lp2/check.py --outguess experiments/records/outguess-keyed-lp2/tool/outguess-guarded-win64.exe --output-dir PATH/TO/outputs
```

This independently checks the original image hashes, all 348 retained output hashes and all 36 planted-key retrievals. To repeat the actual image grid, use `run.py --outguess experiments/records/outguess-keyed-lp2/tool/outguess-guarded-win64.exe --output-dir PATH/TO/new-output --check`. The run compares every receipt with the saved report and prints its counts; it does not replace the saved report. The executable's SHA-256 must match the plan; the [pinned upstream source](https://github.com/resurrecting-open-source-projects/outguess/tree/24810e14327c2bbeedeaadd3e24491f2a4425c02) and [guarded-build specification](experiments/records/outguess-guard-pilot/build-spec.json) document its source and patches. A rebuild under a different toolchain need not yield the same executable hash; compare it as a separate build.

# How much do unresolved LP2 page joins change word-length counts?

The published LP2 word-length census joins adjacent pages when their archived text meets rune to rune. That rule yields **2,896 rune tokens**. If a separator is inserted at each of the **32 rune-to-rune page edges**, the same 12,956 runes yield **2,928 tokens**. This experiment measures how much the statistics depend on that parsing choice. It does not decide which edges actually split words in the manuscript.

![Side-by-side rune-token length counts for joined and separated page edges](experiments/records/page-join-sensitivity/token-lengths.svg)

## Fixed comparison

Use the archived text for LP2-00–55 and the site's 29-rune alphabet. Remove slash and CR/LF row wraps, retain headings and other punctuation, and count rune runs with optional internal apostrophes. There are three prespecified readings: concatenate every page; insert a space at all 32 edges whose archived end and start are both runes; and insert a space at each such edge one at a time. No rune is changed or omitted. The [boundary inventory](#/wiki/transcription-checking?section=page-joins) supplies the distinction between a rune-to-rune candidate and a verified word join.

| Measure | All edges joined | All 32 candidates separated |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Rune tokens | 2,896 | 2,928 |
| One-rune tokens | 83 | 99 |
| Two-rune tokens | 448 | 465 |
| Three-rune tokens | 720 | 726 |
| Tokens at least 10 runes long | 109 | 104 |
| Maximum token length | 14 | 14 |
| 11–11–10 length windows | 1 | 1 |

All 32 individual splits add exactly one token under this tokenizer. Five individual edges—LP2-21/22, 24/25, 42/43, 46/47 and 52/53—each reduce the number of tokens at least 10 runes long by one. The [machine-readable result](experiments/records/page-join-sensitivity/results.json) lists every edge separately. The LP2-21 11–11–10 observation survives both endpoint policies, but this says nothing about its chance frequency or interpretation.

These endpoints are sensitivity cases, not manuscript corrections. A real reading could join some edges and split others. The source text can also omit a mark, and rune-to-rune edges can cross section boundaries. Word counts, repeated-token counts and word-reset cipher inputs depend on the boundary rule; rune frequencies and whole-stream IoC do not, because both versions contain the identical ordered runes. The reported 2,896 tokens are a transparent parsing convention, not 2,896 established words.

## Reproduce and extend

With Python 3 and no packages, run `python experiments/records/page-join-sensitivity/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/page-join-sensitivity/check.py` from the repository root or the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/page-join-sensitivity.zip). The first command checks the source hashes, complete report and figure. The second uses an independent character scanner to verify the 32 candidate edges, the two histograms, every one-edge token count, and the invariant 12,956-rune total. The plan fixes the inputs and three comparisons before interpreting them.

The next useful refinement is to record image-reviewed separators at particular edges and rerun the same script with those decisions frozen. Until then, a word-based cipher claim should specify its page-edge policy and show whether its result survives plausible changes at the relevant edges. See the [word-length guide](#/wiki/word-lengths) for the counting rules and complete token ledger.

records.article:
# Does trimming page margins reveal a special line alignment?

A source discussion suggested reading “shed the circumference” as an instruction to remove manuscript margins and place pages side by side. It described this as something to try, not as a finished decryption. A side-by-side picture is easy to make but easy to overread: text lines can align because pages share a layout. This experiment asks the narrower, measurable question: **do adjacent LP2 pages line up more distinctively than other pages of the same design?**

![All 36 fixed-crop row-alignment scores among LP2-40–48; outlined cells are adjacent pairs](experiments/records/page-margin-row-alignment/row-alignment.svg)

## What was fixed

The nine original JPEGs LP2-40–48 are all 2400 × 3600 pixels. This is a continuous run of text-heavy pages with the same plant-border design; the source proposal did **not** designate these pages. From every image, take the same rectangle, x = 650–1749 and y = 620–2899. This sheds both illustrated sides and keeps the central writing. Preserve the original y coordinates: no page is shifted to fit another.

For each y row, sample every third x pixel. Call the row occupied when more than 12 samples have grayscale value below 90. The similarity of two row masks is their occupied-row intersection divided by their union (Jaccard score). Compare all **eight consecutive pairs** with **all 28 nonconsecutive pairs** from the same run. The [plan](experiments/records/page-margin-row-alignment/plan.json) fixes the crop, threshold, score and controls; [results.json](experiments/records/page-margin-row-alignment/results.json) gives every pair and each page’s row bands.

## What the pages show

The mean score is 0.764 for consecutive pages and 0.672 for controls. That difference by itself is not evidence of a special join: four adjacent pairs score exactly 1.000, **but six nonadjacent controls also score 1.000**. In particular, every pair within LP2-44–48 has the same row mask under this rule. The text grid is reused across multiple pages, so an apparently perfect horizontal alignment cannot identify the correct next page. LP2-40’s enlarged red initial and the larger gaps on some earlier pages also change the measured bands. Every pair, including poor fits, appears in the figure and result file.

This tests only vertical placement of dark text rows after one fixed crop. It cannot tell whether the final rune of one line continues at the beginning of another, whether a word crosses a page boundary, or whether “shed the circumference” refers to physical page margins at all. The source left crop, page order, registration and success condition open. Selecting those *after* seeing an attractive join would create a large search space. The observed score difference has no significance test because pair comparisons share pages and the groups were not random independent samples.

## Reproduce or extend

Run `python experiments/records/page-margin-row-alignment/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/page-margin-row-alignment/check.py` from the repository root or extracted bundle. They require Python 3 and Pillow. `run.py` checks each JPEG’s SHA-256 and the complete saved result; `check.py` scans the image buffers independently and recomputes all 36 scores. `plot.py` regenerates the SVG.

A stronger visual continuation test would need a page sequence and a predeclared rune-level seam rule, plus nonadjacent pages matched for template and line count. The [page-join sensitivity record](#/experiments/page-join-sensitivity) separately measures what happens to word statistics when text transcripts are joined or split at page edges. Neither result supplies an LP2 plaintext.

records.article:
# What does the LP2-40 “FOR EVERY” calculation actually establish?

A [reported attempt](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=page40-for-every-mobius) reads the first two rune groups on [LP2-40](#/reader/lp2-40) as **FOR EVERY**. It interprets mirrored border work as a reason to use Atbash, floral details as the numbers 13 and 31, and their difference, 18, as a shift. It then adds a prime-minus-one stream, treats the initial F as a skipped zero, and suggests a Möbius-directed running key for the difference still needed. Those links from artwork to operations are the solver's proposed interpretation; this audit does not establish them as intended clues.

The source discussion itself describes the example as a working theory built partly backwards from a desired reading. Its linked spreadsheet was described as changing over time. We identify the preserved discussion by SHA-256 `2338de900f4ec231d42791c988640317241880675b35ff68af42ee162cb6573a`; the file is not redistributed here. The replay uses the numerical rows printed in that discussion, the [archived LP2-40 transcription](#/page/lp2-40), and the stored Gematria Primus table.

## Eight positions, one fixed calculation

The first two archived groups contain three and five runes. Their indices are `0, 9, 19 / 26, 6, 23, 25, 8`, matching the source's quoted ciphertext row. The proposed **FOR EVERY** indices are `0, 3, 4 / 18, 1, 18, 4, 26`. On the seven positions after F, shifting each proposed plaintext index by 18 and reflecting with Atbash gives `7, 6, 21, 9, 21, 6, 13`. Adding the source's prime-minus-one stream modulo 29 gives the intermediate row `0, 8, 8 / 25, 15, 2, 18, 0`.

![The fixed rule is compared with eight archived indices. Seven non-F outputs differ; the final row is a residual derived from the observed ciphertext.](experiments/records/page40-for-every-arithmetic/first-eight-trace.svg)

The fixed layers match **zero of seven non-F positions**. The initial F matches because the source holds it at zero rather than transforming it. Subtracting the intermediate row from the observed ciphertext yields residuals `0, 1, 11, 1, 20, 21, 7, 8` modulo 29. The source writes `−8` instead of `21` at the sixth position; these are the same modulo 29. These residuals are calculated *after looking at the ciphertext*. Adding them back necessarily reconstructs the target and is not yet evidence for a running-key rule.

The proposed phrase's GP sums are **FOR = 20** (composite), **EVERY = 251** (prime), and **FOR EVERY = 271** (prime). Thus the whole phrase satisfies a prime-sum filter, while both words individually do not. A prime sum is a property of this candidate, not an independent reading of the runes.

## Where the replay stops

The discussion does not fix the Möbius argument or starting point, how neighboring values form the proposed trigram state, which of the eight possible key formulas belongs to each state, how signs and zero are treated, or exactly when the stream advances over F and separators. Its later notes explore modified Slidefair, Quagmire-like matrices and a Fibonacci autokey as different follow-ups; those are **not** tested here. The incomplete spreadsheet and absent fixed state table prevent an honest end-to-end replay of the proposed running key. The source itself says the state flexibility could make the arithmetic fit.

To turn the running-key idea into a test, choose a complete state table and seed **before** inspecting additional text; specify plaintext-versus-ciphertext feedback, order of operations, F handling and word boundaries; then compare a continuous output on held-out page text with matched controls. A crib fit on these eight positions alone cannot do that work.

## Reproduce this audit

From the repository root or [downloadable experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/page40-for-every-arithmetic.zip), run:

```text
python experiments/records/page40-for-every-arithmetic/run.py --check
python experiments/records/page40-for-every-arithmetic/check.py
python experiments/records/page40-for-every-arithmetic/plot.py --check
```

The [plan](experiments/records/page40-for-every-arithmetic/plan.json) pins the source's printed rows, input hashes, fixed formula, success criterion and stopping rule. The [complete result](experiments/records/page40-for-every-arithmetic/results.json) lists every intermediate and fitted difference. The checker independently reads the rune text, recomputes the seven transformed indices and verifies each congruence and prime sum. This is an **arithmetic audit of one proposed opening**, not a disproof of every artwork-based or running-key method.

records.article:
## What changed from the baseline

The [full-corpus comparison](#/experiments/parallel-languages) used 1,012 evaluation sentences per language. Here we divide that evaluation split into **eight consecutive, disjoint blocks** and compare shorter passages. Each block contains the same sentence IDs in all eight languages. No sentences were chosen because their statistics looked promising.

The first four blocks contain 127 sentences each, and the last four contain 126. Exact one-based sentence ranges are recorded in the results. The tokenization and distance definitions are unchanged.

## Results

**English is the closest of the eight language profiles to the pooled manuscript in all eight blocks, in each of the three representations.** This supports the stability of that relative ranking across these shorter passages. It does not identify the plaintext language.

Using letter units, the block sizes and manuscript distances are:

| Language | Tokens per block, range | Word-length distance, range |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| English | 2,613–3,002 | 0.0710–0.1035 |
| Finnish | 1,927–2,105 | 0.3726–0.4316 |
| French | 3,047–3,318 | 0.1731–0.2079 |
| German | 2,623–2,927 | 0.1696–0.1961 |
| Italian | 2,880–3,181 | 0.2274–0.2467 |
| Portuguese | 2,818–3,147 | 0.2007–0.2300 |
| Spanish | 3,106–3,467 | 0.2091–0.2402 |
| Welsh | 2,884–3,206 | 0.1416–0.1940 |

The target has 2,896 rune tokens. These are smaller aligned passages, not exactly size-matched samples: their token counts range from **1,927 to 3,467**. Translating the same content changes word counts. Keeping the same sentence ranges preserves the content control; truncating every language at exactly 2,896 words would no longer compare exactly the same passages. This design documents that tradeoff rather than hiding it.

## Does the statistic recognize known languages at this scale?

For each block, we compare its word-length histogram against all eight full development-language histograms. The closest development profile is the corresponding language in **64 of 64 decisions**, separately for letter units, accent-folded letters, and GP grouping. The raw report includes every distance and the full confusion matrices, including zeros.

That is a control on these eight translated languages within FLORES. It is not a success rate for cipher language identification. The corpus shares translation practices and source genre; the manuscript does not. The three representations also reuse the same text and are not independent replications.

## Bounds and limitations

- All 1,012 evaluation sentences are used once per language, with no overlap between blocks. Development text is used only for the reference profiles.
- A source article can cross a block boundary. Blocks are therefore not independent draws, and the 64 decisions are not treated as independent trials. No binomial accuracy interval or language posterior is calculated.
- The manuscript remains pooled LP2-00–55, with headings and the baseline boundary convention. This does not test each section separately.
- Word-length comparison requires preserved boundaries and one ciphertext rune per counted plaintext unit. GP grouping remains an orthographic sensitivity, not a validated phonetic transcription.
- No genre-matched corpus or known decoded LP control is included in this variant. The separate [known-reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) now covers the nine documented LP sections. A genre-matched corpus remains open.

## Reproduce

The experiment download includes the aligned corpus, token ledger, baseline helper, independent tokenizer, frozen plan and result ledger. Python 3 standard library only; no network, API or model is used.

```sh
python experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/run.py --check
python experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/check.py
```

The plan was committed before block scoring; its dependency hash was refreshed for a chart-only baseline change before scoring began. The first command verifies input hashes and recomputes the full report. The second independently reconstructs all 192 block profiles with a regex tokenizer and exact rational total-variation distances, checks all nearest-reference decisions, and verifies that the block ranges cover the evaluation sentences exactly once.

[Results and confusion matrices](experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/results.json) · [Frozen plan](experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/plan.json) · [Baseline distributions and source attribution](#/experiments/parallel-languages)

FLORES source text and this derived account are offered under CC BY-SA 4.0. See the source attribution included with the baseline files.

records.article:
## What this comparison tells us

**English has the closest word-length distribution among the eight reference languages tested.** This comparison is useful only if the manuscript's separators correspond to plaintext word boundaries and the encryption preserves one counted unit per rune. Those conditions are unverified for unsolved LP2. The ordering of other close candidates changes when a fixed GP-style grouping is applied to all eight. A nearest distribution is not a plaintext identification or a decoded word.

The experiment uses translations of the **same 997 development sentences and 1,012 evaluation sentences** from FLORES-200. The languages were fixed before scoring: English, Welsh, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and Finnish. They give a manageable Latin-script comparison without adding a transliteration model for other scripts. They are not a shortlist inferred from the manuscript, and the ranking is not a search across all languages.

The plan and source files were committed in `738a812` before any scores were calculated. It is a predeclared comparison within this project, not an external preregistration. Human review is pending.

## Word-length results

The distance is **total variation** between word-length distributions: half the sum of their absolute frequency differences. Zero means identical distributions; one means no overlap. We count lengths 1 through 15 separately and put longer words in a final 16+ bin. A value of 0.084 is a distance, not an 8.4% chance of anything.

| Language | Letters | GP grouping sensitivity |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| English | 0.0840 | 0.1148 |
| Welsh | 0.1721 | 0.1731 |
| German | 0.1757 | 0.1708 |
| French | 0.1827 | 0.1759 |
| Portuguese | 0.2131 | 0.2058 |
| Spanish | 0.2240 | 0.2127 |
| Italian | 0.2359 | 0.2311 |
| Finnish | 0.4022 | 0.3927 |

[Open the comparison chart](experiments/records/parallel-languages/comparison.svg). The chart shows the same results with article-resampling ranges. The JSON also contains the accent-folded letter comparison, which keeps the same language order.

The ordering depends on the counting convention. A language ranking is conditional on both the corpus and the assumed relationship between plaintext units and ciphertext runes. The full table keeps every tested candidate visible.

## Why the rankings differ

The manuscript has a pronounced peak at length three: **24.86% of its tokens contain three runes**. The language profiles differ in how much mass they place at each length. The distribution chart shows the manuscript first, followed by all eight languages alphabetically, using identical scales and the same styling for every language.

The first-place result still has a visible mismatch: English has 19.07% three-letter words, below the manuscript's three-rune share. A ranking measures relative closeness among the tested profiles; it does not establish that the nearest profile is a good explanation of the ciphertext.

[Open all nine distribution panels](experiments/records/parallel-languages/distributions.svg). Lengths 9 and above are combined only for display; scoring retains the original 16 bins. Every full distribution is also available in the results JSON.

## The assumptions that make lengths useful

This comparison requires manuscript word boundaries to preserve plaintext word boundaries, and one counted plaintext unit to correspond to one ciphertext rune. A position-dependent substitution can preserve lengths even when letter frequencies change. Inserted nulls, deleted symbols, word splitting, different spacing, or units representing syllables can break the comparison.

The manuscript target is the existing [rune-token ledger](exports/unsolved-word-tokens.json): **2,896 tokens and 12,956 runes from LP2-00–55**, including headings. Line wraps and slash wraps are removed; tokens can continue across page boundaries. Internal apostrophes count zero, and decimal labels are excluded. See [word lengths](#/wiki/word-lengths) for the exact boundary convention and its historical alternatives. Pooling the pages assumes their aggregate is meaningful; it does not establish that every section has one language or cipher.

For FLORES, letters are lowercased and normalized to NFC. Alphabetic runs are words; internal straight or curly apostrophes are removed without splitting the word. Hyphens and other nonletters separate words. Numbers contribute no letters. Each sentence is tokenized independently. This is an explicit mechanical convention, not a linguist's definition of a word. The comparison retains every aligned sentence; it does not truncate each language to a different passage to equalize word totals.

The GP sensitivity folds combining accents and greedily groups ING, TH, EO, NG, OE, AE, IA, IO and EA, longest first. ING/NG, IO/IA, K/C and Z/S share symbols. Other letters remain. **This is not a validated translation into Gematria Primus.** Pronunciation, ambiguous segmentation and unsupported letters remain unresolved. A supplementary mechanical Welsh-digraph calculation is retained in the raw data as a representation check, not as a separate candidate category or a preferred model. It groups CH, DD, FF, NG, LL, PH, RH and TH and gives a length distance of 0.1466; it does not resolve morphological parsing. The raw-letter and GP profiles can contain more than 29 distinct symbols, so they cannot be literal bijective mappings into a 29-rune alphabet as written. This inventory mismatch is reported in the downloadable results rather than silently repaired by deleting rare letters.

## Repetition gives a different test

IoC is the probability that two different sampled positions contain the same symbol. Adjacent repetition here counts equal neighbors **within words only**. Both require stronger assumptions than lengths: equality must survive a fixed one-to-one substitution. They are not preserved by a general polyalphabetic cipher.

| Text, using letter units | IoC | Equal adjacent pairs |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Unsolved rune target | 0.03448 | 0.63% |
| English | 0.06597 | 2.42% |
| Welsh | 0.06387 | 5.74% |
| German | 0.07344 | 2.33% |
| French | 0.06912 | 2.42% |
| Portuguese | 0.07072 | 1.00% |
| Spanish | 0.07111 | 0.77% |
| Italian | 0.07305 | 4.57% |
| Finnish | 0.07282 | 9.31% |

The language profiles have letter IoCs between **0.06387 and 0.07344**, far from the target's **0.03448**. None of these profiles supplies a close single-substitution explanation of the pooled manuscript. The GP sensitivity does not remove that discrepancy. Spanish is closest on the adjacent-repeat measure, yet has a much poorer word-length match. These conflicting rankings are why we do not blend the measures into an unexplained “language likelihood.”

This does not eliminate Welsh, English or any other language under a different cipher. It weakens the proposed fixed-substitution comparison under these text and unit conventions. See [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants) for what different transformations preserve.

## Controls and sampling sensitivity

Each development-language word-length profile was compared with each evaluation-language profile. The nearest development profile identified the corresponding evaluation language **8 out of 8 times in each of the three representations**. That is a useful check that this dataset and statistic can distinguish the chosen languages at this sample size. It is not 100% accuracy on unknown manuscripts: there are only eight whole-document controls, drawn from the same benchmark, and they are much longer than the target.

For the error bars we resample the **281 source-article URL groups** in the evaluation split, with replacement, 200 times using seed 3301. All sentences from a sampled article are kept. The same article draw is used for all eight languages, preserving the matched-content comparison and avoiding treating every sentence as independent. English has the smallest length distance in all 200 draws in all three representations. This is stability to this corpus resampling—not a 100% probability that the manuscript is English. The target transcription is held fixed; these intervals omit uncertainty about its boundaries, genre and cipher.

FLORES contains translated web material. It controls subject matter across languages, but not the difference between that material and Liber Primus's philosophical style, historical spelling or possible nonstandard prose. Translation practices can also affect lengths. A separately fixed, genre-matched parallel corpus remains a follow-up. The [exact-token control](#/experiments/target-sized-languages) now checks complete 2,896-token samples: all reference samples identify their own language profile, but every manuscript-to-profile distance exceeds the corresponding observed control range. Those ranges are descriptive, not confidence limits or rejection thresholds. The [known-LP reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) is now complete as a computational comparison, with human review pending. A separate [shorter aligned-block variant](#/experiments/parallel-language-blocks) now checks eight disjoint evaluation blocks per language; it preserves matching sentences rather than enforcing exactly equal word counts.

## Reproduce it

Download this experiment's bundle. It includes the source translations, source-article metadata, plan, token ledger, scripts, result JSON and chart. No API, account, model download or network request is needed to rerun the analysis; Python 3's standard library is enough.

```sh
python experiments/records/parallel-languages/run.py --check
python experiments/records/parallel-languages/check.py
python experiments/records/parallel-languages/distribution_figure.py --check
```

The first command verifies input hashes, recomputes the comparisons and the 200 resamples, and checks the saved report and chart. Without `--check`, it writes those two outputs. The second uses a separate regex tokenizer and integer-count formulas to verify the 24 language profiles, additional digraph sensitivity, manuscript profile, IoC, repeated neighbors, distances and ordering. It does not independently reimplement the bootstrap. The final command checks that the distribution chart matches the saved counts; it does not perform another experiment. The ledger itself has a separate [transcription/word-length reproduction](#/wiki/word-lengths).

[Raw results](experiments/records/parallel-languages/results.json) · [Frozen plan](experiments/records/parallel-languages/plan.json) · [Source attribution](experiments/records/parallel-languages/SOURCE.txt)

## Sources and reuse

- [FLORES-200 documentation](https://github.com/facebookresearch/flores/blob/main/flores200/README.md): aligned translation benchmark and language list.
- [Original archive](https://dl.fbaipublicfiles.com/nllb/flores200_dataset.tar.gz): exact extracted translation and metadata files; archive and extracted-file hashes are recorded in the plan.
- [Dataset card and license](https://huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/flores): Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International. Source translations are redistributed unchanged. This derived analysis and its article are also offered under CC BY-SA 4.0.

## Check against known LP readings

The [known-reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) now tests all nine established reading sections and their pool. The pool ranks closest to English, while some individual sections do not. It also documents how LP2-56's embedded hash distorts an unfiltered letter-token count. This supplies a manuscript-specific caution beyond the within-FLORES controls.
records.reader_finding: English had the closest word-length pattern among the eight tested languages. It remained closest under all three counting methods.
records.reader_limit: This comparison assumes that encryption preserves word boundaries and word lengths. It ranks these reference texts; it does not identify the hidden language.

records.title: Do LP2 grid bytes track doublet gaps?
records.question: Do fixed-width or varint readings of the LP2-49–51 payload correlate with distances between adjacent equal-rune events in LP2?
records.summary: Seven declared readings of the pinned 256-byte payload show no strong rank alignment with 85 doublet gaps or the related 86-value sequence.

record_type.label: Method replay
record_type.description: Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading.

family.title: Grid encodings and doublet gaps
family.question: Do integer sequences read from the byte grid track the gaps between repeated runes?

variant.label: Seven readings of one byte version

scope.representation: Pinned 256-byte source grid and 86 within-page equal-rune-pair starts on archived LP2-00–55, concatenated in page order for gap distances.
scope.procedure: Decode seven fixed integer/varint readings at byte zero. Compare first available values with 85 inter-event distances and with the first one-based event coordinate plus those distances using tie-aware Spearman correlation. Audit all 84 nonzero rotations of the 85-gap target with the best-of-seven statistic.
scope.parameters: Seven byte readings; two targets; 14 comparisons; 85 gap distances; 84 alignment controls; published effect-size gate |rho| >= 0.5.
scope.exclusions: Other payload transcriptions, starting offsets, byte permutations, transforms, noncontiguous selections, distinct event definitions, and inference of a cipher mechanism.

records.finding: Among 14 fixed comparisons, the largest absolute Spearman rank correlation is 0.119, below the published 0.5 effect-size gate. For the primary 85-gap target, 83 of 84 nonzero circular alignments have an equal or larger best-of-seven correlation than the unshifted comparison.
records.limitations: Only seven direct readings, byte-zero alignment and two gap definitions are tested. Circular rotations are dependent descriptive controls, not a cipher null. Other byte transcriptions, transforms, offsets, selections and gap definitions remain open.
records.article:
# Do the byte-grid values encode doublet spacing?

**No direct rank alignment was found under seven specified byte readings.** The strongest absolute correlation is **0.119**, below the published 0.5 gate. This checks one way the [LP2-49–51 numerical grid](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids) might encode positions of repeated adjacent runes elsewhere in LP2; it does not assess every possible use of the grid.

![Seven payload readings compared with the gap sequence. All bars fall below the declared 0.5 gate.](experiments/records/payload-doublet-gaps/gap-correlation.svg)

An equal-rune pair is called a *doublet*. There are 86 such pairs within the archived LP2-00–55 page texts. Put their starting rune positions in page order, then subtract each from the next: that makes **85 gaps**. The first few are `85, 249, 197, 129`. We compared this sequence with numbers read from the published 256-byte grid file, beginning at byte zero each time.

| Byte reading | Values used | Correlation with 85 gaps |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| One unsigned byte per number | 85 | +0.043 |
| Two-byte integers, little endian | 85 | −0.018 |
| Two-byte integers, big endian | 85 | −0.026 |
| LEB128, forward / reversed bytes | 85 each | −0.027 / +0.004 |
| MSB-first base-128, forward / reversed bytes | 85 each | −0.040 / −0.004 |

The source's later varint test also prepended the one-based location of the first doublet, **122**, making an 86-value target. The largest absolute correlation across both targets is **0.119**: forward LEB128 against that 86-value sequence. [The full result table](experiments/records/payload-doublet-gaps/results.json) retains all 14 comparisons and the number of values each decoding produced.

## How the comparison was checked

The statistic is Spearman's rank correlation: it asks whether large payload numbers tend to line up with large doublet gaps, without requiring their magnitudes to match. The test fixes the reading direction and starts at the first byte and first gap. It does **not** shift the payload until a favorable match appears. As an alignment check, we circularly shifted the 85-gap target through its other 84 positions, repeating the largest-of-seven comparison each time. **83 of 84** shifted alignments matched or exceeded the unshifted maximum. Those shifts are dependent descriptive controls, not a calibrated cipher null or a p-value.

Encoding all 85 actual gaps into either varint format and decoding them again recovers every gap exactly. A separate checker recomputes all 14 correlations with a different midrank algorithm. This establishes that the tested encoders and rank calculations work; it does not prove the grid cannot hide a transformed gap list.

The [earlier published fixed-width check](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/zeroFP/zerofp_tests.py) used unsigned 8- and 16-bit values. A [later extension](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round28/L5/l5_payload_micro.py) tested the two variable-length readings and both byte directions. This replay uses the pinned source byte file and Liberpedia's separately archived [doublet coordinates](#/experiments/doublet-placement). No inference is made about alternate grid transcriptions, arbitrary offsets, other encodings or a decoder that first transforms the bytes.

## Reproduce

Extract this experiment and the reference-data bundle together, then run:

```sh
python experiments/records/payload-doublet-gaps/run.py --check
python experiments/records/payload-doublet-gaps/check.py
```

Both scripts use only the Python standard library.

records.title: How many periodic affine keys can fit a twelve-rune opening?
records.question: For nine fixed known-reading openings and periods 1–8, how many invertible affine keys fit the first twelve runes of each LP2 page, and how much of the following text is determined?
records.summary: Period-specific affine constraints were counted exactly across 3,960 fixed page, opening and period combinations, then checked for how many following positions a fit forces.

record_type.label: Control
record_type.description: Checks a search, decoder or scorer using synthetic inputs or reference text; it does not identify the cipher of an unsolved page.

scope.representation: First 24 runes including headings on each rune-bearing LP2-00–55 page; first twelve paired with nine fixed reading openings and next twelve inspected only for forced-position count.
scope.procedure: For each period 1–8, enumerate the 812 invertible GP29 affine maps independently at each residue and retain those satisfying its crib observations; multiply residue counts. Count the following positions whose output is identical under every compatible map for its residue. Verify with a planted period-3 known reading and exhaustive F3 small-field key enumeration.
scope.parameters: 55 pages × 9 fixed openings × 8 periods = 3,960 cases. Each residue has 0, 1 or 28 compatible affine maps after the twelve-rune crib; no whole-key brute force and no language score.
scope.exclusions: No other opening, later alignment, period above 8, key clock reset, mixed alphabet, nonlinear transition, feedback model or historical Alberti branch mechanism.

records.finding: No fixed opening fit periods 1–5. At period 6, 287 of 495 page-opening pairs fit, 276 with one key and 11 with 28. Periods 7 and 8 have 262 and 293 fits respectively, all with many keys: at least 784 and 614,656. Compatible fits at those periods force only 6–9 and 3–6 of the next twelve positions. These are algebraic fits, not readings.
records.limitations: Only nine proposed twelve-rune openings at page position zero, periods 1–8, invertible GP29 affine maps and archived page text are examined. A contradiction excludes that exact combination only; compatible openings do not establish an encryption method.
records.article:
## Result

**A twelve-rune opening becomes easier to fit as a periodic cipher gains free maps—but a fit is not a reading.** We paired each of **nine fixed known-reading openings** with the first twelve runes of each of **55 LP2 pages**, then asked whether a period of 1–8 invertible affine maps could produce it. That is **495 page-and-opening pairs per period**.

| Period | No compatible key | One key | Many keys | Compatible keys when a pair fits |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 1–5 | 495 at each period | 0 | 0 | — |
| 6 | 208 | 276 | 11 | 1–28 |
| 7 | 233 | 0 | 262 | 784–21,952 |
| 8 | 202 | 0 | 293 | 614,656–17,210,368 |

At period 8, a visually promising twelve-rune opening can leave **hundreds of thousands or millions of keys**. The opening alone then has little power to identify an intended mechanism. Conversely, an impossible case rules out only that **specific opening at page position zero under that exact period and affine rule**.

![Counts of impossible, unique-key and many-key fits for each period across 495 fixed page-and-opening pairs.](experiments/records/periodic-affine-crib-capacity/fits.svg)

## Why the key count grows

The model is `Pᵢ = aᵣCᵢ + bᵣ (mod 29)`, where `r = i mod p`, `p` is the period, and each multiplier `aᵣ` is nonzero. Each residue has its own affine map. A single ciphertext/plaintext observation leaves **28** possible maps for that residue. Two distinct ciphertext values paired with distinct plaintext values determine **one** invertible map; contradictory observations leave **none**. We count the choices for each residue and multiply them, without attempting `812^p` full keys one by one.

With twelve proposed runes and period 7, two residues appear only once, leaving at least `28² = 784` keys whenever a fit exists. At period 8, **four** residues appear only once, leaving at least `28⁴ = 614,656`. Repeated ciphertext in another residue can leave an additional factor of 28. This is why raw compatibility becomes less persuasive as the period grows.

We also inspected the **next twelve ciphertext positions** without supplying a proposed continuation. Among compatible pairs, the number of output positions forced to a single rune ranged from **10–12** at period 6, **6–9** at period 7, and **3–6** at period 8. These are conditional predictions; we did not call the predicted runes a decipherment or grade them against invented English text.

## Scope and checks

The [frozen plan](experiments/records/periodic-affine-crib-capacity/plan.json) uses the same nine twelve-rune opening vectors as the earlier [known-key test](#/experiments/lp2-known-vigenere-keys), plus the first 24 archived runes of LP2-00–55 except runeless LP2-50. Headings count; punctuation does not. The [case results](experiments/records/periodic-affine-crib-capacity/results.json) retain every residue's 0, 1 or 28 choices, total compatible keys, and number of forced next positions.

A planted period-3 key on a known 24-rune reading was recovered uniquely, with all twelve following symbols forced. Separately, the counting theorem agreed with literal full-key enumeration in **6,561** small-field cases over F₃, including contradictions and ambiguous keys. Run `python experiments/records/periodic-affine-crib-capacity/run.py --check` and the independent algebraic oracle `python experiments/records/periodic-affine-crib-capacity/check.py` to reproduce the census and controls.

Only nine specified openings at the very start of each page and periods 1–8 were tested. Other plaintext openings, later alignments, clock resets, mixed alphabets, nonlinear transitions and noninvertible rules remain outside this result. The historical Alberti-disk proposal has additional branching rules that are not specified here.

# Cicada's PGP key bytes as a repeating rune key

**The four tested public-key byte streams did not produce a complete English-like LP2 page under this simple rule.** Across 119,900 page, key-phase and sign settings, none reached the predeclared English score of −5.5. The best scored −6.456 on LP2-49. In 174 of 199 shuffled-page controls, the strongest result was at least as high. This is a newly defined bounded test of PGP key material, **not** a replay of a claimed historical decryption.

![The highest page score from each of four PGP packet or fingerprint key streams remains below the English gate.](experiments/records/pgp-packet-keys/scores.svg)

The four bars show each material's best *whole-page* score, after trying every starting phase and both arithmetic signs. All remain below the threshold. The 199 controls repeat the **entire search** after shuffling runes within each page, so their 174 comparable maxima include the effect of selecting a favorite key phase and page.

## The exact rule

We extracted the version-4 RSA **primary public-key packet** and **public subkey packet** from the [preserved Cicada key used in the RSA payload audit](#/experiments/public-rsa-payload-e01). Their 20-byte binary fingerprints are the other two candidates. The packet bodies are 525 bytes each; the fingerprints are 20 bytes each. The parser checks both fingerprints against the pinned key record. No third-party PGP keys, signatures or armor text were used as key material.

Each byte becomes one rune-key value by taking `byte mod 29`. For each of the four resulting streams, we tested every cyclic starting phase and both signs in `plaintext = (ciphertext ± key) mod 29`. The key repeats and restarts at the beginning of each page. We scored all runes on each of the 55 nonempty LP2-00–55 pages, including headings. LP2-50 has no runes. There is no skip rule, Atbash step or adaptive word choice.

Before evaluating LP2, all nine 66-rune archived reading controls scored above −5.5. Nine planted tests used those readings with fixed choices of key material, phase and sign; each recovered the reading exactly. A separate direct Latin-string quadgram implementation agreed with the accelerated scorer at fixed settings. This supports the scorer and decoder, but it cannot establish that the manuscript should use PGP key bytes at all.

| Result | Count |
| --- | ---: |
| Complete-page settings | 119,900 |
| Settings at or above the English gate | 0 |
| Shuffled full searches meeting or exceeding the observed best | 174 / 199 |

The [plan](experiments/records/pgp-packet-keys/plan.json) and [results](experiments/records/pgp-packet-keys/results.json) give the exact source hashes, page and key rules, each material's best setting, per-page maxima and all 199 control maxima. Install the [two Python dependencies](experiments/records/pgp-packet-keys/requirements.txt), then run `python experiments/records/pgp-packet-keys/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/pgp-packet-keys/check.py` from the repository root. The checker parses the armored key independently, reconstructs the page streams, verifies all 119,900 scores and reruns every complete-search control. It also scores selected outputs directly as Latin quadgrams.

This result is limited to one lossy `byte mod 29` conversion and a repeating additive key. Packet fields could be parsed differently, used once rather than repeated, combined with another key or applied through a different cipher. None of those alternatives is tested here; the public key's ordinary cryptographic role is also separate from this proposed LP2 use.

records.article:
# Can each rune label a divisor of its position?

**Not with consecutive positions, under the rule tested here.** Every nonempty rune page in LP2-00–55 contains repeated occurrences whose spacing makes a fixed divisor greater than one impossible, regardless of where counting starts. This is a fresh reproduction of the supplied closure archive's C11 claim, not an original discovery.

## Define the rule before testing it

Let i be a zero-based rune position within a page. Choose an integer origin N and a fixed stride s. Assign each rune r an integer divisor q[r] greater than one, then require:

```text
q[r] divides N + s*i whenever position i contains r
```

The same rune must keep the same divisor throughout that page. Divisors need not be prime, distinct, or equal to Gematria Primus values. Allowing all integers greater than one makes this test more permissive than an assignment restricted to primes. Each page may use its own origin, stride and assignment.

This is a necessary condition for a direct smallest-factor or largest-factor labeling proposal. It does not test prime-derived keys combined with plaintext or an arbitrary operation that merely uses prime numbers.

## Why the origin cancels

If q divides both N+s*i and N+s*j, it divides their difference s*(j−i). The unknown N disappears. For several occurrences, q must therefore divide the stride multiplied by the gcd of the position gaps.

For unit stride, a gap gcd of 1 would require q to divide 1. That contradicts q > 1. Running the page backwards changes the origin and stride sign, not this obstruction.

A rune appearing only once has no gap constraint. Two occurrences with gap 1 already suffice; otherwise several gaps may be needed. The report records every occurrence and, where available, a three-occurrence gcd-one witness. It uses gcd 0 for an empty set of gaps; that means no restriction from this particular test, not impossibility.

## A witness on LP2-00

F occurs at zero-based rune positions **7, 17 and 58**. Thus a fixed divisor must divide both 10 and 51 under unit stride. Their gcd is 1. This single repeated rune already rules out the model on that page; the report records the other rune labels as well.

These are positions in the filtered rune stream, including the heading. They are not image coordinates, Latin-letter offsets or positions that count punctuation.

## What the full retest covers

The program reads all 56 archived text files LP2-00–55, retains alphabet runes and headings, and starts each page independently. All **55 nonempty streams** have at least one gcd-one rune. LP2-50 has no alphabet runes in this transcription and is skipped; its alphanumeric grid is not converted into runes.

Every page therefore excludes both forward and reverse unit-stride constructions, even when the origin and arbitrary integer divisor labels are chosen independently for that page. This is an exact contradiction under the stated model, not a low probability or a finite search over origins.

## Why arbitrary strides remain different

With a gcd-one witness, the general condition is **q divides s**. It excludes a stride coprime to that rune's divisor. It does not exclude every nonunit stride.

For a concrete counterexample, set N=2, s=2 and q[r]=2 for every rune. Every position N+s*i is even, so every recorded rune passes the divisibility condition on every page. This construction assigns the same divisor to different runes, which the tested necessary condition permits. It supplies no decoding rule and does not identify which rune to emit at a position.

If a proposal requires distinct labels, literal GP primes, or a deterministic factor-selection rule, those extra requirements need separate analysis. The counterexample refutes the broader claim that this divisibility condition alone excludes all strides; it is not a successful cipher.

## Reproduce and independently check

Download the experiment ZIP and keep its folders intact. Python 3's standard library is sufficient; no network, AI calls or additional packages are needed.

```text
python experiments/records/position-divisor-labels/run.py --check
python experiments/records/position-divisor-labels/check.py
```

The first program uses distances from each rune's first occurrence. The independent checker reads page JSON and computes the gcd of all pairwise occurrence distances. It also verifies every displayed triple, the stride-two counterexample on all 55 pages, a valid unit-stride control, and 450 small synthetic origin/stride cases.

Both text sources share archival ancestry: agreement is a computation check, not an independent manuscript transcription review. The earlier archive cites a Lean proof; this package provides elementary reasoning and fresh integer checks, without claiming that the Lean development was rerun.

## Limits and reopening conditions

Changing which characters advance the clock, resetting within a page, changing a rune's divisor over time, selecting an irregular sequence of integers, or transforming the factor labels changes the model. Such proposals are not ruled out here. A transcription correction also requires a new run. This result belongs alongside other bounded exclusions, not under a heading claiming that prime-based ciphers are impossible.

records.article:
# Why the reported 53-digit reverse-add result is a palindrome

## The precise claim

A [prior LP2-15 discussion](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=lp2-15-prime-distance-palindromes) reports distances from word-level GP sums to nearby primes. After concatenating a selected sequence of those distances, the author added the 53-character decimal string to its reversal and obtained a 53-digit palindrome. The thread corrected an earlier 46-digit claim to 53 digits.

This experiment checks **that arithmetic and one conditional baseline**. The companion [word-by-word source audit](#/experiments/prime-distance-word-derivation) now reconstructs the same section from the archived LP2-15–16 rune text; its complete 57-word sequence differs from the 53 reported digits. This record retains the exact reported string as its input so the historical arithmetic claim remains independently inspectable. The source excerpt is identified in the [structured intake](data/reported-attempts.json) by SHA-256.

## Input and result

```text
  02311171210211215142515300303126131002122052400021111
+ 11112000425022120013162130300351524151211201217111320
= 13423171635233335155677430603477655153333253617132431
```

The addition is correct and the result reads identically in either direction. The first operand's leading zero is retained when constructing the reversal; as an integer it has no value, but dropping it before reversing would define a different operation.

The more informative fact is that **every paired digit sum is at most 7**. No column carries. If a decimal string has digits `d[0] ... d[n−1]`, adding it to its reversal pairs `d[i]` with `d[n−1−i]`. These pair sums are necessarily mirror-symmetric. Whenever all are below ten, and the outer pair is nonzero, the decimal result must be a palindrome. The reported example meets both conditions. Its palindromicity follows from this elementary rule; it does not require a cipher mechanism.

![Fifty-three paired sums from the reported digits mirror around the center and all remain below the decimal carry line of ten.](experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/paired-sums.svg)

## A matched-digit control

The plan fixes 100,000 pseudorandom shuffles of the **same 53 characters**, with Python's `random.Random(3301)` and no restrictions on a leading zero in the shuffled string. Each shuffled string is reversed and added as an integer exactly as above. **50,442 of 100,000** shuffles yield palindromes. In this run, exactly the same 50,442 satisfy the no-carry condition with a nonzero outer pair.

This is a conditional, descriptive control: it preserves the selected digit multiset but not any GP word order. It is not a p-value for the full search that produced the string. That search could choose pages, word boundaries, nearest-prime ties, zero separators, and which examples to present. A null model for the whole idea must include those choices. Randomly shuffling uniform decimal digits would be a different and less relevant comparison, because the reported distances concentrate at small digits (11 zeroes, 18 ones, 11 twos).

## Reproduce

Extract the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/prime-distance-reverse-add.zip) with folders intact, then run from its root:

```text
python experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/run.py --check
python experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/check.py
python experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/plot.py
```

The first command recomputes the arithmetic and all 100,000 fixed shuffles. The independent checker verifies the 53 column sums, their symmetry, the no-carry proof condition, and the saved control's internal consistency. The plotter regenerates the SVG from `results.json`. All use the Python standard library. `plan.json` specifies the original digits, seed, trial count and post-selection scope; `results.json` preserves the full paired-sum list and control counts.

## What remains open

The [companion audit](#/experiments/prime-distance-word-derivation) pins one source-to-digits derivation. Its archived first-section reading has 57 words, compared with 53 reported digits, and also yields a carry-free palindrome. The author's exact transcription or segmentation choices are not preserved in the supplied report. A full cipher test would still need a fixed operation on unsolved text and a comparison that repeats the complete choice of section, grouping and method.

This computational audit was run and checked by Codex on 2026-10-22. Human review of the source grouping and the mathematical interpretation is pending.

# Can the reported prime-distance digits be derived from LP2-15–16?

The earlier [reverse-add record](#/experiments/prime-distance-reverse-add) checks the arithmetic of a reported 53-digit string. It does not show how each digit came from the manuscript. This source audit makes that missing step explicit: read every word in the same first section, sum its Gematria Primus rune values, and record its distance to the nearest prime.

The archived transcription yields **57 word distances**, while the supplied report lists **53**. The two strings have a minimum digit-edit distance of seven under ordinary insertion, deletion and substitution. That discrepancy matters for reproducing the reported derivation. It does **not** make the reverse-add observation disappear: the complete 57-digit sequence also produces a palindrome on the first addition.

## Frozen reading rule

The input is the archived [LP2-15](#/reader/lp2-15) and [LP2-16](#/reader/lp2-16) rune transcription. We use the two-word heading on LP2-15, then every rune word after its `$` section marker through the word before the next section's `ᛈᚹᚷᚷ` on LP2-16. The first five values agree with the report's “red header” sequence; the first three body words are red on the page image. Printed square numbers are not words in this calculation.

A hyphen or period separates words. A `/` followed by a line break is typographic wrapping, so runes on either side remain one word unless a hyphen intervenes. The page boundary also does not split its continuing word. For each word, sum the first 29 primes in Gematria Primus order and use the *absolute* distance to the closest integer prime. A tie between equidistant primes does not change the distance. The [plan](experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/plan.json) pins both text hashes, the rune-to-prime table, the section end marker and the report's 53 digits.

For example, the heading words give `ᚠᚢᛚᛗ → 149 → 0` and `ᚪᛠᚣᛟᚪ → 489 → 2`. The [full token trace](experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/results.json) lists all 57 words, their prime sums and nearest-prime distances, so any disputed separator or rune has an exact place to challenge.

## Where the sequences differ

```text
Reported: 02311171210211215142515300303126131002122052400021111   (53 digits)
Archive:  023111712102410211215142515300303126141002122142400021111 (57 digits)
```

![The reported 53 digits aligned with 57 distances independently derived from archived LP2-15–16 words. Ochre columns mark gaps or differing digits.](experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/word-distance-alignment.svg)

[Open the alignment at full size](experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/word-distance-alignment.svg).

The figure shows **one** minimum alignment: four archive word positions have no partner in the report and three paired digits differ. The minimum edit count is independently checked by dynamic programming. Repeated digits make the precise alignment non-unique, so these positions should not be read as proof of which words the original author skipped or transcribed differently. The reported list and archived source cannot be made identical under the stated rule without additional choices or corrections.

## What happens to the palindrome?

Adding the archive-derived string to its reversal gives:

```text
  023111712102410211215142515300303126141002122142400021111
+ 111120004241221200141621303003515241512112014201217111320
= 134231716343631411356763818303818367653114136343617132431
```

The [independent checker](experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/check.py) verifies the integer sum and each mirrored digit pair. The largest paired sum is eight, so no decimal carry occurs. That is why the 57-digit sum remains a palindrome.

As a conditional baseline, we shuffled the same **57 distance digits** 100,000 times with a fixed seed, reversed and added each shuffle, and obtained **53,845 palindromes**. This preserves the short-digit distribution that makes carry-free addition frequent. It does not reproduce the full historical search over pages, section boundaries and prime-related transformations. The sibling record's 53-digit control gives 50,442 palindromes in 100,000 shuffles of *its* fixed digit multiset. Neither rate is a probability of intentional construction.

## Reproduce and limits

From a full checkout or the [experiment ZIP](downloads/experiments/prime-distance-word-derivation.zip), run:

```text
python experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/run.py --check
python experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/check.py
python experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/plot.py --check
```

The first command recomputes every word and all 100,000 shuffles. The checker uses a separate word scanner, a different nearest-prime search, direct column arithmetic, a minimum-edit calculation and a second control replay. The supplied discussion is identified by SHA-256 in the [reported-attempt intake](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=lp2-15-prime-distance-palindromes); its full pasted transcript is not redistributed. The report may have used a different transcription or unpublished segmentation choices. Image-level verification of every word break and human review are still pending.

This is an **input-derivation audit**, not a decryption of LP2-15–22. A future cipher test would need a fixed way to use these distances on an unsolved passage and evaluate the complete output on text that did not determine the rule.

Require at least 100 Latin quadgrams to score. Compare the best eligible arm to 256 shared within-page-shuffle global maxima and verify planted known-reading extraction.

scope.exclusions: Every-n/phase variants, backwards indexing, alternate page ordering, another cipher layer, alternate languages, using selected positions as a key rather than direct text and claims about unscored short outputs.

records.finding: Page-local prime extraction scored −7.472, the best of three eligible arms. In 201 of 256 page-shuffled trials, the strongest eligible arm scored at least that high (global add-one estimate 202/257≈0.786). The joined Fibonacci arm selected only 20 runes and was not scored.
records.limitations: Direct English quadgram scoring cannot exclude further encryption, another language or alternate position origins/directions. The book-wide Fibonacci stream is too short for the declared scorer. The catalog is an idea list, not a verified historical test record.
records.article:
# Runes at prime and Fibonacci positions

**Question.** If the manuscript's rune positions act as an index, does reading only prime- or Fibonacci-numbered runes reveal English text?

**Result.** The tested extractions did not stand out. The strongest score was from taking prime-numbered runes **afresh on every page**, then pooling the evidence across pages. Its score was **−7.472**. In **201 of 256** shuffled-page trials, the strongest of the same tested methods scored at least as well (global add-one estimate **202/257 ≈ 0.786**). The extracted text does not form a readable passage.

![Prime and Fibonacci extraction scores compared with page-preserving shuffled controls.](experiments/records/prime-fibonacci-position-extraction/selection-scores.svg)

## What we selected

There are **12,956** recorded GP runes on the 55 rune-bearing pages LP2-00–55. Position **1** means the first rune, without advancing for punctuation or page artwork. Prime positions start **2, 3, 5, 7**; unique Fibonacci positions start **1, 2, 3, 5, 8**. We tried each selector twice: restarting at every page, and applying it once after joining the pages in numerical order. This is a fixed four-arm test, not an every-*n* or adjustable-start search.

For page-by-page selection, we scored each page's extracted runes separately and combined the quadgram sums. No four-letter group was allowed to cross a page boundary. Joined selection was scored as one stream. Three arms supplied at least the **100 Latin quadgrams** declared for scoring: page-local primes (2,797 selected runes), joined primes (1,542), and page-local Fibonacci (634). Book-wide Fibonacci selected only **20 runes**, yielding 20 quadgrams, so its score was withheld. Its exact stream remains in `results.json`; this short sample cannot support a negative language finding.

Every control trial shuffled the rune order **inside each complete page once**, keeping each page's rune counts. All four selectors then used those same shuffled pages. We compared the best eligible observed arm with the best eligible arm in each trial, accounting for choosing the most attractive of the three scored variants. The page-local prime score was only **0.025** above its own shuffled median; the other two scored arms were about **0.057 below** theirs. A planted known-reading stream at the selected positions was recovered exactly and scored well above each eligible arm's shuffled median, checking that the extraction and scorer can respond to a real GP-encoded passage.

The outcome is bounded. It tests direct English-like readings at these **one-based, forward** positions under two page-boundary conventions. It does not rule out a second cipher layer, different starting positions, backwards reading, an indexed key rather than direct text, another language, or other ways of treating page divisions. The source catalog lists the idea; it is not evidence that a particular historical attempt used these exact rules.

Run `python experiments/records/prime-fibonacci-position-extraction/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/prime-fibonacci-position-extraction/check.py` from the repository root. Both use Python 3's standard library. The independent check reconstructs pages from the page JSON, computes positions by a separate algorithm, and verifies all 256 shared-control scores. `results.json` preserves every extracted segment, its GP indices and Latin labels, so the precise reading can be inspected without recomputing it.

records.article:
# The circumference substitutions

A [public failed-attempt record](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/bruteforce/2%CF%80R/README.md) applies a circumference-inspired rule to each GP rune: use either its alphabet position or its associated prime as the radius, multiply by `2π`, then reduce modulo 29. The README says **round**, but the repository's [index-radius output](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/bruteforce/2%CF%80R/pages_2piR.txt) and [prime-radius output](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/bruteforce/2%CF%80R/pages_2piR_primes.txt) use **integer truncation** instead. We replay both interpretations so the source discrepancy is visible.

## Finding

![Distinct output runes under index and prime radii with nearest rounding or truncation.](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/mapping-coverage.svg)

The truncated index and prime maps reproduce the **complete Latin rune-label streams on all 57 pages** in each pinned public output, including the source's page 56. The published LP2-00–55 test spans 56 of those pages; LP2-50 has no runic line. The README's nearest-rounding rule does not reproduce those outputs. It produces a different symbol map: the index version reaches 25 of 29 possible output runes instead of 26 under truncation. With GP prime values as radii, both rounding choices reach only **18 of 29** output runes, although the actual mappings differ.

Each rule is a fixed one-rune substitution. In the prime-radius version, 11 output symbols are unreachable. This compression makes the rule non-invertible without additional information; it does not by itself establish that the manuscript was encoded by the inverse rule. The source reports no interesting reading, but supplies no scoring threshold or test that would justify a blanket negative conclusion. Our reproducible result is the exact map and the output agreement.

## Method and limits

The [plan](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/plan.json) pins the public revision, source-output hashes, two radius choices and two rounding choices. The [results](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/results.json) contain all four 29-entry maps and hashes of the transformed text for LP2-00–55. The [independent check](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/check.py) uses a separate floor-based calculation, checks every saved output hash, and compares complete rune-label streams when both source text files are supplied. The [source-output certificate](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/source-output-certificate.json) records all 57 comparisons per source file. Punctuation, line marks and decimal numbers remain unchanged; only runes are substituted.

The original plan's source-file hashes describe a Windows **CRLF checkout**. The pinned Git files have **LF** line endings. The checker verifies the LF Git bytes, then verifies that changing only those line endings to CRLF yields the original plan's hashes. No source content or original plan was changed. For label comparison, it normalizes the archived `IO`/`IA` spelling, excludes structured eight-cell alphanumeric grid rows, and compares complete joined labels without guessing word breaks.

This test neither scores candidate English nor searches secondary keys, alternative page groupings, or a reversible decoding scheme. In particular, a numerical motif is not evidence for a cipher merely because it can be applied to every symbol.

## Reproduce

Run `python experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/check.py`. For the complete source-output comparison, put the two text files named in the [plan](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/plan.json) in one directory and run `check.py --source-directory PATH`. Both LF and CRLF copies are accepted after the two byte receipts are verified.
