records.article:
# Do the manuscript JPEGs hash to the deep-web target?

**Result.** No match in either of two clearly separated JPEG sets. The 75 files used by the [published hash lookup](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/tree/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/deepweb-hash) are now identified exactly: their SHA-512 **and** BLAKE2b-512 digests match all 150 entries in its saved checksum table. None equals the 128-character target printed on LP2-56. A **new, separate follow-up** on 58 preserved seventh-onion JPEGs also found no match among 116 full-file digests. These results cover two specified byte sets, not the search for any web page that might satisfy the manuscript.

![The 75-image source replay and separate 58-image follow-up both return zero LP2-56 target matches under SHA-512 and BLAKE2b-512.](experiments/records/public-deepweb-jpeg-hashes/source-hash-check.svg)

## Which files were checked?

The source script applies `sha512sum` and `b2sum` to `00.jpg` through `74.jpg`. Its image directory was absent from the pinned repository, so an earlier inventory could only confirm that the archived table contained no target string. We compared **complete 128-digit SHA-512 hashes** from that table with the site's JPEGs. Every row maps uniquely and in order: source `00`–`16` are hosted LP1-00–16, and `17`–`74` are hosted LP2-00–57. Recomputed BLAKE2b-512 hashes also match every saved row. That identifies the exact file bytes used for the source lookup without assuming that identically rendered images have identical bytes.

The 58 preserved JPEGs from the seventh-onion archive are **different bytes** and match none of those source SHA-512 entries. Many hosted copies add only a small JFIF segment, which is enough to change a cryptographic hash completely. Neither preserved repository set is independently authenticated as the puzzle creator's original bytes.

The target is read directly from the five hexadecimal lines in the LP2-56 page record, with only the printed line breaks and trailing slashes removed. Both a SHA-512 lookup and a BLAKE2b-512 lookup over the 75 exact files return no match. As a control, replacing the target with either digest of source image `00` correctly finds that image and no other.

## Separate seventh-onion follow-up

The [preserved seventh-onion image set](https://github.com/neuroretransmit/cicada/tree/ade9a02889ef8acbc8cde8edbfd0a785c369f4c3/2014/011-seventh-onion) supplies `0.jpg` through `57.jpg`. We froze their exact paths, byte lengths and SHA-256 values in a [second candidate plan](experiments/records/public-deepweb-jpeg-hashes/followup-plan.json) before comparing with the target. None of their **58 SHA-512** or **58 BLAKE2b-512** full-file digests matches. A separate planted target using archived `0.jpg` recovers that file under each algorithm. The [complete digest list](experiments/records/public-deepweb-jpeg-hashes/followup-results.json) keeps this follow-up auditable without treating it as a historical run by Failed-Attempts.

## Reproduce

From a complete Liberpedia checkout containing `images/lp1-*.jpg` and `images/lp2-*.jpg`:

```text
python experiments/records/public-deepweb-jpeg-hashes/run.py --check
python experiments/records/public-deepweb-jpeg-hashes/check.py
python experiments/records/public-deepweb-jpeg-hashes/followup.py --check
python experiments/records/public-deepweb-jpeg-hashes/followup-check.py
```

The [source-replay candidate manifest](experiments/records/public-deepweb-jpeg-hashes/plan.json) gives every hosted image path, file size, SHA-256 and the two digest values from the [pinned source checksum table](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/deepweb-hash/checksums.txt). Each runner verifies file hashes before the target comparison. The two separate checkers parse the printed target from the page's raw lines and recompute both digest families. For download-based reproduction, extract **Original images (ZIP)** alongside this experiment's ZIP so the declared `images/` and `exports/sources/cicada-2014-seventh-onion/` paths exist. A complete repository checkout already includes them.

The source replay covers only its 75 identified JPEGs; the follow-up covers 58 additional, different JPEG bytes. Both use only full-file SHA-512 and BLAKE2b-512. Neither addresses other files, byte transformations, combined files, web pages or a different meaning of “hashes to.”

# Do common key-stretching recipes unlock LP2's opening?

A short password might generate a much longer numeric key. This [published screen](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/KDF/RESULTS.md) tried that possibility on the **first 120 unsolved LP2 runes**. It crossed a fixed list of puzzle-related secrets with familiar password-to-key recipes, then applied each resulting stream through a decoder that can account for skipped key symbols.

## Finding

**None of the 692,064 LP2 decodes passed the source's English-score requirement.** The best scored **−6.259**, while a candidate needed at least **−5.500** to advance. A message deliberately encrypted with one of the tested recipes *did* come back as the top result at **−4.186**. The control shows this particular search can find one of its own planted messages; it does not establish that every possible real encoding would be found.

![The planted message scores above the advancement bar; the strongest LP2 candidate stays below it.](experiments/records/public-kdf-seed-stretch/scores.svg)

These are English four-letter-pattern scores: higher values are stronger. The strongest LP2 output still does not read as an English continuation. It used the secret `sacrifice`, 100,000 rounds of iterative SHA-256, the secret itself as salt, rejection reduction to rune indices, an Atbash transform, and a reversed key stream. That is the **best measured configuration**, not evidence that any of those choices is a clue.

## What the search actually covered

The code built **534 distinct secret byte strings** from the source's puzzle phrases, solved-page words, numbers, prime sequences and other named artifacts. For each secret it tried **27 key-derivation configurations**: PBKDF2 variants, scrypt, iterated hashes and OpenSSL-style derivation. It then crossed three salts (`empty`, `3301`, and the secret itself), two byte-to-rune reductions, both arithmetic signs, Atbash on or off, and forward or reversed key output. All began at **key offset zero** and were scored against the same 120-rune LP2 prefix.

The source first ran two controls. One recovered a message from a short-seed SHA-256 expander with **98.9%** character agreement; the other planted a PBKDF2 message and searched the *entire same configuration grid* against it, ranking the planted setting first. The latter required another 692,064 control decodes. Those are a power check, not another 692,064 distinct LP2 hypotheses.

The source's 200 shuffled-text comparisons use one fixed control key. They do **not** rerun the full 692,064-choice search on each shuffle, so they do not provide a calibrated probability for the winning LP2 score after selection. The finding here is narrower and cleaner: the executed grid, with its stated English threshold, produced no advancing LP2 result.

This does not test a different secret, salt, iteration count, starting offset, language, changing key by page, or a longer portion of LP2. It says nothing about whether LP2 could use a key-stretching recipe outside this specific grid.

## Reproduce

Download the record's ZIP to inspect the pinned code and inputs. The bundled subset is byte-for-byte source code and the input files that affect this run; its rebuilt **ordered 534-secret dictionary matches the full source checkout by SHA-256**. From a Liberpedia repository checkout:

```bash
python experiments/records/public-kdf-seed-stretch/check.py
python experiments/records/public-kdf-seed-stretch/run.py
```

The checker quickly verifies the saved results, grid count, controls, source dictionary and strongest candidate. The full replay takes much longer and runs in a temporary copy, keeping archived output hashes stable. It executes the source's `K1,K2,A` stages; `--nproc 8` changes worker count, not which configurations are tested. The original K1 program prints its result but does not rewrite the JSON file that the sweep reads. Our runner therefore checks its [live output](experiments/records/public-kdf-seed-stretch/k1_control_output.txt) and exit status against that pinned file before starting the sweep.

Read the [pinned plan](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/KDF/PREREG.md), [source executable](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round15/KDF/sweep.py), [complete Stage A result](experiments/records/public-kdf-seed-stretch/source/liber-primus/analysis/round15/KDF/results_A.json), and [independent checker](experiments/records/public-kdf-seed-stretch/check.py) for exact parameters and values.

records.article:
# Could LP2 be the key to another Cicada text?

The usual question is how to decode Liber Primus. This public test reverses the roles: it treats the **12,956 unsolved LP2 runes as a running key** and asks whether that key reveals a shorter Cicada object. It tests specific objects and rules; it does not directly decrypt LP2.

## Finding

**No tested pairing produced a readable English result.** The best of 40 runs scored **−7.032** on the source's English quadgram scale, below its predeclared **−5.5** advancement bar. The five highest-scoring configurations were also compared with 200 shuffled versions of their target each; none exceeded its corresponding highest shuffle score. A planted message encrypted under the same LP2 key *was* recovered, showing that this decoder can succeed on a constructed example of its assumed mechanism.

![Five target groups and their best English scores, all below the advancement bar.](experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/scores.svg)

The graphic shows each target's best run. Higher scores are stronger *for this English model*; the plotted values do not measure an unconditional probability that a puzzle idea is true.

## What entered the test

The source's key stream was the 55 nonempty unsolved LP2 transcription segments concatenated in page order. It tested four versions of that stream: forward, reversed, rune-index Atbash (`28 − index`), and negation modulo 29. Each was used with addition and subtraction in `plaintext = (target + sign × key) mod 29`. The decoder can skip up to three key positions at a time when searching for synchronization.

Five targets entered the completed run:

| Target | Input to decoder | Length actually scored |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| 2012–13 puzzle texts | English text converted to rune indices | first 500 |
| Five solved LP1 pages | their recorded plaintext transliterations converted to rune indices | first 500 |
| PGP message text | English text converted to rune indices | first 500 |
| “AN END” byte sequence | hard-coded bytes reduced modulo 29 | 63 |
| LP2 opening | first 200 runes of LP2 tested against the LP2 key | 200 |

The source proposed a sixth target, the pages 49–51 payload, but did **not** have the payload bytes needed to run it. It therefore ran five targets × four key variants × two signs = **40 decodes**. Negating the key and changing the sign gives the same arithmetic as an unnegated key with the original sign, so some decodes are equivalent; 40 is the run count, not 40 independent hypotheses. Every run starts at key offset zero.

The “AN END” input is the **63-byte hard-coded sequence in the source script**, which labels it a SHA-512 hash. This record preserves that exact input without asserting that the bytes independently authenticate an external artifact. The text-to-rune conversion is likewise the source's conversion, not a lossless representation of the original messages.

## What the control and scores mean

The source first encrypted a known English sentence with the LP2 stream, including deliberate key skips. Its beam decoder recovered the planted transliteration exactly, scoring **−4.413**. A rigid decoder using the right key but no skip search scored **−7.334**. That is a useful positive control for this implementation; it cannot prove that an unknown real message, if present, would be found under every different skip pattern or encoding.

The strongest real-target result was the 2012–13 text under the forward LP2 stream with addition: **−7.032**. For that *selected* run, 200 target-order shuffles reached a highest score of **−6.972**, slightly stronger than the observed result. The null comparison was computed for only the top five selected configurations, and the shuffled controls do not repeat the whole selection process across all target and rule choices. We therefore report the observed absence of a hit under the source's gate, rather than a universal statistical exclusion.

This replay uses the [pinned F-01 executable](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/F-01/sweep.py) and [its declared plan](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/F-01/PREREG.md). The source's result prose speaks more broadly than its executed grid in places; the figures above come from the machine-readable run and the independent accounting check.

## Reproduce

Download this experiment's ZIP from the record's download control to inspect the pinned code, input texts, result, and checker. From a Liberpedia repository checkout, run:

```bash
python experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/check.py
python experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/run.py
```

The checker is quick. The complete source replay takes several minutes and runs in a temporary copy, so it leaves the archived result bytes intact. It verifies the complete 40-configuration grid, the positive-control gate, the LP2 rune-stream checksum, the five selected null comparisons, and substantive equality with the pinned source output (excluding elapsed wall time).

The bundled [source results](experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/source/liber-primus/analysis/round16/F-01/results.json), [checker](experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/check.py), and [figure script](experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/plot.py) expose the exact values. The [source README and method notes](experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/source/liber-primus/analysis/round16/F-01/PREREG.md) are preserved as evidence of what was proposed, not as broader findings of this replay.

**Remaining scope:** target material other than these five objects, a verified pages 49–51 payload, other key offsets, alternative page boundaries, or using the other objects as key material would require separate tests.

records.summary: The 23,520-setting source sweep found no convincing English reading. A separate power check shows its actual all-equal-seed search misses its own plaintext- and mixed-history plants.

record_type.label: Method replay

scope.representation: Zero-based GP rune indices from the pinned source transcription: 12,956 unsolved runes in 55 nonempty source segments, plus their concatenation.

# Multi-rune feedback and autokey

A feedback cipher can derive each new key symbol from earlier symbols. [This published screen](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round12/C1/RESULTS.md) tested whether LP2 behaves that way when the key depends on the previous two to six runes.

## Finding

**None of the 23,520 source configurations produced a convincing English reading.** The strongest result scored **−6.299**, below the source's required **−5.500**. It came from a **66-rune segment**, not the continuous manuscript: a five-rune plaintext-history XOR rule on the reversed segment, with an all-six seed. The source program recovered all **21 planted cases when given their correct seed**. A further check below shows that its actual limited seed search does **not** recover the plaintext-history or mixed-history plants.

![The planted control clears the score threshold; the highest-scoring LP2 candidate remains below it.](experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/scores.svg)

These are English quadgram scores; higher means the transliterated output resembles the training text more closely. The strongest short fragment is still well below the planted English sample. A score by itself would never establish a solution without a coherent continuation.

### Did the real search pass its planted test?

The source's control encrypts the same 212-rune English passage under each of its seven rules and three history modes, using initial seed **7, 11, 2**. It decrypts each with that exact seed. The real sweep instead tries only **0,0,0** through **28,28,28** for plaintext and mixed history. We ran that actual seed-search step against the source's own planted ciphertexts, holding the correct rule, sign and history length fixed:

![The actual search recovers all seven visible-rune-history plants but none of the seven decoded-rune or seven mixed-history plants.](experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/search-domain-gate.svg)

**Visible-ciphertext history: 7/7 recovered. Plaintext history: 0/7. Mixed history: 0/7.** No tried all-equal seed reaches 90% rune recovery in either of the latter groups, even before selecting the highest English score. The correct non-equal seed still recovers all 21 plants. An [independent recurrence check](experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/check_gate.py) reproduces every candidate's rune recovery and score. This is a **retrospective power check** using the source's already published control passage, not a new blinded trial.

The negative screen therefore has a useful, narrower result: these executed settings produced no persuasive English reading. Its correct-seed control does not show that the **actual all-equal-seed search** could find a plaintext- or mixed-history cipher with a different initial state. The source did not test all 29³ seeds at history length three, let alone all 29^k seeds at larger lengths.

## How the tested rules work

At each position, the program reads the previous *k* symbols, passes them through one of seven fixed functions, then adds or subtracts the resulting value modulo 29. The seven functions are an index sum, prime-value sum, XOR, prime-of-index-sum, prime-of-prime-sum, last-symbol difference and alternating sum. It tries three kinds of history: the visible ciphertext, the plaintext decoded so far, or the modulo-29 sum of the two. The source also tries both directions of the rune stream and both arithmetic signs.

![A five-rune history is mapped to a key value, then combined with the next ciphertext rune to produce a proposed plaintext rune.](experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/feedback.svg)

The screen covers the **12,956-rune continuous unsolved stream** plus its **55 nonempty source segments**. For ciphertext history, symbols after the first *k* positions do not depend on the initial seed. For plaintext and mixed history, the source tries only the **29 all-equal seeds** `0…0` through `28…28` at each *k*, then keeps the best score. That is a thin slice of the possible **29^k** initial states. In particular, a wrong initial plaintext state need not “lock on” to the correct state later; the source's broader claim that a genuine autokey would necessarily reveal itself under these seeds is not established by this test.

The source's 200 shuffled controls score the raw full stream, while its reported best is selected from thousands of configurations, many on short segments. That shuffle maximum is not a full best-of-grid null. The result is therefore **no supported English reading in the executed grid**, not a statistical exclusion of every feedback cipher.

## Reproduce

Download the experiment ZIP and run from its extracted folder:

```sh
python experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/run.py
```

It runs the 21 planted controls before the full sweep, then checks the saved result against the separately archived source output. The independent checker reconstructs the 12,956 source rune indices and **recomputes the winning XOR/plaintext-history decode and score** without calling the source's feedback decoder. For a quick check of the packaged outputs, run `python experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/check.py`. The full sweep takes several minutes.

The code, transcription and scoring table are included from [Dukotah/cicada3301 revision f08b20b](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round12/C1), with the repository's license. This record matches that program's executed parameters; it does not claim to rule out other functions, alphabets, seed states or non-English plaintext.

The [separately frozen gate plan](experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/gate-plan.json), [21-case results](experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/gate-results.json), and source-search check can be rerun without the several-minute LP2 sweep:

```sh
python experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/gate.py
python experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/check_gate.py
python experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/gate_plot.py
```

# How much text does a skip-count test need?

One proposed cipher model sometimes advances the key without consuming a manuscript rune. Its exact decoder permits such a skip only when the skipped key position would reproduce the previous ciphertext rune. A decoder can count those extra advances. This [published experiment](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L2-nskips-crossover-length/RESULTS.md) asks when that count can distinguish a **deliberately planted message and its correct key** from random ciphertext paired with random keys. It tests the measuring tool; it does not decode an unsolved page.

## Finding

For the source's exact `keyskip1` decoder, the planted key first clears its **1% two-sided comparison bar at 6,000 runes**. It does not clear the bar at the preceding measured length, 3,600, and it still clears it at 9,000 and 12,956. Thus the observed crossing lies in **(3,600, 6,000]**, on this ten-point length ladder. This is a bound for this plant and this null model, not a universal minimum length or evidence that LP2 uses the modeled cipher.

![The planted correct-key skip count crosses the wrong-key upper-tail threshold at 6,000 runes, then remains above it.](experiments/records/public-nskips-crossover/crossover.svg)

At 3,600 runes the correct-key path made **94 skips**; the 1% upper-tail threshold of the 300 wrong-key trials was **107**. At 6,000, the correct path made **198**, above a threshold of **176**. The planted plaintext was recovered with at least **99.8% agreement** at every length, so a failed comparison below 6,000 was not caused by a decoder that could not recover its own test message. A reported two-sided value of `0.000` means none of the 300 sampled null trials was as extreme; it is not a zero probability.

## What was tested

The source planted one message at each of **400, 600, 900, 1,200, 1,600, 2,400, 3,600, 6,000, 9,000 and 12,956 runes**, using its fixed skip rule and seed 3301. For each length and decoder mode it compared the correct-key skip count with 300 uniform-random ciphertext and key pairs of the same length. Its criterion required both a two-sided empirical value at or below **0.01** and at least **90%** recovery of the planted message. The two endpoints were checked first: 400 did not separate, while 12,956 did. The source does not cap its doubled-tail statistic at one, so its reported `1.04` at 600 runes is not a probability.

The archive contains **34 reported cells**. Ten lengths were measured for the exact decoder and for a more permissive drift decoder, and a separate ten-length curve planted a `skip_by_two` mechanism. Four additional labels were measured at the 6,000-rune point. Those labels do **not** represent different language corpora in the executable: the plant uses English *Self-Reliance* text for all of them and changes the chosen window with the label. The script also promised an order-preserving shuffle surrogate in its plan, but only the random ciphertext/key null is executed here.

The alternate channels illustrate why a numerical separation cannot stand alone. The permissive drift decoder produces many spurious skips with random keys, so the correct key falls in its **left** tail even at short lengths; that is a different effect from the excess-skip footprint in the exact decoder. The `skip_by_two` plant never reaches the required recovery floor, so its curve cannot establish a crossover for that mechanism. Neither channel should be combined with the exact-channel crossing.

These are **single planted messages per length**, not repeated estimates of how often the method succeeds on arbitrary messages. No LP2 keys were searched, no plaintext language was inferred, and the numerical bound changes if the plant, null, decoder or threshold changes. In particular, this test does not rule out a useful shorter-window statistic or a different skip rule.

## Reproduce

The bundled [result data](experiments/records/public-nskips-crossover/source/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L2-nskips-crossover-length/nskips_crossover.json) retains every discrete null histogram. The [independent checker](experiments/records/public-nskips-crossover/check.py) recomputes the reported thresholds, tails, crossing and endpoint gate, then compares the replay with the pinned source result. From a Liberpedia checkout:

```bash
python experiments/records/public-nskips-crossover/check.py
python experiments/records/public-nskips-crossover/run.py
```

The full runner copies the source to a temporary folder. It reuses a null sample when multiple cells call the source with the **same length, decoder mode, seed and 300-trial input rule**; the source would otherwise recompute identical samples. Every resulting cell is checked against the pinned output. For the exact executable, input files and predeclared rules, inspect the [source driver](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L2-nskips-crossover-length/crossover.py), [plan](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L2-nskips-crossover-length/PREREG.md), and [bundled source files](experiments/records/public-nskips-crossover/source/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L2-nskips-crossover-length/PREREG.md).

# A bounded test of the P20 boundary model

**Question.** In a published P20 analysis, do the supplied numeric boundary states support a single *static affine* rule over the finite field modulo 83?

**Result.** The source's finite calculation reproduces, including its independent check and planted controls. Across **34,020** allowed assignments of state pairs at eight boundary contexts, **six** stated lower-complexity combinations have **no** complete fit. The saturated six-feature/six-feature combination has **five** fits. That count is ordinary under the source's exact conditioned comparison: **4.94** fits expected, with probability **0.552** of five or more. It does not identify a boundary transform or decode a page.

![Eight supplied boundary contexts yield no fit in six lower-complexity static classes; five saturated fits are near the exact null expectation.](experiments/records/public-p20-static-boundary/boundary-fit.svg)

## What the finite test actually says

The [pinned repository](https://github.com/emmanuel6474/liber-primus-p20-analysis/tree/a39e7de90ff9414791fe5f4f8d44540bd0bdb089) describes an **812-rune section it calls P20**. Its bundled numeric file gives eight chosen boundary contexts, six numeric features per context and a menu of permissible pairs of state values. Choosing one pair from each menu gives 34,020 assignments. A proposed *static affine* rule would express each of the two output state coordinates as a fixed linear combination of selected features plus a constant, all modulo 83. The scripts test the declared feature-count pairs `(4,4)`, `(4,5)`, `(5,4)`, `(5,5)`, `(5,6)`, `(6,5)` and `(6,6)` against all eight contexts.

The zeros are exact **within those eight supplied menus and model classes**. The five `(6,6)` fits use all six features for each coordinate plus an intercept. The source separately asks whether the held-out c18 menu’s five fits distinguish it from alternatives. Its independent exact finite-population calculation finds the observed count unexceptional. Two planted low-complexity affine laws are recovered exactly, while one-value mutations break them. These controls show the fitter can recover simple laws when they are present in synthetic data.

We ran the source's [complete cross-validation](https://github.com/emmanuel6474/liber-primus-p20-analysis/blob/a39e7de90ff9414791fe5f4f8d44540bd0bdb089/analysis/33_boundary_complete_crossvalidation.py), [independent exact-null verifier](https://github.com/emmanuel6474/liber-primus-p20-analysis/blob/a39e7de90ff9414791fe5f4f8d44540bd0bdb089/analysis/35_exact_null_independent_verifier.py), and [plant-and-recover control](https://github.com/emmanuel6474/liber-primus-p20-analysis/blob/a39e7de90ff9414791fe5f4f8d44540bd0bdb089/analysis/38_positive_control_plant_and_recover.py) from pinned Git blobs in a temporary directory. Each passed and regenerated a JSON object identical to its committed result. Liberpedia's separate checker recomputes the 34,020 menu product and the exact probability from the saved weight histogram.

The repository calls itself **partial** and [says the original raw workspace is missing](https://github.com/emmanuel6474/liber-primus-p20-analysis/blob/a39e7de90ff9414791fe5f4f8d44540bd0bdb089/PROVENANCE.md). This test **does not independently derive its eight state menus or six features from the manuscript**. It cannot rule out a dynamic or different boundary rule. Its “P20” is the source's section label; this record does not equate it to one Liberpedia page.

## Reproduce from the pinned source

The pinned Git tree has no explicit license, so the experiment ZIP contains our harness, plan and results, **not** copies of the source code or normalized numeric input. Clone the [source repository](https://github.com/emmanuel6474/liber-primus-p20-analysis/tree/a39e7de90ff9414791fe5f4f8d44540bd0bdb089), check out commit `a39e7de90ff9414791fe5f4f8d44540bd0bdb089`, then from the Liberpedia repository root run:

```text
python experiments/records/public-p20-static-boundary/run.py --source PATH_TO_SOURCE_CLONE --check
python experiments/records/public-p20-static-boundary/check.py --source PATH_TO_SOURCE_CLONE
```

The harness reads exact Git blobs, verifies SHA-256 hashes and revision, and executes the three scripts in a temporary directory. The [source's quick `verify.py`](https://github.com/emmanuel6474/liber-primus-p20-analysis/blob/a39e7de90ff9414791fe5f4f8d44540bd0bdb089/verify.py) has a separate defect: its hash manifest names `.gitignore` and `.github/workflows/verify.yml`, but neither file exists in that commit, so the quick check fails before reaching the mathematical assertions. This record runs the mathematical scripts directly; it does not report the quick verifier as passing. [The file-by-file intake](research/source-intake/emmanuel-p20-a39e7de.json) documents all 85 tracked files, 20 active analysis scripts and that limit.

# Seven public PRNG constructions against LP2

Could a seeded software random-number generator supply LP2's 29-symbol key stream? This reruns a [published seven-generator screen](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/prng/RESULTS.md) against the first 120 runes of the unsolved text.

## Finding

**No candidate in the executed grid reached the source's required English score.** The replay screened **52,556 decodes**: seven generator implementations, 1,877 fixed seeds, two addition signs and two key directions. The best candidate scored **−6.347**; a candidate needed at least **−5.500** to advance. A planted English message encoded with the source's PHP-style generator scored **−4.155** and was recovered exactly. The same program can therefore find one of its own planted signals under this setup.

These are English quadgram scores: they measure how much a four-letter pattern resembles the training text. **Higher is better**, but even a high score would still require a readable continuation and independent checks before it could count as a solution.

![Three scores on the same scale: planted control clears the bar; the manuscript's best candidate does not.](experiments/records/public-prng-seed-sweep/score.svg)

The winning seed, generator, sign and direction match the archived run. This is evidence about the **specific seeded generators and seed slice below**, not evidence that LP2 uses no PRNG or no stream cipher.

## What was tested

The seven source implementations are PHP-5-style `mt_rand`, .NET-4-style `System.Random`, a simplified single-integer-seeded ISAAC, Blum–Blum–Shub at two fixed moduli, a 32-bit LFSR and a Geffe combination of three LFSRs. Every stream is reduced modulo 29. The key-skip beam searches up to three rejected key symbols at each rune, using the source's English quadgram scorer. Its first-stage ciphertext is exactly the source's 120-rune LP2 prefix, regenerated from the pinned runic transcription.

The 1,877 seeds are **1,828 daily-spaced Unix seconds from 2011–2015 plus 49 fixed number/string-derived seeds**. The source's earlier plan described hourly sampling and an additional rejection reduction; the actual executable and result cover daily sampling and `mod29` only. That difference matters. The test also fixes key offset at zero and does not check other starting positions.

The source calls all seven generators “validated,” but most reference vectors in this script are computed by the same implementation being tested. Self-consistency and a planted decode show that the local program works consistently; they do **not** independently verify exact PHP, .NET or standard ISAAC runtime compatibility. The ISAAC variant expressly uses a simplified seed procedure. We therefore name them as the **source implementations**, not all production runtimes bearing those names.

## Reproduce

Download this experiment's ZIP and run from its extracted folder:

```sh
python experiments/records/public-prng-seed-sweep/run.py
```

The command executes the archived test program, then independently checks the reconstructed ciphertext, case count, control, winning configuration and score against the separately archived original result. It takes several minutes. For a quick integrity check of saved results, run `python experiments/records/public-prng-seed-sweep/check.py`.

The packaged source files are pinned to [Dukotah/cicada3301 revision f08b20b](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/prng). The original generator code, documented plan and result are retained with this record. The only regenerated source input is `ct.bin`, constructed byte-for-byte from that revision's `krisyotam_runes.txt`; the checker confirms its 12,956 rune indices and SHA-256.

records.article:
# The 256-byte grid payload as an RSA block

## Finding

The [published E-01 test](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round18/L5-payload/PREREG.md) interprets the **whole 256-byte payload from LP2 pages 49–51** as an RSA value. We reproduced its **162 structural checks** under Cicada's 4096-bit PGP primary key and subkey. **None** produced a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature frame, a PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption frame, or the tested PSS frame. The source's genuine-signature controls fired; 10,000 random control blocks produced no strict hits.

![The two 4096-bit PGP moduli each support 81 evaluated checks with zero structural hits. The 432-bit 2013 modulus supports none because the whole payload is larger than the modulus.](experiments/records/public-rsa-payload-e01/rsa-scope.svg)

The third modulus in the source grid, from the **2013 welcome message**, is only **432 bits**. Every whole-payload value is at least as large as it, so **zero** valid RSA inputs are evaluated under that modulus. The test also skips six left-aligned encodings that are too large for their 4096-bit modulus. Altogether it records **12 excluded encodings** before crossing valid inputs with three exponents and three structural checks.

## What was checked

The source specifies three pinned 256-byte payload readings: the majority transcription, decimal-preferred transcription, and its resolved reading. For each valid byte order and zero-extension convention it calculates `s^e mod n`, with public exponents **65537, 3, and 17**, and examines the resulting block for the specified padding structure. The full [source results](experiments/records/public-rsa-payload-e01/source-expected.json) and our [replay summary](experiments/records/public-rsa-payload-e01/results.json) agree on every evaluated row, not just the headline count. The 3 and 17 exponents are exploratory alternatives; the PGP keys themselves specify 65537.

This is a **public-power structure test**. If the payload were an RSA-encrypted ciphertext, applying the public exponent again would not decrypt it; decryption would require the private exponent. The null result covers these whole-payload representations under these two PGP moduli and structural predicates. It does not rule out an internal 54-byte RSA block, a private-key operation, a different encoding, or another role for the number grid. The separate [54-byte window test](#/experiments/rsa-window-54-source-replay) covers a different construction.

## Reproduce

The [plan](experiments/records/public-rsa-payload-e01/plan.json) pins the source revision, minimal source files, PGP armor, 2013 witness, payload bytes and historical output by SHA-256. The source is included under its MIT license. Run `python experiments/records/public-rsa-payload-e01/run.py --check` from the repository root to execute the original program in a temporary copy and compare its stable rows with the archived output. Run `python experiments/records/public-rsa-payload-e01/check.py` to independently extract the PGP modulus and fingerprint, verify the 2013 modulus, recompute all 162 public-power outputs, and check the padding predicates. The original source's planted controls require the `cryptography` Python package; the independent checker uses only Python's standard library.

# A public 43-key Vigenère sweep

An archived attempt tried Liber Primus-related words as repeating Vigenère keys. Its [README](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/bruteforce/vigenere/README.md) describes a wordlist; its [output archive](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/bruteforce/vigenere/vigenere-bruteforce-results.zip) contains **43** rune keys across 58 page files. The archive includes an additional DIVINITY key after the listed words. We take the keys from the archived output, rather than silently reducing the set to the README list.

## Finding

![A fixed-key sweep: 43 keys across 55 rune-bearing unsolved pages, with no 12-rune known-opening match.](experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/key-sweep.svg)

The **complete decoded rune streams** match the pinned public output in all **2,494 page–key cases** (43 keys across 58 archived pages). That includes **2,408 cases** on LP2-00–55; LP2-50 contains only the alphanumeric grid and has no rune output. None of the 2,365 rune-bearing page starts equals any of nine predeclared, 12-rune known-reading openings: **0 of 21,285 comparisons**. A planted MOUNTAIN plaintext encrypts and decrypts correctly with the first source key.

This verifies the public arithmetic throughout each archived output and rules out **these keys, at page-start phase zero, for these nine exact openings** on our transcription. It does not mean that every wordlist Vigenère attempt has failed. A different key, phase, word-boundary reset, alphabet, page segment, or plaintext beginning is outside this check. The source's “no good result” is an editorial observation, not a numerical language score, so we do not present it as a measured threshold.

## What was done

For every rune position *j* on each page, we computed plaintext index `P[j] = C[j] − K[j mod length(K)] (mod 29)`. Non-rune marks and the number square remain visible but do not advance the key. We kept the GP rune order and the printed page boundaries fixed. The [plan](experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/plan.json) pins all 43 rune keys and the public repository revision. The saved [results](experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/results.json) give every LP2-00–55 page/key prefix and its input hash. The independent [check](experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/check.py) recomputes those prefixes; with the source ZIP, it compares the **full Latin rune-label stream** on all 58 archived pages. The [source-output certificate](experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/source-output-certificate.json) records that wider audit. The archive uses both `IA` and `IO` for one GP rune. We normalize that label, omit the separately structured eight-cell alphanumeric grid rows, and keep letters in lines with inline numbers; rune labels are not unambiguously separable by greedy spelling, so the comparison uses complete joined label strings.

This is related to the [two known Vigenère keys and nine openings](#/experiments/lp2-known-vigenere-keys), but it is a different fixed source key list and a narrower phase rule. The nine openings are a diagnostic: their absence does not prove that no decoded output contains meaningful text elsewhere.

## Reproduce

From the repository root, run `python experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/check.py`. To verify every complete archived output, download the ZIP from the pinned GitHub revision and pass it with `--source-archive PATH` to the checker; the source ZIP and page inputs are hash-checked.

records.article:
# Python 2.7 priority seeds against fixed LP2 openings

**Finding.** None of the **45,975 priority words** in the published [R21-L3 sweep](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L3-py27-reducers-plus-64bit-map/sweep.py) produces any of nine fixed 12-rune known-reading openings at the start of the 55 nonempty pages in LP2-00–55. We checked all four source generator settings—**183,900 generated cases**—under the source's key-skip rule. The closest match reaches five runes.

![No Python 2.7 priority-seed case matches a complete twelve-rune opening; the longest match is five.](experiments/records/py27-prior-front-opening-cribs/prior-front-prefixes.svg)

## What was checked

The source orders 433 proposed 32-bit words, then adds the ±512 neighbourhood around its first 64 words, removing repeated values. That yields **45,975 words** before its later dense-from-zero search. We reconstructed the order from the pinned `seedprior20.json` and checked its SHA-256 digest against the earlier source audit. For each word we used exactly the source's four settings:

| Setting | How the key starts |
| --- | --- |
| `grb5_mod_i386` | One 32-bit seed word; five random bits modulo 29 |
| `grb5_rej_i386` | One 32-bit seed word; reject five-bit values 29–31 |
| `shuffle29_i386` | One 32-bit seed word; repeated shuffled rune alphabet |
| `random29_amd64` | Multiply the word by the source constant into 64 bits; seed with its low and high 32-bit words |

We generated the first **45 key symbols**, enough to allow 12 accepted symbols with up to three rejected symbols between them. A rejected symbol is permitted only if it would have repeated the preceding ciphertext rune. The test searches every valid skip path, without ranking or discarding one because its English score looks poor. It uses the source's subtraction direction, zero starting offset, no Atbash, and the same nine predeclared openings used in other site experiments.

## What the result means

| Best opening prefix per case | Generated cases |
| --- | ---: |
| 1 rune | 115,884 |
| 2 runes | 64,488 |
| 3 runes | 3,409 |
| 4 runes | 108 |
| 5 runes | 11 |
| All 12 runes | **0** |

There are **183,356 different first-45-symbol streams** among the 183,900 generated cases. The counts above are settings and seeds tested, not separate solving ideas. The useful conclusion is limited: *this priority seed grid cannot produce any of these nine exact openings at those page starts under the stated skip rule.* Other plaintext openings, later positions, further seeds and other key rules are outside the result.

R21-L3 originally screened **884,000** word-and-setting cases on LP2-00 with an English-language panel. This record does **not** reproduce that language-panel claim: its model inputs are unavailable in the pinned source. The fixed-opening criterion here is independent of that panel and asks a narrower, directly checkable question.

## Reproduce

From the repository root:

```bash
python experiments/records/py27-prior-front-opening-cribs/run.py
python experiments/records/py27-prior-front-opening-cribs/check.py
python experiments/records/py27-prior-front-opening-cribs/plot.py --check
```

The record bundles the pinned source seed list and Python 2.7 generator under their MIT license. `results.json` gives each setting's prefix counts and a digest over all 183,900 case results. The separate checker rebuilds the whole grid, uses its own exact path-state search, checks 400 small cases against brute tree search, verifies a reference MT19937 output vector, and recovers planted openings with and without a forced skipped key symbol.

records.question: Does the pinned four-configuration Python 2.7 keystream sweep provide an independently reproducible negative with a validated screening gate?
records.summary: The source reports 884,000 screened words and saves 95 promotions with no final-bar clearance. Those rows reconcile, but the original scoring model is unavailable and the planted controls bypass the sweep's first gate.

record_type.label: Source or input audit
record_type.description: Checks image provenance, extraction or input coverage against a declared reference; it does not establish a decryption.

scope.representation: The source's canonical LP2 numeric stream; first 120 runes of LP2-00 screened and first 240 assessed after promotion. This audit inspects pinned source outputs and code, not a fresh cipher decode.
scope.procedure: Hash the pinned source files; independently reconcile all saved survivor rows and aggregate counts; reconstruct the proposed-seed front; inspect source call paths for the two-stage gate; inventory unavailable model inputs.
scope.parameters: Four pinned reducer/map configurations; source-reported 884,000 screened words; 95 saved promoted rows; screening score bar 5.0 and final score bar 7.6342.

records.finding: All 95 pinned Stage-B rows reconcile with the source aggregate; none reaches the 7.6342 final score bar. The 45,975-word proposed-seed front reconstructs. The source-reported 884,000 Stage-A tests cannot be replayed from public bytes, and the 4/4 saved positive controls do not exercise Stage A. The source prose also counts 71 perfect-recovery rows where its receipt contains 67.

records.article:
## Finding

The pinned source reports a sweep of **884,000 seed words** across four Python 2.7-style keystream configurations. It saved **95 candidates** that passed its first screen. We can check those saved rows: they divide into **21, 25, 24 and 25** by configuration, and none clears the source's final score bar of **7.6342**. Their highest final score is **6.248**. The underlying 884,000 first-stage scores were *not* saved, so the sweep total and the claim that no omitted candidate passed remain source-reported rather than independently recomputed here.

The source's planted-key control passes **4/4** in its saved output, but it begins at the **full 240-rune evaluation**. The actual sweep first applies a **120-rune, narrower-beam screen** and promotes a word only when that score reaches **5.0**. The control never calls this screening function. It therefore shows the final evaluator can recognize its own planted text; it does **not** measure whether the first gate would pass that text. The exact model file needed to try the gate is missing from the pinned public repository, as are three of the corpus files required to rebuild it.

![The actual sweep has a first screening gate that the planted control skips.](experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/screen-control-gap.svg)

This is a **source-method audit**, not a new negative decryption result. The saved rows support a narrower statement: *among the 95 recorded promotions, no candidate met the published final score threshold.* They do not establish a measured false-negative rate for Stage A or a ruling on Python-derived keystreams in general.

## What was in the source sweep

| Rune reducer / seed map | Screened, reported | Saved promotions | Best saved final score |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `getrandbits(5) % 29`, one word | 288,000 | 21 | 6.089 |
| Reject `getrandbits(5)` values 29–31, one word | 216,000 | 25 | 5.260 |
| Repeated shuffle of 29 values, one word | 186,000 | 24 | 6.248 |
| `int(random() × 29)`, two-word seed map | 194,000 | 25 | 5.341 |

The source orders **433 proposed seed words**, expands neighborhoods around its top 64, and deduplicates them to **45,975** words before a dense count from zero. We independently reconstructed that ordering from the pinned seed-prior file. The recorded screen counts are each larger than 45,975, consistent with the source's statement that it completed this front in every configuration. Because only promoted rows were persisted, their actual first-stage scores and the rest of each scan cannot be audited from the receipts alone.

There is a small but concrete reporting error: the prose says **71 of 95** promotions had both recovery fields equal to 1.000. The pinned rows contain **67**. This does not change the observed zero final-bar clearances, but it illustrates why the rows matter more than summary prose.

## Scope and how to retest

The source decodes the **first 120 runes of LP2-00** for screening and the **first 240** for its final gate. Its key is a seed word passed through one of the four specified reducer/map combinations. The searched fractions of each nominal 2³²-word space are roughly **0.004–0.007%**. The two-word map is a deterministic 32-bit-to-64-bit fold used by the source, not an enumeration of all 64-bit Python hash values. Other seeds, other reducers, other cipher relations and plaintexts outside the source's scoring panel remain untested here.

The [pinned sweep code](experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/source/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L3-py27-reducers-plus-64bit-map/sweep.py), [planted control](experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/source/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L3-py27-reducers-plus-64bit-map/poscontrol.py), [saved rows](experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/source/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L3-py27-reducers-plus-64bit-map/reducers_sweep.jsonl) and [aggregate](experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/source/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L3-py27-reducers-plus-64bit-map/out_reducers.json) are included with hashes. Reconcile them without the absent model using:

```text
python experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/run.py --check
python experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/check.py
python experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/plot.py --check
```

To establish the broader negative, first restore the original `panel.npz` or its exact training inputs, then run the **complete planted control through Stage A and Stage B**. Persist each screened word's first-stage score or a verifiable checkpoint before repeating the bounded sweep. The original [preregistration](experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/source/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L3-py27-reducers-plus-64bit-map/PREREG.md) describes that intended bound; the [source manifest](experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/source-manifest.json) identifies the bytes audited here.

records.article:
# How far does the QuagMirror draft run?

**Result.** The pinned public script processes the first **six runes of LP2-00**, then deliberately stops. An independent replay obtains the same index streams and the transliteration **DCBWJO**. That is a match to the draft program's output, not a reading of the page. The code does not run its proposed method across a complete word or page.

The idea combines an autokey calculation with one of nine handwritten 29-symbol substitution tables. At each position, Möbius values associated with the position and a prime-derived totient choose the table. Previous cipher and output symbols feed the next autokey calculation. The first two positions contain explicit overrides in the source. Those choices are retained here; silently removing them would replay a different method.

![A five-row diagram traces the six cipher indices through the autokey indices, selected mirror tables, output indices and Latin fragments.](experiments/records/quagmirror-six-rune-replay/six-rune-trace.svg)

| Stage | Six values |
| --- | --- |
| Archived LP2-00 rune indices | 15, 8, 18, 3, 6, 19 |
| Autokey indices | 15, 28, 2, 10, 3, 14 |
| Output indices | 23, 5, 17, 7, 11, 3 |
| Latin fragments | D C B W J O |

The replay checks the source's first six input indices against this site's LP2-00 transcription. It stores all nine permutation tables and every fixed choice in the [plan](experiments/records/quagmirror-six-rune-replay/plan.json), then calculates each row in the [result](experiments/records/quagmirror-six-rune-replay/results.json). The tables are permutations, but that property alone does not make the output intelligible or prove an encryption mechanism.

This is a **WIP source-version replay**. The repository contains several changing scripts; it would be misleading to combine their rules into one historical "QuagMirror" result. The particular file [Mobius_AT_QuagMirror.py at pinned commit 88ef1e60](https://github.com/sgroveman/cicada3301_lp/blob/88ef1e60b0738b8b28db96bc9dc44dc4da8dd307/Solving%20Attempts/Mobius_AT_QuagMirror.py) has SHA-256 `e317878190994910afbbdc5707a66af73a684b29abdd9d7e443563aba9d15a66`. Its `break` after six processed positions is part of the code, so this record cannot test its remaining page output, any later revisions or proposed thematic keywords. A complete candidate needs one frozen version, a declared rule for every position, full output and an untouched-text check.

Run `python experiments/records/quagmirror-six-rune-replay/run.py --check` from the repository root. Python's standard library suffices. The saved plan and results make this exact six-position variant available offline without shipping the source discussion or changing its unfinished state.

records.article:
# Three QuagMirror drafts beyond the six-rune example

The [six-rune draft](#/experiments/quagmirror-six-rune-replay) is one of four scripts in the same [pinned public repository](https://github.com/sgroveman/cicada3301_lp/tree/88ef1e60b0738b8b28db96bc9dc44dc4da8dd307/Solving%20Attempts). We ran the other three **as written**, including their fixed debug stops and handwritten mirror tables. All start from the same 729 source rune indices covering LP2-00–02. The indices match Liberpedia's page transcription after treating the two printed forms of the J rune as the same alphabet position.

## Finding

The scripts process **49, 153 and 500 positions** respectively. Each produces short English-like fragments mixed with unreadable text. None processes its whole 729-rune input, supplies a planted recovery control, or checks a reading on held-out text. Reproducing these outputs establishes what the drafts actually do; it does not establish a plaintext for LP2.

![The original script stops after 153 runes, version 4 after 49, and the WIP script after 500; page boundaries occur after 262 and 528.](experiments/records/quagmirror-variant-continuations/coverage.svg)

| Script | Positions | Beginning of its output |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Original | 153 | `DIUINITY WITHIN HAUING BOTH IHING...` |
| Version 4 | 49 | `DIUINITY WITHIN PRAY FOR ANY CORRUPTIBLE...` |
| WIP | 500 | `DIUINITH WITHIN EUEN DIATH OSW...` |

These are **three different drafts**, not three confirmations of one decryption. Their rules and stopping points differ. Version 4 contains a pass-through at source index 17 that uses `continue` before the loop counter advances. Its nominal `index >= 48` debug stop therefore occurs after **49 input positions**. We retain that behavior; silently changing it would create another method. The [complete outputs and numeric streams](experiments/records/quagmirror-variant-continuations/results.json) are saved so a promising fragment can be read in context rather than selected in isolation.

## What the replay checks

Each script contains nine 29-symbol substitution tables, a hard-coded 729-index ciphertext, a numerical recurrence, and a Latin-fragment mapping. The [checker](experiments/records/quagmirror-variant-continuations/check.py) confirms that the tables are permutations, the source ciphertext matches the 729 runes on LP2-00–02, the printed numeric rows have the stated lengths, and the printed final text follows from those numeric outputs and the script's own spacing marks. This independently checks the **input and output trace**; it is not an independent proof that the recurrence recovers meaningful plaintext.

The first fragments may look deliberate. Assessing them requires the full output, a fixed method for every rune, a criterion chosen before seeing the result, and a positive control showing that the program can recover a known message made with its proposed cipher. The source drafts provide no such control. The longer WIP output is valuable evidence of how the apparent opening continues under the same code, but it does not by itself validate or refute every QuagMirror-style method.

## Reproduce

From a Liberpedia checkout with Python 3 and SymPy installed:

```bash
python experiments/records/quagmirror-variant-continuations/check.py
python experiments/records/quagmirror-variant-continuations/run.py
```

The runner executes the three bundled [pinned scripts](experiments/records/quagmirror-variant-continuations/source/OG_quag_mirror.py), extracts their complete printed output tables, and compares the results with the saved file. Their source revision is `88ef1e60b0738b8b28db96bc9dc44dc4da8dd307`; the record lists every file hash. No word choice, table, or stop point is adjusted during the replay.

records.title: Can skipped key draws shift a page start?
records.question: When earlier runes consume extra key draws, does a drift-corrected offset recover a planted key and improve previously reported keys on LP2?
records.summary: A planted key is recovered only after correcting for skipped draws. Replaying 1,371,030 real-page decodes over 230 previously ranked candidate keys yields no supported reading under the source score gate.

scope.representation: Gematria Primus indices from the source transcription; 55 nonempty LP2-00–55 pages, with source ordinal 52 mapped to LP2-53.
scope.procedure: Run F0 parity gate, replay the three-page planted offset control, and search 230 source-mined key candidates at 5,961 offsets each over first 100 runes of every nonempty page; compare all candidate rows with pinned source output.

# Does key skipping move a page's starting position?

If an encryptor discards some key draws to prevent repeated output runes, the key position at a later page is **not** simply the number of preceding runes. This [published Round 18 test](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round18/L2-filter-leak) searches a predicted band of later key positions. We replayed its planted-key control and its search over previously reported candidate keys.

## Finding

![Three planted pages score much better at the corrected key position than at the uncorrected one. In the real manuscript, neither the best corrected score nor the best overall score reaches the source's reading bar.](experiments/records/r18-drift-ladder-replay/drift-ladder.svg)

The correction matters **when the simulated key is known to be right**: on three planted pages, the true offset ranks first, scoring about −4.0. Starting at the uncorrected position scores around −7.0 to −7.3 on those same pages. The planted control therefore shows that an otherwise good key could be missed by a rigid page-start test under this particular skip model.

On the real LP2 transcription, the source tests **230 candidate keystreams** mined from its earlier top lists. Each is checked at **5,961 positions** across the first 100 runes of each of **55 nonempty pages**: **1,371,030 decodes**. The best result in the newly corrected positions is **−6.012**. The best overall, **−5.885**, is at a previously tested page-restart position. Both remain below the source's declared **−5.5** reading bar. No candidate in this bounded set supplies a supported reading.

The source numbers the nonempty text segments from zero. Its “page 52” is **LP2-53** in the manuscript: LP2-50 has no rune text and drops out of that numbering. We checked this mapping against all 56 LP2-00–55 page records.

## Scope and limits

The offset band assumes one continuous 29-value key stream, a per-draw skip probability derived from the manuscript's low adjacent-repeat rate, and a maximum of three skipped draws at a step. The source searches a predicted four-standard-deviation band plus uncorrected and page-restart controls. It inspects 100 runes per text page. The 230 keys came from earlier score-ranked lists; they are **not every possible key**. A low score here does not reject every key-skip method, other global starts, page rules, or later text.

The **−5.5** bar is the source's historical English-score gate, not a fresh held-out calibration for all choices behind this search. The plant verifies recovery under its synthetic rule, not that LP2 used that rule.

## Reproduce

The [source-read replay plan](experiments/records/r18-drift-ladder-replay/plan.json) pins the source revision, candidate-list inputs, KJV text, and original output hashes. This B4 publication scope was derived from the [combined plan frozen before our replay](experiments/records/r18-drift-ladder-replay/combined-plan-as-frozen.json); neither plan is an independent preregistration of the published method. The first isolated pass exposed one missing staged input for the PRNG candidates. The [dependency amendment](experiments/records/r18-drift-ladder-replay/plan-amendment.json) pins an archived `ct.bin` that independently matches the source's `prep.py` output. We retained the 210 completed rows and retried the 20 affected candidates. The runner checks these bytes, stages files in a temporary directory, and leaves the source checkout untouched. Use the pinned source checkout as `SOURCE`:

```text
python experiments/records/r18-drift-ladder-replay/run.py --source-root SOURCE --kjv exports/sources/gutenberg-10-kjv.txt --stage gate
python experiments/records/r18-drift-ladder-replay/run.py --source-root SOURCE --kjv exports/sources/gutenberg-10-kjv.txt --stage b4pc
python experiments/records/r18-drift-ladder-replay/run.py --source-root SOURCE --kjv exports/sources/gutenberg-10-kjv.txt --stage ladder --nproc 6
python experiments/records/r18-drift-ladder-replay/check.py
python experiments/records/r18-drift-ladder-replay/plot.py --check
```

The complete [source ladder](experiments/records/r18-drift-ladder-replay/source-b4_ladder.json) and [our replay](experiments/records/r18-drift-ladder-replay/replayed-b4_ladder.json) are retained. The checker compares all **230** candidate rows independent of multiprocessing order and derives the offset count from the page records. It also verifies the source's ordinal-to-page mapping.

# What can an entropy budget tell us?

A [published Round 18 calculation](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round18/L2-filter-leak) counts bits in a proposed key-skip cipher and labels some key models “determined.” We replayed every number with the recovered exact source text. The arithmetic reproduces; the determinacy labels do **not** follow from it.

## Finding

![The source estimates 62.6 thousand ciphertext bits under a full random-pad model. The same output estimate is then reused for a 256-bit seeded key, whose English-plus-key input proxy is only 33.5 thousand bits. A deterministic model cannot have more output entropy than counted input entropy.](experiments/records/r18-entropy-budget-replay/budget-models.svg)

The source estimates **62,617 bits** of output entropy from a 29-rune filtered Markov model fitted to LP2's repeat rate. It separately measures **2.568 bits per rune** as the lowest test-set cross-entropy among six short Markov models of one King James Bible encoding, then scales that value to **33,269 bits** for a manuscript-length English proxy.

For a full independent random pad, its estimated input sum is about **98,025 bits**. Replacing the pad with a **256-bit seed** reduces that sum to about **33,525 bits**, but the source keeps the same **62,617-bit output estimate** and calls the negative difference “determined.” Those numbers cannot all describe one deterministic seeded-key model: output entropy cannot exceed the entropy of its inputs. A random rejection coin could supply additional randomness, but it must be counted explicitly, and the output law must be recalculated for that model. The source's 40-, 64-, and 32-bit seed rows have the same issue.

Even within one consistent model, an entropy difference is **not an if-and-only-if test for a unique plaintext**. The expression `H(P) + H(K) − H(C)` equals remaining *joint* uncertainty only with the requisite independence and deterministic-channel assumptions; positive joint uncertainty can coexist with a uniquely known plaintext, while a negative value signals incompatible assumptions. It does not certify a readable LP2 decryption.

## What the corpus measurement covers

The source encodes a fixed KJV text in Gematria Primus runes, trains Markov orders **0–5** on the first **400,000** runes, and scores the next **200,000**. Order **3** has the lowest measured cross-entropy on that test segment. Selecting the best order on the same test segment is a model-selection step, and one Bible segment is not a measured distribution for unknown LP2 plaintext. The source also simulates **1,000** constant-text and **1,000** English-text filters; their low adjacent-repeat rates are a control for the specified model, not a way to infer LP2's text.

The source's **323-bit** “filter information injection” is the reduction in *ciphertext entropy* under its fitted Markov law. It is not 323 bits about plaintext. The separate [exact conditional-channel result](#/experiments/rejection-channel-information) proves that, with independent uniform key draws and the stated filter, the visible next-rune law is identical for every plaintext rune. That proof has narrower assumptions than a claim about every possible LP2 cipher.

## Reproduce

The ZIP includes the exact [KJV input](exports/sources/gutenberg-10-kjv.txt), preserved from [Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/10/10-0.txt). The runner verifies its hash; the source-code checkout and NumPy are still required.

The [replay plan](experiments/records/r18-entropy-budget-replay/plan.json) pins revision `f08b20b`, every imported source file, the recovered KJV bytes, and the original output hash. It was frozen before our run after we inspected the published source. With that checkout at `SOURCE`:

```text
python experiments/records/r18-entropy-budget-replay/run.py --source-root SOURCE --kjv exports/sources/gutenberg-10-kjv.txt --check
python experiments/records/r18-entropy-budget-replay/check.py
python experiments/records/r18-entropy-budget-replay/plot.py --check
```

The runner uses a temporary source tree and leaves the original checkout untouched. The [complete source output](experiments/records/r18-entropy-budget-replay/source-results.json) and [replay](experiments/records/r18-entropy-budget-replay/replayed-results.json) match in every field. The independent checker recomputes the entropy formulas and flags the model mismatch; it does not turn the KJV proxy into a claim about LP2's language or key.

# Where could a repeat filter act?

LP2-00–55 contains **86 equal adjacent rune pairs among 12,955**. One [published seven-model comparison](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round18/L2-filter-leak) asks whether that scarcity looks like a filter on the output, the key, or the input text. We reproduced its complete 200-replicate simulation and saved every result field.

## Finding

![The observed repeat rate is 0.664 percent. Key skip and output rewrite are near it; fixed nudge also matches repeats but fails another statistic. No filter, key filter and text filter are around 3.5 percent; hard ban produces zero.](experiments/records/r18-filter-locus-replay/filter-loci.svg)

Two **output-stage** models reproduce the observed repeat rate within this setup: discard a key draw and retry (**0.633%** simulated), or overwrite a repeated output with a fresh random rune (**0.668%**). The manuscript has **0.664%**. The source's classifier has only **17.5% in-sample power** to distinguish the rewrite model from key skipping at its stated 5% false-positive threshold. That is weak separation, not evidence that either mechanism was used.

A third output rule—always nudging a repeated rune by one—also matches the repeat count (**0.659%**). But it makes one modular rune-to-rune difference far too common: its mean largest standardized deviation is **16.5**, versus **2.64** in the manuscript. The unfiltered, key-filtered, and plaintext-filtered source models leave roughly **3.5%** adjacent repeats. A hard output ban leaves **zero**. Those are mismatches for these precisely defined models, not exclusions of every possible filter or cipher.

## What this test actually compares

Each model encrypts the same Gematria Primus encoding of a pinned King James Bible text using simulated uniform 29-value key draws. Where the model has a suppression parameter, the source tunes it to the manuscript's repeat rate before measuring 200 seeded streams of 12,956 runes. Five preselected measurements then include adjacent repeats, other short-distance repeats, alternation, and the distribution of modular differences. The complete [source output](experiments/records/r18-filter-locus-replay/source-results.json) and our [replayed output](experiments/records/r18-filter-locus-replay/replayed-results.json) match in **every field except elapsed time**. These linked copies encode the source's infinite hard-ban deviation as `null`; the exact [source bytes](experiments/records/r18-filter-locus-replay/source-output-raw.txt) are preserved separately.

The source fits each classifier's means, spreads, and threshold on those same simulated streams used to report power. Its **17.5%** and **100%** figures are therefore *in-sample discrimination within this seven-model comparison*, not held-out performance. The manuscript's repeat rate is also used to tune some models; matching that same rate cannot validate a model. Our separate [probability-law check](#/experiments/rejection-channel-information) shows why idealized key-skip and fresh-random-output rules can have the same visible ciphertext distribution. This simulation does not identify which, if either, produced LP2.

## Reproduce

The ZIP includes the exact [KJV input](exports/sources/gutenberg-10-kjv.txt), preserved from [Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/10/10-0.txt). The runner verifies its hash; the source-code checkout and NumPy are still required.

The [frozen plan](experiments/records/r18-filter-locus-replay/plan.json) pins source revision `f08b20b`, exact code and input hashes, the 200-replicate command, and the preserved result hash. Use a checkout of that revision and the exact `kjv.txt` named in the plan. With the source repository at `SOURCE`:

```text
python experiments/records/r18-filter-locus-replay/run.py --source-root SOURCE --kjv exports/sources/gutenberg-10-kjv.txt --check
python experiments/records/r18-filter-locus-replay/check.py
python experiments/records/r18-filter-locus-replay/plot.py --check
```

The runner verifies SHA-256 inputs, stages only the required source files in a temporary directory, and runs the source there, leaving its tracked result file untouched. NumPy is needed for the source simulation. The independent checker uses the repository's LP2 transcription to recount the **27 manuscript measurements** and the conditional draw-count arithmetic; it does **not** independently re-estimate the source classifier's power.

# Can a correct key survive skipped draws?

In a proposed key-skip cipher, a key value is consumed without producing a rune when it would create an adjacent repeat. A correct key then drifts out of alignment with the visible text. The pinned [Round 18 test](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round18/L2-filter-leak) planted a known key and plaintext to ask whether its skip-aware decoder could recover them as the text grows to LP2 length.

## Finding

![Rigid key alignment detects 70 percent of 25-rune plants but only 0.5 percent of 400-rune plants. The skip-aware beam detects all 200 plants at every tested short length and recovers over 99.9 percent of plaintext runes in three full-length plants.](experiments/records/r18-keyskip-drift-power/drift-power.svg)

With the **correct planted key**, rigid decoding crosses the source's reading threshold in just **1 of 200** tests at 400 runes. The skip-aware beam crosses it in **all 200**. At **12,956 runes**, its three planted tests recover a mean **99.97%** of plaintext rune positions; all three satisfy the source's predeclared score and 90% recovery gates. A different SHA-256-counter key scores **−7.30**, below the **−5.5** reading threshold. This shows the beam can retain a known correct key at this length *under the specified simulated filter*.

The source also simulates how far the key index drifts. Its 200 full-length plants consume a mean **374.47** extra draws; the fitted geometric calculation predicts **373.61** over 12,955 transitions. That agrees with the source simulation and the separate [draw-count probability check](#/experiments/rejection-channel-information). It is a model calculation, not a measurement of an LP2 key stream.

## What was tested

The source encodes one exact King James Bible text as Gematria Primus runes, encrypts it with a seeded SHA-256-counter key, and conditionally skips draws when a candidate output repeats the previous rune. The skip probability **0.8129** was chosen from LP2's low repeat rate. A preliminary **F0 gate** checks the faster beam against the source's reference decoder on **24** seeded cases: scores agree to better than 10⁻⁹ and every plaintext path matches. Only then does the full run measure 200 drift samples, 200 planted windows at each of six lengths, and three planted full-length decodes at each of another six lengths. The source's original grid is preserved in the [complete output](experiments/records/r18-keyskip-drift-power/source-results.json).

This is a **power test for the synthetic model**. It does not show that LP2 used key skipping, identify its key, or turn a low-scoring real-page search into a proof that all possible keys fail. The planted plaintext comes from one known English corpus, and the beam's quadgram score rewards that corpus's writing. The source's own score threshold is not a family-wide error rate for an arbitrary later search.

## Reproduce

The ZIP includes the exact [KJV input](exports/sources/gutenberg-10-kjv.txt), preserved from [Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/10/10-0.txt). The runner verifies its hash; the source-code checkout and NumPy are still required.

The [replay plan](experiments/records/r18-keyskip-drift-power/plan.json) pins revision `f08b20b`, the exact source files, the recovered KJV input hash, F0 gate receipt, and B output hash. It was frozen before our replay, after inspecting the published source, so it is a source replay specification rather than a fresh preregistration. With that source checkout at `SOURCE` and its exact `kjv.txt` available:

```text
python experiments/records/r18-keyskip-drift-power/run.py --source-root SOURCE --kjv exports/sources/gutenberg-10-kjv.txt --check
python experiments/records/r18-keyskip-drift-power/check.py
python experiments/records/r18-keyskip-drift-power/plot.py --check
```

The runner verifies every input hash, stages the source in a temporary directory, runs F0 and B, then compares **every non-timing field** with the archived output. It does not change the source checkout's tracked result files. The separate checker recalculates the drift and window-survival formulas and verifies the declared length, beam, threshold and control gates.
records.reader_finding: Given the correct key, the skip-aware decoder recovered 99.97% of the plaintext on average in three full-length simulations.
records.reader_limit: These simulations use one English source and one proposed skip rule. This result does not show that LP2 uses that rule or identify its key.

records.summary: The known planted key has 362 inferred skips versus 240–348 for forty wrong keys on its synthetic text. The best of twenty real LP2 candidates has 353, within the 260–357 wrong-key range, and produces no supported reading.
