# Can inferred key skips identify a correct key?

A [Round 18 source test](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round18/L2-filter-leak) proposes counting how many key draws a skip-aware decoder uses. If a key is right, its winning path may use a different number of skips from a wrong key. We ran the pinned source's full B5 program, including the candidate-ranking loop left unfinished in its saved receipt.

## Finding

![The planted correct key has more beam-inferred skips than the 40 wrong keys on planted text. The best of 20 real candidates overlaps the 40 wrong keys on LP2.](experiments/records/r18-skip-channel-power/skip-counts.svg)

On a **synthetic text encrypted with a known key**, the decoder reports **362 skips**, one away from the planted process's actual **361**. Forty deliberately wrong keys on the same text average **296.3 skips** (range **240–348**). The true-key count is **3.08** of those samples' standard deviations above their mean. This demonstrates separation for this one planted construction.

On the real **12,956-rune LP2 stream**, forty wrong keys average **297.8 skips** (range **260–357**). The finished source run also checks **20 candidates** selected from earlier key searches. Their highest count is **353**, within the wrong-key range and **2.78** standard deviations above its mean; none reaches 3. Their English scores remain around **−7.25 to −7.32**. This bounded test gives no supported LP2 reading or key.

The source describes skip count as a second, English-independent channel. The executable decoder actually **scores plaintext quadgrams while choosing each beam path**, then counts skips on the winning path. The count is therefore affected by that English-based path choice. It is useful as a diagnostic of the decoder, but this implementation does not establish a language-independent measurement.

## What was checked

The [plan frozen before our run](experiments/records/r18-skip-channel-power/plan.json) pins the source revision, dependencies, original result, controls and search bounds. The first B4 stage exposed a missing ignored generated input; the [separate amendment](experiments/records/r18-skip-channel-power/plan-amendment.json) pins its recovered bytes. B5 was run in the same disposable staging process, without changing the source checkout. The source's saved B5 file contains both complete 40-key null samples but an incomplete candidate loop. We reproduce the saved sample statistics exactly and retain the completed 20-candidate output.

The source's stored expected-skip projection differs by **0.0077 skips** from the current pinned executable; the reason for that small difference is unverified and it does not affect the counts above. Its reported “92% screening power” comes from a fitted approximation around one planted true key, rather than repeated held-out true-key trials, so we do not treat that as an observed power estimate.

This checks one skip rule, one synthetic true key, forty specified wrong keys per stream, twenty previously selected real candidates, and an English-scored beam width of 400. Other keys, skip laws, language models and held-out texts remain outside this result. The earlier [drift-ladder test](#/experiments/r18-drift-ladder-replay) covers candidate offsets; this record covers the distinct full-stream skip-count question.

## Reproduce

Use the [pinned source revision](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1) as `SOURCE`. This complete source stage is long-running. The runner checks exact dependency hashes and stages a temporary copy; it does not overwrite the checkout:

```text
python experiments/records/r18-skip-channel-power/run.py --source-root SOURCE --kjv exports/sources/gutenberg-10-kjv.txt --stage skipchannel
python experiments/records/r18-skip-channel-power/check.py
python experiments/records/r18-skip-channel-power/plot.py --check
```

The [saved source receipt](experiments/records/r18-skip-channel-power/source-b5_skipchannel.json) and [completed replay](experiments/records/r18-skip-channel-power/replayed-b5_skipchannel.json) are available. The independent checker rebuilds the original null means, spreads, ranges and all twenty candidate standard scores without calling the beam decoder.
records.reader_finding: None of the 20 tested LP2 key candidates produced a supported reading. The largest inferred skip count, 353, was within the wrong-key range of 260–357.

records.article:
# Which part of a decode does the fold check verify?

**Finding.** The source's fold helper compares **overlapping right-hand tails** of a decoded page. It omits the final fold and never compares the first fold's reference indices. On six new known-key plants, all 30 fold-count trials recover the true text exactly, but changing the first 40 reference indices leaves every measured tail agreement unchanged. Changing every reference index drops every measured tail agreement to zero.

![The five-fold helper compares four overlapping right tails; the first 48 reference indices are never compared.](experiments/records/r21-fold-tail-scope-controls/fold-domains.svg)

The [Round 21 source](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L1-seal-realmode-proxy/hitfn21_folds.py) describes a disjoint-fold check of the held-out complement. Its executable helper first decodes the prefix ending at a fold boundary, then decodes the remaining tail from that prefix's ending key pointer. A final fold has no right-hand tail, so it returns `None`. Earlier prefixes contain all preceding folds, and the compared tails overlap.

| Requested folds | Measured tails | Reference positions compared at least once |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| 2 | 1 | 120–239 |
| 3 | 2 | 80–239 |
| 4 | 3 | 60–239 |
| 5 | 4 | 48–239 |
| 6 | 5 | 40–239 |

Positions above are zero-based. At five folds, for example, four comparisons cover tails starting at 48, 96, 144 and 192. The first 48 reference indices do not enter any agreement calculation. They still affect prefix decoding and the attributed key phase: this is a limit on the **reference comparison**, not a claim that the first ciphertext runes are ignored.

We supplied one fixed 240-rune English plaintext window, three deterministic key seeds and the source's no-suppression or 83% repeat-suppression encoder. The six newly generated ciphertexts use the source `exact` decoder at beam width 400. All six full-page decodes recover 100% of the planted rune indices; every measured tail agrees with its full-page decode at 100%. The three aggregation rules—minimum, mean and fraction above 90%—all return 1.0 for each fold-count trial.

The reference-change controls call the same unmodified source helper on the same ciphertext and key. They change the supplied comparison vector only. Changing its first 40 indices is outside every tested tail, so all tail agreements remain 1.0; changing all indices gives 0.0. These diagnostic controls expose the comparison's scope. They are not wrong-key trials, candidate hallucinations or estimates of a real candidate's correctness.

The runner executes selected source definitions unchanged using Python's syntax tree: the actual `HitDecode` class, baseline held-out helper, fold bounds and fold helpers. It uses the actual bundled beam decoder and English quadgram table. It does not import or replace the unavailable nine-register panel. The separate checker reconstructs each encryption, verifies the traced prefix/tail inputs and key offsets, and independently recounts every agreement and aggregate.

This does **not** replay the original 45 hallucinations, 15-cell catch surface or held-out surrogate, which still require the exact source language panel. The result establishes the executed helper's finite comparison domains; it does not demonstrate that a wrong manuscript reading passes the complete hit gate or that every no-oracle gate must fail.

Run offline with Python 3:

```bash
python experiments/records/r21-fold-tail-scope-controls/run.py
python experiments/records/r21-fold-tail-scope-controls/check.py
python experiments/records/r21-fold-tail-scope-controls/plot.py --check
```

The source, model table, fixed plaintext, plan, traces and MIT license are bundled. No manuscript candidate is searched.
records.reader_finding: The helper checks overlapping right tails; it never compares the first fold of reference indices and skips the final fold.
records.reader_limit: Known-key diagnostic controls; no manuscript key, complete hit decision or original hallucination catch surface is tested.

record_type.description: Applies a fixed decoding, extraction or payload-retrieval rule to declared unsolved material, or excludes a specific direct-generation rule. Its result covers only those bounds.

Each generated case gets exact/keyskip1 and pair/keyskip2 preset. 24,231 generated cases (19,986 distinct first-100-symbol streams); 48,462 rows; 55 nonempty page starts in LP2-00–55; nine cribs.

An independent full-grid path-state check verifies the result. The source's planned count, 49,302, includes 840 Perl and TeX rows the executable loop skips for string seeds.

It only tests nine specific page-start openings with source sign -1, no Atbash, zero initial key offset, the saved seed grid, and the two source skip presets. records.article:
# Older random generators against fixed LP2 openings

**Finding.** We rebuilt the [R26-A source grid](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round26/A/sweep.py) of Perl, TeX and Python 2.7 keystreams and asked whether any could begin an unsolved LP2 page with one of nine known 12-rune readings. Across **24,231 generated key cases**, each checked under the source's two skip rules, **none matched a complete opening**. The closest matched four runes.

![The longest opening matched four of twelve runes; no source-defined configuration matched all twelve.](experiments/records/r26-derived-generators-opening-cribs/opening-prefixes.svg)

This is a **fixed-opening check**, not a rerun of R26-A's English-scoring test. The source tested a 333-rune page with a language panel and reported an interim result. Here the question is narrower and exact: *could a named plaintext opening be structurally produced at a page start?*

## What went into the check

The source's ordered dictionary has **347 entries**: puzzle numbers, the first 200 primes, sparse dates, prime sums of solved-text words and those words as Python 2 string seeds. Its **400 integers from 0 to 399** add a small baseline. Some entries repeat values under another label. We preserved the complete executable generator grid:

| Source generator | Generated key cases | Two skip rules |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Eight Perl `rand` reductions | 5,696 | 11,392 |
| Four TeX random generators | 2,848 | 5,696 |
| Three Python 2.7 reductions, seven offsets each | 15,687 | 31,374 |
| **Total** | **24,231** | **48,462** |

Those cases contain **19,986 different first-100-symbol streams**; repeated seeds and equivalent settings make some duplicate prefixes. The case count describes the source grid, not 24,231 independent ideas or keys.

Perl and TeX accept integer seeds here; Python 2.7 also accepts the 35 word seeds. Python 2.7 uses the source's 64-bit seeding path and offset list **0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 13**. The source's `count_decodes()` announces 49,302 rows because it counts all 347 dictionary entries for Perl and TeX. Its actual loop skips their 35 string seeds, removing **840** rows. We counted the executable loop, not the announced estimate.

For every key stream, we tested the first 12 runes on all **55 nonempty pages in LP2-00–55**—LP2-50 is blank—against the same **nine predeclared 12-rune openings** used in the site's other fixed-opening experiments. We kept the source's subtraction direction, no Atbash, and zero starting offset. The `exact` rule may reject up to three key symbols before an accepted rune; each rejected symbol must otherwise repeat the previous ciphertext rune. The `pair` rule may reject up to eight in pairs; the first symbol of each rejected pair must make that repeat. Every feasible path is considered, without an English-score beam that could prune one.

Only the first **100 key symbols** are needed to test a 12-rune opening under the larger eight-rejection bound. Generating a longer forward stream would leave those symbols unchanged. This shortens the computation without truncating any possible 12-rune path.

## Result and meaning

| Longest feasible prefix among the nine openings and 55 pages | Configurations |
| --- | ---: |
| 1 rune | 30,680 |
| 2 runes | 16,909 |
| 3 runes | 842 |
| 4 runes | 31 |
| All 12 runes | **0** |

A one-rune match says little: each key is compared with many page-and-opening pairs. The decisive fact for this specific test is that **no complete 12-rune opening is possible anywhere in the declared grid**. That does *not* show that these generators cannot encrypt LP2. The unknown pages might begin with other words, use another offset or direction, reset the key, or follow a different transition rule. The original R26-A language-panel outcome is a separate claim.

## Reproduce and inspect

From the repository root:

```bash
python experiments/records/r26-derived-generators-opening-cribs/run.py
python experiments/records/r26-derived-generators-opening-cribs/check.py
python experiments/records/r26-derived-generators-opening-cribs/plot.py --check
```

The ordered seed manifest and original generator modules are bundled with the record under the source's MIT license. The results file records each generator/preset distribution, every complete match (there were none), and a digest over all 48,462 configuration results. An independent checker regenerates the full grid with a separate path-state implementation, compares that implementation with brute tree search on 400 small cases, verifies generator vectors against independent arithmetic or a captured Python 2.7 vector, and recovers planted no-skip and forced-skip openings. Current site rune transcriptions and the published reading cribs are the target inputs; changing either requires a new run.
records.reader_finding: None of the tested older random-generator keys reproduced a complete known 12-rune opening. Across 24,231 generated key cases and two skip rules, the closest match was four runes.
records.reader_limit: Only nine specified beginnings at the starts of 55 pages were checked, with the saved seeds, subtraction direction and starting offsets. This does not test unknown openings or repeat the source’s broader English-scoring search.

records.article:
# Can the compiled generator ports reproduce their reference streams?

**Finding.** The pinned Round 28 C generator code matches all **144,000 symbols** in a finite Python-model comparison, and all **8,192 symbols** in the earlier Round 27 archived reference vectors. A separate checker reproduces every symbol using independently constructed expectations. This validates the extracted generator code on this finite grid.

![All finite C generator comparisons match exactly.](experiments/records/r28-c-generator-port-controls/port-checks.svg)

We compiled the unmodified generator and reducer region of [the pinned source](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round28/L4/grind28.c) in a small portable harness. The full sweep engine requires POSIX functions and an unavailable language-panel file; this harness only calls its generator functions.

The grid contains nine output modes and eight fixed seeds: 0, 1, 777, 3301, 123456789, 2147483647, 2147483648 and 4294967295. Each emits 2,000 symbols, crossing MT's 624-word state reload several times. The modes are Python 2.7 single-word MT with random29, five-bit modulo, five-bit rejection and shuffle29; canonical and historical PHP MT with scaling or modulo; and glibc's additive generator modulo 29. The archived comparison separately tests the first 128 random29 symbols for all 64 Round 27 reference seeds.

Both PHP twist modes produce different streams for every tested seed. This matters because checking the canonical twist does not establish that the historical PHP generator was implemented correctly. The independent checker uses the standard-library MT engine with an explicitly constructed state for canonical PHP, a separate historical-twist implementation, and an unbounded history recurrence for glibc rather than the source's ring buffer. The familiar MT19937 seed-5489 reference also passes.

This is a **generator-port control**, not a decoding control or a manuscript result. It does not rerun native PHP, native glibc or Python 2.7; the native-runtime assertions in the source remain source-reported evidence. It does not reproduce the language scores, plant-recovery gates, full seed spaces, checkpoint behavior or the source's LP2 negatives. In particular, no fresh coverage is assigned to the orphaned Round 28 run.

Run offline from the repository root with Python 3 and GCC:

```bash
python experiments/records/r28-c-generator-port-controls/run.py
python experiments/records/r28-c-generator-port-controls/check.py
python experiments/records/r28-c-generator-port-controls/plot.py --check
```

All source files and the MIT license are bundled. Generated executables live only in a temporary directory. The checker recompiles the C region and checks every emitted symbol and saved digest.
records.reader_finding: The C implementations produced the same output as the reference models in every comparison: 152,192 symbols checked.
records.reader_limit: This verifies these generator implementations on a fixed test set. It does not rerun the seed search or recover manuscript text.

records.title: Rail-fence readings of visible LP2 words
records.question: Do conventional two- through ten-rail fence decodings improve English word matches at the printed LP2 word alignment?
records.summary: The best rail count matches 70 fixed-dictionary words; 195 of 199 page-rotated, best-of-nine controls match at least 70.

record_type.label: Method replay
record_type.description: Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading.

scope.representation: LP2-00–55 GP rune indices; each visible hyphen-delimited segment is a fixed word slot, preserving page boundaries. The English lexicon is a pinned, filtered public word list.
scope.procedure: For each page, apply the standard rail-fence inverse with rail counts 2–10; transliterate the resulting runes in the original word slots and count exact English-list hits. Compare the printed-order best of nine with 199 seeded controls that independently rotate each page by a nonzero offset before repeating the identical nine-way selection. Verify the inverse on LP1-03 and check manuscript counts through a separate permutation implementation.
scope.parameters: 56 LP2 pages; 12,956 runes; 2,776 visible word slots; 369,652 dictionary entries; 2–10 rails; 199 controls, random.Random(3301); ties count against the proposed alignment.
scope.exclusions: Other rail counts, grouping pages, changed word boundaries, keyed or other transpositions, preceding substitution layers, other languages and alternate lexicons. Original source counts are not claimed as reproduced because its dictionary and input paths are unavailable.

records.finding: The best printed-alignment score is 70 words for rails 2, 4 and 9, compared with a control median of 78. There are 195 of 199 control maxima at least as large as 70; a one-sided plus-one tail is 196/200.
records.limitations: The score uses exact dictionary membership, not sentence coherence. The dictionary includes obscure words and the page-rotation null is an alignment comparison, not a cipher generator. This result cannot exclude a layered or differently segmented rail cipher.
records.article:
## Finding

**A straightforward rail-fence reading does not stand out in this bounded test.** Across LP2-00–55, the best of nine rail counts matched **70** words in a fixed English list. The same nine-way search on page-rotated controls had a median of **78** matches; **195 of 199** controls matched at least 70. The unchanged rune order matched 57. These are dictionary matches, not a translation.

![The best rail-fence word count is below the median of the alignment controls.](experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/comparison.svg)

## The proposal and the actual test

[TheronEagle's public rail-fence script](https://github.com/TheronEagle/liber-primus-research/blob/a6c5d13f7591030367daace993c887af20a5e0ab/experiments/2026-09-24/rail_fence_test.py) decrypts each page using two through ten rails and scores the resulting letters as words in a dictionary. Its saved result names two rails as the highest scorer. The repository points to an absolute local path for its word list and another for its transcription; neither file is part of that repository. Its numeric result therefore cannot be exactly replayed from its published checkout.

Here the input is Liberpedia's pinned LP2-00–55 rune text: **12,956 runes** arranged into **2,776 visible word slots**. As in the source code, a hyphen ends a slot; line-break marks and punctuation do not. The [fixed 369,652-word list](experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/lexicon.txt) is derived from the [Unlicense English-words repository](https://github.com/dwyl/english-words/blob/20f5cc9b3f0ccc8ce45d814c532b7c2031bba31c/words_alpha.txt), with the exact transform and source hash in [SOURCE.txt](experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/SOURCE.txt). A decoded slot counts only when its exact GP Latin transliteration is in that list. The denominator includes short slots that cannot score, so the counts should be compared only under this same scoring rule.

| Reading | Matched slots |
| --- | ---: |
| Printed order, no rail transform | 57 |
| Two, four, or nine rails | 70 each |
| Median of 199 control maxima | 78 |

Each control rotates the rune stream of *each page* by a seeded, nonzero offset, keeps its visible word lengths, tests all nine rail counts, and retains the best score. The page's rune inventory and contiguous ciphertext order remain intact; the rotation changes the alignment with word slots. This comparison asks whether the printed alignment of the proposed rail reading is better than the same method applied at other alignments. It is not a model of how Cicada composed the manuscript. The saved control maximum scores range from **67 to 90**. The complete nine-rail counts and all 199 control maxima are in [results.json](experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/results.json).

## What this does and does not exclude

The decoder was checked two ways: the main script encrypts an actual solved-page rune sequence and recovers it at each rail count, while the separate checker recomputes all manuscript outputs through a different index permutation. This rules out a broken rail inverse as the explanation for the ordinary score.

The test covers **only** conventional page-by-page rail-fence decryption with two through ten rails, this word segmentation, this GP transliteration and this fixed dictionary. It says nothing about keyed columns, a rail count outside the range, combining pages, moving word boundaries, a preceding substitution layer, or a non-English plaintext. In particular, the source repository's wider statement that all transpositions are ruled out does not follow from these nine cases.

To reproduce offline, use the experiment ZIP and run `python experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/run.py --check`, followed by `python experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/check.py`. Both need Python 3 and the archived source files; no network call is made during the run.

records.title: LP2 red initials: corrected page-order test
records.question: Do the pages bearing large red initials have unusual spacing compared with a uniform 13-of-58 page placement?
records.summary: The corrected 13-page list has ordinary spacing under four specified measures; one compressed-bit measure has almost no resolving power at this length.

record_type.label: Manuscript measurement
record_type.description: Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule.

family.title: Order of visual page markers
family.question: Does a precisely identified visual marker occur on pages in an unusual order?

variant.label: Large-red-initial page presence; uniform placement null

scope.representation: Binary page presence from the archived JPEG image audit: at least one red component of 10000 full-resolution-equivalent pixels, measured with four-connectivity after half-resolution sampling. The original JPEG SHA-256 values are recorded per row in the audit CSV.
scope.procedure: Compare 13 corrected page positions with uniform 13-page subsets of 58; test internal-gap variance in both directions and packed-bit compression with 100000 seeded samples; count span and adjacent-run tails exactly; run evenly spaced and consecutive planted controls.
scope.parameters: Pages 00–57; 13 selected; random.Random(3301) with 100000 subsets; zlib level 9; plus-one Monte Carlo tails; five tail directions with Bonferroni correction.
scope.exclusions: Initial-rune identities, multiple initials on one page, red centroids, nonuniform authorship or section-placement models, alternate image segmentation, arbitrary encodings and any complete decryption rule.

records.finding: No declared spacing measure is unusual for a uniform 13-of-58 subset. The internal-gap variance is 12.85 (upper-tail estimate 0.328); the longest run is two (exact upper-tail 0.968); the span is 57 (exact lower-tail 1). The zlib score is 16 bytes, matched by 99977 of 100000 random subsets. These are narrow page-order results, not a proof against hidden information.
records.limitations: Exploratory after source misclassification was noticed. Uniform page placement is only a reference, not an authorship model. The presence bit discards the two second initials and the locations of later initials. Compression has almost no discrimination here; a spaced control also uses 16 bytes. None of these statistics tests a general code.
records.article:
## Result

**The thirteen pages with large red initials do not have unusual spacing under this uniform-page comparison.** Their largest consecutive run is two pages; a random set of thirteen pages has a run of at least two **96.8%** of the time. Their first and last marked pages are LP2-00 and LP2-57, so their span is the full release; that cannot be unusually short. The variance of the twelve internal gaps is **12.85**; **32.8%** of 100,000 random sets have at least that much variance. This tests page placement, not whether the artwork carries a message.

![The published total-red selection, corrected large-initial pages, and two planted spacing controls on the same 58-page axis.](experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/page-order.svg)

The top row reproduces the [published total-red page list](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round22/D-illustration-dropcap/RESULTS.md). Its highlighted LP2-07 and LP2-53 are [small red text, not large initials](#/wiki/red-initials). The corrected row has thirteen pages. LP2-03 and LP2-33 each have two large initials; this test deliberately reduces each page to a single yes/no mark.

## What was compared

The [image audit](research/red-initials-audit.csv) freezes which of the 58 LP2 pages contain a large red connected shape. The comparison draws **100,000** uniform 13-page subsets without replacement. It asks whether the actual pages have unusually variable internal gaps, a short overall span, a long run of adjacent pages, or an unusually compressible 58-bit presence string. Span and run probabilities are also counted exactly over all **3,155,581,562,280** possible 13-page subsets. Five declared tail directions are considered together; none approaches the adjusted threshold.

| Measure | Observed | Comparison result |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Variance of the 12 gaps | 12.85 | 32.8% of random sets are at least as variable; 67.4% are no more variable. |
| Span, last minus first | 57 pages | All 13-page sets have a span of 57 or less. |
| Longest consecutive run | 2 pages | 96.8% of random sets have a run of at least two. |
| zlib size of the packed page bits | 16 bytes | 99,977 of 100,000 random sets also occupy 16 bytes; this score has almost no resolving power here. |

The comparison deliberately assumes every 13-page placement is equally likely. It is a baseline for visible spacing, **not** a model of how the manuscript was composed. A rule based on section boundaries, the identities of the initials, or two initials on one page is outside it.

## Can these checks detect a planted pattern?

The lower two rows of the figure are fixed controls with the same thirteen marks. Approximately even spacing gives a very small gap-variance tail in the sampled comparison, while thirteen consecutive marks give an exact short-span and long-run probability of **46 / 3,155,581,562,280**. But both controls have low gap variance: that one statistic cannot tell even spacing from a single compact block. The evenly spaced control still compresses to 16 bytes, so the compression check would miss that visible regularity. These limitations matter when interpreting the ordinary manuscript result.

The earlier study also tested red-pixel centroids and an initial-rune string. Those are **not** reproduced here: its total-red mask includes two pages without initials, its centroids include all red marks rather than only the large shapes, and several pages have a second or later initial. A corrected identity or position test needs explicit annotation of each large initial before scoring.

## Reproduce

Download the [original JPEGs](downloads/original-images.zip) if you want to repeat the image classification itself. With Python 3 and Pillow, NumPy and OpenCV installed, run `python scripts/audit_red_initials.py > research/red-initials-audit.csv`. The page-order test then needs only Python's standard library:

```text
python experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/run.py --check
python experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/check.py
python experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/plot.py
```

# What a missing doublet can—and cannot—tell us

## Finding

The joined rune stream for **LP2-00–55** has **86 equal adjacent pairs among 12,955 pairs**. The pinned [Round 18 filter analysis](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round18/L2-filter-leak) considers an encryptor that avoids some repeated ciphertext runes by discarding a key draw and trying again. We checked the exact probability law behind that idea.

**If key symbols are independent and uniformly distributed**, every plaintext rune produces the same distribution of visible ciphertext runes after this filter. The unusually few repeats can reveal something about a *possible filter*, but the filter alone gives no clue about which plaintext rune produced an output. This does not show that LP2 uses such a key or that its text cannot be solved by other means.

![The same observed repeat rate can be produced by a skip filter that consumes roughly 374 extra key draws, or by a rewrite filter that consumes no extra key draws. The visible ciphertext law is identical under the stated independent uniform-key model.](experiments/records/rejection-channel-information/channel-comparison.svg)

## Why the same output can hide different mechanisms

Let the alphabet have 29 runes and let a candidate ciphertext rune be the plaintext rune plus a fresh uniform key symbol, modulo 29. A **skip filter** rejects a candidate matching the preceding output with probability *s* and draws another key symbol. Fitting its expected repeat rate to 86/12,955 gives *s* ≈ **0.8129**. The probability of a visible repeat is then `(1 − s)/(29 − s)`; each particular nonmatching rune has probability `1/(29 − s)`. Neither probability depends on the plaintext rune.

A different **rewrite filter** can match the same output law: when a candidate repeats, sometimes replace it with a new uniform rune. The fitted replacement probability is about **0.8363**. Here that replacement randomness is separate from the key stream. These mechanisms have the same visible one-step distribution. They differ in a testable way if an independent key stream is known: the skip model would consume about **374 extra key symbols** over 12,955 transitions on average, while the rewrite model would consume none. The source's fixed *s* = 0.8129 gives the same approximate drift; our exact calculation reproduces its preserved analytic mean.

This is a model comparison, not a claim that doublet suppression was actually performed. A key with structure, a plaintext-dependent filter, or a different reset rule changes the argument. The observed count was used to fit both models; it cannot independently validate either one.

## What was checked

The [plan](experiments/records/rejection-channel-information/plan.json) pins the source code and preserved numerical receipts. We re-derived the conditional probabilities, matched the source's closed repeat-rate and draw-count formulas, and checked both filters by independently enumerating every key, plaintext and previous-output combination in a nontrivial three-symbol control model. Zero suppression correctly returns a uniform output.

Run `python experiments/records/rejection-channel-information/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/rejection-channel-information/check.py` from the repository root. The source's English-text entropy estimates and corpus-based simulations are **not reproduced** here because their exact corpora are not in the pinned source. Those estimates must not be read as a measured amount of LP2 plaintext leaked by the filter.

## Finding

The eight saved LiberPrayground autokey databases contain **2,412 candidate rows**. Every saved score reproduces to its five-decimal display precision. That confirms the score calculation for these rows; it does **not** show a decoded LP2 passage. The files preserve candidate interruption choices and starting values, but provide no independent execution log for the search that selected them.

![A known 96-rune message recovers in all eight variants when the three inserted interruptions are supplied.](experiments/records/relikd-autokey-interrupt-database/control.svg)

On a constructed **96-rune known reading**, each of the eight rules recovers every rune after three inserted interruptions are removed. With those positions fixed, the correct starting value has the highest coincidence score in **six of eight** rules. The other two place it second. This is a useful check of the arithmetic, but the test **supplies** the interruption locations. It does not establish that the saved search can find them in a real ciphertext.

## The rule that was checked

At each accepted rune, the previous decoded rune sets the next shift. The shift is either its GP **index** or its GP **prime value**. The saved filenames specify adding or subtracting that shift; `_inv` first maps each ciphertext index `c` to `28 − c`. Candidate F positions are deleted before feedback runs. The source examines only the first **16 occurrences** of its interruption rune and may stop the section at the 17th. A row's `keylen` field is its starting value, except that the source computes field **0 using starting value 1**.

The pinned [source function](https://github.com/relikd/LiberPrayground/blob/719380ebee0523ad7f2fbf389c6f960d51bea5a4/LP/InterruptDB.py) actively calls only the **subtract-prime, non-inverted** file. Its adjacent comment describes the other signs, index values and inversion switch, and seven other database files are committed. We reproduced their saved scores under those stated variants, but cannot verify from this revision that those seven branches were executed by its active entry point.

The plain previous-plaintext-prime recurrence overlaps the [GP-prime feedback test](#/experiments/gp-prime-plaintext-feedback). This record's added scope is the source's selected interruptions, inverted input and saved alternative value/sign variants. It does not retest the full unskipped page search.

## How much of the manuscript entered a score

We matched all nine source section streams to the site transcription, then mapped the **actual runes used** by the saved rows back to pages. Across all eight files, **13 pages** entered completely, **8 pages** partly and **35 pages** not at all. In the one actively called source file, **12 complete and 8 partial pages** entered. The long section filenames do not mean every page in those sections was tested: the first-16-interruption cutoff often stops early.

The saved scores are normalized coincidence counts (random-uniform reference near 1). They are selected maxima over starting values and interruption choices. We have not calibrated that whole selection against a matched null or found readable output, so a high row score is **not evidence of a cipher or a solution**. The [complete row data](experiments/records/relikd-autokey-interrupt-database/results.json) and [page coverage](experiments/records/relikd-autokey-interrupt-database/coverage.json) let readers inspect precisely what was checked.

## Reproduce

The [frozen plan](experiments/records/relikd-autokey-interrupt-database/plan.json) pins the source revision, Git-blob hashes, interpretation and control. The original project has no license in the pinned revision, so its source and corpus remain an explicit external prerequisite rather than being repackaged. Obtain that revision of [LiberPrayground](https://github.com/relikd/LiberPrayground/tree/719380ebee0523ad7f2fbf389c6f960d51bea5a4), then from this repository root run:

```text
python -X utf8 experiments/records/relikd-autokey-interrupt-database/control.py --source-root PATH_TO_LIBERPRAYGROUND --check
python -X utf8 experiments/records/relikd-autokey-interrupt-database/target.py --source-root PATH_TO_LIBERPRAYGROUND --check
python -X utf8 experiments/records/relikd-autokey-interrupt-database/coverage.py --source-root PATH_TO_LIBERPRAYGROUND --check
python -X utf8 experiments/records/relikd-autokey-interrupt-database/check.py --source-root PATH_TO_LIBERPRAYGROUND
```

The independent checker re-reads the pinned Git objects, recalculates every score and decoded-output digest, and reconstructs all eight known-message controls. It does not infer a new skip pattern or verify the historical search process.

# The saved interrupt-key candidates did not pass a known-text check

The [original LiberPrayground program](https://github.com/relikd/LiberPrayground/blob/719380ebee0523ad7f2fbf389c6f960d51bea5a4/probability.py) contains a second search path: remove selected `ᚠ` runes, fit a repeating Vigenère or affine key to the remaining text, then decode the full section while preserving the removed runes. **That path never ran in the original main loop.** A broken earlier call raises an error, and an unconditional `continue` would skip it even after that call is repaired. We extracted the saved-row operations without claiming the original program had tested them.

The source database supplies **nine candidate rows** from three sections. Each is tried with the source's two key fitters, for 18 outputs. The key fit uses only about 404–455 runes before the twenty-first `ᚠ`; it then applies the inferred key to sections as long as 3,008 runes.

![Six known-text controls are only partly recovered, although thirteen LP2 fits clear the source limit.](experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-db-keyfit/control-power.svg)

The source fitters recovered an authentic 95-rune solved page with a one-rune identity key. They also reproduced a small skipped-`ᚠ` clock example. At the saved candidates' more demanding key lengths **14, 20 and 26**, however, all six constructed known-text messages failed complete recovery. The Vigenère fits recovered 69–86% of their runes; affine recovered 35–59%. These language controls are slightly easier than the target fits because they do not delete any `ᚠ` before estimating the key.

Despite that weak control result, **13 of 18 LP2 fits clear the source's similarity limit**. This means the source limit readily reports candidate keys without demonstrating that its fitter can recover a complete known message at comparable lengths. A reported fit is **not** a reading, and the five misses do not rule out either cipher family.

The nine source rows, key lengths, skip positions, code and inputs are frozen in the [plan](experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-db-keyfit/plan.json). The [results](experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-db-keyfit/results.json) retain each fitted key, score, threshold decision and full decoded-stream hash. The source database scores that selected these rows were historical candidate metadata; we did not regenerate or broaden its interrupt search. The controls were run before these LP2 key fits. The plan records earlier exploratory known-text calibration, so its timing should not be read as independent preregistration of control choices.

To reproduce, obtain the pinned source Git revision `719380ebee0523ad7f2fbf389c6f960d51bea5a4` and substitute its path below. The scripts read and hash-check Git objects, including files omitted from a sparse checkout; they do not redistribute the unlicensed source.

```text
python -X utf8 experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-db-keyfit/run.py --source-root SOURCE --phase all --check
python -X utf8 experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-db-keyfit/check.py --source-root SOURCE
python experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-db-keyfit/plot.py --check
```
records.reader_finding: Thirteen saved LP2 key fits pass the source score limit, but six comparable planted known messages are only partly recovered. No readable message has been established.
records.reader_limit: The original branch was unreachable and these are nine saved candidates, not a full interrupt search. The control failure prevents a negative claim about Vigenère or affine ciphers.

# Mirror and alternating-group scores in the saved interrupt database

The [pinned LiberPrayground source](https://github.com/relikd/LiberPrayground/blob/719380ebee0523ad7f2fbf389c6f960d51bea5a4/LP/InterruptDB.py) stores candidate ways to omit `ᚠ` or `ᛠ` runes and then group what remains. One group rule mirrors a repeating key position; two others alternate positions in pairs or threes, differing in whether the chosen runes are removed before or after that split. **A high score means the groups have striking rune frequencies. It does not reveal a key or words.**

![Known-period detection: mirror 4/4, remove then split 10/10, split then remove 8/10.](experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-pattern-database/control.svg)

On a 600-rune known reading encrypted with a five-position pattern, the correct period scored above periods 2–8 in **22 of 24** source-rule controls. The two misses both use the “split, then remove” rule with the source's normal-frequency score. A separately labeled **post-result** check shuffled the same planted ciphertext values, kept the inserted `ᚠ` positions fixed and repeated the period search 49 times. The planted score beat every shuffled maximum in 19 of 24 arms; five had at least one shuffled result as high. These are checks of the score's ability to find a *known* pattern. We supplied the interrupt positions, so they do not show that the method can discover interruptions in LP2.

We then recounted **all 7,407 rows** in the 24 committed mirror/modulo database files. Every score agrees with the pinned source calculation to the displayed five-decimal rounding (absolute difference at most 0.000005). This verifies the saved arithmetic and the source-to-site rune streams, not how the database's best skip sets were originally selected. Across its nine sections, **44 complete LP2 pages and parts of seven more** contribute at least one rune to a saved score; five other pages were verified against the source but entered no saved score. The [exact page coverage](experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-pattern-database/coverage.json) and [all row results](experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-pattern-database/results.json) are available for inspection.

**No reading follows from the saved high scores.** The source selected over many skip sets and periods, and we did not repeat that expensive selection on shuffled LP2 pages. Comparing its best saved score with a fixed-rule random baseline would make chance patterns look more convincing. The positive controls establish only structural period detection under a supplied skip mask; they are not a complete-message decryption test. Two source-rule controls failed even that narrower gate. The saved files are evidence of candidate data, without an independently recovered execution log proving every historical search ran as documented.

The [base plan](experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-pattern-database/plan.json) fixes all 24 source files and the row recount. The [shuffle addendum](experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-pattern-database/shuffle-plan.json) was frozen after the LP2 row scores were inspected and must be read as a control-power diagnostic, not prior statistical confirmation. To reproduce, obtain the pinned Git revision `719380ebee0523ad7f2fbf389c6f960d51bea5a4` separately. These scripts hash-check its Git blobs and do not redistribute the source:

```text
python -X utf8 experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-pattern-database/control.py --source-root SOURCE --check
python -X utf8 experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-pattern-database/target.py --source-root SOURCE --check
python -X utf8 experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-pattern-database/shuffle.py --source-root SOURCE --check
python -X utf8 experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-pattern-database/coverage.py --source-root SOURCE --check
python -X utf8 experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-pattern-database/check.py --source-root SOURCE
python experiments/records/relikd-interrupt-pattern-database/plot.py --check
```
records.reader_finding: Every saved score can be reproduced, but a high rune-frequency score is not a decrypted message. The known-period control is imperfect, and the original skip-mask selection was not repeated on controls.
records.reader_limit: The score archive covers 44 whole pages and parts of seven more. It cannot tell whether the selected high scores reflect a cipher, chance after a large search, or an untested rule.

# A rotating-key search stopped at its first screen

The [original program](https://github.com/relikd/LiberPrayground/blob/719380ebee0523ad7f2fbf389c6f960d51bea5a4/probability.py) proposes a key whose column order rotates as the text advances. It tests key lengths 3–18, rotation steps 1 through length minus one, and every starting position. On each of nine LP2 section files it first looks for the repeat-frequency band **1.6–2.1**; only settings in that band proceed to key fitting.

The published script actually passes a number where its grouping function expects a generator, so it raises `TypeError` on its first section. We tested an **explicitly repaired variant**: supply the source's own `shift_pattern(length, step)` generator at that call. We preserved its input files, first-970-symbol cutoff, group assignment and screen. The source and independent schedules agree across all 1,936 settings per section.

![The planted known text crosses the source gate, but neither the LP2 settings nor the shuffles do](experiments/records/relikd-rotated-key-source-gate/gate.svg)

On a constructed **970-rune known reading**, the declared seven-column rotating key recovered all 970 runes. Its repeat score was 1.73, and it was the only setting reported by the full 1,936-setting source grid. The plant is longer than every actual section prefix (308–796 runes). It demonstrates the mechanics on a clean example, not matched-length detection power for these sections or other plaintexts and interruptions.

Across the nine source LP2 sections, **none of 17,424 settings** reached the source's 1.6 lower gate. The highest was **1.30**, so no LP2 key was fitted and no proposed reading emerged. Forty-nine shared full-grid shuffles also produced no gated settings; their highest repeat score was 1.48. Zero source reports in both target and controls is a bounded screen result, not evidence that LP2 cannot use rotating keys. A different plaintext distribution, generator, punctuation clock or ciphertext layer could fall outside this source band.

The nine committed source rune streams match the site's LP2 rune arrays in full. For the actual search, we retain the source's punctuation and take its first 970 non-newline symbols **before** removing non-runes. This yields between 308 and 796 runes per section. Only **33 pages contributed runes**: 26 in full and seven in part. The other 22 nonempty pages were verified against the source but did not enter the search; LP2-50 is empty. The [prefix coverage receipt](experiments/records/relikd-rotated-key-source-gate/prefix-coverage.json) identifies every contributing page and the last used line and rune of each partial page. The nine source files, not hand-selected page fragments, define the test.

## Inspect and reproduce

The [control plan](experiments/records/relikd-rotated-key-source-gate/control-plan.json) and [target plan](experiments/records/relikd-rotated-key-source-gate/target-plan.json) fix the repair, scope and 49 shared shuffles. [Control results](experiments/records/relikd-rotated-key-source-gate/control-results.json), [section results](experiments/records/relikd-rotated-key-source-gate/results.json) and [null results](experiments/records/relikd-rotated-key-source-gate/null-results.json) retain the corresponding outcomes. The [separate coordinate check](experiments/records/relikd-rotated-key-source-gate/ioc-diagnostic.json) reports each section's maximum and is marked as post-result description.

With a separate checkout of the pinned LiberPrayground revision, run:

records.article:
# Testing a three-rune shift display

The pinned LiberPrayground program displays possible readings **three runes at a time**. For each block it tries all 29 alphabet shifts and ranks them by a rune-trigram frequency table. It repeats the display from three starting positions. Each block chooses its own ranked shift; the program does not require one key to connect adjacent blocks.

We checked that display on **17 already decoded page streams** (15 LP1 pages and solved LP2-56–57). Adding 7 to every known rune gave every block a known correct shift. The original program's block output matched a separate enumeration of all 29 shifts. Yet its first-ranked row recovered only **50.4%** of known runes on average across the 51 page/starting-position displays (range 32.1–64.5%). Five blocks had ties for the top frequency; stable source ordering chooses one displayed alternative without resolving the tie.

![The selected row scores well but falls short of exact recovery](experiments/records/relikd-trigram-shift-control/comparison.svg)

We also scored all 29 displayed rows per starting position with a fixed English quadgram table. Blank source cells broke text into separate runs; a row needed at least 100 scored quadgrams. The best-scoring row was on LP1-06: **129 of 207 runes matched, leaving 78 wrong**. Its score was higher than the maximum of each of 49 complete searches on within-page shuffled controls. That is a finite comparison of this display and score, not a probability that it decoded a page. The scorer's training overlap with these known readings has not been excluded.

The selected row starts **“OANDEDNDEEDWEDTSES…”**; the known reading starts **“OANAMANDECIDEDTOGO…”**. The resemblance is real, but so are the mismatches.

The fixed control rule required both score separation from at least 47 of 49 shuffled maxima **and 70% exact recovery** before screening unsolved LP2. The 70% line is a practical threshold chosen for this control, not a universal decoding standard. The score condition passed; recovery did not. We did **not** run this setup on unsolved LP2. The +7 construction verifies a simple known shift and source arithmetic; it does not test whether an unknown cipher uses an interrupted or changing key. Likewise, plausible-looking fragments can arise because every three-rune block is independently selected from a language table.

This is a control audit of a local-fragment display, not a failed Liber Primus decryption. A proposed decoder would need an explicit rule connecting blocks and a known-reading recovery control for that rule before an unsolved-page result could carry weight.

## Inspect and reproduce

The [frozen control plan](experiments/records/relikd-trigram-shift-control/precontrol-plan.json) fixes the 17 pages, three starts, 29 ranked rows, score eligibility, +7 plant and 49 shared shuffles. [Complete measurements](experiments/records/relikd-trigram-shift-control/results.json) preserve every first-ranked page/start display and every shuffle maximum. The original program is [pinned at revision 719380e](https://github.com/relikd/LiberPrayground/blob/719380ebee0523ad7f2fbf389c6f960d51bea5a4/LP/FailedAttempts.py); it has no license file in that Git tree, so its code is not copied into this record.

With a separate checkout of that exact revision, run Python in UTF-8 mode. This matters on Windows because the original frequency loader does not declare its file encoding.

```text
python -X utf8 experiments/records/relikd-trigram-shift-control/run.py --source-root PATH_TO_LIBERPRAYGROUND --check
python experiments/records/relikd-trigram-shift-control/check.py --source-root PATH_TO_LIBERPRAYGROUND
python experiments/records/relikd-trigram-shift-control/plot.py --check
```

The runner executes the original method from verified Git objects in a temporary directory and compares its entire saved result. The checker separately derives the 29 shifts, all selected rows and all 49 complete-search maxima without importing that method. No manuscript target or external service is needed.
records.reader_finding: The highest-scoring row still had 78 wrong runes out of 207. The tool found some correct fragments, but did not recover the known page well enough for the planned LP2 test.
records.reader_limit: Only known readings were tested; the scorer's training overlap is unknown.

records.title: Are the long LP2 rune repeats unusual?
records.question: Do the published repeated five- and six-rune sequence counts exceed section-matched adjacent-step controls?
records.summary: The published six five-rune repeats and one six-rune repeat reproduce; 361 of 999 section-matched step-shuffle controls reach either selected threshold.

record_type.label: Manuscript measurement
record_type.description: Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule.

scope.representation: 12,956 GP rune indices, concatenated in manuscript order from LP2-00 through LP2-55; non-runes removed.
scope.procedure: Count distinct repeated contiguous rune-index tuples at lengths 5, 6 and 7, including overlapping windows and joins. Rebuild 999 sectionwise step-shuffled controls, count each length, and compare fixed-length and either-length selection thresholds.
scope.parameters: Nine declared unsolved sections; 29-symbol modular steps; 999 random.Random(3301) controls; upper-tail ties included; one planted six-rune copy.
scope.exclusions: Other transcriptions, gaps and noncontiguous motifs, alternate segmentation, longer lengths, specific plaintext or key tests, and selection over further search choices.

records.finding: The source counts reproduce: six distinct five-rune repeats, one six-rune repeat (DJUBEI), no seven-rune repeats. Of 999 sectionwise step-shuffled controls, 300 meet the five-rune threshold, 150 meet the six-rune threshold, and 361 meet either; the combined plus-one proportion is 362/1,000.
records.limitations: The control conditions on observed step inventories and nine section boundaries; it is a comparison distribution, not a cipher simulator. The combined threshold covers selection between lengths five and six only, not all possible methods or motifs.
records.article:
## Finding

**The long repeats are real, but their number is not unusual under a control that preserves each section’s adjacent rune steps.** The 12,956-rune LP2-00–55 transcription contains **six distinct repeated five-rune sequences**, **one repeated six-rune sequence**, and **no repeated seven-rune sequence**. These match the [published inventory](https://github.com/Leo-Y-Zhang/LiberPrimusAnalysis/blob/a32bdc0e06ea58532fbaf4329acae4a0b1020513/results/characterize.txt), including the six-rune `DJUBEI` at zero-based corpus positions **6,555** and **12,950**.

![How often the matched controls produce at least as many long repeated sequences.](experiments/records/repeated-long-ngrams/repeats.svg)

The two overlapping five-rune sequences `DJUBE` and `JUBEI` come from that same `DJUBEI` repeat. They are **not three separate pieces of evidence**. Of 999 controls, 300 reached at least six five-rune repeats, 150 reached at least one six-rune repeat, and 361 reached either threshold. The last comparison counts the decision to notice whichever of the two lengths looks more interesting. The corresponding plus-one proportions are 301/1,000, 151/1,000 and **362/1,000**.

## What was compared

Each control keeps the nine manuscript section lengths, each section’s first rune, and the **exact inventory of its adjacent modular differences**, including rare zero steps. It shuffles the order of those steps within each section, rebuilds the rune stream, joins the sections in manuscript order, and counts distinct repeated sequences of lengths five, six and seven. Windows may overlap and cross joined section boundaries in both the manuscript and controls, matching the source’s corpus-wide counting rule. A planted six-rune copy makes the checker’s repeat count rise from zero to one.

This control asks whether *these counts* distinguish the manuscript from streams with the same step composition. It does not model every possible cipher or decide whether a particular repeat is meaningful. A future claim about `DJUBEI` should specify its predicted location, transformation and successful decoding criterion before inspecting another position. The [complete results](experiments/records/repeated-long-ngrams/results.json) contain every repeated tuple and all 999 control counts.

Run `python experiments/records/repeated-long-ngrams/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/repeated-long-ngrams/check.py` from the repository root. The second script independently extracts the rune stream, recounts the observed tuples, and reconstructs the first twelve shuffled controls.

records.article:
# Rotating and folded wordlist keys

Can the 43 archived keys recover a familiar 12-rune opening if each key changes shape as it repeats?

## Finding

**No exact opening match.** We tested **6,272 key schedules** at every phase of their actual repeating cycles on the 55 rune-bearing unsolved pages. Their **3,104,640 comparisons** with nine fixed known-reading openings produced zero exact matches. The closest opening agreed for four runes. This is a narrow exclusion of the stated keys, schedules, positions and target readings; it does not judge other plaintext openings.

![For key-01, left rotation changes the next nine-rune cycle; folding walks back through key positions.](experiments/records/rotating-folded-key-openings/clock.svg)

The diagram shows the *key position* used at each of the first 12 ciphertext runes for the first archived key. A left rotation uses slots 0–8 once, then begins the next cycle at slot 1. Folding goes forward and then back. We also tested right rotation and a fold that does not repeat either end. For each key, we reduced identical repeated cycles to their true period before testing every phase. The result file separates **6,272 declared settings** from duplicated 12-step clocks; variants are counted independently because they specify different rules.

## Scope and reproduction

The key list is the 43-rune-key list pinned in the [public wordlist replay](#/experiments/public-wordlist-vigenere). Each page starts its own clock. Non-rune marks do not advance it; each output is the ciphertext rune index minus the scheduled key index modulo 29. We compare only the first 12 runes with the nine openings selected before this test. The original public attempt used ordinary repeating keys; **these rotating and folded schedules are new tests here**, not a claimed historical replay. They do not test other keys, shifts, word resets, interruptions or a language score.

The [manifest](experiments/suites/classical-key-schedules/manifest.json) fixes the schedules and inputs. [Results](experiments/records/rotating-folded-key-openings/results.json) retain per-variant totals, planted recovery controls and a digest of every decoded page start. From the repository root, run `python experiments/records/rotating-folded-key-openings/run.py --check` and `python experiments/suites/classical-key-schedules/check.py rotating-folded-key-openings`. The independent checker rebuilds runes from page JSON and computes the schedules separately.

records.article:
# Does the pair-skip decoder preserve a known correct key?

The [Round 19 source test](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round19/I1) creates readable rune text, encrypts it with a known key, and sometimes discards a key draw to avoid repeating the last ciphertext rune. It then gives the correct key to six decoders. A decoder that expects skipped draws in **pairs** is intentionally mismatched to this one-draw construction.

## Finding

![With the correct key, the matching decoder recovers all runes at 240 and 400 positions; the pair-skip decoder recovers 37.9 and 41.2 percent.](experiments/records/round19-decoder-baseline-control/decoder-baseline.svg)

At the source's 0.83 suppression setting, the matching decoder recovers **100%** of the planted runes at both 240 and 400 positions. The pair-skip decoder recovers **37.9%** and **41.2%**, respectively. At 240 positions its median language score falls from **−4.303** to **−6.631**, below the source's −5.5 reading bar. The correct key is present throughout: changing the permitted alignment rule alone causes the failure.

We replayed the source's entire **336-decoding G-BASE grid**: four suppression settings, two lengths, six decoder modes and seven seeds. Every non-timing row matches the pinned output; an independent recount matches all 48 cell summaries. A separate [36-case decoder-equivalence receipt](research/control-preflights/i1-2026-10-23.json) finds the same plaintext paths as the two earlier implementations, with scores agreeing within 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁴. Those 36 cases are an instrument control and are not included in the 336.

## What this establishes

A negative search using one skip rule does not exclude a different skip rule. The pair decoder fails **this particular one-draw plant**, not every pair-skip cipher. These are synthetic known-key controls, with English-derived text and a source-selected language threshold. **No LP2 ciphertext or unknown key is tested here.** A high language score can also coexist with poor exact rune recovery, so both measurements matter.

## Reproduce

The [plan](experiments/records/round19-decoder-baseline-control/plan.json) pins the source revision, inputs and original 336-case grid. It was written after the source outcome was known, so it is a retrospective replay specification. A later packaging amendment bundled the exact source code with its MIT license, plus the pinned text and score model, without changing the grid; the [original plan](experiments/records/round19-decoder-baseline-control/original-plan-before-bundle.json) is retained. From the extracted experiment ZIP, run:

```text
python experiments/records/round19-decoder-baseline-control/run.py --nproc 6
python experiments/records/round19-decoder-baseline-control/run.py --check
python experiments/records/round19-decoder-baseline-control/plot.py --check
```

The full run stages the bundled source in a temporary folder and compares each result with the [archived source output](experiments/records/round19-decoder-baseline-control/source/liber-primus/analysis/round19/I1/out_base.json). `--check` independently recounts the saved 336 rows and 48 summaries without running the decoder or changing files. Only wall times are excluded from parity. This is a decoder-power control, not an LP2 solve result.

records.article:
# How often do wrong keys look promising?

A language score can rise because a decoder has more freedom to choose English-like output. The [pinned Round 19 test](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round19/I1) ran wrong keys through several decoders, then fitted a separate score threshold for each one. We replayed its fit from all **34,000 saved score rows** and checked the arithmetic independently.

## Finding

![Wrong keys crossing the same score line under five decoders.](experiments/records/round19-decoder-null-bars/decoder-null-bars.svg)

The source used **−5.5** as a reading line. With a permissive drift decoder, all **500 of 500** wrong keys in one setting scored above that line; at a stricter drift setting, **230 of 2,000** did. The source's repository decoder yielded **0 of 2,000** above the same line. The chart counts scores, **not readable decipherments**. Its point is that a fixed language-score line has very different behavior under different decoders.

These archived comparisons use 240-rune samples and beam width 400, with the same declared SHA256-counter wrong-key family. They do not calibrate whole-book outputs.

The source therefore fitted wrong-key score tails separately for each of **13 decoder modes** on real ciphertext and synthetic controls: **26 cells** in all. Our full source replay matches every saved fit field. An independent implementation, using the same stated block sizes and random seeds, also matches all 26 cells. For example, the fitted one-percent bar for **one million** wrong-key trials is **−6.02** for the repository mode and **−4.05** for the most permissive drift mode. Those bars are **model projections** from 500–2,000 scores per cell, not observed million-trial error rates.

As a separate check fixed before we computed it, we fitted on alternating rows and compared predictions with the reserved rows at block sizes **10, 25 and 50**. Median absolute score errors were **0.012, 0.015 and 0.016**. This checks short-block behavior inside the saved arrays; it cannot validate the source's million- or billion-trial extrapolation. The source fit was already known when we wrote the replay plan, so this is a retrospective replay with a new internal diagnostic.

## What it means

For this specific language score and decoder family, the threshold must be calibrated **after** the decoder rule and search size are fixed. A score above an unadjusted line is insufficient evidence of a correct key. The saved wrong-key arrays come from the source's beam searches; we did not rerun those 34,000 decodes or test a new LP2 key. The Gumbel model's tail and its independence assumptions remain unverified at million-trial scale. This result does not identify or exclude an LP2 cipher.

## Reproduce

The [plan](experiments/records/round19-decoder-null-bars/plan.json) pins the source revision and exact saved arrays. The downloadable experiment includes the original MIT-licensed source and score data. From the extracted folder, run:

```text
python experiments/records/round19-decoder-null-bars/run.py
python experiments/records/round19-decoder-null-bars/check.py
python experiments/records/round19-decoder-null-bars/plot.py --check
```

The first command executes the original fit script in a temporary folder and compares its entire 26-cell output with the archived source. The second independently recomputes the fits and reserved-row diagnostic, then compares the saved [results](experiments/records/round19-decoder-null-bars/results.json). The chart is generated as responsive SVG from the same pinned rows. The related [known-key decoder control](#/experiments/round19-decoder-baseline-control) tests a different question: whether each decoder can recover planted text at all.

records.article:
# A correct key can fail in the wrong decoder

The [Round 19 I1 source](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round19/I1) encrypts known English-derived rune text with several ways of skipping key draws, then supplies the **correct key** to ten decoders. If a decoder cannot follow a planted message, its failure on an unknown LP2 key would tell us little.

![The source's original beam passes none of its twenty gated construction and length groups. Several permissive drift modes pass all twenty.](experiments/records/round19-decoder-repair-controls/decoder-repair-controls.svg)

**Finding:** On one 240-rune paired-skip message (seed 0), the original beam recovered **45.8%** of runes with the correct key; a permissive drift decoder recovered **100%** from that same message and key. Across the source's twenty gated construction-and-length groups, the original beam passed **0** and the permissive decoder with cost 8 passed **20**. Its cost-4 sibling also passed twenty; other exact or paired settings passed fewer. A group pass means the median of seven seeded messages met both exact-rune recovery of at least 90% and a language score of at least −5.5. It does not mean every message was fully recovered. The pictured seed was selected for explanation after the source results were known; the full grid supports the broader comparison.

The 2,100 decodes cover **15 constructed cases**, ten decoder settings, two lengths (240 and 400 runes), and seven seeds. Ten constructions per length belong to the source's positive gate; the baseline and four extra probes are measured separately. The constructions include paired skipped draws, free drift, occasional pointer jumps, key-dependent two-draw decisions, and keys with long repeated runs. Every result uses synthetic ciphertext with the known construction and correct key supplied. This is an instrument-power test, **not an LP2 decryption**. The separate [full-book control](experiments/records/round19-full-book-decoder-power/article.md) tests two rules at 12,956 runes; it does not establish full-length power for all ten rules here.

The exact source command was replayed without changing its functions or its pinned Self-Reliance text. The [frozen retrospective plan](experiments/records/round19-decoder-repair-controls/plan.json) demanded bit-exact non-timing JSON. **That exact condition failed:** 88 of 2,100 row scores and eight of 300 summary score fields differ at the final floating-point bits, by at most 2.665×10⁻¹⁵ and 1.777×10⁻¹⁵ respectively. The cause of those tiny differences is not established. All other non-timing fields, construction/seed coverage, group decisions and skip limits match exactly. A [post-result comparison](experiments/records/round19-decoder-repair-controls/precision-addendum.json) bounds the score differences at 3×10⁻¹⁵; it does not change the original acceptance rule.

Allowing more key-pointer movement helps these known-key plants, but it also creates more ways for a **wrong key** to fit. This replay does not run wrong-key controls for all ten modes. The [separate Round 19 null-bar audit](experiments/records/round19-decoder-null-bars/article.md) examines that calibration question. A language score or 90% recovery gate here does not give a false-positive rate for unknown keys, other languages, other message lengths, or the actual LP2 cipher. The complete case grid and source bytes are included so a different decoder rule can be checked without treating these 2,100 settings as 2,100 independent ideas.

From the extracted experiment folder, run `python experiments/records/round19-decoder-repair-controls/run.py --check` to verify saved source/replay rows and independently recompute all 300 group summaries. To repeat the 2,100 decodes, run `python experiments/records/round19-decoder-repair-controls/run.py --nproc 4`. The runner copies the pinned source into a temporary directory and leaves the archived output unchanged. Use `python experiments/records/round19-decoder-repair-controls/plot.py --check` to verify the chart.

# Can this decoder keep a known key aligned across the full book?

The [Round 19 source test](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round19/I1) encrypts **12,956 runes of known text**, deliberately skipping some key draws, then gives the correct key to two decoders. One permits the source's one-draw skip; the other permits a broader drift rule. This is a long-message power check for the decoder, not an LP2 key search.

![At full-book length, both decoders recover more than 99.8% of a planted message with the correct key; wrong-key controls recover less than 5%.](experiments/records/round19-full-book-decoder-power/full-book-power.svg)

**Result:** With the correct key, median exact rune recovery was **99.98%** for the source's exact skip rule and **99.82%** for its permissive drift rule, across three planted seeds per mode. Every correct-key run cleared the source's 90% recovery and −5.5 language-score bars. The one wrong-key control per mode recovered **3.77%** and **4.88%**, respectively. These controls show the two decoders can follow this specific skip construction over a full-book length when given the right key. They do not establish the correct key or rule for LP2.

The exact replay matched **all eight archived source rows** on every field except elapsed wall time. It used the source's `self_reliance.txt` English text, GP29 converter, SHA-generated key, 0.83 doublet-suppression setting and width-400 beam. The modes differ: `repo_ms3` allows up to three source-style skipped draws; `drift_l8` allows additional free drift with its source-defined cost. These are not interchangeable decoder rules. The earlier [short-message control](experiments/records/round19-decoder-baseline-control/article.md) tested six decoders at 240 and 400 runes; this record verifies the separate **12,956-rune** source arm.

This is a retrospective source replay: the eight archived outcomes were known before its [plan](experiments/records/round19-full-book-decoder-power/plan.json) was saved. It validates a long planted-message gate, not a false-positive rate for searching unknown keys or another cipher model. A readable score on synthetic English-derived text does not identify the LP2 plaintext.

The experiment ZIP includes the pinned source code and data under its MIT license. To rerun the eight decodes from the extracted folder, use `python experiments/records/round19-full-book-decoder-power/run.py --nproc 6`; the runner stages a disposable source copy and does not rewrite the archived [source output](experiments/records/round19-full-book-decoder-power/source/liber-primus/analysis/round19/I1/out_book.json). Use `python experiments/records/round19-full-book-decoder-power/run.py --check` to verify the saved replay, source rows and independently recounted gate summaries without rerunning the beam.
