records.article:
# Does removing one rune type reduce LP2’s adjacent repeats?

No, under the fixed rule tested here. For each of the 29 rune types, remove **every occurrence of that type** from LP2-00–55 and recount equal adjacent runes within pages. The archived stream has **86 doublets**. Every one-type deletion leaves **92 to 109**, so none reduces the raw count. This closes a small, explicit class of null-removal suggestions; it does not test arbitrary null positions or whether deletion before a later cipher could help.

![Adjacent equal-rune counts for every fixed one-type deletion](experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/single-rune-null-doublets.svg)

## What was fixed

The inputs are the 56 archived LP2-00–55 page texts and the stored 29-rune alphabet. Headings are included. Within each page, remove non-runes as in the [published doublet census](#/wiki/doublets); never count a pair across pages. For each rune type, delete all its occurrences, leave all surviving runes in order, and count adjacent equal pairs again. The rule has exactly **29 configurations**, not a search over individual positions. The [plan](experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/plan.json) and source hashes make the corpus and comparison explicit.

| Result | Value |
| --- | ---: |
| Original adjacent equal pairs | 86 of 12,901 within-page edges |
| Lowest after a one-type deletion | 92 (G, W, S or NG) |
| Highest after a one-type deletion | 109 (R) |
| Fixed-count shuffle expectation after deletion | 437.08–440.80 pairs, depending on type |

Deleting a type can destroy an existing pair of that rune, but it can also bring two formerly separated surviving runes together. For G, five old G–G pairs disappear while 11 new equal pairs form across deleted runs, giving **86 − 5 + 11 = 92**. For R, two old pairs disappear and 25 new bridges form, giving **109**. The [complete result](experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/results.json) records the removed symbols, destroyed pairs, new bridges, surviving edges, rate and reference expectation for every type. Its exact bridge accounting is checked independently.

The fixed-count shuffle expectation is calculated separately from each **retained** page’s rune frequencies. The observed-to-expected ratio stays between **0.209 and 0.248** across the 29 deletions. That comparison says the low-adjacency feature is still visible after this transformation relative to a within-page shuffle of the retained symbols. It is **not** a probability that a null model is false, and a shuffled stream is not a plaintext-language model.

## What this does and does not close

If the proposal is specifically “one rune type is padding, and deleting all of it will remove the low-doublet feature from the raw LP2 stream,” these 29 exhaustive cases do not support it. A different claim could delete only selected positions, delete several rune types, preserve word boundaries differently, or delete before applying a cipher whose alignment then changes. Those have much larger search spaces and need separate bounds and controls. A readable fragment after hand-selecting deleted positions would not be comparable with this fixed sweep.

This record measures a ciphertext statistic. It does not recover plaintext, identify a null symbol, or rule out nulls in general. The [null-removal guide](#/wiki/method-nulls) explains the larger family and the order-of-operations issue; the [doublet guide](#/wiki/doublets) defines the 86-pair baseline.

## Reproduce

From the repository root or extracted [experiment ZIP](downloads/experiments/single-rune-null-doublets.zip), using Python 3 standard library:

```text
python experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/run.py --check
python experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/check.py
```

The producer checks every input hash and reproduces the report and SVG. The separate checker extracts rune streams through a different parser, verifies the destroyed-pair and bridge identity for all 29 cases, and recalculates every edge count and exact fixed-count shuffle expectation. Both compare the same declared source files; neither re-reads the manuscript images.

records.title: Solved manuscript readings as a running key
records.question: Does any complete unsolved LP2 page decode under a contiguous offset of the established GP29 readings?
records.summary: The highest-scoring whole-page output is not readable English. It exceeds the limited control scores but does not establish a decryption.

record_type.label: Bounded solving test
record_type.description: Applies a fixed decoding, extraction or payload-retrieval rule to declared unsolved material, or excludes a specific direct-generation rule. Its result covers only those bounds.

scope.representation: 2,892 canonical GP29 rune indices from eight established readings in manuscript order; 55 nonempty LP2-00–55 ciphertext pages.
scope.procedure: At every fitting contiguous source offset, add or subtract one key index per rune modulo 29 and score the entire page with the pinned English quadgram model. Compare the global best to 16 whole-key shuffled full-grid maxima. A separate post-observation diagnostic searches four disjoint 2,892-GP-rune windows of preserved Emerson English.
scope.parameters: 55 complete pages; 292,318 observed page/offset/sign alignments, 16 complete shuffled-key grids (seeds 33017100–33017115), both arithmetic signs, four post-observation English GP-key windows.
scope.exclusions: Other source orders, substrings of pages, wrapping, key skips, word resets, alternate languages or score models, source text variants and any claim of general running-key exclusion.

records.finding: Across 292,318 whole-page offset/sign alignments, the best English quadgram score was −5.897 on the 66-rune LP2-49. No one of 16 shuffled-key global maxima reached it (add-one estimate 1/17), but the output is not coherent English. Four later GP-encoded Emerson windows also scored below it.
records.limitations: The winning page contains only 66 runes, and 16 key shuffles plus four post-observation English windows are weak controls for the broad choice of structured keys. No independent continuation or readable plaintext was found. Only this source order, direct additive GP29 rule, and complete pages were searched.
records.article:
# Solved manuscript readings as a running key

**Question.** Can the eight established readings of Liber Primus serve, in order, as a key that reveals a complete unsolved page?

**Result.** No complete reading was established. The best of **292,318** whole-page alignments used 66 runes of LP2-49 and had an English score of **−5.897**. That exceeds the best scores from all 16 shuffled versions of the same key and four GP-encoded windows of unrelated English. It is a signal to investigate, not a reading: the resulting text begins `EOAHIAEOSMASTHOOHYSOEMUNEADEALT…`. A short, selected page can score well by chance or by a feature the controls fail to model.

![The solved-reading key scores above the two limited reference groups, but yields no readable page.](experiments/records/solved-reading-running-key/key-comparison.svg)

## The test

We joined **2,892 runes** from eight established readings in manuscript order: Warning, Welcome, Some Wisdom, First Koan, Loss of Divinity, Second Koan, Instruction and LP2-57. These are their recorded Gematria Primus indices, not an English transliteration. For each of the **55 rune-bearing pages LP2-00–55** (LP2-50 has no rune text), we tried every contiguous key position that could cover the *entire* page, with both addition and subtraction modulo 29. The key did not wrap, skip, or restart at word breaks. We scored each complete output with the same pinned English quadgram model; the highest score across the whole grid was the reported result.

The 16 controls each shuffled the **whole 2,892-rune key once**, then searched the same page/offset/sign grid. Their highest scores ranged from **−6.426 to −6.070**; none reached the observed −5.897. Sixteen trials give only coarse resolution: the add-one global estimate is **1/17**, about **0.059**, and the shuffle removes the real key's language and structure. It cannot establish that the solved readings uniquely explain LP2.

As a separate *post-observation* check, we converted four nonoverlapping windows of the archived Emerson text into GP indices using one frozen greedy rune rule, then searched the identical grid. Their maxima ranged from **−6.430 to −6.150**. This small comparison also leaves many other structured keys untested; it is not part of the 16-trial probability estimate. An earlier ASCII-letter version of this plan was superseded **without being run**, because ASCII indices would not match the GP-index key.

Before looking at LP2, we encrypted the complete 184-rune Warning reading using a First Koan key segment, with Warning excluded from the *control key*. The same full search recovered the correct offset, sign and every rune. This avoids matching the control plaintext to itself. Warning remains part of the actual eight-reading LP2 key.

The result only covers this ordered source, direct additive GP29 arithmetic, all fitting offsets, and complete pages under one English model. A high score without a coherent plaintext and independent continuation is not a decryption. It does not eliminate other source orderings, key derivations, page subsets, interrupted clocks, or languages.

## Reproduce

From the repository root, run `python experiments/records/solved-reading-running-key/run.py --check` for the portable full computation (Python 3 standard library). Install NumPy and Numba to run `python experiments/records/solved-reading-running-key/fast_check.py`, which independently checks the same complete grid with a numeric scorer and compares six arbitrary nonwinning cases to the portable scorer. `english_key_control.py` reproduces the separate Emerson diagnostic with those optional libraries. `plan.json`, both diagnostic plans, `results.json`, and the pinned source traces document every input and bound.
records.reader_finding: The highest-scoring output was not coherent English. LP2-49’s 66 runes nevertheless scored above all 16 shuffled-key search maxima.
records.reader_limit: The search used one fixed 2,892-rune key order on 55 pages, trying every fitting whole-page offset and both arithmetic directions. It did not test wrapping, skips, partial pages or other languages.

records.title: Solved-text selections: what the source controls prove
records.question: Did published selection and printed-line acrostic searches validate their final decision rule on planted messages?
records.summary: Two source sweeps replayed: 3,508 character/rune selections and 48 line/word reads. Zero final hits, but the planted controls only passed an earlier length-specific threshold, not the final rule.

record_type.label: Source or input audit
record_type.description: Checks image provenance, extraction or input coverage against a declared reference; it does not establish a decryption.

family.title: Messages selected from decoded text
family.question: Does a fixed selection rule recover a second message from already-decoded text?

variant.label: Pinned R22-A character selections and R23-A2 printed-line/word acrostics

scope.representation: Five decoded source sections spanning ten LP1 images. Source section order is 01, 05, 06–09, 03–04, 14–15; the concatenation is not manuscript order.
scope.procedure: Replay and audit the pinned R22-A every-k/diagonal selections and R23-A2 first/last printed-line/word reads. Compare planted-control scores with both the length-specific bars they were tested against and the final family bars actually applied to manuscript reads.
scope.parameters: R22-A: 1,754 selection functions for each of letter and rune streams (3,508); R23-A2: four read types × six scopes × two directions (48). Both use seed 3301 and 1,000 source null shuffles per distinct length.
scope.exclusions: No new LP1 image-checked transcription, no new whole-search null or end-to-end power estimate, no LP2 ciphertext search, and no claim that all acrostic or selection methods have been excluded.

records.finding: The four planted examples clear their own length thresholds and all miss the final bars. The source therefore established that it can extract and score these planted reads, but not its claimed power to detect them at the threshold used for the manuscript. Its zero-hit result is a bounded report, not a control-validated exclusion.
records.limitations: This checks the source's saved rows and the decision rule against the independently replayed output from 2026-10-22; the 1,000-shuffle nulls were not rerun for this packaging step. Its decoded source sections cover ten LP1 images, with line geometry that differs from Liberpedia's current reading exports. No LP2 unsolved text was tested.
records.article:
## What this source search actually establishes

Two published searches tried to read a message from **already-decoded Liber Primus text**. One selected every *k*th character or a diagonal from the joined text. The other read the first or last rune of each printed line or word. We replayed the pinned source sweeps: **3,508 selection reads and 48 line/word reads; none crossed the source's final threshold.** That count describes the run. It does not, by itself, establish that these hiding places are empty.

![The four planted examples clear their own length thresholds but fall below the final thresholds.](experiments/records/solved-text-selection-source-gate/gates.svg)

The source tested whether its detector could find a planted message. **All four plants passed a threshold for reads of their own length. None passed the stricter threshold used for the final result.** The controls therefore show that the extraction and first scoring step work; they do not measure the chance that a message of the planted strength would survive the decision rule applied to the manuscript. The source's “control-validated null” wording goes beyond that evidence.

The line/word search had one read just above its own length threshold: a reversed word-last string from the section labelled 06. It was unreadable and far below the final threshold. The source describes one crossing as below an expected 0.048 crossings. It is **above** 0.048; that expectation is not a probability bound, and the 48 reads are dependent. Neither point makes the string a solution.

## Exactly what was searched

The earlier search used 1,754 selectors on Latin letters and 1,754 on rune indices: every-*k* positions, reversals, and diagonal folds. The later search used line-first, line-last, word-first and word-last reads on each of five decoded **source sections** and on their concatenation, in both directions. Those sections span **ten LP1 images**: 01, 05, 06–09, 03–04 and 14–15. The source's five-section order is not manuscript order. These tests did **not** try the unsolved LP2 ciphertext.

Both searches used the source's English quadgram score and 1,000 shuffled-letter controls per length. Its final bar is the highest null score across lengths; the plants were checked against their own length bars. A calibrated replacement would repeat the *entire selection and scoring process* on each null sample and on planted examples, then test whether the plants cross that same final bar. For the line/word version, first check the line breaks against the manuscript images: the source geometry differs from Liberpedia's current LP1 reading exports.

## Check the record

Run `python experiments/records/solved-text-selection-source-gate/check.py` from the repository root. It checks the two pinned [source result files](experiments/records/solved-text-selection-source-gate/source-r22-results.json) and [line/word result file](experiments/records/solved-text-selection-source-gate/source-r23-results.json) against the recorded counts and threshold comparisons. The [earlier replay audit](research/dukotah-r23-a2-source-audit-2026-10-22.md) records the original commands and their observed outputs. To regenerate the null sweeps, use the pinned source scripts linked below; this record does not silently change their geometry, model or rule.

records.article:
## Finding

The published D2 audit asks whether the unusual rune statistics were caused by counting the wrong text or joining pages incorrectly. Its source script runs from the pinned files here, and its planted-English scoring control passes. An independent Unicode-rune count confirms **12,956 runes** and **86 equal adjacent pairs among 12,901 within-page pairs**. None of the 54 extra pairs made by joining pages is equal. Its index of coincidence (multiplied by 29) is **0.9999** and entropy is **4.8565 bits**.

That supports the *measurements*. It does not reproduce the report's stronger statement that the low doublet rate excludes **every plaintext-independent key**. D2's `recompute.py` never calculates the cited plaintext-difference floor. The separate B4 script requires four English corpus files absent from the pinned repository, so its corpus numbers cannot be regenerated from this source package. We retain those numbers as reported results, not measurements made in this replay.

## What the bound actually says

Let `Δp` be a plaintext difference and `Δk` a key difference modulo 29. If their distributions are independent under the specified sampling model, then the **expected** ciphertext repeat rate is

```text
P(Δp + Δk = 0) = Σ P(Δp = d) P(Δk = −d) ≥ min P(Δp = d).
```

The inequality is correct under that factorization. It is not a minimum imposed on *each finite ciphertext*. A small complete example makes the distinction visible. In an alphabet of three symbols, take plaintext `0, 0, 1, 0`: its three successive differences are `0, 1, 2`, so the minimum difference frequency is **1/3**. Enumerate all **81** four-symbol keys drawn independently and uniformly, without looking at that plaintext. The expected ciphertext repeat rate is **1/3**, yet **24 keys (8/27)** yield **zero** repeats. No plaintext-aware choice was needed for those outcomes to be possible.

![The count of adjacent repeats across all 81 keys in the finite example.](experiments/records/source-independent-key-floor-audit/finite-key-control.svg)

This logical distinction does **not** make an independent uniform additive key a good explanation for LP2. The separate [exact uniform-key test](#/experiments/uniform-additive-doublets) assigns 86 or fewer repeats among 12,901 positions a probability near **1.07 × 10⁻⁹⁸** under its precisely defined model. The source's corpus floors may also help specify useful language models. What they cannot do without a declared stochastic model and error threshold is turn one observed manuscript rate into an impossibility proof for every independent key generator or every possible plaintext.

## Source coverage and limits

The [B4 preregistration](experiments/records/source-independent-key-floor-audit/source/liber-primus/analysis/round10b/B4-otp-steelman/PREREG.md) required **at least five independent English encodings of at least 100,000 runes each**. Its [G3 implementation](experiments/records/source-independent-key-floor-audit/source/liber-primus/analysis/round10b/B4-otp-steelman/b4_identifiability.py) names **four** large external corpora, plus a 180-rune solved-page sample explicitly excluded from the large-corpus minimum. None of the four corpus text files is present in the pinned Git tree; `git ls-tree -r --name-only f08b20b -- liber-primus/data/kjv.txt liber-primus/data/moby.txt liber-primus/data/pride.txt liber-primus/data/war.txt` returns no paths. The earlier [saved B4 output](experiments/records/source-independent-key-floor-audit/source/liber-primus/analysis/round10b/B4-otp-steelman/b4_results.json) reports a KJV minimum of **1.5025%**. A [later source audit](experiments/records/source-independent-key-floor-audit/source/liber-primus/analysis/round18/L7-redteam/RESULTS.md) calls that figure stale and reports **1.386%** using a longer KJV sample. This replay verifies the provenance and revision, but neither source corpus is available here to recalculate the revised value.

D2 also labels the `p* ≈ 400` period-detection threshold reproduced in its saved report. The D2 script prints column IoC for selected periods; it does not rerun the separate detection-power simulation behind that threshold. This record therefore does not validate that claim. The page inventory is based on the pinned rune text, not a new inspection of each manuscript image.

## Reproduce

The [pinned source inventory](experiments/records/source-independent-key-floor-audit/source-manifest.json), [D2 output](experiments/records/source-independent-key-floor-audit/source-replay.txt), [result data](experiments/records/source-independent-key-floor-audit/results.json), and [finite control](experiments/records/source-independent-key-floor-audit/finite-key-control.svg) are included. Python 3 and the standard library suffice:

```text
python experiments/records/source-independent-key-floor-audit/run.py --check
python experiments/records/source-independent-key-floor-audit/check.py
python experiments/records/source-independent-key-floor-audit/plot.py --check
```

The first command reruns the source D2 code and makes its printed positive control a hard gate. The second extracts rune characters with an independent parser, verifies source hashes and counts, and checks the finite-key example by enumerating ciphertexts directly. Neither command fills in the absent four corpora.

records.article:
## What is being tested?

The Spirals and Branches text, followed by the nine-rune heading before the Möbius number panel, contains 2,883 runes. Spiral Branches also has 2,883 runes after its 125 F runes are removed. A source discussion suggested pairing the streams, reversing Branches like a musical retrograde, or applying Atbash before modular subtraction. We test five *specified* ways to do that pairing and ask whether the best output has unusually high whole-stream index of coincidence (IoC) relative to two controls.

This is a new computation of suggestions in that discussion, not a replay of a reported successful decryption. The two long runic strings pasted in the supplied source thread match the archived Spirals and Branches-plus-heading transcriptions exactly: 1,145 and 1,738 runes, respectively. Their hashes are fixed in the [plan](experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/plan.json). The second 2,883-rune stream is rebuilt from LP2-40–53 after removing every F; the discussion did not supply a complete scored sweep of it.

## Inputs and five variants

Use zero-based positions in the 29-rune alphabet. Let **A** be the 1,145 Spirals runes, then the 1,729 Branches runes, then the nine-rune pre-Möbius heading. Let **B** be the 3,008 Spiral Branches runes after deleting its 125 F runes. Retain all other headings. Punctuation, page breaks and the number panel are not rune positions. At every aligned position output `(B − A) mod 29`.

| Variant | What changes in A |
| --- | --- |
| Direct | Nothing; printed order. |
| Reverse Branches | Reverse its 1,729 runes; leave the nine-rune heading at the end. |
| Reverse tail | Reverse Branches and the heading together as one 1,738-rune block. |
| Atbash Branches | Replace each Branches index `x` by `28 − x`; leave the heading unchanged. |
| Atbash tail | Atbash the entire Branches-plus-heading block. |

The two reverse and two Atbash treatments make the thread's “Branches” versus “Branches + Table” boundary ambiguity explicit. A head-of-Spirals-to-tail-of-Branches pairing is covered by reversal of the relevant tail. We do not search starts, other page ranges, arbitrary offsets, keys, multiplication, XOR, or different F handling.

## Score and controls

For each complete output, count ordered pairs of identical runes and divide by `2,883 × 2,882 = 8,308,806`. This is whole-stream IoC, not a language score. The chosen statistic is the **largest** of the five variant scores. Each control repeats all five variants and takes its own maximum:

1. **Every nonzero circular shift of B:** 2,882 comparisons preserve its rune sequence and frequencies but change its alignment with A. The observed unshifted alignment is the remaining position.
2. **999 within-page shuffles of B:** each LP2-40–53 non-F page chunk is independently shuffled, preserving its size and rune counts. These disrupt local order while retaining page-level composition. The pseudorandom seed is recorded in the plan.

These controls ask whether the observed *alignment* stands out under their respective assumptions. They do not estimate how rarely a researcher might discover some equal-length sections and some promising operation after searching many alternatives.

## Result

| Variant | Ordered equal-rune pairs | IoC |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Direct | 286,654 | 0.034500 |
| Reverse Branches | 286,132 | 0.034437 |
| Reverse tail | **287,504** | **0.034602** |
| Atbash Branches | 286,138 | 0.034438 |
| Atbash tail | 286,280 | 0.034455 |

Reverse tail is the best of the five on this measure. But 921 of the 2,882 nonzero circular shifts reach at least its score; including the observed alignment gives **922/2,883 ≈ 0.320**. Similarly, 341 of 999 within-page shuffles reach it; the usual add-one estimate is **342/1,000 = 0.342**. The selected score is ordinary under both comparisons. Neither number is a probability that the full historical idea is correct or incorrect.

![Two horizontal box plots show the best-of-five score inside both control distributions.](experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/score-controls.svg)

The boxes span each control's middle half, their central lines mark medians, and the whiskers reach the saved minimum and maximum. The dashed line is the observed 287,504. The figure displays the distribution of the **maximum over five** for every control input, not the distribution of a single selected variant. [Download the figure](experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/score-controls.svg), [all candidate streams and source coordinates](experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/candidate-streams.json), or [the complete results and control scores](experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/results.json).

## Reproduce and interpret

From a full checkout or the [experiment ZIP](downloads/experiments/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction.zip), run:

```text
python experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/run.py --check
python experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/check.py
python experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/plot.py --check
```

The first command rebuilds all five outputs, 2,882 shifted maxima and 999 shuffled maxima. The independent checker verifies each stored source coordinate against the archived text, all 14,415 output runes by re-encryption, every observed score through direct rune-pair comparison, sampled controls and both complete tail counts. The [source-bound section-count guide](#/wiki/section-rune-counts) checks the 2,883 construction separately. The [reported-attempt entry](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=spirals-branches-2883-alignment) identifies the supplied discussion without republishing its full transcript.

This result does **not support an unusual IoC peak** for the five subtraction variants and exact representation above. It does not test n-gram scores, additions, multiplication, XOR, periodic IoC, alternative page spans, partial readings or different interruption rules. Even a high whole-stream IoC would need a complete, stable reading and a prediction on text not used to choose its operation. Keep a later variant as a separate test with its own search scope and controls.

records.article:
# Does 331 / 133 point uniquely to STUDY HERE?

**Result.** On the archived 464-word solved LP1 sequence, forward word **331** is STUDY and reverse word **133** is HERE. The reverse position is forward word 332, so the two directions pick adjacent words. The phrase appears at **five** positions in this already-decoded text, not only at the reported 331 / 133 split. At the selected cut, the final 133 cipher words have the reported Gematria Primus (GP) sum **26,893**. The first 331 sum to **72,065**, which is **102 above** the reported 71,963.

![A line marks the five locations of STUDY HERE in the 464-word reading; the chosen 331/133 split is highlighted with the two measured GP block sums below.](experiments/records/study-here-bidirectional-pointer/pointer-locations.svg)

| Forward STUDY word | Reverse HERE word | First block GP sum | Remaining block GP sum |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 196 | 268 | 42,503 | 56,455 |
| 227 | 237 | 48,700 | 50,258 |
| 262 | 202 | 56,114 | 42,844 |
| 293 | 171 | 62,910 | 36,048 |
| **331** | **133** | **72,065** | **26,893** |

The source conversation links the selected split to two purported prime sums, 71,963 and 26,893. Only the latter reproduces from this archive's nine-page ciphertext transcription. The reporter's exact 464-word input list was not supplied, so the 102-point difference is an **unresolved source discrepancy**; it does not prove the original calculation was impossible on another transcription.

The pointer arithmetic is less selective than it first looks: for any cut after forward word *k* in a 464-word list, reverse word *(464 − k)* is automatically the next forward word. The audit therefore checks every adjacent STUDY HERE occurrence and every one of the 463 possible cuts. Thirteen cuts have prime GP sums on both sides, while the selected 331 cut has a prime on only the final side. These are descriptive counts, **not a probability**: the positions, phrase and number links were discussed after the solved text was available.

The [plan](experiments/records/study-here-bidirectional-pointer/plan.json) fixes the four-section word order and counting rule. The [result](experiments/records/study-here-bidirectional-pointer/results.json) records input hashes, all five phrase locations and the prime-cut count. Reproduce it from the repository root with `python experiments/records/study-here-bidirectional-pointer/run.py --check`; the underlying independent word/token audit is `python scripts/audit_464_pointer.py --check`. This tests the reported **LP1 pointer**, not whether it specifies an LP2 decryption.

records.article:
## Why match the number of tokens?

The [aligned-language baseline](#/experiments/parallel-languages) compares the manuscript with much longer reference texts. This control asks a narrower question: how do those reference languages behave when each sample contains exactly **2,896 tokens**, the size of the unsolved rune-token target?

Every complete reference sample is nearest to its own language profile. However, **the manuscript is farther from every language profile than any of that language's reference samples are**. English is still the nearest of the eight candidates, but nearest does not mean that its profile closely explains the manuscript. These are observed distances, not probabilities or statistical rejection thresholds.

## What is held fixed

The languages, translations, development profiles, three common representations and total-variation distance are inherited from the baseline. There is no fitted classifier or new language selection. Each evaluation translation is tokenized sentence by sentence, then divided in original order into disjoint blocks of 2,896 tokens. Every complete block is retained; the final incomplete remainder is counted and reported but not scored as an equal-size sample.

This produces seven blocks each for English and German, eight each for French, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish and Welsh, and five for Finnish. The three representations reuse the same texts. The resulting 177 profile checks are **not 177 independent trials**, and they are not pooled into a claimed general classification accuracy.

Equal token counts do not preserve identical translated passages: different languages use different numbers of words for the same content. This control addresses size. The [aligned-block variant](#/experiments/parallel-language-blocks) separately preserves sentence ranges across languages. Neither controls for the difference between translated web material and Liber Primus's style.

## Reading the distances

Each sample is compared with all eight full development profiles using length bins 1 through 15 and 16+. Total variation is half the sum of the absolute differences in bin proportions. Zero means matching distributions; larger values mean greater separation. All distances are stored as exact rational numbers, and ties would be retained rather than broken by language order.

| Language | Complete blocks per representation | Largest letter-control distance | Manuscript to letter profile |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| English | 7 | 0.0508 | 0.0831 |
| Finnish | 5 | 0.0466 | 0.4051 |
| French | 8 | 0.0514 | 0.1781 |
| German | 7 | 0.0561 | 0.1665 |
| Italian | 8 | 0.0436 | 0.2375 |
| Portuguese | 8 | 0.0426 | 0.2114 |
| Spanish | 8 | 0.0456 | 0.2230 |
| Welsh | 8 | 0.0404 | 0.1650 |

“Largest control distance” means the farthest observed sample from its own language's development profile. It is not a confidence limit. The manuscript lies beyond those observed ranges for all eight languages in all three representations, including GP-style grouping. That grouping is an orthographic sensitivity, not a validated conversion of each language into runes.

Within this corpus, all complete samples have a unique nearest profile matching their known language. The manuscript's nearest profile is English in all three representations. The report preserves every competing distance and the margin over the nearest competing language, so this statement can be checked without relying on a winner-only table.

## A Unicode exception found before scoring

The original follow-up plan assumed that all three representations would preserve token boundaries. The implementation stopped when that check failed. Lowercasing the capital dotted I in “İzmir” creates an i followed by a combining dot; the inherited raw-letter tokenizer treats the mark as a separator. Accent folding removes it, joining the word. Three source sentences are affected.

An amendment was committed after inspecting that tokenization issue and before inspecting follow-up scores. The baseline tokenizer was not silently changed. Each representation is partitioned independently, its endpoint ledger is retained, and the report states whether boundaries agree. Folded letters and GP grouping do share boundaries. The original plan remains available alongside the amendment.

## What this does not establish

The control does not identify the manuscript's language, eliminate the eight languages, or estimate a posterior probability. The sample ranges are small, adjacent blocks can share a source article, and both reference splits come from the same benchmark. The manuscript has different genre, spelling, unit and boundary uncertainties. Even its closest reference profile can therefore be a poor match for reasons other than language.

The [known-reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) supplies a complementary warning: some short, established English sections rank nearest to other language profiles. The [cipher-invariants guide](#/wiki/cipher-invariants) explains which transformations preserve lengths and which change the assumptions behind this comparison.

## Reproduce and inspect

Python 3's standard library is sufficient; no API or model is involved. From the repository or extracted reproduction bundle, choose new output filenames:

```sh
python scripts/run_target_sized_languages.py --output my-language-controls.json
python scripts/check_target_sized_languages.py my-language-controls.json --receipt my-language-audit.json
python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_target_sized_languages.py
```

The independent checker imports neither the producer nor the baseline tokenizer. It reconstructs words with a regex tokenizer, calculates distances from integer histogram counts, and checks all sample boundaries, remainders, 177 profiles, competing distances, margins and summary decisions. Its saved receipt records the report and checker hashes. Computational verification has passed; human review remains pending.

FLORES translations and this derived account are provided under CC BY-SA 4.0. The baseline's source attribution is included with the reproduction files.

family.title: 27 × 27 totient-map methods
family.question: Can fixed geometric rules recover and predict a reading of LP2-00–02?

scope.procedure: Replay supplied nodes and ciphertext; independently check arithmetic; recompute three transition rules; compare three documented SOON centers; census mirrors and 99 frequency-preserving shuffled controls.
scope.parameters: Pinned commit d5eed3f10428372c7202ceebc65cc3bdead0819d; 17 primary blocks plus alternative SOON; 16 primary transitions; phase thresholds 7,14; four mirror axes/radii 1..13; seed3301; ordered signature keys indices1..28.

records.finding: The selected words reproduce, including the alternative SOON reading: 65 rune calculations across 18 blocks. All 16 primary transitions match the stated signature, axis and boundary rules. However, three nodes giving the same SOON key predict different next axes; the route still needs selection rules.

records.article:
## What was tested

The proposed 27 × 27 reading can be reproduced **when its selected cells and key nodes are supplied**. This experiment checks that arithmetic, the map itself, and the additional rules for predicting properties of the next block. It does not find the route from the manuscript without those selections.

The source is pinned to commit `d5eed3f10428372c7202ceebc65cc3bdead0819d`. Later edits to that repository are outside this result. The downloadable input records the coordinates, keys, source-file hashes and proposed output rune indices. No language model or language scorer chooses words in this replay.

## Results at a glance

| Check | Result | What it establishes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Map compared with archived LP2-00–02 | 729 of 729 cells agree | The selected matrix uses our transcription in page order |
| Main reading | 17 blocks, 61 rune subtractions reproduce | Correct arithmetic for supplied choices |
| Alternative SOON block | 4 further subtractions reproduce | A second supplied route produces the same word |
| Next-key signature | 16 of 16 transitions match | Fit to the recorded route |
| Next axis and boundary role | Each matches 16 of 16 | Further fit to the same route, not independent discoveries |
| Ciphertext coverage | 54 distinct cells of 729, about 7.4% | The proposed reading is a selection, with reused cells |
| Same SOON key from three nodes | Horizontal / diagonal / diagonal | Key equality does not settle the node choice |

**Outcome: inconclusive as a decryption claim.** Successful arithmetic is a real result. The supplied rules do not yet uniquely select and read the full matrix, and this experiment does not establish whether the proposed passage was intended.

[Open the full-size coverage map](exports/figures/totient-map-coverage.svg) · [Open the node-choice diagram](exports/figures/totient-map-node-choice.svg)

## How the map is made

Read [LP2-00](#/page/lp2-00), [LP2-01](#/page/lp2-01) and [LP2-02](#/page/lp2-02) in that order. Keep every rune, including the heading, remove punctuation and spacing, and fill rows of 27 from left to right. Coordinates start at (1,1). This gives exactly 729 cells; the repository's displayed map agrees cell by cell. It is a rearrangement of the text, not the original page layout.

The coverage figure highlights only ciphertext cells used in the primary route. Keys and navigation landmarks can use other cells. There are 61 output positions but only 54 distinct ciphertext cells because several are read more than once. Reuse is not automatically an error in a geometric cipher; it needs an explicit rule, just as skipping cells does.

For the functions themselves, see [Euler’s totient](#/wiki/totient) and [the Möbius function](#/wiki/mobius-function).

## A complete arithmetic example: WEATHER

The node at row 14, columns 4–6 is X–OE–X, with indices 14,22,14. Replace the middle index by its totient: φ(22)=10, giving X–I–X. Apply μ(φ(k)) to each derived key index. The signature is (1,0,1), whose sum modulo 3 is 2. Rotate the key left twice to get X–X–I and repeat it.

| Cipher cell | Cipher index | Key index | Difference modulo 29 | Output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (14,14) | NG = 21 | X = 14 | 7 | W |
| (14,15) | P = 13 | X = 14 | 28 | EA |
| (14,16) | EO = 12 | I = 10 | 2 | TH |
| (14,17) | O = 3 | X = 14 | 18 | E |
| (14,18) | E = 18 | X = 14 | 4 | R |

Five output runes spell WEATHER. This calculation does not itself explain why those five cells are chosen, why the block stops there, or which block follows. The opening block also crosses a row boundary, whereas later selections include vertical and diagonal segments. TURNS uses its three node indices directly rather than transforming the center. Those choices are preserved in the replay instead of silently replacing them with a uniform rule.

The output trace retains rune tokens such as TH and EA. Spaces and punctuation in the proposed English reading are editorial interpretations, not separate decoded symbols.

## What the transition rules add

The source provides more than word examples. It predicts a next-key signature using Möbius values of current block coordinates. It switches between direct and half-turned positions at cumulative phase totals 7 and 14. A quarter-turn calculation updates the outer signature state. A separate formula involving the current beginning, end and original node center predicts horizontal, vertical or diagonal; another predicts whether the next block's leftmost cell is its beginning or end.

We recomputed all 16 primary transitions, treating OF and THE separately and using the primary SOON route. All three checks match. The starting state, block boundaries, node centers and phase thresholds are inputs. The source states that the thresholds were identified from this route. Consequently, **16 matches are an in-sample fit, not 16 held-out predictions**. The signature, axis and boundary checks also share inputs and must not be multiplied as independent probabilities.

### How many keys share a signature?

A signature constrains a key without identifying its runes. For example, (0,0,0) is shared by 4,096 ordered triples of positive rune indices; (1,0,1) by 1,296. These counts enumerate indices 1–28 only. They exclude F=0, for which the standard positive-integer totient is not defined here. They are not counts of reachable nodes: geometric restrictions can reduce the candidates considerably.

For each derived key index k, compute μ(φ(k)). Among indices 1–28, 16 give zero, 3 give −1, and 9 give +1. An ordered key with signature (0,0,0) can independently select any of the 16 zero-class indices in each slot: 16 × 16 × 16 = 4,096. Repeated indices are allowed in this algebraic count. The signature (1,0,1) similarly gives 9 × 16 × 9 = 1,296.

[Inspect the signature-class diagram](exports/figures/totient-signature-classes.svg). These are derived key triples before phase rotation; equal outer signature values do not require equal outer rune indices. They do not enumerate manuscript locations, enforce mirror-node geometry, or measure how many alternatives survive the complete proposed traversal. Therefore they cannot be used as the denominator of a chance probability for the reading.

### Check one transition by hand: WEATHER → TURNS

WEATHER occupies absolute positions 365–369, where position is `27 × (row − 1) + column`. Its original key-node center is (14,5), position 356, and contains OE with rune index 22. The cumulative phase total before this transition is 2, so the direct-position mode with offset 1 applies.

| Quantity | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Next phase | `(1 + μ(365) + μ(366) + μ(367) + μ(368) + μ(369)) mod 3` = `(1 + 1 − 1 − 1 + 0 + 0) mod 3` | 0 |
| Next outer state | Quarter-turned positions are 365, 392, 419, 446, 473; minimum 365 has μ = 1. Update `(1 + 1) mod 2`. | 0 |
| Next signature | Phase 0 and outer state 0 force the middle component to 0. | (0,0,0) |
| Next axis | `μ(365 + 356) + μ(gcd(473,361))` = `μ(721) + μ(1)` = 1 + 1 | Positive: vertical |
| Next boundary role | Three-quarter-turned endpoint has position 257. `(μ(257) + φ(22)) mod 2` = `(−1 + 10) mod 2` | 1: beginning |

For a vertical block, the minimum quarter-turned position corresponds to its bottommost cell. Calling that cell the beginning therefore predicts upward reading. The supplied TURNS block does read upward, from (14,19) to (10,19), and its key has signature (0,0,0). These properties agree; the calculation still does not choose column 19, the block's starting row, its length, or the exact key.

Every transition now has the same level of detail in the report's `calculation` object: coordinates, transformed positions, individual Möbius values, cumulative state, gcd arguments and boundary selection. The independent checker reconstructs these entries by rotating coordinates directly instead of using the replay's formulas for rotated absolute positions.

## A controlled ambiguity: three SOON nodes

The source documents L–C–EA, L–I–EA and L–EO–EA. Their center indices 5, 10 and 12 all have totient 4. All therefore derive L–R–EA, align to EA–L–R, and turn the same X–D–W–H ciphertext into SOON.

However, the next-axis formula also uses the original center's **position**. With the documented centers (25,7), (20,15) and (25,14), the scores are respectively 0, −1 and −1: horizontal, diagonal, diagonal. The published transition fit chooses (25,7), which agrees with THEN's horizontal block. The source explicitly identifies that choice.

This is a bounded example of a selection that affects the result. It does not prove that any desired sentence can be produced, or that all three choices satisfy every proposed navigation condition. It shows why a full decoder needs a rule selecting the original node before the next block is inspected.

## Are three-rune mirrors unusual by themselves?

We counted equal outer runes around any center, along rows, columns and the two diagonals, at every in-bounds radius from 1 to 13. Each unoriented triple is counted once. The map has **507** such mirrors.

As a control, we shuffled the same 729 rune indices 99 times using seed 3301. This preserves rune frequencies but removes their original positions. Mirror counts ranged from **458 to 568**. The observed count is inside that range.

This control is deliberately narrow. It tests the abundance of this simple geometric pattern, not the quality of the proposed English, the complete traversal, or the combined transition rules. It supplies no chance probability for the selected reading. Testing that stronger claim would require a completely specified search procedure, the same search budget on controls, and a scoring rule chosen before inspecting the results.

## How to reproduce

Download this experiment's bundle and extract it without changing its folder structure. Python 3 and its standard library are sufficient; no network, API or model is required.

```text
python experiments/records/totient-map-route/run.py --check
python experiments/records/totient-map-route/check.py
python experiments/records/totient-map-route/signature_figure.py
```

The first command rebuilds the report and coverage image in memory and compares them with the saved versions. It checks all selected key nodes and subtractions, recomputes transition matches, enumerates signature classes, and repeats the mirror controls. Running without `--check` writes the report and coverage image. The explanatory node-choice diagram is an authored illustration of the reported three-node comparison.

The second command independently derives totients through prime factorization, checks all 65 recorded rune subtractions and node-derived keys, and compares totients with coprime counting for 1–729. It also independently verifies all 16 transition calculation records, all 18 key-node midpoints, and rotation identities for all 729 cells. It does not independently rediscover the route or certify the author's navigation choices. The JSON report includes all rune traces, transition inputs/results, the 99 control counts, reused cells, and phase-rotation ablations. Those ablations deliberately change the phase rule; they are sensitivity checks, not alternatives permitted by the fixed phase formula.

The third command independently calculates totients by counting coprimes and Möbius values by factorization, checks all six reported signature-class counts, and verifies the saved diagram. Add `--write` only to regenerate that diagram. It does not search for map nodes or produce plaintext.

## What would strengthen the claim

A useful next variant would freeze a deterministic procedure for choosing the initial node, subsequent anchors, node transformations, distance expressions, block lengths, directions, stopping condition and tie-breaking. It should specify how to handle zero-valued runes and every branch that remains possible.

Run that fixed procedure on an unseen continuation before adjusting it. Report all outputs, not only readable ones. If alternatives remain, bound the enumeration and apply an explicit score to every candidate and to matched controls. This is the distinction between a reproducible selected reading and a decoder capable of making a new prediction. See [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) and [planning a first experiment](#/wiki/first-experiment).

The numerical and thematic correspondences in the source's “Strongest Plaintext Evidence” discussion are not assigned significance here. Nor does this test rule out other 27 × 27, totient or geometric methods. Revisions that change node selection or traversal belong as related variants in this experiment family, with their changed choices stated explicitly.

records.article:
# Do the stored transcription corrections change the published LP2 word-length statistics?

For the **seven currently stored LP2 reviewed-text layers**, no. Applying them all leaves the ordered rune stream, rune-token sequence, 2,896-token length distribution, and whole-stream IoC pair counts unchanged under the site's published counting rule. The one LP1 reviewed layer is a useful positive control: LP1-10 swaps two neighboring runes, changing six ordered-bigram type counts, while retaining its rune multiset and token-length sequence.

This is a sensitivity measurement of the stored layers, **not** a fresh verification of the manuscript images. It says nothing about corrections not yet recorded. A method that treats every punctuation mark as a key reset can change even when this particular word-length statistic does not.

![Per-page correction effects: mark edits, rune order, and rune-token sequence](experiments/records/transcription-correction-sensitivity/correction-effects.svg)

## Inputs and rules

Use the archived `raw` and separate `reviewed_text` in the eight page records: LP1-10; LP2-05, 07, 11, 15, 35, 37 and 38. These are the only eight records with a distinct reviewed layer in the current [75-page inventory](#/wiki/transcription-checking?section=coverage). Every input page record and the 29-rune alphabet are pinned by SHA-256 in `plan.json`.

For word lengths, concatenate LP2-00 through LP2-55 in order, remove slash and CR/LF row wraps, keep headings, and identify runs of the 29 runes with optional internal apostrophes. Other punctuation separates tokens. Count runes, not Latin transliteration letters. This is the same rule used by the [word-length census](#/wiki/word-lengths). No alternative punctuation policy or page-local tokenization is included in the main comparison.

The seven LP2 corrections consist of added or removed notation marks, with no rune substitution. The LP1-10 correction swaps the runes at zero-based rune indices 116 and 117; it is outside the LP2 corpus. The independent checker reconstructs all seven LP2 reviewed strings from the documented edit offsets and checks the LP1 adjacent swap separately.

## Measured effect

| Page | Stored change | Ordered runes | Rune-token sequence | Token count |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| LP1-10 | Adjacent rune swap | Changed | Changed | 40 → 40 |
| LP2-05 | Add `-` | Same | Same | 59 → 59 |
| LP2-07 | Add `.` | Same | Same | 50 → 50 |
| LP2-11 | Add `-` | Same | Same | 55 → 55 |
| LP2-15 | Add `.` | Same | Same | 37 → 37 |
| LP2-35 | Add an apostrophe | Same | Same after omitting the apostrophe | 61 → 61 |
| LP2-37 | Remove three `-` and one `.` | Same | Same | 53 → 53 |
| LP2-38 | Add `.` | Same | Same | 47 → 47 |

Across LP2-00–55, both versions contain **12,956 runes**, **2,896 rune tokens**, and a maximum token length of **14**. Their complete token-length histograms match. Their whole-stream IoC numerator and denominator are **5,787,026 / 167,844,980** in both versions. The ordered rune stream and normalized token sequence have matching SHA-256 values. LP2-35's literal token text contains an extra apostrophe; the apostrophe is not a rune, and its normalized rune token is unchanged.

LP1-10 demonstrates that the audit can register a real ordered-rune difference: the two-rune exchange changes six ordered-bigram type counts. Because it is a swap, its rune count, multiset and whole-page IoC remain unchanged. Its word lengths remain 40 tokens with the same length sequence, even though the token containing the swapped symbols has different rune order.

## What follows—and what does not

For these exact stored LP2 corrections, recomputing the site's joined-page word-length histogram will not change the result. A rune-only frequency or IoC calculation also receives the same symbols in the same order. This is stronger than merely saying that punctuation changes *might* affect word lengths: it measures the actual published corrections under a declared tokenizer.

It does **not** prove that punctuation is irrelevant. A period, hyphen or apostrophe can drive a reset or extraction rule that this experiment does not run. Different tokenization, image-derived separators, or a newly corrected rune can change later measurements. Nor does matching a reviewed layer establish that the image was transcribed correctly everywhere. See [the transcription guide](#/wiki/transcription-checking) for the distinction between archived text, reviewed correction and original-image evidence.

## Reproduce

From the repository root or extracted experiment ZIP, with Python 3 and no packages:

```text
python experiments/records/transcription-correction-sensitivity/run.py --check
python experiments/records/transcription-correction-sensitivity/check.py
```

The first command recomputes every page and the complete LP2 corpus, then compares `results.json` and the SVG. The second independently reconstructs the reviewed strings and scans rune tokens with a separate parser. `run.py` without flags prints a compact summary. The full machine-readable result includes per-page histograms, correction fields, hashes and the exact IoC pair counts.

The next variants should test a *specified* punctuation-sensitive key clock or tokenization policy, then add newly image-reviewed disputed marks one at a time. Retain this archived-versus-reviewed baseline so any changed conclusion can be attributed to the exact edit that caused it.

For a more specific statistic on the same seven LP2 reviewed layers, the [doublet boundary audit](#/experiments/doublet-boundaries) checks all 86 equal-rune pairs and whether any stored mark edit changes the intervening-separator class.

# Typed seeds and Python Random streams

**Finding.** A published seed sweep tries words, byte strings, integers and dates as Python `random.Random` seeds. We generated its **15,408 seed–stream–sign configurations** and checked four source-defined F-rune interrupter choices for each. Across **55 nonempty LP2-00–55 page starts** and nine fixed, 12-rune known-reading openings, **none reaches 12 runes**. The longest match is five.

![The typed-seed candidates rapidly thin from first-rune matches to no complete 12-rune opening.](experiments/records/typed-seed-random-opening-cribs/typed-seed-opening-funnel.svg)

## The bounded question

The [pinned source program](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/seed_sweep/string_seeds.py) specifies **1,284 typed seed values**: 68 words as strings and as bytes, 1,145 integers including the source's date grid, and three floats. Each feeds six Python Random output modes: `randrange`, `randint`, `random`, `choice`, `shuffle`, and five-bit `getrandbits`. The source tests two decode signs, making 15,408 configurations. Its decoder also tries four masks: keep or remove each of the first two F runes before the key advances.

We held the nine published 12-rune reading openings fixed and tested each against the first 12 output runes of every included page under those same interrupter choices. We used the shared exact-prefix checker with **no key skips**; the F-mask operation is the source rule here. This is a new fixed-opening test across pages, distinct from the source's original English-score test on LP2-00. It also differs from the site's separate seven-generator public PRNG sweep.

| Longest opening prefix | Mask paths |
| --- | ---: |
| 1 rune | 39,208 |
| 2 runes | 21,388 |
| 3 runes | 1,000 |
| 4 runes | 30 |
| 5 runes | 6 |
| 12 runes | **0** |

Four mask paths per configuration give **61,632 paths**. Many paths and several Python Random output modes can coincide; those paths are not independent discoveries. The test excludes these *specific* source streams as producers of the *nine chosen openings* at the *included page starts*. It does not assume the unsolved pages must begin with those readings, and it does not rule out other seeds, plaintexts, offsets or interruption rules.

## Repeat it

```bash
python experiments/records/typed-seed-random-opening-cribs/run.py
python experiments/records/typed-seed-random-opening-cribs/check.py
python experiments/records/typed-seed-random-opening-cribs/plot.py --check
```

The runner executes only the seed literals, date loop and stream function extracted from the pinned MIT-licensed source file; it does not need the source's unavailable English-scoring model. `check.py` reconciles the source's 15,408-configuration count, compares each stream mode with an independently written Python Random sample, and verifies plaintext reconstruction under all four F masks and both signs. Python **3.12** seed behavior is part of this result; the copied source code does not execute a Python 2 string-seeding implementation.

records.title: LP2-00–55: uniform additive keys and adjacent matches
records.question: Does the observed number of within-page adjacent matches agree with independent uniform additive keys modulo 29?
records.summary: 86 adjacent matches versus 444.86 expected under one fixed model. Exact lower-tail calculation, page-boundary proof and independent finite controls.

record_type.label: Manuscript measurement
record_type.description: Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule.

family.title: Models for the number of adjacent matches
family.question: Which explicit symbol-generation models agree with the observed within-page repeat count?

variant.label: Independent uniform additive keys modulo 29

scope.representation: Archived rune-only page streams; headings included; remove non-runes; count overlapping equal neighbors; never join pages.
scope.procedure: Recount all pages and evaluate the inclusive lower binomial tail using exact integer arithmetic; independently check by integer-mass recurrence and regex recount.
scope.parameters: 29-symbol alphabet; independent uniform additive keys, independent of fixed plaintext; fixed observed page lengths; lower tail includes ties; 80-digit Decimal rendering; 12 finite distribution controls.
scope.exclusions: Nonuniform or dependent keys, fixed-count shuffles, other cipher equations, altered boundaries, output filters, plaintext identification and correction for historical feature selection.

records.finding: The observed 86 matches among 12,901 edges strongly disagree with this uniform model: expected 12,901/29 ≈ 444.86; conditional P(D≤86) ≈ 1.0708e-98. This is not logical impossibility or a probability about language.
records.limitations: Low count and prior claim known before replication. Conditional tail is not adjusted for prior feature selection. Archived transcription is assumed. Other key models and multiplicative running sums remain outside the result; human review pending.
records.article:
## What was tested

The archived LP2-00–55 text has **86 adjacent equal-rune pairs across 12,901 within-page edges**. Independent uniform additive keys modulo 29 would produce about **444.86 matches on average**. The exact probability of 86 or fewer under that model is approximately **1.0708 × 10⁻⁹⁸**.

This is a strong disagreement with one precisely defined model. It does not rule out encryption, random choices in other constructions, or any particular plaintext language. The low count and an earlier statement of this model were known before the replication. The probability is conditional on the model and is not adjusted for the historical search across manuscript features.

## The model in ordinary terms

For every plaintext rune, independently choose a key uniformly from 0 through 28 and add it modulo 29. The plaintext may be any fixed sequence. Each resulting ciphertext rune is uniform, and different positions are independent. Keep the observed page lengths fixed.

The prediction concerns fresh, independent uniform symbols. A shuffle that preserves the manuscript's observed rune counts asks a different question. So does a generator that forbids repeats, uses nonuniform keys, reuses key values dependently, or changes its output according to the plaintext.

The [EA running-sum control](#/experiments/ea-frequency-control) examines an especially different equation: nonzero multiplicative keys and an EA offset make repeats depend on plaintext EA frequency. Its required EA count should not be tested with this record's independent-uniform-additive-key tail.

The [short-lag profile](#/experiments/doublet-lag-profile) uses that different, fixed-count page-shuffle reference. It shows the deficit at adjacent positions but not at rune distances two through five. Its bands must not be read as the exact uniform-key probability computed here.

## Why overlapping pairs still give a binomial law here

Adjacent comparisons share positions: the first pair of ABC uses A and B, and the next uses B and C. Shared positions do not automatically make these match indicators dependent under this particular uniform model.

Within one page, replace the ciphertext sequence by its first rune and the successive differences modulo 29. This transformation is reversible: start at the first rune and add each difference to recover the page. A reversible transformation of the uniformly distributed full sequence remains uniform over all such coordinate tuples. The differences are therefore independent uniform residues. A pair matches exactly when its difference is zero, which has probability 1/29.

Apply this separately to each page. There are 12,956 runes on 55 nonempty pages, hence **12,956 − 55 = 12,901 differences**. LP2-50 has no alphabet runes and adds no edge. Their zero count has the binomial distribution with 12,901 trials and success probability 1/29.

Uniformity matters. For independent binary symbols with probabilities 3/4 and 1/4, one pair matches with probability 5/8. Both overlapping pairs match with probability 7/16, which is different from (5/8)² = 25/64. The corresponding independence argument fails for that nonuniform model.

## Reading the figure and the probability

The bars show probabilities for ten-count intervals under the uniform model. The observed count is far to the left of the main mass; its tiny probability cannot be resolved at this linear plotting scale. Values 650 and above are retained in one overflow bin in the JSON but omitted from the displayed range. The exact lower tail includes every count from zero through 86, not just the probability of exactly 86.

The numerator is the integer sum `Σ comb(E,j) × 28^(E−j)` for j from 0 through D, and the denominator is `29^E`, with E = 12,901 and D = 86. The script uses exact integers for that sum and 80-digit decimal arithmetic to render the ratio. It records hashes of both exact integers and supplies their reconstruction formulas. No normal approximation is used.

The separate checker reconstructs the same integer masses using a recurrence. It verifies the entire set of plotting bins against exact integer totals, independently recounts all 56 source files with regular expressions, and exhausts twelve small uniform-alphabet/page-length cases. Those controls include overlapping edges, multiple pages, empty pages and single-rune pages. They check the calculation and boundary handling; they do not authenticate the underlying handwriting.

## What remains possible

The model assigns this event a very small but nonzero probability. That is statistical evidence against the model, not a mathematical impossibility certificate. It neither selects an alternative model nor explains the suppression.

In particular, the [multiplicative running-sum model](#/wiki/doublets?section=ea-constraint) has a different equation. There, with nonzero keys modulo 29, a repeat can be determined by a particular plaintext rune. Uniform selection of its nonzero keys does not imply a repeat probability of 1/29. This experiment must not be used to reject that construction.

## Reproduce the comparison

Download this experiment's bundle and preserve its folders. Python 3 standard library only; no network, API, or model is required.

```text
python experiments/records/uniform-additive-doublets/run.py --check
python experiments/records/uniform-additive-doublets/check.py
python experiments/records/uniform-additive-doublets/plot.py --check
```

The first verifies the input hashes, per-page counts, exact tail and saved bins. The second uses the independent recurrence and controls. The third checks the chart against the saved probabilities. To regenerate, run the producer with `--write` and the plotter without `--check`.

The [committed plan](experiments/plans/uniform-additive-doublets.md) was fixed before these new calculations, after the prior count and claim were known. This is computationally checked replication; human review is pending. See [doublet definitions](#/wiki/doublets), [null-model selection](#/wiki/null-models), and [what a scoped exclusion means](#/wiki/first-experiment?section=exclusions).

records.article:
# Do fixed affine rune maps produce literal web markers?

One map produces one literal **HTTPS** window: LP2-36, rune start 226 using zero-based positions, under `P=(24C+28) mod 29`. **HTTP** is the prefix of that same window. WWW and ONION have no matches. These are literal marker counts, not recovered URLs: punctuation and hostname grammar were not tested.

The frozen readout covers all 812 invertible GP29 affine maps at every fitting rune position in original LP2-00 through 55. Fifty-five pages contain 12,956 runes; LP2-50 has none. Every non-rune separator is removed, headings retain their original order, and searches never cross page boundaries. One ASCII letter uses its canonical one-letter GP rune. A digraph-labelled rune is one separate rune slot, not two searchable letters. No alternative spellings or marker variants were added after counting.

The sole cipher window has indices `4,14,14,3,20`, whose GP labels are `R X X O L`. The map sends it to `8,16,16,13,15`, or `H T T P S`. The saved snippet is `W H IA TH Y M B A [HTTPS] EO M F X U EO A`; spaces here delimit rune slots, and brackets mark the tested token. They do not recover original word spacing or punctuation. The HTTP and HTTPS rows share one page, key and start and therefore are not independent candidate locations. Both rows, exact source line/column positions and their bounded snippets are retained in `matches.json`.

WWW has a stronger pattern constraint. Every static bijective substitution preserves symbol equality: three decoded W runes require three identical adjacent ciphertext runes. The original page streams contain **zero equal-symbol triples**, even after separators are removed. Literal WWW is therefore incompatible with any static bijective rune substitution in these page streams, including every affine map. This does not exclude web addresses without WWW or a cipher whose symbol map changes by position. ONION's absence is established only for the declared affine maps.

All 3,248 planted map/token cases recover their fixed-offset markers: each of 812 maps enciphers synthetic contexts containing each of the four tokens, and the scanner recovers the marker at rune offset 8. A separate implementation translates every complete page into a one-codepoint-per-rune decoded stream and performs overlapping substring searches. Its 45,472 page/map streams, including 812 empty-page streams, reproduce every match tuple, index window, source location and snippet. It independently repeats all 3,248 synthetic controls and checks the equal-triple invariant.

This is one grouped marker-readout follow-up to the existing whole-page affine GP29 English-score record. It reuses the same 812-map keyspace for a different fixed output predicate. The earlier nine opening-crib capacity checks do not supply an all-position marker census. This record makes no p-value, language-score or URL claim; other key layers, transpositions, alphabets and spellings remain untested.

Run `python experiments/records/url-marker-affine-census/run.py`, then `python experiments/records/url-marker-affine-census/check.py`. The plan pins `data/index.json` and all 56 original page files before target counting. Both scripts verify those hashes and use only the Python standard library.
records.reader_finding: One five-rune stretch on LP2-36 reads HTTPS. Its HTTP prefix is the same candidate, not a second hit. WWW and ONION have no matches under the tested maps. The short marker does not establish a web address or confirm the plaintext.
records.reader_limit: Only four fixed literal rune spellings and static affine maps were tested. No punctuation or hostname grammar was inferred, and no chance/significance claim is made. This reuses an already tested keyspace for a new marker readout.

records.title: Every static affine map on complete LP2 pages
records.question: Does any invertible affine transformation of the 29 GP rune indices yield English-like complete text on an unsolved LP2 page?
records.summary: All 812 invertible GP29 affine maps were scored over all 55 rune-bearing LP2-00–55 pages, with solved-reading controls and a full-search shuffled baseline.

record_type.label: Bounded solving test
record_type.description: Applies a fixed decoding, extraction or payload-retrieval rule to declared unsolved material, or excludes a specific direct-generation rule. Its result covers only those bounds.

scope.representation: Original archived GP29 rune order including headings on each rune-bearing LP2-00–55 page. LP2-50 has no runes.
scope.procedure: Apply P=(aC+b) mod 29 for every a=1..28 and b=0..28 to each complete page. Score canonical GP Latin text with a pinned English quadgram table. Gate on nine complete archived readings and nine planted affine encipherments. For 199 null trials shuffle each page's rune order, run the whole census, and retain one global maximum.
scope.parameters: 812 maps, 55 pages, 44,660 candidate outputs; fixed English threshold −5.5; 200 shuffles per positive control and 199 complete-search null replicates.
scope.exclusions: No time-varying affine rule, general substitution, wordwise transforms, non-English score, altered transcription or hidden intermediate operation.

records.finding: Nine complete archived readings cleared the English-score gate and all nine planted affine encipherments ranked the true map first. None of 44,660 LP2 outputs reached the fixed −5.5 threshold. The highest score was −6.543, and 144 of 199 shuffled-page full-search controls had an equal or higher maximum.
records.limitations: The test covers one static affine map per complete page and English-like canonical GP transliteration. Pagewise rune shuffles are positional controls, not cipher models. Periodic or contextual maps, other languages and hidden layers remain open.
records.article:
## Result

**No fixed affine map made a complete unsolved LP2 page resemble the archived English readings.** We tried every invertible map of the 29-rune alphabet on each of **55 rune-bearing pages**: **44,660 page/map outputs**. None reached the fixed English-score threshold of −5.5. The best, on LP2-55 with `P = 12C + 22 (mod 29)`, scored **−6.543**.

That winner is ordinary for a search this large. We shuffled rune order separately within every page, reran the **entire 44,660-output search** 199 times, and kept each trial's highest score. **144 of 199** trials matched or exceeded the manuscript maximum. The result limits this particular static-alphabet English reading; it does not eliminate changing alphabets or other ciphers.

![The best LP2 affine score falls among the full-search shuffled controls, far below the weakest complete known reading.](experiments/records/wholepage-affine-gp29/scores.svg)

## What the search covers

For each archived rune index `C`, the proposed plaintext index is `P = aC + b (mod 29)`. We tested **all 28 nonzero multipliers** and **all 29 offsets**. Because 29 is prime, each of these 812 maps permutes the alphabet. They include all constant shifts (`a = 1`) and ordinary Atbash (`a = 28, b = 28`) without listing those cases twice. Each map acts uniformly across one complete page, including headings. LP2-50 has no runes and contributes no candidate.

Before scoring LP2, we tested the scorer and search on all **nine complete archived readings**. All nine scored above −5.5 and above 99% of 200 rune-order shuffles of their own text. We also constructed a ciphertext for each reading whose intended decoding map was `P = 7C + 13 (mod 29)`; the search ranked the planted true plaintext first among 812 maps **nine times out of nine**. These controls show the procedure can recover a similar English reading if this sort of map generated it. They do not establish English as the language of every unsolved page.

The shuffled controls preserve each page's rune frequencies and length. Comparing **global maxima** accounts for selecting the most attractive page and map after seeing all results under this positional null. A rune shuffle is not a simulation of Cicada's possible encryption process. The 44,660 outputs are parameter settings within one method, not 44,660 independent ideas.

## Reproduce and limits

The [plan](experiments/records/wholepage-affine-gp29/plan.json) pins all 56 page transcriptions, nine reading traces, alphabet and score model by SHA-256. The [complete case ledger](experiments/records/wholepage-affine-gp29/cases.jsonl) gives every page, map, score and decoded-index hash; the [summary and null maxima](experiments/records/wholepage-affine-gp29/results.json) are separate. Run `python experiments/records/wholepage-affine-gp29/run.py --check`, then `python experiments/records/wholepage-affine-gp29/check.py` for an independent reconstruction. Both use NumPy and Numba for the full search; the runner crosschecks fixed cases against a separate ordinary Latin-string scorer.

This does not test a map changing by position, word, line or page state; arbitrary substitutions; transposition; alternate rune assignments; hidden layers; or non-English plaintext. The visible text may also require more than one operation.

scope.procedure: Decode every full page with the documented Welcome and second-koan keys under both signs and all phases. Score the complete canonical GP Latin transliteration with the pinned English quadgram model. Gate on nine archived 66-rune readings and nine planted encipherments. Compare the single maximum over all pages/settings with 199 full-search pagewise rune shuffles.

Across 2,310 whole-page outputs, the highest English score was −6.675 and none reached the fixed −5.5 threshold. A complete 2,310-setting search on each of 199 independently page-shuffled controls produced an equal or higher maximum 68 times.
