records.article:
## Result

**Neither documented LP1 key produced an English-like complete page in this search.** We decoded all **55 rune-bearing pages from LP2-00–55** with the Welcome and second-koan keys, both arithmetic directions and every key phase: **2,310 complete-page outputs**. None reached the fixed −5.5 score that recognized the archived readings. The highest score was **−6.675**, on LP2-55 with the Welcome key.

That best result was not unusual after allowing the search to choose among all 2,310 outputs: **68 of 199** shuffled-page controls scored at least as high under the same entire search. This comparison does not exclude other keys or forms of Vigenère.

![The LP2 best score sits within the full-search shuffle range, well below the weakest archived English control.](experiments/records/wholepage-known-vigenere-keys/scores.svg)

## Why this is a different test

The earlier [known-key opening test](#/experiments/lp2-known-vigenere-keys) asked whether a page *began* with one of nine exact twelve-rune readings. A page could fail that test yet still contain English elsewhere. Here the score uses **every rune on each page**, including headings. Punctuation and line breaks do not advance the repeating key; each page starts a fresh phase. LP2-50 has no runes and therefore contributes no candidate. The shortest tested page has 66 runes.

We first checked whether the scorer could recognize texts of that minimum length. All **nine** archived 66-rune reading excerpts cleared the fixed threshold and beat all 200 of their own rune-order shuffles. When each excerpt was enciphered with one declared key, its true plaintext ranked first among the same 42 key/phase/sign settings **nine times out of nine**. Those controls establish sensitivity to similar known plaintext; they cannot show that every valid LP2 reading must resemble the English training corpus.

For each of 199 null trials, we shuffled rune positions **separately within every page**, preserving each page's length and rune counts. We then tried all 42 settings on all 55 pages and kept only that trial's highest score. This is a comparison against the entire chosen search, not 2,310 individual unadjusted comparisons. A shuffle is a positional control, not a model of the unknown cipher.

## Reproduce and limits

The [frozen plan](experiments/records/wholepage-known-vigenere-keys/plan.json) pins the page transcriptions, nine reading traces, keys and quadgram model by SHA-256. The [results](experiments/records/wholepage-known-vigenere-keys/results.json) contain every candidate score and output hash, the nine controls and all 199 global null maxima. Run `python experiments/records/wholepage-known-vigenere-keys/run.py --check`, then `python experiments/records/wholepage-known-vigenere-keys/check.py` for an independent reconstruction. The [plot script](experiments/records/wholepage-known-vigenere-keys/plot.py) regenerates the figure.

The test assumes the archived GP rune order, direct repeating-key addition or subtraction, a page-level reset, one of **two** known keys, and English-like output under the pinned scorer. It does not test key interruption, other keys, transposition, cross-page state, a hidden intermediate layer, or another language. It provides no decryption of the unsolved pages.

scope.representation: Original archived GP29 rune order including headings on each rune-bearing LP2-00–55 page. Non-runes do not advance the page-local position; LP2-50 has no runes.
scope.procedure: Apply Pᵢ=Cᵢ+k·i+b modulo 29 for every k=1..28 and b=0..28 to each complete page. Score canonical GP Latin text with a pinned English quadgram table. Gate on nine complete archived readings and nine planted schedules. For 199 null trials shuffle each page's rune order, run the whole census and retain one global maximum.

records.finding: All nine complete archived readings and all nine planted progressive-shift controls passed. None of 44,660 LP2 outputs reached the fixed −5.5 English threshold; the best scored −6.426. Seventy of 199 page-shuffled full-search controls had an equal or higher maximum.

records.article:
## Result

**A constant-rate rotating alphabet did not make any complete unsolved LP2 page read like the archived English passages.** We tested **44,660 outputs**: 812 distinct progressive shifts on each of 55 rune-bearing pages. None reached the fixed −5.5 English-score threshold. The best was **−6.426**, on the short 66-rune LP2-49 page with step `k = 17` and starting offset `b = 11`.

Selection matters: **70 of 199** controls made by shuffling runes within each page produced an equal or higher best score after the **same complete search**. This is a narrow result for a linear position clock, not a verdict on Alberti disks or every changing-alphabet method.

![The best LP2 progressive-shift score lies within complete-search shuffled controls and well below the weakest whole known reading.](experiments/records/wholepage-progressive-caesar/scores.svg)

## The exact rule

At rune position `i`, counted from zero at the start of each page, we decode `Pᵢ = Cᵢ + k·i + b (mod 29)`. Only runes advance `i`; headings are included. We tested every **nonzero step** `k = 1…28` and every offset `b = 0…28`. A negative step is another value of `k` modulo 29, and changing the starting phase only changes `b`, so neither needs a duplicated case. Constant shifts (`k = 0`) were already covered by the [static affine census](#/experiments/wholepage-affine-gp29). LP2-50 has no runes and was excluded.

We validated the score before inspecting LP2. All **nine complete archived readings** exceeded −5.5 and beat more than 99% of 200 rune-order shuffles of their own text. After enciphering each reading with the fixed schedule `k = 7, b = 13`, its true plaintext ranked first among all 812 tested schedules **nine times out of nine**. These controls show that a comparable English reading generated by this rule would register; they do not prove LP2's hidden language or structure.

For each of 199 null trials, we shuffled positions independently within every page, preserving its length and rune counts, then retained the single highest score over all **55 × 812** outputs. This controls selection over both page and schedule under that positional model. It is not a simulation of the manuscript's encryption. The tested schedules are variants of one method, not thousands of independent hypotheses.

## Reproduce and limits

The [plan](experiments/records/wholepage-progressive-caesar/plan.json) pins all page transcriptions, solved readings, alphabet and score model by SHA-256. The [case ledger](experiments/records/wholepage-progressive-caesar/cases.jsonl) contains every schedule, score and decoded-index hash; [results](experiments/records/wholepage-progressive-caesar/results.json) retain all 199 global null maxima. Run `python experiments/records/wholepage-progressive-caesar/run.py --check`, then `python experiments/records/wholepage-progressive-caesar/check.py` for an independent reconstruction. Both full searches use NumPy and Numba; fixed outputs are also checked by a separate ordinary Latin-string scorer.

The position clock here increments once per rune and resets at each page. It does not test word or line resets, nonlinear clocks, extra key layers, mixed alphabets, transposition, non-English text, or the branching disk proposal's unspecified transitions.

records.article:
# Public wordlist keys on complete LP2 pages

## Finding

None of the **43 archived rune keys**, tested at every phase and in both GP29 arithmetic directions, made a complete rune-bearing LP2-00–55 page reach the predeclared English-score threshold. The best output scored **−6.50**. In a matched control that reran the entire search after shuffling rune order within each page, **105 of 199** searches found a score at least that high. This does not identify an English reading from this key list.

![Best complete-page score from the public keys alongside the median full-search shuffle result and the weakest genuine solved-reading control.](experiments/records/wholepage-public-wordlist/score-comparison.svg)

The earlier [public key replay](#/experiments/public-wordlist-vigenere) checked exact openings at phase zero. Here every phase of each of the same **43 fixed keys** is used to decode every rune on each of **55 pages**; LP2-50 has no runes. That is **618 key, phase, and direction settings** and **33,990 complete-page outputs**. This is one bounded extension of the public wordlist, not 33,990 independent ideas. Of the two keys in the earlier [known-key whole-page test](#/experiments/wholepage-known-vigenere-keys), `welcome` is exactly source key 43; `second-koan` is absent from this wordlist.

## What the score means

The score averages English four-letter log likelihoods over the canonical Latin transliteration of each decoded page. Larger values look more like the archived English controls. All nine genuine solved-reading examples passed the predeclared −5.5 threshold and beat at least 198 of 200 individual shuffled controls. All nine planted encipherments were recovered as the highest-ranked setting among the same 618 candidates. The best actual LP2 output stayed below −5.5; **none** of the 33,990 outputs reached it.

The 199 full-search shuffles address selection: with this many pages and key settings, the single highest score will look better than an ordinary random output. A shuffle preserves each page's rune counts and length while disrupting its order. The observed best score was near the middle of the shuffled full-search maxima. A shuffle is a comparison device, not a model of Cicada's encryption. This result does not exclude a different key, a word reset, a second layer, a different alphabet, or a non-English plaintext.

## Reproduce

The [frozen plan](experiments/records/wholepage-public-wordlist/plan.json) declares exact input hashes, score, controls and global null before the LP2 run. [Results](experiments/records/wholepage-public-wordlist/results.json) include all 199 null maxima; [cases](experiments/records/wholepage-public-wordlist/cases.jsonl) retain every output score and decoded-rune hash. Run `python experiments/records/wholepage-public-wordlist/run.py` from the repository root to regenerate them. `python experiments/records/wholepage-public-wordlist/check.py` independently reconstructs every decoded-rune hash, sampled portable scores and three separated full-search null maxima. The run uses Python, NumPy and Numba.

# Eleven-rune windows in the Wing and Tree section

Across six pages, **seven windows sum to 563 and ten sum to 569**. This record supports recurrence under the rules below, not statistical significance, intent or decipherment.

## What changed from the grid experiment?

The baseline rearranges LP2-32 into an 11×11 grid and selects a row, column and perimeter. This variant expands the input to LP2-27–32 and selects every consecutive eleven-rune window within each page. It retains prime values and fixed targets 563 and 569. It does not test the perimeter target 1136. The family comparison lists every changed scope field.

## Complete counting rules

Read the archived text in order, including headings. Keep only the 29 alphabet runes. Remove punctuation and line markers, but start a fresh stream at each page. Sum runes 1–11, then 2–12, continuing to the last complete window. A page with N runes contributes N−10 windows. Do not reverse, pad, wrap or cross a page boundary.

| Page | Runes | Windows | Sum 563 | Sum 569 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| LP2-27 | 234 | 224 | 0 | 2 |
| LP2-28 | 269 | 259 | 2 | 2 |
| LP2-29 | 277 | 267 | 1 | 2 |
| LP2-30 | 263 | 253 | 0 | 1 |
| LP2-31 | 269 | 259 | 3 | 3 |
| LP2-32 | 121 | 111 | 1 | 0 |
| Total | 1433 | 1373 | 7 | 10 |

All window sums total 784505, giving a mean of approximately 571.38. The ledger retains all 1373 windows, including nonmatches. Each includes its rune sequence, sum, one-based rune interval and zero-based source character offsets.

## Why the 569 column is not counted on LP2-32

The first grid column selects positions 1, 12, 23, …, 111. Those positions sum to 569, but are not consecutive. The first grid row uses positions 1–11 and is counted here. A column and a sliding window use different selection rules.

## Limits

Both the targets and section were chosen after the original correspondence was noticed. Adjacent windows share ten runes. Counts cannot be treated as independent trials or p-values. There is no shuffled corpus or adjustment for other targets, lengths and layouts searched. This record does not resolve image-only claims about unspecified row alignments.

## Reproduce and independently check

Extract the experiment ZIP with folders intact, or use the repository. No external packages, images, network requests or AI calls are needed.

```text
python experiments/records/wing-tree-eleven-rune-windows/run.py --check
python experiments/records/wing-tree-eleven-rune-windows/check.py
```

The first command runs the shared census implementation and compares the saved report. The independent checker reads page JSON, constructs intervals by their ending position and sums each directly. It verifies every sequence, coordinate and total without importing the census implementation. Both text representations derive from the same archive: agreement is a computational check, not an independent visual review of the manuscript.

# Affine relations across twelve rune distances

## Finding

Across **12 distances and 841 formulas per distance**, the strongest excess is a **same-rune repeat five positions later**: 102 matches versus 60.6 expected after shuffling runes within each visible word. Only **4 of 999** shuffled-word searches found a result at least this strong (**p = 0.005**, including the one-count Monte Carlo correction). The earlier six-rune rule ranked below this repeat; 23 shuffled searches reached its score somewhere in the full search.

![Histogram of the strongest score in each shuffled-word search, with markers for the actual maximum and the proposed six-rune rule.](experiments/records/word-internal-affine-all-lags/selection-null.svg)

The test finds word-internal structure that this shuffle does not explain. **It does not identify the encryption algorithm.** A shuffle breaks ordinary sequence patterns too, so an elevated count alone cannot distinguish a cipher rule from other structure in the manuscript.

## Why scan the full range?

The [earlier lag-six measurement](#/experiments/word-internal-affine-lags) compared the proposed rule c′ = 24 − 2c (mod 29) against all 841 affine maps **at distance six**. That comparison did not account for choosing the distance after exploration. Here every shuffle must compete over the same 12 distances and 841 maps as the actual transcription. The proposed rule has 77 matches against a shuffle mean of 44.8; its standardized score is 4.763. The complete-search reference reaches at least that score in **23 of 999** trials (corrected tail 0.024). This is a comparison to a wider search, not a fresh independent test of the original idea.

The largest observed score, 5.272, comes from the identity relation at distance five: the rune repeats. It is 102 matches against an exact within-word shuffle expectation of 60.6. Four controls have a maximum score at least this high after repeating the **entire** search. That 4/999 count belongs to the strongest relation, not specifically to the original six-rune formula.

## How the comparison works

Use the archived rune order on LP2-00–55. A hyphen or full stop ends a word; a slash or line break does not. Each page remains separate. For each distance from 1 through 12, count rune pairs that stay within a visible word. Try all maps c′ = ac + b (mod 29), with a and b each 0–28. These are pattern measurements, including noninvertible maps, rather than candidate decryption keys.

For each map and distance, calculate its expected count under independent random order inside each word, keeping that word's exact rune counts. Divide the excess count by the square root of expected count plus one. Select the largest of the **10,092** scores. The denominator is a ranking scale, not a claim that scores follow a normal distribution; the full selection is calibrated by 999 seeded shuffles that repeat the same scan. The [frozen plan](experiments/records/word-internal-affine-all-lags/plan.json) records this score, search range, word rule, seed, stopping rule, and threshold before the run.

## What remains open

The word rule follows the archived transcription, which has disputed separators. Other segmentations, page subsets, relations, and prior exploratory choices were not included in the selection control. The shuffled words preserve local rune counts and word lengths but are not simulated ciphertext. The high same-rune count at distance five should be tested on held-out material or against a more realistic generative control before treating it as a mechanism. Neither result supplies a key, plaintext, or explanation for missing adjacent doublets.

## Reproduce

From the repository root with Python 3.12 and the standard library:

```text
python experiments/records/word-internal-affine-all-lags/run.py --check
python experiments/records/word-internal-affine-all-lags/check.py
```

The first command reruns all 999 complete searches and compares the full [saved result](experiments/records/word-internal-affine-all-lags/results.json) and chart byte for byte. The second independently checks the word and pair counts, the earlier 77-match rule, the exact shuffle expectation on a small exhaustive example, and the saved tail arithmetic. Input hashes and exact bounds are in the plan and download bundle. The run reached its planned 999 trials; the score, range, and stopping rule were not changed after seeing the result.
records.reader_limit: Other word boundaries, earlier exploratory choices, and realistic encryption models were not tested. A shuffled word is only one reference for ordinary sequence structure.

records.article:
## Finding

The relation **c′ = 24 − 2c (mod 29)** appears **77 times in 1,267 eligible pairs**, compared with **44.8 expected** when runes are shuffled within each word. It ranks first among 841 affine maps at lag six; only **3 of 2,000 shuffles** reached 77 matches after choosing their best map.

## What six places apart means

The fourth word on [LP2-02, line 1](#/page/lp2-02?line=1) is `ᛒᛇᛚᛞᚻᛒᛗ`. Its alphabet indices are **17, 12, 20, 23, 8, 17, 19**. Compare positions **1 and 7**: six steps apart, with five runes between them.

The rule gives **24 − 2 × 17 = −10**. Adding 29 gives **19**, the seventh rune’s index. This calculation uses alphabet indices **0–28**; prime values aren’t used. This is one matching pair, not proof of a cipher. The full count is compared with shuffled words below.

![Observed lag-six count compared with fixed-map and best-of-841 word-shuffle means.](experiments/records/word-internal-affine-lags/comparison.svg)

This is a reproducible pattern in the archived transcription. It is **not a recovered encryption rule**. The formula and lag were supplied after exploration; the 841-map comparison does not account for trying other lags, word rules, page subsets, or formula families. The simple 1-in-29 reference would predict 43.7 matches, but it ignores each word's rune composition, so the within-word shuffle is the more relevant comparison here.

## What counts as a word

We split at printed hyphens and full stops, join text across slashes and line breaks, and never connect different pages. This follows the archived transcription's visible separators; it does not settle disputed breaks in the source images. Splitting at **every** non-rune character instead leaves 965 opportunities and 58 matches. That choice would incorrectly turn layout wraps into word breaks. The supplied figure of **80 against 45.7** was not reproduced under either explicit rule and may use a different page range or transcription. The report keeps the rules and exact inputs visible so a differing count can be traced.

At the same six-rune distance, **389 of 11,359** pairs *crossing* a word gap also satisfy the formula. Thus “zero across word gaps” is false if it means all lag-six pairs whose ends lie in different words. A more specific boundary test would need its own definition.

## What the comparison does and does not show

The formula's count is elevated relative to a fixed-map word shuffle, and it remains unusual against the **best of 841 maps at this one lag**. The report also records the same formula at lags 1–12 and counts on each page, so readers can check whether a few long words or pages dominate it. These are exploratory diagnostics; they do not establish that preventing doublets *causes* the lag-six relation. A causal proposal needs a fully specified generator that predicts both the missing adjacent repeats and the excess lag-six pairs, plus a held-out test.

For the adjacent-repeat baseline, see [equal rune pairs at lags one through five](#/experiments/doublet-lag-profile) and [doublet placement](#/experiments/doublet-placement). Those records measure different events and cannot by themselves confirm the proposed link.

## Reproduce

With Python 3.12 and no extra packages, from the repository root:

```text
python experiments/records/word-internal-affine-lags/run.py --check
python experiments/records/word-internal-affine-lags/check.py
```

The first command rebuilds every count, the 2,000 seeded shuffles, and the figure in memory, then compares them with the saved outputs. The second independently scans the transcription to verify the 77 internal and 389 crossing-gap matches. The [machine-readable result](experiments/records/word-internal-affine-lags/results.json) includes page counts, all lag counts, selection-control ranks, and input hashes.

records.article:
# What do the missing word repetitions constrain?

**Every selected ciphertext token is distinct:** 1,589 tokens when apostrophes are boundaries, or 1,591 when apostrophes are transparent. Allowing anagrams adds four pairs of four-rune tokens, but no pairs of five or more runes. These are constraints on particular word-local models, not a proof that every word-based cipher is impossible.

## Exactly which tokens are counted?

Read archived LP2-00–55 one page at a time, retaining headings. Slashes and CR/LF line wraps do not break a token. Other nonrune characters are boundaries. Run the analysis twice: once with apostrophes as boundaries, once with apostrophes ignored. No Latin expansion is used: TH and NG each count as one rune.

Drop the first and last nonempty token of each page before comparing. Those units may be fragments at page edges. This deliberately omits some complete words too; it avoids assuming that the printed page edges are word boundaries. Do not join pages. Keep only the remaining tokens containing at least four ciphertext runes.

| Apostrophe policy | Selected tokens | Distinct exact tokens | Equal pairs | Anagram pairs, length ≥4 | Anagram pairs, length ≥5 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Boundary | 1589 | 1589 | 0 | 4 | 0 |
| Transparent | 1591 | 1591 | 0 | 4 | 0 |

A pair means two distinct token occurrences, even if they are on the same page. A group of k equal signatures contributes k(k−1)/2 pairs. The ledger identifies every selected token, its original page-local token index and each rune's source offset, plus all collision groups.

## Model 1: a deterministic cipher reset for each word

Suppose each printed ciphertext token comes from one plaintext unit through the same deterministic function F, with identical key and reset context:

```text
ciphertext unit = F(plaintext unit)
```

Equal inputs to the same function produce equal outputs. Therefore, if two ciphertext units differ, their plaintext units cannot have been equal under that model. Since all selected ciphertext tokens differ, their corresponding plaintext units must differ wherever the same F applies.

The function may contain a complicated composition, deterministic padding, fractionation or hashing. None of that changes the equal-input implication. F need not be invertible, and plaintext length need not equal ciphertext length. The four-rune cutoff is a selection rule on the observed ciphertext only.

This does **not** prove the unknown plaintext repeats. It supplies a necessary condition for this model, rather than a general exclusion of deterministic word ciphers.

## Model 2: a shared symbol map plus word-local shuffling

A different proposal applies the same symbol map to every word, then independently rearranges each word's output. Identical plaintext words may now give different ordered ciphertext, but they must give the same multiset of ciphertext symbols: they must be anagrams.

For example, A B A mapped to 2 5 2 can be rearranged into 2 2 5 or 5 2 2. The order changes, but the two 2s and one 5 remain. This implication does not require an injective symbol map; each input rune only needs one fixed output rune.

There are no selected anagram pairs of length five or more. Thus no two such tokens can encode the same plaintext rune word under this shared-map-and-shuffle model. Among length-four-or-longer selected tokens, at most four occurrence pairs can represent repeated plaintext words. An anagram match is only necessary, not proof that a pair encodes the same word.

Unlike Model 1, this model preserves rune length. Padding, fractionation, or a different substitution for each word changes its assumptions.

## The four anagram pairs

Both apostrophe policies produce these same pairs. Spaces below separate rune labels; NG, EA, TH, OE and AE each denote one rune. Token indices are zero-based in the original per-page token list, before removing edge tokens.

| First occurrence | Second occurrence |
| --- | --- |
| [LP2-42](#/page/lp2-42), token 4: **F A NG E** | [LP2-53](#/page/lp2-53), token 16: **E F A NG** |
| [LP2-12](#/page/lp2-12), token 40: **EA TH W Y** | [LP2-46](#/page/lp2-46), token 59: **Y EA TH W** |
| [LP2-10](#/page/lp2-10), token 60: **S N OE X** | [LP2-12](#/page/lp2-12), token 33: **OE S N X** |
| [LP2-09](#/page/lp2-09), token 17: **J Y T AE** | [LP2-49](#/page/lp2-49), token 9: **T Y AE J** |

These are ciphertext comparisons, not proposed readings. The resemblance of a label sequence to a familiar word is not evidence of plaintext.

## What changing context does

An algorithm can be deterministic while its output depends on position, carried state, a different key, or a nonce. Those inputs belong to the effective context. If they differ, equal plaintext words need not give equal ciphertext. A Vigenère key continuing between words is not automatically a reset-per-word cipher.

Likewise, allowing a different symbol map for each word can destroy the anagram relationship. Two copies of A B A could map to 0 1 0 and 2 3 2; their multiplicity patterns agree, but their named-symbol multisets differ. This experiment does not test that more flexible model.

## Reproduce and independently check

Download and extract the experiment ZIP with folders intact. Python 3's standard library is enough; no packages, network requests or AI calls are required.

```text
python experiments/records/word-reset-repetition/run.py --check
python experiments/records/word-reset-repetition/check.py
```

The main script scans characters and groups sorted rune sequences. The independent checker reads page JSON, tokenizes with a regular expression, and compares 29-component count vectors. It verifies source positions and every collision group, and checks the anagram implication over 4,374 small mapping/permutation cases, including noninjective maps.

Both input formats share their archival source; this is not a second visual transcription audit. The supplied closure archive reports the same observations in C31 and C33. This record freshly reproduces them and explains the elementary implications. It does not rerun or claim verification of the archive's Lean project.

## Scope of the conclusion

The counting is exact for these token rules. No English frequency model, likelihood, p-value, or assumption that a particular word must appear is used. Changed boundaries, page-edge inclusion, a corrected transcription, different contexts, or a different output construction require an explicitly recorded retest. The word-length article uses a different boundary convention for a different purpose; its total should not be substituted for the counts here.

# How many words fit the selected magic-square totals?

The proposed phrase **PROVE WORTHIER FIND TRUTHS** fits the LP1 square values 131, 151, 151, 131. That arithmetic is already [checked word by word](#/experiments/selected-phrase-word-sums). It leaves a different question: how many *other* words would also fit those values if a solver searched a large list and chose a pleasing phrase afterward?

This control counts candidates in a [preserved revision of the Liber Primus Crib Assist word list](https://github.com/mortlach/Liber-Primus-Crib-Assist/tree/9c10cafce02e512840cc9e173127930594a56281/data/1_grams-full). The supplied discussion linked an older `data/1_grams` path and mentioned a separate `worddata.csv`. Those exact historical bytes are unavailable in the supplied transcript. This is therefore a **pinned-corpus control**, not a reconstruction of every historical search or its dictionary.

## What the census found

The sixteen preserved CSVs contain **138,466 distinct word rows**. Every stored GP total agrees with summing its stored rune values after accounting for one source-font difference: the corpus writes J as `ᛂ`, while this site's manuscript alphabet writes J as `ᛄ`; both carry value 37. The source glyph occurs in 2,217 rows. That mapping is declared in the plan, not silently normalized.

| Phrase slot | Target GP total | Stored rune length | Matching corpus words |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| PROVE | 131 | 5 | 38 |
| WORTHIER | 151 | 7 | 15 |
| FIND | 151 | 4 | 10 |
| TRUTHS | 131 | 5 | 38 |

All four proposed words occur in the preserved corpus. At the four fixed totals **and** rune lengths, there are **38 × 15 × 10 × 38 = 216,600 ordered word combinations**. If the first and fourth words must differ, there are **210,900**. These are combinations of dictionary entries, not 216,600 grammatical sentences. They have not been scored for meaning, syntax or relation to the manuscript.

If rune length is discarded, 105 corpus words have GP 131 and 133 have GP 151, giving 195,021,225 ordered combinations for the same four total slots. This illustrates why a claim must state its length constraint before a phrase is chosen. The corpus has only one row with GP 809, **DETECTABILITY** at 13 runes. The proposed **MYRMELEONTIDAE** is absent from this corpus; absence from a bounded word list is not evidence against that separately verified arithmetic assignment.

![Three histograms of corpus word counts by GP sum for four-, five-, and seven-rune words, highlighting the selected 131 and 151 totals.](experiments/records/word-sum-corpus-control/candidate-space.svg)

The graph shows GP totals 80–220 so the selected values remain legible. The downloadable result keeps the complete count distribution for every rune length and observed total. Neither the displayed interval nor the source frequency column is used to select candidate words.

## What was counted

The [plan](experiments/records/word-sum-corpus-control/plan.json) fixes the four word slots, totals and rune lengths. Each distinct CSV row counts once, including rows in the `2a1` and `3a1` files. The script checks the SHA-256 of all sixteen CSVs, the source manifest, its GPL-3.0 license and the manuscript alphabet before reading them. It validates every row's printed GP sum against the stored rune sequence. The opaque source count and flag columns are retained in the output but are not interpreted as independent evidence about language or author intent.

The ordered product lets any word fitting one slot combine with any word fitting the others. It does not test whether a coherent four-word sentence is common. Conversely, finding many alternatives does not prove the proposed phrase accidental. A sentence-level test would need a predeclared grammar or language score, the original vocabulary and all candidate phrases retained, plus matched square-value controls.

## Reproduce

From the repository root or the standalone experiment ZIP, run:

```sh
python experiments/records/word-sum-corpus-control/run.py --check
python experiments/records/word-sum-corpus-control/check.py
```

The runner checks the saved JSON and SVG byte for byte. The separate checker reads the preserved CSVs afresh, verifies each stored GP value and recomputes the target counts and products without importing the runner. Both use Python's standard library and require no network or AI model. The CSVs are redistributed unchanged with their source revision, per-file hashes, attribution and GPL-3.0 text in the experiment bundle.

## Limits and next test

This corpus is a surviving version of the linked tool's word data, not proven identical to the forum attachment called `worddata.csv`. It ends at 14 stored runes and its vocabulary is neither all English nor an unbiased sample of possible keys. The result measures **candidate freedom under one explicit list**. It does not reconstruct how the phrase was selected, apply a word to LP2, or judge any unsolved reading.

The next defensible variant is to recover the historical CSV or document that it is lost, then fix a phrase-generation and scoring procedure before seeing its winners. A separate cipher test must specify which selected word maps to which target, exactly how the word acts as a key, and what held-out output would count as success.

# Does the archived fractionation test reverse its own shuffle?

The archived proposal puts the 29 rune values in a keyword-mixed 6×5 grid. Each rune becomes a row and column number; the proposal then tries several ways to rearrange those numbers. We replayed its **14 keywords on six intended LP2 pages**. The historical page filenames were checked against the rune streams: source `page_38`, for example, is LP2-21, not LP2-38.

## The decisive control

Before looking for a reading, a reversal must be able to undo the matching forward shuffle. We planted a known rune message at each target length, each keyword and each of the seven column widths. The archived reversal restored **112 of 588** messages exactly. It failed the other **476**, because it allocates a full-height slice to short columns. A separately labeled inverse using the columns' actual lengths restored **all 588**. The correction is an implementation repair, not evidence that this is the manuscript cipher.

![The archived reversal restores 112 of 588 planted messages; the corrected inverse restores all 588.](experiments/records/wulfic-adfgvx-fractionation/reversal.svg)

## What the manuscript run found

The source names **1,260 settings**. Its own length rule skips **336** split settings, leaving **924 scored settings**. Two cross its vocabulary-score gate: `CABAL`, width 7 on LP2-28, and `CONSUMPTION`, width 19 on LP2-30. Both produce invalid grid cells (8 and 33 respectively). The score omits invalid cells when forming words, so these hits need inspection rather than a reading claim. The source's other gate, **raw IoC above 1.3, can never fire**: its IoC formula always returns a value between 0 and 1.

The separate corrected inverse has **588 settings** on the same pages, keys and widths. Two cross that same heuristic gate: `CARNAL`, width 29 on LP2-27, and `CABAL`, width 7 on LP2-28. They produce 15 and 8 invalid cells. The `CABAL` row is identical under both reversals at that particular stream length. No setting here provides a verified coherent page reading.

The direct route simply fractionates and defractionates each observed rune, returning the original cipher stream. It is a useful identity control, not a decipherment. Four named split points always produce too few pairs and are skipped by the source rule. The source also includes two running-key tests after this grid; those are different methods and are outside this record.

## Repeat the check

Download the experiment files and run `python experiments/records/wulfic-adfgvx-fractionation/run.py --check` to verify the saved outputs against the pinned page JSON. `python experiments/records/wulfic-adfgvx-fractionation/check.py --checkout PATH_TO_WULFIC_CLONE` additionally reads the pinned source commit, verifies all six historical page mappings, and independently checks all 1,512 scored route outputs and source scoring. Omit `--check` on the first command to regenerate the outputs. The source checkout must resolve commit `bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c`.

This bounds the specified keys, six pages, widths, split rules, and coordinate shifts. It does not test other transposition keys, coordinate encodings, null conventions, or a general fractionation cipher family. The source's vocabulary score and unnormalized IoC are exploratory filters; neither is a calibrated probability of a correct decryption.

# Four source texts as running keys

An archived [cipher program](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/legacy/advanced_cipher_solver.py) treats **Liber AL**, an authored collection of solved Liber Primus text, Emerson's *Self-Reliance*, and *Deor* as possible running keys. It samples locations in each text, picks the direction and offset with the highest whole-page coincidence, then scores that one output. We replayed this complete source branch on its **18 named pages**.

**Finding:** the best retained output was LP2-08 with Liber AL at offset 2,688. It received source rank score **117.9**. **41 of 49** complete searches over within-page rune-order shuffles scored at least that high. No output is an established reading. The shuffles are a selection reference, not a model of a cipher.

![Four of four full known readings were found at a sampled key offset, none at the tested unsampled offset; the LP2 source score is below the middle shuffled-search score.](experiments/records/wulfic-advanced-running-keys/comparison.svg)

The control is crucial here. We encrypted the unchanged **209-rune First Koan reading** with each of the four texts at offset **300**. The source selector recovered the entire message, correct direction and offset **four times in four trials**. A complete 18-page, four-key synthetic search also ranked its planted reading first. But when the same reading started at offset **137**, between the source's 100-step sampling points, the selector missed it for **all four texts**. These eight plants and the full-grid control were written before the manuscript scores. Thus this replay tests the source's *sampling-and-selection rule*, not every location in the texts.

For each page and text, the program tries offsets `0, 100, 200…` in subtraction, addition and Beaufort directions. It keeps the one with highest normalized `29 × IoC`; only then does it search offsets within 100 places of that winner, in the selected direction. This yields **one retained candidate per page/text pair, 72 in all**. The final score counts English substrings in run-together GP labels and whole words at the page's visible rune separators, then adds `50 × IoC`. It is a rough ranking heuristic, not evidence that an English message has appeared.

The 18 pinned source page streams match the current **LP2-04–17, 26–27, 32 and 37** rune arrays exactly. All four source key streams have distinct byte digests, and the 72 retained decoded outputs are distinct. The authored solved-LP key is the script's own English text, not the independently audited solved rune readings. Existing [Deor/Emerson](#/experiments/wulfic-p21-running-key-layers), [Liber AL](#/experiments/wulfic-liber-al-offset-sweep) and [audited-reading](#/experiments/solved-reading-running-key) records use different programs or key representations; this is one grouped replay of the remaining source branch, not four newly invented cipher ideas.

The [plan](experiments/records/wulfic-advanced-running-keys/plan.json) fixes corpus bytes, page mapping, source offset selection, both planted positions and 49 complete shuffled searches. The [results](experiments/records/wulfic-advanced-running-keys/results.json) retain all 72 source winners and each shuffle's best score; the [control results](experiments/records/wulfic-advanced-running-keys/control-results.json) were produced first. From a full checkout or experiment bundle, provide a separate Git checkout containing the pinned Wulfic revision:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-advanced-running-keys/run.py --source-root PATH_TO_PINNED_WULFIC_CHECKOUT --check
python experiments/records/wulfic-advanced-running-keys/check.py --source-root PATH_TO_PINNED_WULFIC_CHECKOUT
python experiments/records/wulfic-advanced-running-keys/plot.py --check
```

The original source has no declared license in that checkout, and the three external texts remain in its repository rather than this experiment bundle. The runner checks their Git-blob hashes and executes the original source conversion, decryption and scoring functions. The independent checker reconstructs the key conversion, adaptive offset search, source score, all controls and all 49 complete shuffles without importing that program.
records.reader_finding: This program found no established reading using its four proposed key texts. Its best manuscript score was matched or beaten by 41 of 49 shuffled searches. More importantly, it missed the same known message for all four texts when that message began between its sampled offsets.
records.reader_limit: The search samples every hundredth text position, then refines around only one selected candidate. These results do not rule out the key texts at other offsets or under different selection rules.

records.title: Short seeds for autokey ciphers
records.question: Do the pinned source keyword, two-rune, or three-rune autokey seeds pass their one-rune and IoC screens on the selected LP2 pages?
records.summary: Four related archived search branches were replayed on verified LP2 page streams. None passed the source-defined hit screen; the gate and ciphertext-feedback design sharply limit what that result can exclude.

record_type.label: Method replay
record_type.description: Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading.

scope.representation: Pinned archived source GP29 page values verified against current LP2-04–37 text; source pages old21–54 map to LP2-(old−17). Source isolated-word positions retained.
scope.procedure: Replay six GP29 plaintext/ciphertext feedback recurrences for 22 source keyword seeds, every two-rune seed, every three-rune seed on source-eligible pages, and the one distinct four-rune P21–30 DEOR array. Preserve source gates, strict IoC threshold and page resets; compare 49 full-search shuffles.
scope.parameters: 4,488 named-keyword, 171,564 two-rune, 4,536,354 three-rune, and 60 distinct P21–30 DEOR settings; 49 within-page shuffled complete searches, seed 20261023.
scope.exclusions: Other seeds or lengths, alternate alphabets, word resets and segmentations, different singleton assumptions, English scoring, the P21–30 running-key/double-layer branches, and manuscript-derived numerical autokey rules without an exact recurrence.

records.finding: Across the four source branches, zero manuscript outputs passed their strict IoC > 1.3 hit threshold. The 4,488 named-keyword settings had 135 one-rune-compatible cases; 171,564 two-rune settings had 5,058; 4,536,354 three-rune settings had none on 31 source-eligible pages. The distinct four-rune DEOR vector gave zero hits among 60 IoC-only settings. A planted reading-like control passed in all six feedback modes.
records.limitations: The source requires visible one-rune words to decode to I or A, which assumes this word segmentation and language. Ciphertext-feedback seeds alter only their own short output prefix, so the whole-page screen cannot reliably identify those seeds. Forty-nine full-search shuffles are coarse controls, not a cipher model. Other seed lengths, pages, boundaries and autokey rules remain untested.
records.article:
# Autokey seeds from an archived search

**Result.** Four related source searches found no output that passed their stated hit screen. This is a result for those seeds, pages, six feedback rules, and the source's one-rune and frequency checks. It does not rule out autokey on Liber Primus.

![Four source search branches and their hit counts](experiments/records/wulfic-autokey-seed-families/screen.svg)

| Source branch | Settings | Passed its one-rune check | IoC above 1.3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 22 named keyword seeds | 4,488 | 135 | 0 |
| Every two-rune seed | 171,564 | 5,058 | 0 |
| Every three-rune seed | 4,536,354 | 0 | 0 |
| A distinct four-rune DEOR seed | 60 | Not required | 0 |

The first three branches come from an [archived comprehensive autokey script](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/legacy/autokey_comprehensive.py). It tries plaintext and ciphertext feedback, each with subtraction, addition, and Beaufort arithmetic modulo 29. Each page restarts its seed. For the named, two-rune, and three-rune branches, **every isolated one-rune word** must decrypt to I or A before the output's normalized index of coincidence (IoC) is considered. The fourth row is the one [P21–30 source variant](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/legacy/p21_30_autokey_solver.py) with a different DEOR seed; its screen uses IoC alone.

These are four **search branches**, not millions of independent solving ideas. The 34 archived source pages numbered 21–54 correspond to LP2-04–37 in this site. The comprehensive script skips pages with fewer than three isolated one-rune words for its three-rune seed search, leaving 31 pages. The P21–30 variant covers ten pages. Seventeen of its other keyword arrays duplicate the comprehensive branch on those pages, so they were not counted again here.

## What the controls show

A constructed 261-rune passage, derived from an independently recorded solved reading, passed the source's screen after we encrypted it under each of the six feedback rules. Two- and three-rune planted seeds were also recovered by their complete searches. The detector can therefore find a deliberately planted, reading-like example with its declared assumptions.

For the manuscript, we repeated each **whole branch**, including its seed search, on 49 within-page rune shuffles. The best named-keyword IoC (1.121) was equaled or exceeded by 44 controls; the two-rune best (1.177) by 24; the four-rune DEOR best (1.064) by 42. The three-rune branch had no candidate past its one-rune gate, so a best-IoC comparison is not informative. These controls preserve page lengths and rune counts; they are a search comparison, not a model of how the manuscript was encrypted.

There is a further limit to this screen. With **ciphertext feedback**, the decoded runes after the seed-length prefix depend only on ciphertext and the selected rule. Changing the seed changes just that short prefix. On a long page, the whole-page IoC and one-rune positions beyond it therefore cannot identify a ciphertext-feedback seed. The planted test verifies this: a wrong seed still passes those ciphertext-feedback screens.

The one-rune I/A requirement is also a hypothesis about the visible word breaks. A seed eliminated by that condition may still be relevant under another segmentation or language. No branch produced an established reading, and the source's zero-hit result is not evidence against every autokey design. A more discriminating follow-up would specify an independent predicted passage or another feature that changes with the seed.

## Reproduce and inspect

The [frozen plan](experiments/records/wulfic-autokey-seed-families/plan.json) states the page mapping, six recurrences, gates, controls, and exclusions before the manuscript results. [Full results](experiments/records/wulfic-autokey-seed-families/results.json) include every page's counts and each complete-search control. Run `python experiments/records/wulfic-autokey-seed-families/check.py` for an independent scalar check, or `python experiments/records/wulfic-autokey-seed-families/run.py --check` to repeat the full grid. [Source parity checks](experiments/records/wulfic-autokey-seed-families/source_parity.py) additionally require a checkout of the pinned upstream commit.

records.question: Do 25 archived number or byte sources recover LP2 under the pinned phase-averaged stay/advance/skip key detector?
records.summary: Exact accelerated replay of the pinned Stage R source grid finds no candidate above its declared +30 line; all planted controls pass.

record_type.label: Method replay
record_type.description: Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading.

scope.representation: Source GP29 rune transcript in sections 7–15 and their continuous join, covering unsolved LP2-00–55; section labels are not manuscript page numbers.
scope.procedure: Read 25 pinned number/byte sources into modulo-29 and rejection-mapped key streams. For each of 50 keys and ten section alignments, score three arithmetic modes and all 29 shifts with the pinned phase-averaged stay/advance/skip HMM. Replay 200 planted positive/negative pairs with exact seed. Compare all serialized rows against the pinned Stage R tables.

The highest score, +2.41, is on the nine-rune title; its absolute score ceiling is only +11.19, so its 4,350 settings could never pass. This screen uses only the source's 25 inputs, two GP29 mappings, ten transcript alignments, three arithmetic modes, 29 shifts, solved-LP1 unigram model, drift probabilities and uniform start-phase prior. records.article:
# Can archived Cicada numbers and byte streams serve as LP2 keys?

**Finding.** In this exact Stage R search, none of the 43,500 source settings reached the declared +30 detection score. The strongest LP2 score was **+2.41** on a nine-rune title section, but that section is **too short to reach +30 with this scorer under any key**. Among the other sections, the best was **−50.75**; the complete joined stream peaked at **−1,479.67**. All 200 planted positive controls exceeded +30 and all 200 wrong-key controls stayed below it. This is a result about the specified detector and inputs, not a claim that these sources cannot be used in another construction.

![Three detection-score extrema against the source pass line.](experiments/records/wulfic-cicada-byte-key-phases/comparison.svg)

The figure shows the lowest positive-control score, the highest LP2 score, and the highest negative-control score. Each point is an extremum of a different group, not one representative trial. The LP2 maximum comes from the title section, whose score ceiling is below the pass line.

## What was tested

The [pinned Stage R program](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/run_stage_r.py) collected 25 numerical or byte sources connected to earlier Cicada material. They include the published prime product and RSA modulus as decimal digits, cookie values, a source hash, two hex strings, a hint, and several archived byte files. A file name such as `page_17.bin` is the archive's label for a candidate key file; it is not itself proof of a Liber Primus page number or of an authenticated hidden payload.

Each source became two GP29 key streams: values reduced modulo 29, and values above the largest divisible range rejected before reduction. For each of those 50 streams, the test tried three arithmetic modes (`sub`, `add`, `beaufort`) and all 29 shifts against nine source sections separately and their continuous join. This gives **50 × 3 × 29 × 10 = 43,500** settings. Source section labels 7–15 refer to that program's transcript divisions; they are not manuscript page numbers. Together they cover the unsolved LP2 text through page 55, with some section boundaries inside pages.

The scorer allows the key stream to stay, advance once, or advance twice between runes, with probabilities 0.02, 0.96 and 0.02. It averages over **every** possible cyclic starting phase instead of choosing the most flattering one. It compares decoded-rune frequencies with those of the solved LP1 text and reports a log likelihood ratio; **+30** was the source's fixed pass line.

The nine-rune title accounts for **4,350** of the 43,500 settings. Its largest possible per-rune emission ratio is 3.467, so even a perfect path cannot exceed **9 × ln(3.467) = 11.19 nats**. The +30 line is mathematically unreachable there. The longer sections can reach the line in principle, though the planted controls test detection power only at 729 and 3,316 runes. Neither kind of evidence makes all 43,500 settings equally informative.

## What makes the screen interpretable

The source first encrypted solved LP1 text with each key under its own stay/advance/skip model, then measured the correct key and an independent wrong key. It used two lengths (729 and 3,316 runes) and two anti-doublet rekey settings. That produced 200 positive–negative pairs. The weakest correct-key score was **+169.09**; the strongest wrong-key score was **−60.86**. The positive controls show that this detector can recover keys generated by its own model at the tested lengths. They do not establish equal power against every possible real encryption scheme.

Our separately written compiled forward-sum implementation agreed with the pinned original scorer on 108 real cells spanning short and long source keys, short and joined LP2 sections, all three modes, and multiple shifts (largest absolute difference **2.27 × 10⁻¹² nats**). Synthetic equal-mass and skewed-emission cases check ties and pruning. It preserved the source control generator and random seed. The replay then checked every rounded candidate and control row against the two original source tables. These checks verify the computation; they do not establish that any candidate source was the actual LP2 key.

## Read or rerun the data

- [Full source candidate table](experiments/records/wulfic-cicada-byte-key-phases/source-stage_r_candidates.tsv) — one row per setting.
- [Source control table](experiments/records/wulfic-cicada-byte-key-phases/source-stage_r_controls.tsv) — 200 positive–negative pairs.
- [Packaged numeric inputs](experiments/records/wulfic-cicada-byte-key-phases/source-profile.npz) — the exact 50 key streams, section runes, and emission ratios used by the checker.
- [Result summary](experiments/records/wulfic-cicada-byte-key-phases/results.json) and [declared plan](experiments/records/wulfic-cicada-byte-key-phases/plan.json).

Run `python experiments/records/wulfic-cicada-byte-key-phases/check.py` to verify full-table hashes, controls and a spread of independently computed cells. Add `--full` to recompute all 43,500 LP2 scores from the packaged numeric inputs. To repeat source construction and planted controls from the pinned checkout, use `replay.py --source PATH --workers 4 --output PATH`; it writes only to the given output directory. The compiled scorer needs NumPy and Numba. `plot.py --check` verifies the figure against the result summary.

This screen does not test other starting distributions, source preprocessing, key schedules, language models, interruption probabilities, or later cipher layers. A proposal using one of these sources with a different specific rule remains a separate test.

records.title: Can a guessed word seed a short feedback key?
records.question: Does a source-defined crib-derived GF(29) linear recurrence predict a language-like 128-rune continuation on 11 named unsolved LP2 pages when the key phase and J-rune parsing are corrected?
records.summary: The corrected crib rule produced 13 two-rune-validated candidate fits, but its best 128-rune continuation scored 18; 126 of 199 complete shuffled searches did at least as well. A separate post-result known-reading plant ranked first across a mixed 11-page search in all 12 mode/order cases, showing this exact screen can detect a clean positive.

record_type.label: Method replay
record_type.description: Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading.

scope.representation: Pinned source page-number mapping separately preserves the source's J-dropping rune sequence on 11 LP2 pages plus solved LP1-15. Corrected scan uses canonical GP29 site arrays for the 11 LP2 pages; each source array equals its canonical counterpart with J removed.
scope.procedure: Replay the source's original crib-drag Berlekamp-Massey and IoC gate. Separately fit the first m-2 key symbols from each selected source crib, verify the last two, predict the next 128 runes and score only that continuation; rerun the complete page/crib/mode/offset selection on 199 shared seeded page shuffles.
scope.parameters: Original 21 source cribs length>=4, 3 directions and 12 mapped pages; corrected 13 source cribs length>=6, 3 directions, recurrence order 2–5, all offsets leaving 128 runes, 11 LP2 pages; 199 shuffle trials seed 20261023.
scope.exclusions: Other LP2 pages, other cribs, order>5, non-GP alphabets, key skips/resets, unrelated recurrence laws, a trained language model, and proof of full decryption.

records.finding: The pinned source's original 21-crib normalized-IoC-gated branch produced zero candidates on 174,141 placements across 11 LP2 pages and solved LP1-15. After preserving all canonical J runes and aligning the key to each crib, a 13-crib, three-direction, order-2–5 screen found 13 candidate fits across 52,527 placements on the 11 LP2 pages; additive and subtractive sign forms can represent the same decoded text. The best continuation score was 18 on LP2-05; 126/199 shared whole-search shuffled controls scored at least 18. On an unchanged decoded 226-rune LP1-14 passage containing the source crib CIRCUMFERENCE, all 12 planted mode/order cases recovered the next 128 runes exactly and ranked first at score 119 across a mixed grid with ten unchanged LP2 pages. That post-target grid replaces the original 273-rune first target, so the original 199 shuffle maxima are not calibrated to it.
records.limitations: The original source gate scores a page containing its own guessed crib and uses a rune parser that drops J. The corrected search still covers only 13 words, feedback lengths 2–5, three arithmetic directions, 11 pages and one approximate GP bigram/trigram score. The page-frequency shuffle is not a cipher generator. The post-result positive is one known 226-rune reading under a clean page-local clock, shorter than the replaced 273-rune LP2 page, and cannot prove power against every LP2 plaintext. No LFSR family or alternate key clock is excluded.

# Can a guessed word reveal a repeating feedback rule?

**Result:** Correcting two problems in a [public crib-and-LFSR program](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/legacy/lfsr_alberti_solver.py) did not produce a strong continuation on the 11 LP2 pages that program named. The best score was **18** on LP2-05; **126 of 199** shuffled-page searches scored at least as high. A separate known-reading plant scored **119** and ranked first across an 11-page mixed grid, showing that this exact search can find a clean example of the proposed rule. It does not exclude other LFSR constructions.

![On a planted message, only the corrected rune reader and aligned key recover all 128 following runes. The best LP2 score is below the middle of the shuffled-search results.](experiments/records/wulfic-crib-lfsr-recurrence/result.svg)

The idea is concrete: suppose a word such as **EMERGE** appears somewhere in the ciphertext. Under an additive cipher, that guess reveals a short piece of the key. A linear feedback rule might then continue the key. We tried every placement of **13 source words**, three arithmetic directions and feedback lengths **2–5** on the source's **11 unsolved LP2 pages**. We learned a rule from the first part of each guessed word, required it to predict the last two key values under that word, then decrypted and scored **128 runes after the word**. Those 128 runes, not the guessed word, determine the score. Across **52,527 placements**, 13 candidate fits passed the two-rune recurrence check. They are not 13 distinct key rules: the additive and subtractive directions can represent the same decoded text with negated keys. The highest score came from an EMERGE guess at LP2-05 rune 62 in the Beaufort direction.

The original program's separate scan used **21 shorter-or-longer cribs** on 12 archived page files, including the solved LP1-15, and reported candidates only when its **29× normalized whole-page index of coincidence** exceeded 1.4 (a uniform-rune reference is about 1). We replayed **174,141 placements** and reproduced its **zero gated candidates**; the unchanged source function agreed on all 12 page counts. That zero is a fact about that program, not a sound exclusion of the proposed cipher. Its rune reader drops the manuscript's J glyph (`ᛄ`) because it expects a different glyph (`ᛂ`), losing **1–13 runes per page**. It also starts a key inferred at a later crib as if the crib were at page position zero. A known planted message isolates the errors: the source reader and source key position recovered only **6 of 128** following runes; fixing both recovered **128 of 128**. Twelve more planted cases recovered the full continuation for every arithmetic direction at feedback lengths 2 and 3; twelve additional endpoint plants did so at lengths 4 and 5.

The comparison shuffled each LP2 page's rune order once per trial and repeated the **entire page, word, direction and position search** with the same 199 trial seeds. Its median best score was **19**, and its highest was **40**. Page shuffling preserves rune totals but not the manuscript's word structure, so this is a conditional search control rather than a cipher simulation. The result does not rule out another word, longer feedback, a different key start, interruptions, a better language model or a full-page plaintext revealed by other evidence.

**Power check, added after the LP2 result:** The existing decoded rune text of LP1-14 contains **CIRCUMFERENCE**, one of the 13 original source words, at rune 52 with at least 128 known runes after it. We encrypted that **unchanged 226-rune reading** with planted page-local keys for all three directions and lengths 2–5. Every planted case recovered the next 128 runes exactly. On the planted page alone, the real candidate scored **119** and ranked first in all 12 searches (sharing first with an equivalent sign-form candidate in eight, not a competing plaintext). No F runes were inserted or replaced. The separate [power plan](experiments/records/wulfic-crib-lfsr-recurrence/power-plan.json) and [single-page results](experiments/records/wulfic-crib-lfsr-recurrence/power-results.json) preserve that first check.

**Full-grid power amendment, also after the LP2 result:** We replaced the first of the 11 tested page slots (LP2-11, **273 runes**) with the 226-rune known-message plant, leaving the other ten LP2 pages and the entire crib, direction and position search unchanged. Across **50,694** examined placements per planted arm, the true candidate still ranked first in all 12 mixed-grid searches. The ten unchanged pages contributed 13 eligible recurrences and a best score of 18, so none outranked or tied the planted score of 119. The [mixed-grid plan](experiments/records/wulfic-crib-lfsr-recurrence/power-grid-plan.json) was added after the single-page power review; [results](experiments/records/wulfic-crib-lfsr-recurrence/power-grid-results.json) give each arm's rank and ties. This shows detection power for a clean 226-rune known reading in a grid containing ten actual LP2 pages. Because the replaced page is shorter, the **199 original LP2 shuffles are not a calibrated null for this mixed grid**; their maximum of 40 is only background context. This check cannot establish the unknown LP2 plaintext style or exclude other feedback rules.

The [original plan](experiments/records/wulfic-crib-lfsr-recurrence/plan.json) and [indexed inputs](experiments/records/wulfic-crib-lfsr-recurrence/inputs.json) preserve both the source's rune readings and the site's corrected readings separately. Run `python experiments/records/wulfic-crib-lfsr-recurrence/extended_controls.py --check` for the feedback-length endpoint plants, then `python experiments/records/wulfic-crib-lfsr-recurrence/check.py` for an independent check of all page findings and ten fixed null trials. Add `--full` to the latter command to repeat all 199 null trials. Run `python experiments/records/wulfic-crib-lfsr-recurrence/power_check.py` for an independent check of the known-reading plant and its source text, then `python experiments/records/wulfic-crib-lfsr-recurrence/power_grid_check.py` for an independent full-grid check. The saved [LP2 result data](experiments/records/wulfic-crib-lfsr-recurrence/results.json) includes all control maxima and the best 128-rune continuations.
records.reader_finding: The best continuation from the guessed words scored no better than many shuffled pages: 126 of 199 shuffled searches matched or exceeded it. A separate planted known reading was recovered correctly.
records.reader_limit: This covers 13 fixed words and short feedback rules on 11 pages. Other words, key clocks and feedback rules remain untested.

records.article:
# Can one rune stream unlock another?

An [archived test](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/legacy/p20_interlocking.py) divides one LP2 page by each rune’s zero-based alphabet index. Indices **2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19 and 23** go into one stream; all others go into another. These are alphabet positions, not Gematria Primus prime values. It tries a passage from the Old English poem *Deor* as a key for the first stream, then reuses its best output as a repeating key for the second.

**The original script cannot report a hit.** Its coincidence score is between 0 and 1, but its two hit checks require scores above **1.3** and **1.5**. We reproduced its exact output, including zero hits. That zero says nothing about whether the idea works; the gates are unreachable for *any* input.

![The source splits 217 runes into two streams; its original score gates are impossible, while a separate normalized comparison finds no distinctive final-stage score.](experiments/records/wulfic-deor-interlocking-streams/comparison.svg)

## What a corrected comparison shows

We separately multiplied the same coincidence score by 29, a conventional normalization that makes a threshold such as 1.3 possible. We kept the source's key directions, offsets and choice of the best first-stream result. The second-stream maximum is **1.17**. In **110 of 199** seeded shuffles of the page, the *whole two-stage search* reached at least that score. The amended 1.3 screen found no second-stream candidate here. The selected first-stream score, **1.88**, was reached by 18 of 199 shuffles. The first-stage peak alone does not turn into a distinctive final-stage result.

The shuffles preserve the page's rune counts and redo both stages, including the adaptive choice of first key. They show how this exact search behaves under a simple control; they are not an encryption model or a proof that every interlocking cipher fails.

## Exact bounds and reproduction

The source's “page 20” is **current LP2-03**: its 217 rune values match the archived input. It yields 65 prime-index and 152 other runes. The source tries three directions at 600 *Deor* offsets, then three directions at 65 repeat-key offsets. Only the Old English section of the pinned poem is parsed, producing 960 rune values. The separate Caesar-shift check cannot change coincidence score, so all 29 shifts tie on that measure.

Our [pinned plan](experiments/records/wulfic-deor-interlocking-streams/plan.json) and [saved results](experiments/records/wulfic-deor-interlocking-streams/results.json) preserve the source calculation and label the normalized comparison as a later diagnostic. An [input-parser amendment](experiments/records/wulfic-deor-interlocking-streams/input-parser-amendment.json) records that an initial exploratory run mistakenly included the poem's modern translation; the published diagnostic uses the source's 960-value stream. The original source output is saved as a short [trace](experiments/records/wulfic-deor-interlocking-streams/source-run.txt), and `python experiments/records/wulfic-deor-interlocking-streams/check.py` repeats the independent computation and controls. The pinned external checkout can be used with [the source replay wrapper](experiments/records/wulfic-deor-interlocking-streams/replay_source.py).

This is one page, one poem, a value-based split and a fixed repeating-key rule. It does not test other partitions, poems, word boundaries, feedback rules or language-based readings.

# What separates LP2’s surviving doublets?

**Finding.** Wulfic's pinned H/O tests find no source-defined concentration of the **86 surviving adjacent equal-rune pairs** by other difference value, written-line break, short period or marked section. Two named key-switch constructions make too few repeats on solved text. A specific “skip to the next key value” model disagrees with LP2's nonzero differences. None of these checks identifies the encryption method.

The blue marks show where each surviving repeat occurs in nine manuscript sections, labeled by the feature used to recognize each part of the book. A section with more runes has a longer bar. The very short number-square section has no repeat; the others do not show a single concentrated pocket.

![Eighty-six equal-rune pairs marked along nine proportional manuscript sections.](experiments/records/wulfic-doublet-leak-h-o/distribution.svg)

Line endings were one proposed place for a special rule. Here, their repeat rate is nearly the same as elsewhere and well below that rule's 2.5% decision line.

![Repeat rates within written lines and across line breaks, with the proposed line-end threshold.](experiments/records/wulfic-doublet-leak-h-o/line-breaks.svg)

The count here is **86 / 12,947 adjacent pairs**. The source joins pages *within* each of nine marked manuscript sections and never compares across a section boundary. Liberpedia's page-only doublet records use **86 / 12,901** instead. The source's **48 page-break pairs** are part of its line-break category; they should not be added again as separate opportunities. Our independent extractor reproduces every one of the source's 12,947 pair records from the site page text and its written-line markers.

| Source check | Result and decision line | What that establishes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **H1 · Where did missing repeats go?** | Largest departure among 28 nonzero difference bins: **z = −2.58** at residue 17; source line is absolute z of 3.5 | No single nonzero residue shows the source's proposed compensating nudge. |
| **H2 · A rule at line ends?** | **82/12,362** within lines, **4/585** across written-line breaks, **0/48** across page breaks; source line-end rule requires at least 2.5% | The line-break rate, about 0.68%, does not rise to that rule. |
| **H3 · A repeating phase?** | Best of periods 2–32 under two position clocks: **p = 0.0355** at period 27, joined clock; corrected line **0.000161** | No period passes the declared 62-way selection threshold. |
| **H4 · Section clusters?** | Nine-section χ² **5.33** on 8 df, **p = 0.721**; 500-pair window dispersion **1.022**, inside the source's 0.5–2 band | Surviving pairs are not unusually uneven by either specified summary. |
| **H5 · Two-key collision switch?** | On 2,901 solved runes, DIVINITY/CIRCUMFERENCES gives **6/2,900** repeats under the ideal rule and **10/2,898** under the literal code; φ(primes)/primes gives zero under both | Those two named switch constructions, transferred to this solved text, produce too few repeats to match LP2's source rate. |
| **O · Skip-next-key rule?** | LP2's specified 28-bin difference log-likelihood ratio is **−21.34 nats**, below the source's **−10** exclusion line | The stated model, with a 19% key-repeat parameter and solved-text difference distribution, fails its own prediction. |

The source's **16 relevant assertions pass**, including planted controls for the H patterns and three skip-next versus fresh-rekey simulations. The O result also stays below its line when its plaintext-difference distribution is estimated from either of two disjoint solved-text subsets. These controls support the *specific* tests, not every way a cipher might suppress repeated runes. H5's “literal” implementation can leave positions unset; its eligible-pair denominator is therefore smaller and is reported separately.

## Reproduce and limits

The [plan](experiments/records/wulfic-doublet-leak-h-o/plan.json) fixes all source rules and thresholds. [Inputs](experiments/records/wulfic-doublet-leak-h-o/inputs.json) preserve the pair ledger and solved-text control stream; [results](experiments/records/wulfic-doublet-leak-h-o/results.json) contain all 62 period/clock rows and numerical summaries. An independent standard-library checker re-extracts source-defined pairs from the archived page text, recalculates every row, regenerates the two named key-switch streams, and recomputes the skip-next score:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-doublet-leak-h-o/check.py
python experiments/records/wulfic-doublet-leak-h-o/plot.py --check
```

For a complete unchanged-source run, use [Wulfic's checkout at the pinned revision](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/tree/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c):

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-doublet-leak-h-o/replay_source.py --source PATH_TO_CHECKOUT
```

The relevant source is [`tests/test_leak.py`](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tests/test_leak.py) and [`tools/lpcore/leak.py`](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/lpcore/leak.py). The model assumptions matter: H5 tests only two specified key pairs, on solved text rather than unknown LP2 plaintext; O assumes its fixed 19% repeat rate and solved-text difference profile. The period correction covers the declared 62 phase scans, not all earlier ideas considered about doublets. Other transcriptions, boundary rules and multi-layer ciphers remain outside this result.

records.question: Do Wulfic's specified running-key, small-key, ciphertext-autokey and selected-alphabet diagnostics find their expected LP2 signal?
records.summary: Pinned J/K/L source controls pass; two pooled unigram models fail their source line and two within-section lag searches find no corrected detection.

record_type.label: Method replay
record_type.description: Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading.

scope.representation: Source GP29 canonical rune values in nine segments 7–15 over LP2-00–55; 12,956 positions, checked against all site page raw texts.
scope.procedure: Run unchanged pinned test_keyspace.py (13 assertions with synthetic controls); retain its exact C10–C13 manuscript score grids and model inputs; independently recalculate every score and compare source/site runes.

records.finding: All thirteen pinned test assertions pass. The strongest C10 and C13 pooled frequency LLRs are −14.38 and −14.27, below the source's −10 line.
