# Four early keyspace checks on LP2

**Finding.** The pinned Wulfic source tests pass, but none of their four specified models identifies a reading. Two frequency models disagree with LP2 under their fixed −10-nat rule. Two lag scans find no value past their multiple-test thresholds. These are checks of particular statistical predictions, not a search of all possible keys.

![Four distinct Wulfic keyspace checks and their nearest results against source decision lines.](experiments/records/wulfic-early-keyspace-diagnostics/comparison.svg)

| Source claim | What is actually measured | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **C10 · English-like running key** | Pooled rune frequencies for three key-value mappings, three arithmetic directions, three mixtures of solved-text and uniform key letters, and 29 offsets | Best log-likelihood ratio **−14.38**, below the source's −10 exclusion line |
| **C13 · small key alphabets** | Pooled frequencies for uniformly chosen decimal digits, hex digits, Latin A–Z, or source English letter weights; three directions and 29 offsets | Best ratio **−14.27**, below −10 |
| **C11 · ciphertext autokey** | A 29-bin combination of ciphertext runes separated by each lag 2–1000, both signs, within the source's nine sections | Smallest unadjusted **p = 0.000559** at lag 880; above the corrected **0.00000501** pass line |
| **C12 · ciphertext-selected alphabet** | Off-diagonal rune transitions at each lag 1–1000, within those sections | Smallest approximate **p = 0.003916** at lag 142; above **0.00001** |

The source's thirteen test assertions all pass, including synthetic encryptions that the four diagnostics detect and a random-stream calibration for C12. An independent checker recalculates **all 27 C10, 1,998 C11, 1,000 C12 and four C13 manuscript rows** from the preserved numerical inputs. It also confirms that the source's 12,956 GP29 rune values are exactly the sequence in Liberpedia's LP2-00–55 page records.

## What the findings mean

The C10 and C13 scores compare *one-rune frequencies* with a model based on solved LP1 text. They depend on the assumed independence of plaintext and key values and the stated key-letter distributions. They do not test every English passage as a running key. C13's wider base-60, two-digit and byte alphabets have too little predicted signal for this same frequency check; the source explicitly marks them **untestable by this criterion**, not excluded.

C11 tests the frequency pattern expected from a particular additive ciphertext-feedback relation. C12 tests a distinct transition pattern expected when a prior ciphertext rune selects one of 29 substitution alphabets. Neither test tries to decrypt LP2 or excludes arbitrary feedback or alphabet-selection rules. Their smallest raw p-values must be compared with the source's thresholds across the full lag search, not read as individual discoveries. The later [AC/AD lag study](#/experiments/wulfic-lag-reuse-models) tests different pair laws and stretch scores; it does not replace these source checks.

## Reproduce

The [plan](experiments/records/wulfic-early-keyspace-diagnostics/plan.json) fixes the model grid and decision lines. [Inputs](experiments/records/wulfic-early-keyspace-diagnostics/inputs.json) preserve the source-derived rune stream, section boundaries and solved-text model; [results](experiments/records/wulfic-early-keyspace-diagnostics/results.json) include every manuscript statistic. Run the independent calculation with:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-early-keyspace-diagnostics/check.py
python experiments/records/wulfic-early-keyspace-diagnostics/plot.py --check
```

To rerun the **unchanged pinned source tests** and rebuild the data bundle, use a checkout of [Wulfic's repository at this revision](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/tree/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c):

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-early-keyspace-diagnostics/replay_source.py --source PATH_TO_CHECKOUT
```

The source test is [`tests/test_keyspace.py`](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tests/test_keyspace.py). The model arithmetic is in [`tools/lpcore/stats.py`](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/lpcore/stats.py). The replay uses the source's nine section boundaries; those are not individual page resets. Other transcriptions, plaintext priors, nonadditive rules and later cipher layers are outside these tests.

records.question: Do the printed number-grid bytes form a complete raw DEFLATE, zlib, gzip, bzip2 or LZMA stream in any of four fixed routes?
records.summary: Exact Wulfic Stage X4 component replay and an independent checker find no end-of-stream across five decoders and four full-grid routes.

record_type.label: Method replay
record_type.description: Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading.

scope.representation: The 256 printed base-60 grid cells parsed to bytes in row/reversed-row/column/reversed-column order.
scope.procedure: Replay the pinned Stage X4 component with 100,000 seeded uniform-byte calibration blocks for each decoder. Test each complete grid route with raw DEFLATE, zlib, gzip, bzip2 and LZMA; also preserve Stage N offset-zero signature rows. Independently reconstruct the grid and every decoder result.
scope.parameters: Five source decoders × four routes = 20 complete-stream calls, plus four signature checks. One bounded call per decoder with 1 MiB output cap; source PASS requires EOF and empirical null rate ×20≤0.01.

The source's 100,000-block calibration yielded 552 raw-DEFLATE EOFs and zero observed for each other decoder; independent recomputation matches. Synthetic complete/truncated/trailing-junk controls pass as separately labeled post-replay diagnostics.
records.limitations: Only 256 exact printed-grid bytes, four source routes, five decoder APIs, offset zero, a single call and 1 MiB output cap. Source EOF does not require consuming all input; zero calibration hits is finite-sample evidence, not a true zero rate. Other byte constructions, offsets, keys, formats and larger outputs remain untested.

# Does the printed grid contain a compressed stream?

The 256 cells on [LP2-49–51](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids) can each be read as one base-60 byte. Wulfic's Stage X4 passes the **complete 256-byte grid** to five standard decompressors in four fixed reading orders. It also checks the same four streams for known file starts.

**Finding:** none of the **20 decoder calls** reaches the end of a compressed stream. None of the four streams matches the source's offset-zero file signatures. We reran the pinned X4 component and reproduced all **24 published rows** exactly; an independent checker rebuilt the grid from Liberpedia's tokens, repeated the five 100,000-block calibrations and checked every decoder result.

![Four complete grid routes under five decoders; none reaches the end of a compressed stream](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-compression-source-replay/decoder-screen.svg)

The four orders are printed rows, reversed rows, columns of the 32 × 8 grid, and reversed columns. The five decoders are **raw DEFLATE, zlib, gzip, bzip2 and LZMA**. No byte is skipped, reordered within a route, keyed, or prefixed with a header. The [complete X4 result table](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-compression-source-replay/source-stage_x4_rows.tsv) keeps each decoder error and verdict.

## Why the random-stream check matters

The source applied each decoder to **100,000 seeded random 256-byte blocks**. Raw DEFLATE reached end-of-stream **552** times; the other four decoders had **zero observed hits** in their respective samples. A raw DEFLATE end marker alone would therefore be weak evidence here. Zero observed calibration hits is a sample result, **not** proof that a format can never accept random bytes.

The source accepts `eof=True` from a single bounded decoder call, with at most **1 MiB of output**. It does **not** require every input byte to be consumed. Our separate synthetic controls confirm that all five implementations recognize a complete compressed message, reject a truncated one, and still report EOF when junk follows a complete stream. These controls were added **after** the source replay to check the implementation; they were not part of Stage X4's original power gate.

The result excludes only an end-of-stream under these five APIs on these four exact 256-byte readings. A stream beginning at another offset, a different rendering of contested grid cells, a keyed transform, a larger output stopped by the cap, or another compression format remains outside this test. This also differs from the [direct-byte screen](#/experiments/grid-direct-bytes), which checks text and file headers rather than running full decompressors.

## Reproduce

From the repository root, with Python and NumPy:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-compression-source-replay/run.py --check
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-compression-source-replay/plot.py --check
```

The [plan](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-compression-source-replay/plan.json) fixes the input export, decoder APIs, routes, output cap, random seed and verdict rule. The [independent report](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-compression-source-replay/results.json) separates the manuscript results from calibration and the later diagnostics.

With the [pinned Stage X program](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/run_stage_x.py) at commit `bf89d3d`, this command reruns **X4 only**, compares every row with the committed Stage X table, and writes no file into the external checkout:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-compression-source-replay/replay_source.py PATH_TO_WULFIC_CLONE
```

# Can archived byte streams unlock the number grid?

The [number grid on LP2-49–51](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids) contains 256 printed cells that can be read as bytes. Wulfic's Stage Y uses six specified byte streams as repeating keys, starting at **every possible position** in each stream. It checks four ways to traverse the grid and four byte operations.

**Result:** none of the **96 source × route × operation cells** contains a phase that meets the source's pass rule. The lowest decoded block has **139 distinct byte values**; the declared cutoff is **120**. All **24 planted positives** pass, and all **18 random-grid negatives** stay above the cutoff. The original two result tables were reproduced byte-for-byte, and our checker independently recomputed all **2,865,136 phase trials** from the site's grid transcription.

![The lowest distinct-byte count from each of six source files remains above the declared cutoff](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-long-byte-sources/comparison.svg)

Here “distinct” means how many different byte values appear in a complete 256-byte output. A block restricted to ordinary text or a small alphabet may have few; a nearly uniform block generally has more. This is a **screen for low byte diversity**, not a text decoder. An intelligible answer with more than 120 different byte values would not pass this screen.

## What was tested

The six inputs are three archive files named `page_17.bin`, `page_21.bin`, `page_43.bin`, the archived wisdom hint, 991 bytes parsed from the `page_00` hex text, and 256 bytes parsed from the second-onion hex string. The file numbers are **source archive names**, not a claim that they belong to manuscript pages LP2-17, LP2-21 or LP2-43. Their exact bytes and hashes are bundled with this record.

For each source, the key starts at every cyclic phase. The grid is read in printed row order, its reverse, column order, or its reverse. Each route is combined with XOR, grid minus key, grid plus key, or key minus grid modulo 256. This gives **16 cells per source**, each covering every phase. The [full 96-cell table](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-long-byte-sources/source-stage_y_results.tsv) preserves the lowest count, its source phase, and the exact-source verdict. The best cell uses `page_43.bin`, printed row order and XOR at phase 43,059; its count is 139.

The source's rule treats a cell as excluded when none of its phases has at most 120 distinct values. Its controls are part of that claim: every planted text, rune, hex and base64 case must pass at its planted location; random grids must produce no passes, with a mean distinct count within 0.5 of 162. The [42-row control table](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-long-byte-sources/source-stage_y_controls.tsv) records those checks. The source run reports a valid gate. This does **not** rule out a message that remains high-diversity under the chosen operation.

## Reproduce

The [plan](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-long-byte-sources/plan.json) fixes the six inputs, four routes, operations, all-phase rule and threshold. The experiment download includes all six exact byte inputs. The checker reads Liberpedia's 256 grid tokens, parses them independently as base-60 bytes, calculates every phase, and checks each published minimum, phase, mean, printable fraction, probability and verdict. It also tests 24 separately planted known-byte controls. Run from the repository root with Python and NumPy:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-long-byte-sources/run.py --check
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-long-byte-sources/plot.py --check
```

We also reran the [pinned Stage Y program](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/run_stage_y.py) at commit `bf89d3d`. With that external checkout, the optional wrapper recomputes the source's own controls and results in a temporary directory and verifies them against its committed tables:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-long-byte-sources/replay_source.py PATH_TO_WULFIC_CLONE
```

This only covers the six byte streams, the printed grid, these four routes and operations, and the source's diversity cutoff. It does not test other keys, another grid construction, inserted or skipped bytes, decompression after a keyed transform, or a plaintext whose bytes remain diverse.

# Do native Cicada keys read the number grid?

The 256 printed cells on LP2-49–51 can be converted to bytes under the documented base-60 convention. Wulfic's Stage N tests whether several keys drawn from earlier Cicada material make those bytes resemble text, a file, or runes. **None of its 456 fixed settings reaches its own reading screen.** This is a bounded keyed-grid check, not a claim that the grid has no encoded message.

![Best byte-printability and GP29 likelihood compared with the original source thresholds](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-native-keys/comparison.svg)

## The two screens

The **byte screen** uses the printed 32 × 8 grid in row order or its full reversal. For each, it repeats one of 12 source keys and applies XOR, byte subtraction or byte addition. Those **72 outputs** are screened for at least 90% printable bytes or an offset-zero signature such as PNG, JPEG, gzip, ZIP, PDF or a length-consistent OpenPGP packet header. The best printable fraction is **42.6%**; no signature is reported. A printable result would only be a candidate, not a proven reading.

The **rune screen** takes either the 256 grid bytes modulo 29 or the 512 individual base-60 digits modulo 29. In each representation it tests forward and reversed order. It then scores three GP29 decoding directions under every constant shift, plus the source's prime, `DIVINITY` and `FIRFUMFERENFE` streams. These **384 settings** use the source's drift-tolerant solved-LP1 rune-frequency detector. The largest log-likelihood ratio is **4.63 nats**, below the source pass level of **+30**.

The [complete 456-row source result](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-native-keys/source-stage_n_results.tsv) retains each key, operation, direction, screen value and verdict. The byte screen uses a permissive printable threshold; the rune screen is a unigram detector. Neither tests whether a longer decoded phrase is meaningful or whether a key derived from different puzzle material works.

## What this does and does not establish

The original Stage N run did **not** include a planted detector-control gate. We regenerated its table exactly, then added separate, **post-replay** checks that its byte operations can recover synthetic printable text and that its rune likelihood can recognize a simple planted high-signal case. Those diagnostics catch broken implementations; they are not a preregistered LP2 power study and do not justify rejecting a whole cipher family.

The result is about the source's row-order grid, full reversal, named keys, operations, two rune encodings and two fixed thresholds. It does not cover other grid routes, uncertain glyph readings, offsets within a file, key starts and drift models beyond the source, decompression after decryption, or different languages. The [direct-byte experiment](#/experiments/grid-direct-bytes) checks unkeyed whole-stream formats over more routes and stem choices; this record answers the separate keyed question.

## Reproduce

We ran the [pinned Stage N source](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/run_stage_n.py) at commit `bf89d3d`; its 456-row TSV matches the pinned repository byte-for-byte. The bundled [numerical input profile](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-native-keys/source-profile.json) records the exact key streams and unigram distribution exported from that checkout; no upstream source code is copied. The site’s own 256-cell [grid export](exports/alphanumeric-grids.csv) independently reproduces every source grid byte and base-60 digit.

With Python's standard library, run from the extracted Liberpedia repository:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-native-keys/run.py --check
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-native-keys/check.py
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-native-keys/plot.py --check
```

The checker rebuilds the grid, replays every byte operation, and independently calculates all 384 GP29 likelihood scores from the recorded numerical inputs. It also runs the explicitly post-replay planted byte and rune diagnostics. The [plan](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-native-keys/plan.json) pins files, source revision and exact thresholds; `prepare_source.py` regenerates the numerical profile when supplied a matching external checkout.

# Does the number grid retain a repeating alphabet's pattern?

The 256 printed cells on LP2-49–51 can be read as bytes. Wulfic's Stage X2 asks whether those bytes could come from a plaintext stream through a **different one-to-one byte substitution at each position of a repeating period**. A one-to-one substitution changes byte values, but it cannot change whether two bytes encrypted with the *same* substitution are equal. That gives a test without guessing any of the substitutions.

**Finding:** across both declared ways to traverse the grid and every period **1–128**, no equality count exceeds the maximum from 100,000 uniform-byte controls. The source's lower-tail rule excludes **241 of 256 reading/period cells** under its English control, **247** under solved LP1 runes, **247** under hexadecimal digits, and **78** under Base64. These are conditional exclusions of this one model; many Base64 cells remain open, and no byte stream has been decoded.

![Conditional exclusions by plaintext control class among 256 grid-reading and period cells](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-periodic-byte-invariant/comparison.svg)

The [full table](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-periodic-byte-invariant/source-stage_x_periodic.tsv) gives the observed pair count, uniform-null maximum, control cutoff and verdict for each of the 256 cells. A cell is one reading order and one period, **not a separate puzzle idea**.

## What was compared

The two reading orders are the printed row order of the 32 × 8 grid and a column-major traversal of the same cells. For each period `p`, the test groups positions by their remainder after division by `p` and counts equal-byte pairs *within* those groups. If a fixed, one-to-one alphabet is reused at each residue, that count is unchanged by encryption.

The source compares the observed count with 100,000 seeded blocks of uniform random bytes. It calls a structural hit only when the grid exceeds **every** such block at the same period. It also compares with 256-byte plaintext windows from Emerson, the solved LP1 rune stream, and generated hexadecimal and Base64 streams. Its exclusion rule asks whether the grid falls below a class's **lower 0.1% control cutoff**. English and LP1 therefore test specific source representations, not every possible language, text encoding or symbol frequency.

The source supplies 9,024 Emerson windows, 2,646 LP1 windows, and 10,000 each of the hexadecimal and Base64 controls. Our independent checker rebuilds the grid bytes from Liberpedia's printed-token export, recalculates **all 256 observed equality counts and pair capacities**, checks every reported decision against its cutoff, and plants residue-specific bijections to verify the invariant. That planted test is a **post-replay mathematical diagnostic**; it is not an original source power study.

## What remains open

An exclusion only applies if the bytes really represent the proposed plaintext class and every residue uses a fixed bijection with no extra processing. It does not rule out a changing alphabet, non-bijective mapping, transposition, compression, keyed stream or a different grid traversal. The uniform-null maximum is a finite-control threshold, not a decryption score. This record replays **Stage X2 only**; the source's X1 byte-uniformity, X3 integer and X4 decompression screens are separate questions.

## Reproduce

From the repository root, Python's standard library checks the bundled source result and rebuilds the figure:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-periodic-byte-invariant/run.py --check
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-periodic-byte-invariant/plot.py --check
```

The [plan](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-periodic-byte-invariant/plan.json) pins the exact source revision, grid export, control counts and rules. The 256-row table was generated with the unmodified [pinned Stage X program](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/run_stage_x.py), calling only its X2 component. To repeat the full 100,000-draw source calculation from a matching external checkout, run:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-periodic-byte-invariant/replay_source.py PATH_TO_WULFIC_CLONE
```

The optional source replay requires NumPy, verifies the checkout revision and its four input hashes, then compares its regenerated table **byte-for-byte** with the bundled one. Source code stays in its original repository.

# What do the unkeyed number-grid bytes tell us?

The [256-cell number grid](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids) can be read as 256 bytes. Two parts of Wulfic's Stage X inspect those bytes directly: seven measurements against random blocks, and four readings as a possible RSA modulus. We reproduced all **eleven source rows exactly** and independently checked the measurements and divisibility tests.

**Finding:** none of the seven measurements crosses the source's threshold for rejecting its uniform-byte reference. But all four integer readings have small prime factors, including **3 and 7**. They therefore fail the proposed interpretation as a conventional RSA modulus formed from large primes. These are structural checks, not a decryption.

![The grid has 161 distinct byte values versus about 162 under the random reference; all four integer readings have small factors.](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-rsa-modulus-screen/byte-checks.svg)

## What the byte measurements establish

The source generated **100,000 independent, uniformly random 256-byte blocks**. It compared the printed grid with those blocks using seven fixed measurements and a two-sided cutoff of **0.01 / 7**, allowing for the seven comparisons.

| Measurement | Printed grid | Random-reference mean |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Different byte values | 161 | 162.00 |
| Byte-count chi-square | 254 | 254.97 |
| One bits among 2,048 bits | 1,017 | 1,023.98 |
| High-nibble chi-square | 14.625 | 14.98 |
| Low-nibble chi-square | 18.75 | 15.00 |
| Equal adjacent bytes, rows | 0 | 0.99 |
| Equal adjacent bytes, columns | 3 | 0.99 |

A nibble is half a byte: the high and low four-bit parts. The chi-square measurements compare how evenly values appear. None of these results rejects the declared reference. That **does not prove randomness**, encryption, compression, or a one-time pad. Many constructed messages can pass a small collection of statistical tests.

## Could the grid itself be an RSA modulus?

An RSA modulus is the public integer formed by multiplying prime factors; it is different from an RSA ciphertext or signature. The source tests printed row order and column order, each interpreted with the first byte most significant or least significant. It requires an odd, exactly 2,048-bit integer with no prime factor below one million.

| Reading | Bits | Examples of exact prime divisors |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Rows, big-endian | 2,048 | 2, 3, 7, 13 |
| Rows, little-endian | 2,047 | 3, 7, 11 |
| Columns, big-endian | 2,048 | 2, 3, 7, 19 |
| Columns, little-endian | 2,047 | 3, 7, 13, 61 |

We tested all **78,498 primes below one million** against each integer. The [results](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-rsa-modulus-screen/results.json) retain every divisor found and the complete integers. A divisor such as 3 is an exact witness against a product made only from large primes; it is not a probabilistic primality result. This does not supply a full factorization, and it does not exclude arbitrary weak RSA parameters, another ordering, changed grid cells, or use of the bytes as ciphertext. [Applying public RSA keys to the payload](#/experiments/public-rsa-payload-e01) is a separate experiment.

## Reproduce

From the repository root, with Python and NumPy:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-rsa-modulus-screen/run.py --check
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-rsa-modulus-screen/check.py
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-rsa-modulus-screen/plot.py --check
```

The producer reconstructs the grid from Liberpedia's tokens, uses vectorized count tables for the random reference, and exhausts the small-prime screen. The separate checker uses scalar counts and incremental prime generation. The [plan](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-rsa-modulus-screen/plan.json), [X1 scope amendment](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-rsa-modulus-screen/amendment.json), and [source rows](experiments/records/wulfic-grid-rsa-modulus-screen/source-x1-x3.tsv) preserve the exact bounds.

To repeat the original [Stage X1 and X3 code](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/run_stage_x.py), use a checkout at that revision:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-grid-rsa-modulus-screen/replay_source.py PATH_TO_WULFIC_CLONE
```

The wrapper verifies that the source's grid parser and Liberpedia's export produce identical bytes, reruns these two components only, and compares all eleven rows with the committed source table. It writes no files into the external checkout.

# What did the archived keyword-and-route search actually test?

The archived program first applies a proposed repeating keyword to each page, then tries column orders, a magic-square order, spirals, rails, diagonals and other rearrangements. Its files named `page_21` through `page_30` contain **LP2-04 through LP2-13**, respectively. We matched all ten rune streams exactly before replaying the program. The keyword assignments are proposals, not established decryption keys.

## Result

The complete source loop produced **585 reported route rows** across the ten pages. The program also tries all column orders for six short keywords before retaining only each page's best such order. Its highest numerical score differs across pages, but **none of the 585 rows matched even one word** under the program's own word test. The numbers rank English letter pairs in an unbroken stream; they are not evidence of a reading.

![Across ten actual target pages, selected routes raise the source bigram score, while every output has zero recognized words.](experiments/records/wulfic-keyed-transposition-cohort/comparison.svg)

The zero is a property of this *test design*: the program removes spacing and passes the whole output to a function that looks up entire space-separated words. Its pinned repository does not contain the optional `data/wordlist.txt`, so this replay uses its built-in 95-word fallback. The selected strings are far longer than any word in that fallback. A different, explicitly specified word-segmentation test might find short substrings, but that would be a different experiment.

## What the controls establish

We planted known rune messages at each of the ten source lengths. The source keyword-column reversal restored each one, and the source's 25-position magic-square inverse restored each one. Six other route functions preserved full length and the multiset of rune values on every planted stream. **All 80 controls passed.** These checks show the implemented routes run as claimed; they do not validate the proposed page keywords or the English ranking rule.

The source comments promise Myszkowski and disrupted transposition, but `solve_page` never calls either. Its prime-position extraction is not a full-message permutation. We report only the operators actually executed.

## Reproduce and limits

Run `python experiments/records/wulfic-keyed-transposition-cohort/run.py --check --source-file PATH_TO_PINNED_SCRIPT` to repeat the full source loop. Omit `--source-file` to fetch the exact script from its pinned GitHub revision; the runner rejects a different SHA-256. `python experiments/records/wulfic-keyed-transposition-cohort/check.py --source-file PATH_TO_PINNED_SCRIPT` independently checks the page alignment receipts, unchanged-keyword baselines, route selection, and zero-word result. With `--source-repo PATH_TO_PINNED_CLONE`, it also compares all ten archived page files rune by rune with the current LP2 pages. The scripts and saved results are included in the experiment download.

This replay covers the source's exact ten input streams, fixed keyword assignments, routes and scoring rule. It does not test all transpositions or prove that no output can be read under another language or segmentation rule. Four nearby scripts are not silently counted as the same experiment: `p21_30_transposition.py` overlaps the columnar/prime route subset; `p21_30_rearrange.py` requires an absent wordlist for its own score; `p21_30_verified_rearrange.py` additionally requires an absent `verified_keys.json`; and `refine_and_batch.py` adds a stochastic monoalphabetic optimizer and unavailable training inputs. Their unresolved differences remain outside this result.

# A keyword that feeds a shifting register

The archived [advanced cipher program](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/legacy/advanced_cipher_solver.py) tries a keyword-seeded *linear feedback shift register* on ten manuscript pages. **None of its 400 settings crossed the program's reporting cutoff** on LP2-04–13. The best normalized coincidence value on any page was **1.10**, below the required **greater than 1.20**. This is a result for the source's fixed keywords and register rules, not for every feedback cipher.

![Each page's highest normalized coincidence value is below the source gate of 1.20; a known-reading control reached 2.06.](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-lfsr/comparison.svg)

The keyword gives the first register values. At each rune, the register emits its first value as the key, then calculates a new value from selected positions before shifting. With `CABAL` as `5, 24, 17, 24, 20` and taps at zero-based positions 1 and 4, the key starts `5, 24, 17, 24, 20, 15…`; the new value `15` is `(24 + 20) mod 29`. The program tries register lengths **4–8**, four tap lists at each length, and two directions of subtraction. Each page starts its own register.

We tested the reporting rule on a full message first. A **209-rune established reading** was encrypted with one of the declared CABAL settings. The same 400-case search recovered every rune, cleared the coincidence cutoff at **2.06**, and ranked the correct case first. This shows that the gate can find a clean in-family message. It does not prove the gate would catch a noisy, interrupted, differently encoded, or layered message.

The archived page files 21–30 match the current LP2-04–13 rune arrays exactly. The 400 source settings yielded **396 distinct decoded outputs**, because four pairs of settings coincide on particular pages; they are still one method family. The source reports and English-substring-scores an output only after its whole-page normalized `29 × IoC` exceeds 1.20. **Zero** manuscript outputs cleared that rule. In **199** complete searches over independently shuffled pages, zero outputs cleared it there too. With no reported scores on either side, the shuffles do not provide a useful score-ranking or significance claim. They only show that this cutoff is stringent for these page lengths and frequencies.

The [plan](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-lfsr/plan.json) fixes the ten pages, 400 settings, full-message control and whole-search shuffle procedure. The [results](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-lfsr/results.json) retain the coincidence measurement and decoded-output digest for every setting; the separate [control result](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-lfsr/control-results.json) was written before the manuscript scan. The related [keyword-ramp](#/experiments/wulfic-keyword-ramp) and [crib-inferred recurrence](#/experiments/wulfic-crib-lfsr-recurrence) tests use different key clocks.

From the full checkout or experiment bundle, supply an exact checkout of the pinned public Wulfic revision separately:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-lfsr/run.py --source-root PATH_TO_PINNED_WULFIC_CHECKOUT --check
python experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-lfsr/check.py --source-root PATH_TO_PINNED_WULFIC_CHECKOUT
python experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-lfsr/plot.py --check
```

The source checkout does not provide a license, so its script is not copied into the bundle. The runner imports only the SHA-256-verified Git blob. The independent checker rebuilds the register, both decryption directions, all 400 outputs, the planted reading and all 199 shuffled searches without importing the producer.

# Keywords combined with a prime stream

Could a familiar keyword remove one layer of LP2 while a prime-derived stream removes another? An [archived public script](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/legacy/combined_cipher_test.py) defined a finite version of that question. We ran its fixed settings on the corresponding manuscript pages with a known-reading control and a whole-search comparison.

**None of the 224,128 tested settings crossed the script's IoC screen of 1.40.** The best was 1.29 on LP2-32. A planted 515-rune known reading decoded completely and scored 1.72, so the test can detect that example made with its own rules. The control is longer than any target page and does not establish equal detection power on short pages. The highest LP2 score is not an unusual search peak under our page-shuffle comparison: 42 of 49 shuffles reached at least that value.

![The best LP2 IoC is 1.29, below the 1.40 source screen; a planted known reading scores 1.72.](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-prime-layer-grid/comparison.svg)

## What the script tried

At each rune position, it adds or subtracts one of **16 fixed keyword sequences** and one of **103 second streams**, modulo 29. The second streams include ordinary primes, prime minus one, cumulative prime-minus-one values, a linear count and Fibonacci values. Both signs are tried for both components. Each setting starts again at the beginning of each page. The script used the index of coincidence (IoC), a measure of repeated symbols, to screen its outputs; a high IoC alone would not establish a reading.

The named keywords are CABAL, DIVINITY, ENCRYPTION, OBSCURA, ENCRYPT, SHADOWS, DEOR, TOTIENT, MOURNFUL, VOID, AETHEREAL, BUFFERS, CARNAL, ANALOG, MOBIUS and FORM. We use their [literal source rune vectors](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-prime-layer-grid/keys.json). Those labels are not a separate spelling check: for example, the source’s AETHEREAL vector includes both TH and a following H. A conventional re-encoding of that word is a different setting.

The source calls its inputs pages 21–54. Those names came from an older file layout. A rune-by-rune length and SHA-256 check shows they are **current LP2-04–37**, in order. This correction matters: testing today's LP2-21–54 would test different text. Our [input-mapping amendment](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-prime-layer-grid/input-mapping-amendment.json) preserves the initial mistaken plan and records that an exploratory run on the wrong range was discarded before this result. The saved result uses only the verified mapping.

## How to read the result

The result covers exactly the source's keyword arrays, 103 stream definitions, four sign choices and 34 matched pages. Its 1.40 line is a candidate screen, not a proof that all layered ciphers fail below it. We also shuffled runes *within each page* and repeated the entire search 49 times. Those controls preserve each page's rune frequencies, so they reveal how large a best score can appear after searching many settings. They do not simulate every possible cipher.

The archived script is explicitly marked untrusted by its own repository and has a broken old directory assumption. We reimplemented its finite arithmetic on verified inputs. That is a new bounded test of the archived proposal, not a claim that its original historical output was correct.

The [plan](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-prime-layer-grid/plan.json), [saved measurements](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-prime-layer-grid/results.json) and [reproduction script](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-prime-layer-grid/check.py) give the exact settings. Run `python experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-prime-layer-grid/check.py` to repeat the full grid, input checks and shuffle controls.

# Do named keyword alphabets fit LP2?

Wulfic's Stage V builds substitution alphabets from **34 specified words and phrases**, including `DIVINITY`, `KNOW THIS`, `CICADA`, and the known parable. After collapsing duplicates, those give **68 distinct alphabets**. The test checks every source-defined choice of plaintext, ciphertext and key alphabet for each of six key-value distributions. It scores **whole LP2 rune frequencies**; it does not assemble or read a plaintext sentence.

**Finding:** the source's calibration gate passes, but **no tested member reaches its +10 lead threshold**. For English-rune, prime-value, English Latin-letter and decimal-digit key distributions, every named-alphabet combination is both control-powered and below the source's −10 exclusion cutoff. Hexadecimal digits leave **135** powered combinations above that cutoff; uniform A–Z leaves **10,197**. Neither group supplies a reading or a positive lead. Many A–Z combinations lack enough control power, so they remain untestable.

![Control-qualified outcomes for six named-alphabet key distributions](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-quagmire-models/comparison.svg)

Each family has **314,432 alphabet combinations**. That is the size of one bounded search, **not** a count of independent solving ideas. The chart shows the share of each family that is both below the exclusion cutoff and powerful enough to judge, above the cutoff with power, or untestable. Hexadecimal's 135 powered survivors are too small to distinguish at the chart's scale; their exact count remains in the data.

## How the screen works

The source considers an identity alphabet and each keyword alphabet or its inverse. It combines three of those alphabets, tries its three arithmetic sign modes and all 29 constant offsets, then keeps the best **single-rune frequency** score for each combination. Six declared key-value distributions come from English runes, their prime values, English Latin letters, decimal digits, hexadecimal digits and uniform A–Z letters.

Before looking at LP2, the source tested **50 generated messages per family** under their own model; none fell below the −10 cutoff. For each alphabet combination, at least **18 of 20** flat-key controls must fall below the cutoff before a low LP2 score counts as a *powered exclusion*. The source's raw “excluded” count also includes some combinations without that power. We keep those in the untestable part of the chart. This distinction matters especially for uniform A–Z.

The [source result table](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-quagmire-models/source-stage_v_results.tsv) contains the gate results, six family summaries, and **10,332** listed powered non-exclusions. Those listings are candidates within this frequency screen, not decoded messages. The highest LP2 score is **+6.51**, below the source's +10 lead rule. A different keyword set, a non-independent key sequence, another alphabet construction, page-specific resets or layered encryption remains outside this test.

## Reproduce

The bundled checker independently counts the **12,956** LP2 runes from Liberpedia's page files, audits all source gate and family summaries, and checks every listed survivor against its cutoff and power label:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-quagmire-models/run.py --check
python experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-quagmire-models/plot.py --check
```

We also reran the [pinned source program](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/run_stage_v.py): all **10,357 rows match its published table byte-for-byte**. The [plan](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-quagmire-models/plan.json) fixes its inputs, key rules and thresholds. With a matching external checkout and NumPy, repeat that source computation in a temporary output file:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-quagmire-models/replay_source.py PATH_TO_WULFIC_CLONE
```

# A keyword that shifts with each rune

The archived [advanced cipher program](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/legacy/advanced_cipher_solver.py) assigns one keyword to each of ten pages, then changes that keyword's shift at every rune. We replayed **all nine steps on each page**. No output establishes a reading. The strongest source word score was **86** on LP2-11; **10 of 199** complete shuffled searches scored at least as high.

![The strongest manuscript source word score is 86, compared with 61 at the middle and 95 at the highest of 199 complete shuffled searches. A known-reading plant recovered exactly and scored 380.](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-ramp/comparison.svg)

The rule is simple: take the keyword's rune value at position *i*, add *i* times a fixed step, and subtract that total from ciphertext modulo 29. Each page restarts at position zero. The source's steps are **1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, −1, and −2**. For example, with CABAL and step 7, the key begins `5, 2, 2, 16, 19, 11…`. This is a repeating keyword plus a steady position ramp, not a plain progressive Caesar shift.

We checked the source scoring path before the manuscript sweep. Encrypting the complete, established **209-rune first-koan reading** with CABAL and step 7, then testing all nine steps, recovers every rune only at step 7. That true candidate ranks first under the source score, at **380**. It demonstrates power for this clean example, not for every possible reading or language. The source score counts selected English substrings in a run-together GP transliteration; it is a rough screen and can reward accidental fragments.

The ten pinned source rune files numbered **21–30** match the site's **LP2-04–13** arrays rune for rune. Each of the 199 seeded controls shuffles each page once, retains its original keyword, tests all nine steps, and saves the highest score across the entire ten-page search. The shuffles keep each page's rune frequencies but destroy its order; they are a selection reference, not a cipher model. The source script's other autokey, running-key, F-skip and LFSR branches are separate questions, many already tested in bounded records. These nine steps do not exhaust other keywords, step schedules, boundary resets, or layered methods.

The [plan](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-ramp/plan.json) fixes the exact branches, pages, known-reading control, and shuffle procedure. The [results](experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-ramp/results.json) give all 90 candidate scores and decoded-output hashes plus 199 full-search control maxima. From the full checkout or experiment bundle, with an exact checkout of the public Wulfic revision supplied separately:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-ramp/run.py --source-root PATH_TO_PINNED_WULFIC_CHECKOUT --check
python experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-ramp/check.py --source-root PATH_TO_PINNED_WULFIC_CHECKOUT
python experiments/records/wulfic-keyword-ramp/plot.py --check
```

The original source has no license in that checkout, so the bundle does not copy its script. The runner executes its exact key and score functions from a SHA-256-checked Git blob. The independent checker rebuilds the arithmetic, all outputs, the known-reading plant and all shuffled maxima without importing those functions.
records.reader_finding: The nine tested step sizes produced no established reading on LP2-04–13. The best word score was matched or beaten by 10 of 199 complete shuffled searches. The same search recovered a 209-rune known message when it used the tested key rule.
records.reader_limit: Only the ten assigned keywords and nine fixed step sizes were tested. Other keywords, changing step schedules, resets and languages remain open.

record_type.label: Method replay
record_type.description: Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading.

scope.representation: The source's continuous 12,956 GP29 rune values for LP2-00–55, verified identical to the site page transcription.
scope.procedure: Repair only AC's one-row control cumsum allocation in memory. Reproduce AC and AD full original planted-control grids, four anti-doublet null streams each, all forward lags 11 through N−11 and all eligible reverse anti-diagonals. AC tests three pair laws ×29 shifts; AD tests four ×29. Compare every generated lag, top and control TSV byte with the pinned source; independently recompute representative scores.
scope.parameters: AC: 12,935 forward lags, 3 relations, 29 shifts, 138 control rows, Pmax 12,500/Mmin 3,000. AD: same 12,935 lag rows, 4 relations, 29 shifts, 184 control rows, Pmax 12,900/Mmin 200. Fixed +30 positive line and −10 calibrated exclusion line; four null streams per stage. Source-provided control draws and seeds retained.

records.finding: After correcting only an original one-row control-array allocation in memory, all six AC/AD source result tables reproduce byte-for-byte. AC's best whole-lag, forward-stretch and reverse-stretch scores are +7.05, +19.86 and +18.23; AD's are +5.30, +22.49 and +23.16. All are below +30. AD's +5.30 whole-lag maximum has only 14 pair opportunities and an absolute +17.41 ceiling, so cannot pass at any key. The 138 AC and 184 AD planted-control rows match; both four-null gates are valid. Source/site GP29 text agrees across 12,956 positions, with selected pair-law scores independently recomputed.

The in-memory shape correction is disclosed and all original tables must match before accepting a result. AC's whole-lag exclusions are calibrated only through gap 12,500 and its all-cell reused-stretch detection only from 3,000 runes; AD's corresponding bounds are 12,900 and 200. The AD maximum whole-lag score comes from an underpowered 14-pair tail. Other pair laws, word resets, changing keys, language models or later decoding layers remain untested.
records.article:
# Distant key reuse and ciphertext autokeys

**Finding.** Two related source searches find no LP2 score at their declared **+30** pass line. The highest whole-lag scores are **+7.05** for a repeated-key relation and **+5.30** when an earlier ciphertext rune serves as the key. The strongest shorter-stretch scores are higher, but still below +30. These are bounded screens of particular pair laws, not a rejection of every autokey or repeated-key cipher.

![Best whole-lag and stretch scores for both source models, all below the source pass line.](experiments/records/wulfic-lag-reuse-models/comparison.svg)

## The idea behind the test

If ciphertext is formed by adding plaintext and a key modulo 29, and the same key rune is used again after a gap of **L** runes, subtracting the two ciphertext runes cancels the key. This gives a testable relation between rune pairs **L** places apart. The source's **AC** search also tries shifted or reflected key relations. Its **AD** search asks whether an earlier *ciphertext* rune itself supplied the later key, in forward or reverse order. Both are more specific than searching for a high count of repeated runes.

For every forward gap from 11 through 12,945 in the continuous 12,956-rune LP2 text, the programs score all allowed pair relations and 29 shifts. They also inspect reverse pairings where two positions have a fixed sum. **F** measures evidence over an entire forward diagonal, as a long periodic key would require. **S** finds the best contiguous stretch on a forward or reverse diagonal, as a shorter reused piece would require. The test uses a solved-LP1 rune-frequency model and scores complete declared diagonals or stretches, rather than selecting words that look promising.

| Source model | Best whole gap F | Best forward stretch S | Best reverse stretch S |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| AC · repeated key relation | +7.05 | +19.86 | +18.23 |
| AD · ciphertext as key | +5.30 | +22.49 | +23.16 |

The source fixed **+30** as a positive screen and **−10** as an exclusion only where planted controls establish enough power. Four flat anti-doublet null streams per model had to stay below +30 for a valid run. The original control grids reproduced exactly: AC's periodic tests support exclusions only through gap **12,500**, and its planted reused stretches all pass only at **3,000** runes; AD's corresponding figures are **12,900** and **200**. Shorter, different or more elaborate key reuse remains outside those calibrated exclusions.

The top AD whole-gap score comes from lag **12,942**, leaving only **14 rune pairs**. With the source's largest possible per-pair emission ratio, even its theoretical ceiling is **+17.41**. It cannot meet +30 under any such key. The table preserves the source's maximum, but it is not a near-hit from a fully testable long diagonal.

## A source-code repair that matters

The pinned AC and AD programs each encounter the same one-row array error during their planted-stretch controls, in both quick and full modes. The source helper allocates 29 rows even when the caller passes a single shift. We changed that allocation to the actual row count **in memory only**, leaving the pinned checkout untouched. After that correction, all **138 AC** and **184 AD** original control rows match the published tables exactly. The full source scans and output formatting remain unchanged; the replay checks every row of all six published source tables before accepting the finding. This is an **amended-source replay**, not an unchanged execution of a program that currently crashes.

The independently checked input is Liberpedia's page text: its LP2-00–55 GP29 rune sequence matches the source's 12,956 positions exactly. A separate checker rebuilds the pair-law score tables and recomputes sampled whole-gap and forward/reverse-stretch values from that sequence, including the leading source results.

## Inspect or reproduce

- [AC lag table](experiments/records/wulfic-lag-reuse-models/source-stage_ac_lags.tsv), [top scores](experiments/records/wulfic-lag-reuse-models/source-stage_ac_top.tsv), [controls](experiments/records/wulfic-lag-reuse-models/source-stage_ac_controls.tsv).
- [AD lag table](experiments/records/wulfic-lag-reuse-models/source-stage_ad_lags.tsv), [top scores](experiments/records/wulfic-lag-reuse-models/source-stage_ad_top.tsv), [controls](experiments/records/wulfic-lag-reuse-models/source-stage_ad_controls.tsv).
- [Exact rune numbers](experiments/records/wulfic-lag-reuse-models/source-stream.bin), [frequency model](experiments/records/wulfic-lag-reuse-models/source-model.json), [result summary](experiments/records/wulfic-lag-reuse-models/results.json), and [scope plan](experiments/records/wulfic-lag-reuse-models/plan.json).

Run `python experiments/records/wulfic-lag-reuse-models/check.py` for the independent source/site and sampled numerical checks. With the [pinned upstream checkout](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/tree/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c), run `python experiments/records/wulfic-lag-reuse-models/replay_source.py --source PATH --output PATH` to repeat the full amended-source screens and check all six generated TSV files against the archived tables. NumPy is required. Use an output directory separate from the checkout.

The test does not consider word resets, other pair laws, keys that change between spans, a different language model, or a later decoding layer. A finding below +30 does not mean every one of those possibilities was tried.

records.question: Do visible rune repeats mark one plaintext rune, or can a fixed set of dedicated homophones explain LP2 rune frequencies?
records.summary: Two source-defined rules make predictions about visible runes; neither fits under its stated assumptions.

record_type.label: Bounded solving test
record_type.description: Applies a fixed decoding, extraction or payload-retrieval rule to declared unsolved material, or excludes a specific direct-generation rule. Its result covers only those bounds.

scope.procedure: Replay original C3 and C15 source tests. Independently count LP2 repeats and word classes, run all 29 C3 marker candidates with the original Poisson and position cutoffs, and enumerate/verify the best C15 ciphertext-symbol allocation.

The marker result uses solved-reading frequencies and word positions as plaintext proxies and assumes a fixed marker with nonzero multiplier. records.article:
# Can simple letter-encoding rules explain LP2?

Two precise proposals make predictions about the visible runes. We replayed both from the [pinned source tests](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/tree/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tests) and independently rebuilt their manuscript measurements. **Neither rule fits under its stated assumptions.** This does not rule out other ways to handle repeated runes or homophones.

![Two checks: 29 possible repeat markers narrow to three by count and zero by word position; the best dedicated-homophone model predicts a frequency mismatch far above the observed one.](experiments/records/wulfic-letter-encoding-bounds/comparison.svg)

## A repeated rune as a marker

In the first proposal, one chosen plaintext rune makes the ciphertext repeat its previous rune. If that rule operates throughout LP2, the *number* and *positions* of visible repeats should resemble occurrences of that plaintext rune. We tested each of the 29 possible markers. Only **NG, IA and EA** survive the source's repeat-count test. None fits the source's word-position test: their scores are −106.4, −149.4 and −67.7, respectively, against its −10 decision line. Thus the proposed marker rule has no surviving rune in this fixed model.

This relies on solved-page rune frequencies and word positions representing the unknown plaintext, and on a nonzero multiplier in the proposed recurrence. A different rule for avoiding or generating repeats would need its own test.

## One-to-many letters with fixed choices

The second proposal gives each plaintext rune its own dedicated set of ciphertext runes, with equal use of the choices within that set. We gave the model every allocation of the 29 available ciphertext symbols across the 26 plaintext rune types seen in the solved sample. Even the **best allocation predicts a frequency mismatch of 4,802** on the source's chi-square scale. The actual LP2 rune counts score **26**. The source's cutoff for this model is 200.

The best allocation gives O two ciphertext symbols and E three; the other used plaintext runes get one each. This is an expected-frequency bound, not an attempted decryption. Unequal choices, context-dependent homophones, extra cipher layers or a different plaintext distribution are outside this result.

## What we checked

The reconstructed sample has 2,901 known plaintext runes. LP2-00–55 has 12,956 runes, with 86 repeats in 12,947 within-section adjacent opportunities. The original six targeted source tests pass, including planted marker examples. An independent calculation checks the count and position tests, and a separate dynamic program checks the optimal homophone allocation. Source and site measurements agree at the decision points.

To check the saved result and figure, run `python experiments/records/wulfic-letter-encoding-bounds/check.py` and `python experiments/records/wulfic-letter-encoding-bounds/plot.py --check`. The [record files](experiments/records/wulfic-letter-encoding-bounds/plan.json) state exact bounds and source revisions. The original source replay additionally needs the pinned external repository.

records.article:
# Can single-rune words pin down an LFSR key?

An [LFSR](#/wiki/method-seeded-generators?section=lfsr) generates a key from a short memory of earlier values. Here it remembers one to five rune indices and calculates each next value modulo 29. The test assumes that every visible one-rune word in the unknown plaintext is **I** or **A**.

**Finding.** With one or two values of memory, no tested setting fits all the one-rune words on any of the three pages. With five, LP2-21 admits about **5.8 million** fitting parameter settings and LP2-24 about **27,400**. LP2-28 admits **four**, all under the Beaufort direction. A fit means only that those few positions read I or A; none is an established reading of the page.

![Number of LFSR parameter settings satisfying every visible one-rune word as I or A, by page and key memory length.](experiments/records/wulfic-lfsr-singleton-constraints/fits.svg)

The source's historical labels P28, P24 and P21 refer to **LP2-28, LP2-24 and LP2-21**. In the pinned repository's current global page folders, those are scans **45, 41 and 38**. We checked the rune streams and the precise positions of the 12, 9 and 7 one-rune words against the unchanged source parser before scanning. Using today's `page_28` folder would instead test LP2-11.

| Page | One-rune words | Complete fits at L3 | L4 | L5 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| LP2-28 | 12 | 0 | 0 | **4** |
| LP2-24 | 9 | 0 | 24 | **27,424** |
| LP2-21 | 7 | 6 | 6,846 | **5,808,457** |

These counts combine the source's subtraction and Beaufort directions. Its addition direction gives the **same decoded streams** as subtraction with every initial key value negated, so it is reported in the result file but not counted twice in the table. At L1 and L2, none of the three pages has a complete fit. Every L5 row includes all **20,511,149** ordered feedback tuples, including zero coefficients.

The four LP2-28 candidates have normalized full-page indices of coincidence **0.978–1.142**, below the source's `>1.3` shortcut. That observation is descriptive: we did not calibrate the source's other dictionary shortcut over the entire selected grid, and neither shortcut would establish a decryption by itself. The [result file](experiments/records/wulfic-lfsr-singleton-constraints/results.json) gives each of those four full-page decode hashes, key parameters, and exact singleton values. It also preserves example decodes for the larger rows.

## What the calculation covers

For state length L from **1 through 5**, the source defines each next key value as a linear combination of the previous L key values modulo 29. Its solver tries all tap tuples and all I/A assignments for the first L one-rune words, solves for the starting state, then checks every remaining one-rune word. We reproduced that **first-L invertible** procedure in all three directions. Planted streams recovered their exact taps and starting states for every length and direction. An independent checker recalculates every L1/L2 result, the first 100 tap tuples at L3–L5, every published full-page example, and the pinned input positions. It also exhausts small GF(3) and GF(5) tap/state spaces against a direct recurrence oracle and tests nonconsecutive singleton positions in GF(29). These checker controls were completed after the manuscript scan; the small-field oracle had been specified in the frozen plan.

This is a test of a **specific English singleton crib and source search rule**. If one-rune words use other plaintext symbols, the state advances across pages, the key skips, or the first-L basis is singular, these counts do not decide the model. In particular, millions of L5 fits on the page with only seven one-rune words show why satisfying a small crib is not evidence of a solution. A candidate needs a rule fixed in advance that predicts substantial text outside the singleton positions.

To repeat the saved-output checks, run:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-lfsr-singleton-constraints/run.py --check
```

The full four-minute sweep needs a C++17 `g++` compiler:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-lfsr-singleton-constraints/run.py
```

The [plan](experiments/records/wulfic-lfsr-singleton-constraints/plan.json) fixes the bounds and assumptions. The [input ledger](experiments/records/wulfic-lfsr-singleton-constraints/inputs.json) pins the page text and one-rune positions. The [pinned source script](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/legacy/lfsr_gf29_solver.py) defines the historical proposal; its archived execution and old optimizer output are not treated as verified results.

# Does the Liber AL text work as a key for LP2-08?

An archived program turns *Liber AL vel Legis* into rune values, slides that key across a page, and scores the results for six common English letter triples. Its archived `page_25` file matches **LP2-08**, not LP2-25. We ran the program's complete offset-selection rule on the corrected 255-rune page and the exact text bytes pinned in its repository. This is a new test on corrected inputs; the original output file is unavailable.

## What happened

The best output scored **670** on the program's common-trigram scale. That is ordinary under a simple order control: **154 of 199** shuffled versions of the same rune sequence scored at least as high when the *entire* search was rerun. The shuffle comparison asks whether this score stands out from rearranged page symbols. It is not a model of encryption or a probability that the book is irrelevant.

![The source's offset selection misses an off-grid planted message, while the page score sits below the shuffle median.](experiments/records/wulfic-liber-al-offset-sweep/comparison.svg)

The program samples offsets 0, 100, 200, and so on through 5,000, then searches within 200 positions of its six strongest first-stage rows. On this page it examined **2,104 distinct refined offsets** in two cipher directions, producing **4,310 scored rows** including the coarse rows. It does not examine every possible starting position.

That limit mattered in a direct test. Four known messages planted at sampled offsets 300 and 1,700, in both directions, were recovered. The same clear message planted at offset **137** was missed in both directions: its neighborhood never qualified for the finer search. So this result does **not** rule out an offset the source procedure skipped.

## What this covers

The source's exact rune alphabet, greedy text-to-rune conversion, two decryption directions, weighted `THE`/`AND`/`ING`/`ION`/`ENT`/`TIO` score, IoC tie-break, first six coarse rows, and ±200 refinement were retained. We only redirected paths moved by the source repository's own archiving. The page file and book text were verified against pinned Git objects before use. The source's old optimizer outputs are explicitly disclaimed in its archive, so none was treated as a confirmed key or reading.

A high score here means those short letter triples appeared in an unbroken transliteration. It is not a readable passage by itself. Other page identities, editions, key encodings, offsets outside the selected neighborhoods, and the follow-on substitution hill climber remain untested by this record.

## Reproduce

From a clone of the [pinned Wulfic revision](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/tree/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c), run `python experiments/records/wulfic-liber-al-offset-sweep/run.py --source-repo PATH_TO_CLONE --check`. The runner verifies the source script, page and book hashes, then recomputes the complete result. `check.py` independently rebuilds all selected rows and all 199 shuffle controls; it also compares 40 short random cases with the source's own decryptor and scorer. The exact search bounds and input hashes are in the bundled plan and results. `plan-frozen.json` preserves the byte-for-byte plan saved before scoring; `plan.json` adds only the archive's dependency-list format.

record_type.description: Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading.

records.article:
# Do fixed local rules preserve too many repeats?

A fixed rule that treats the same input unit the same way tends to preserve repeats. Wulfic's Stages AA and Z turn that idea into two precise tests on the unsolved LP2 text. **The controlled tests exclude the simplest short-context and short-block versions. Longer contexts and blocks usually cannot be distinguished from the controls.** This is a limit on those models, not a reading of the manuscript.

![Controlled repeat tests for local context widths, repeated words and aligned blocks](experiments/records/wulfic-local-codebook-invariants/comparison.svg)

## What was tested

**Stage AA: local context.** Suppose each output rune comes from a fixed, position-independent rule applied to nearby plaintext runes. If the same input window appears twice, the resulting output window must repeat. The source checks context widths 0–12, output groups of 3–7 runes, and two scopes: compare only inside each manuscript section or join the nine sections. It first measures the repeated output groups, then asks whether a proposed width would have produced more of them.

**Stage Z: fixed codebooks.** A fixed word table gives the same ciphertext to every copy of a word. A fixed, invertible block table likewise gives the same output to every copy of an aligned block. The source checks repeated words of at least two runes and aligned blocks 2–8 runes long at every starting offset. Each block length is tested both within sections and across the joined text. This covers **72 declared cells**: two word comparisons and 70 block comparisons.

These are structural tests. They do not look for English words or choose a key after seeing a promising passage. The source also lets its simulated encoder redraw 81% of adjacent repeat collisions, a measured LP2 feature. That matters: a simple fixed-codebook test without the collision rule would be easier to reject and less relevant.

## Result

| Source test | Excluded by its controls | Not resolved |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| AA context-width cells | 5 of 26 | 21 of 26 |
| Z repeated-word cells | 2 of 2 | 0 |
| Z aligned-block cells | 24 of 70 | 46 of 70 |

The AA exclusions are widths **0–2 within sections** and **0–1 in the joined stream**. Every other declared width lacks enough control power for an exclusion. In Z, the two word-codebook comparisons are excluded. All cells for blocks of 2–4 runes are excluded. Six of ten five-rune cells are excluded; the remaining four and every cell for lengths 6–8 are unresolved. **Unresolved does not mean compatible:** there are too few preserved repeats in the positive examples to separate those cases reliably from random text.

For each cell, the source generated 1,000 flat-rune null samples and 200 positive samples from each of two sources: Emerson prose and decoded LP1. It applies the same collision rule to the positive samples. An exclusion requires both positive sources to separate cleanly from the null and the LP2 count to lie below both positive lower bounds. The [exact result tables](experiments/records/wulfic-local-codebook-invariants/source-stage_z_results.tsv) show every cell; the [compact summary](experiments/records/wulfic-local-codebook-invariants/results.json) groups the verdicts. No LP2 repeat statistic is reported as a positive cipher identification.

## How to read the finding

Equal plaintext need not give equal ciphertext if the rule also depends on position, a running key, previous ciphertext, a changing alphabet, or some other state. Such a cipher is outside these fixed local-codebook tests. Different word boundaries or a corrected transcription would also change the measured repeats. Stage AA's 21 unresolved cells and Stage Z's 46 unresolved cells should remain open until a stronger control or another invariant makes them testable.

The supplied anti-doublet model is a control, not a demonstrated account of how LP2 was made. The controls check whether this particular repeat test can reject its proposed construction. They do not establish that the construction is the only way to create the manuscript's low repeat rate.

## Reproduce

The bundled AA and Z tables were regenerated by executing the [pinned Stage AA](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/run_stage_aa.py) and [Stage Z](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/run_stage_z.py) programs at commit `bf89d3d`, with the source's complete grids, seeds and controls. Every output table was compared byte-for-byte with the pinned repository. The source repository and its code are linked rather than copied into this ZIP.

From the extracted Liberpedia repository, Python's standard library is enough to verify the bundled results and independently recount every LP2 word, sliding group and aligned block:

```text
python experiments/records/wulfic-local-codebook-invariants/run.py --check
python experiments/records/wulfic-local-codebook-invariants/check.py
python experiments/records/wulfic-local-codebook-invariants/plot.py --check
```

The [plan](experiments/records/wulfic-local-codebook-invariants/plan.json) pins input hashes and the exact grids. The optional `replay_source.py` script runs both upstream programs from a checkout at the recorded commit, or compares completed rerun tables with `--verify-output-dir`; a full source rerun requires that repository and its dependencies. The independent checker reads Liberpedia's page text afresh and checks the manuscript counts against the source tables. It also checks a small planted example in which a fixed one-to-one relabelling must preserve word and block repeats.

record_type.label: Method replay
record_type.description: Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading.

scope.procedure: Replay pinned Stage I and M complete candidate grids, then measure a separately identified post-replay planted-key diagnostic within each finite key's usable length.

records.article:
# Do Cicada's own numbers work as a key?

**No setting crossed the reading threshold, but the short keys leave whole-section claims inconclusive.** We replayed [Wulfic's Stage I](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/run_stage_i.py) and [Stage M](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus/blob/bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c/tools/run_stage_m.py) from one pinned source revision. Their **5,742 recorded settings** test prime numbers, values derived from solved LP1 text, and three readings of the LP2 number grid. None reaches the program's **+30 reading threshold**. Both complete tables reproduce the published source files byte-for-byte.

![Six source keys: each LP2 score stays below the reading threshold, while planted key controls are higher.](experiments/records/wulfic-native-key-streams/comparison.svg)

The blue point for each key is its best LP2 score on an alignment of at least 100 runes. Gray shows the range from 20 planted encryptions under that **same key and detector**. Control texts have different lengths because the source keys do.

## What was actually tried

Stage I starts at the beginning of three streams: consecutive primes; one Gematria sum per solved LP1 word; or the prime value of each solved LP1 rune. Stage M starts at the beginning of three streams read from the printed 256-cell grid: its base-60 bytes, their regrouped five-bit values, or the individual base-60 digits. The grid streams contain **256, 409 and 512 values**, respectively. The [independent checker](experiments/records/wulfic-native-key-streams/check.py) confirms that the source's grid tokens match Liberpedia's 256 transcribed tokens, then constructs all three numeric streams from those tokens.

For each key, the source applies three arithmetic directions and 29 shifts. Stage I scores nine manuscript sections separately and as one joined stream; Stage M also tests positions immediately after and ending at the grid. The detector tolerates occasional skipped or repeated key steps and scores whether decrypted rune frequencies resemble known LP1 text. Its key starts at **position zero**. These are six source-defined streams under one decoder, not a general search of possible Cicada-derived keys.

**Key length matters here.** Once the detector runs off the end of a key, later runes contribute a neutral score. In particular, Stage M's long-page result mostly measures what its first few hundred grid-derived values do, not a complete-page decryption. Stage I's LP1 word-sum stream likewise has only 726 values. The highest LP2 score in either complete table is from the **nine-rune** section 10 (+4.83), far too short to carry a strong reading. Among alignments of at least 100 runes, the best scores are **−65.54** for Stage I and **−13.75** for Stage M.

## Did the detector have enough power?

After inspecting the source results, we added a **supplemental diagnostic**. It plants each exact key in 20 anti-doublet encryptions, using text lengths that fit within the key: **729, 650 and 729 runes** for the three Stage I keys, and **230, 368 and 460** for the grid keys. **All 120 planted scores pass +30; none of the 120 wrong-key scores does.** This shows the detector can recognize these keys within those bounded lengths. Because the diagnostic was designed after the LP2 replay, it is a power check, **not** a preregistered source control or a correction for selecting a promising key after the fact. The [plan](experiments/records/wulfic-native-key-streams/plan.json) and [control table](experiments/records/wulfic-native-key-streams/supplemental-controls.tsv) state its exact rules and values.

This excludes no alternate start position, repeated grid key, other base-60 reading, different plaintext model or cipher. Stage I also performs a separate **nine-rune square-title vocabulary check**; it is not part of these stream scores and deserves its own treatment if used as evidence.

## Reproduce

From the repository root, run `python experiments/records/wulfic-native-key-streams/run.py --check`, `python experiments/records/wulfic-native-key-streams/check.py` and `python experiments/records/wulfic-native-key-streams/plot.py --check`. The bundled [candidate tables](experiments/records/wulfic-native-key-streams/results.json) and controls are hashed in the record. To rerun the historical programs, check out the [source repository](https://github.com/Wulfic/Cicada3301-Liber_Primus) at commit `bf89d3d13aad2b8f2c95ab195cf1b092f250775c` and run `python experiments/records/wulfic-native-key-streams/replay_source.py --source-dir PATH_TO_CLONE`. The wrapper writes into a temporary directory and checks both full output tables byte-for-byte. Run `calibrate.py --source-dir PATH_TO_CLONE --check` to repeat our supplemental diagnostic.
